title: Unhandled application startup failure re-thrown without security logging
description: The application bootstrap catches any error from the startup process (dependency validation, server initialization) in a .catch handler at line 15. Instead of logging the error before re-throwing, the handler simply does `throw err` with no call to any logging or monitoring system. If the application fails to start due to a security-relevant cause (e.g., missing security dependencies, failed integrity checks from validateDependencies, misconfigured security middleware in server.start), there is no structured security log entry created. The error is surfaced only through the process crash and natural stderr output, with no audit trail, no correlation ID, and no alerting. This means operators cannot reconstruct from application logs why the application failed to start or whether a security control was missing at boot time.

trace.description: The app() function is invoked at module load time. It calls validateDependencies() and server.start() (lines 6-11). If either fails, the promise rejects and control reaches the .catch handler.
app is declared async, so any thrown error inside it causes the returned promise to reject. Control enters the function body.
await validateDependencies() is the first operation that can throw a startup error (e.g., failed dependency or integrity check). If it rejects, the promise from app() rejects immediately.
await server.start() is the second operation that can throw a startup error (e.g., misconfigured security middleware, port binding failure). If it rejects, the promise from app() also rejects.
throw err re-throws the error with no prior call to any logger, monitoring service, or security event recorder. The startup failure — a security-relevant event — produces no auditable log entry.

The .catch handler on line 15-16 catches the startup error but performs no logging or monitoring before re-throwing it on line 16. There is no call to any logger, no security event recorded, and no alert triggered for the application startup failure — a security-relevant event (availability/integrity of the application at boot).

title: Exported raw database collections with no access-control wrapper, validation layer, or audit logging
description: The file creates two MarsDB collections (`reviewsCollection` for 'posts' and `ordersCollection` for 'orders') and exports them directly as bare data-access objects. There is no intermediate abstraction layer that enforces who may read, create, update, or delete documents in these collections, no validation of document structure or ownership, and no logging of security-relevant database events (creation, modification, deletion of orders or reviews). Any module that imports these exports gains unrestricted CRUD capability over orders and reviews. Given the application context (a shop with orders and product reviews), the orders collection in particular should enforce per-user ownership rules and the reviews collection should enforce constraints on who can post or modify reviews. The design as written — exporting raw collections with no guard layer — permits any importing caller to bypass whatever business rules the route handlers are supposed to enforce by calling the collection methods directly. Additionally, because no logging exists at the data layer, modifications made through direct collection access are completely unauditable.

trace.description: MarsDB is imported. The caller (outside this file) will import the exported collections and use them. The collections are the entrypoint for data flowing into and out of the database.

`new MarsDB.Collection('posts')` creates a raw collection with default options and exports it as `reviewsCollection`. No access-control wrapper, no schema/ownership validation, and no logging of insert/update/remove operations is applied. Any importing module can perform unrestricted CRUD on reviews. This is the insecure-design sink: the design exports a raw data primitive where a guarded repository should be, and the logging-monitoring gap: no security-relevant events on the reviews collection are logged anywhere in this file.

`new MarsDB.Collection('orders')` creates a raw collection with default options and exports it as `ordersCollection`. Same design flaw and logging gap as line 9, but for orders — a financially sensitive resource where unrestricted access or modification has direct business impact (order tampering, data exfiltration, deletion).

title: MarsDB collections initialized with default (no security) configuration
description: Both collections are created via `new MarsDB.Collection(name)` with no options object passed. MarsDB (a MongoDB-like client-side/server-side database) accepts configuration options, and the defaults provide no access control, no validation hooks, and no audit configuration. In a production shop application handling orders and user-generated reviews, initializing the data store with zero configuration — no schema enforcement, no permission rules, no indexes for lookup integrity — is a security misconfiguration. The dangerous default is the absence of any configuration where security-relevant options should be set. An attacker who can reach these collections (directly or through auto-generated CRUD endpoints suggested by the null handler routes in the architecture context) exploits this by performing operations the database never restricts.

trace.description: MarsDB is imported as the database library. Its collections will be configured here.

`new MarsDB.Collection('posts')` — the collection is constructed with only a name argument and no options. No security configuration is passed: no access-control rules, no validation function, no schema constraints. The default configuration (no restrictions) is the dangerous setting.

`new MarsDB.Collection('orders')` — same pattern: collection created with only a name, no security options, relying entirely on defaults that impose no restrictions on a financially sensitive collection.

title: Delivery list fetch has no pagination or result limit
description: The `get()` method issues an unparameterized GET request to `/api/Deliverys` with no pagination, offset, or limit parameters. If the backend endpoint returns all delivery method records without enforcing a maximum result set, a single request can pull an unbounded number of records into client memory. Because this frontend service never requests bounded results, the design contributes to an unrestricted resource consumption path: an attacker (or even a normal user under load) triggers a response whose size scales with the total record count, with no client-side or application-level cap.

`hostServer` is assigned from `environment.hostServer` — the base API origin. No size limit or pagination default is introduced here.
`host` is constructed by concatenating `hostServer` with the fixed path `/api/Deliverys`. The resulting URL has no query parameters for page size, offset, or limit, and none are appended later.

`this.http.get(this.host)` issues a GET to `/api/Deliverys` with no query parameters for page size, offset, or limit. The response is mapped directly to `response.data` (an array of DeliveryMethod) with no bound on array length. If the backend returns all records, the client receives and holds an unbounded result set in memory.

title: getAll() requests unbounded result set without pagination
description: The getAll() method issues a GET request to /api/Hints/ and returns the entire result set without any pagination, limit, or offset parameter. If the backend endpoint also lacks pagination (the architecture context shows GET /api/Hints/:id but no explicit pagination handler), a single request can retrieve an arbitrarily large number of records into browser memory. An attacker can call this endpoint repeatedly to consume server-side database query resources and client-side memory. This is a frontend service, so the confidence is tempered by the possibility that the backend enforces its own limits.

The target URL is constructed using this.host, which is initialized to environment.hostServer + '/api/Hints'. No pagination query parameters are appended or configured here.

The response is mapped directly from response.data, implying the entire dataset is returned in one call. No rate limiting, pagination, or result-size cap is applied at this layer.

title: Client-controlled 'unlocked' flag in Hint model enables trust assumption violation
description: The Hint interface declares an 'unlocked?: boolean' field (line 11). Hints in a CTF/challenge context are typically unlocked based on server-side state — challenge progress, points spent, or admin action. Placing an 'unlocked' boolean on a frontend-facing model is a design smell: if any route handler or component trusts this client-provided value to decide whether to display or serve a hint, an attacker can simply set 'unlocked: true' to bypass the intended unlock gating without completing the prerequisite challenge or paying the required cost. This is a trust assumption violation — the server should re-derive unlock status from its own state rather than accept it from the caller. The interface itself does not enforce any rule, but its design makes client-controlled unlock status the path of least resistance. Without server-side re-derivation visible elsewhere, the current design permits hint access bypass.

trace.description: The Hint interface receives an optional 'unlocked?: boolean' field. This field is part of the data model consumed by frontend components and potentially by API handlers (caller logic is outside this file). If a route handler (e.g., GET /api/Hints/:id listed in the architecture) returns or accepts this model, the 'unlocked' value is attacker-controllable.

The 'unlocked' field has no accompanying constraint in the interface (no server-derivation marker, no read-only annotation, no validation). The model design treats unlock status as plain data that can flow in either direction (server→client for display, or client→server for state updates).
The Hint interface is declared, establishing the data contract for hint objects exchanged between the frontend and backend (caller logic is outside this file).

If a handler trusts the 'unlocked' boolean from the client to decide hint visibility/access, an attacker submits 'unlocked: true' to retrieve hints they have not earned, bypassing the challenge prerequisite workflow. The design defect is that unlock status is modeled as a mutable client field rather than a server-derived property.

title: Arbitrary URL fetch in notification service with no validation or logging
description: The CtfSystemWideNotificationService.fetchNotification method accepts a caller-provided URL string and passes it directly to this.http.get() without any validation, allowlisting, or sanitization. The service's stated purpose is to fetch system-wide notifications, yet its design delegates the choice of endpoint entirely to the caller. If the caller is attacker-controlled or can influence the URL parameter, the service becomes a generic SSRF proxy that can be directed at internal endpoints, cloud metadata services, or arbitrary external hosts. The URL is never checked against an allowlist of legitimate notification endpoints, nor is the scheme restricted (http vs https). Additionally, no security-relevant logging occurs for this fetch operation — there is no record of which URLs were requested, whether a request failed, or whether unexpected responses were received. This means an attacker abusing the service to probe internal endpoints would leave no audit trail. The root cause is a design that trusts the caller to specify the resource location rather than having the service determine or constrain it. The trace is two lines because the code is a direct pass-through: the parameter on line 22 flows immediately into the HTTP call on line 23 with no intermediate assignment, transformation, conditional check, or validation step. The absence of any such intermediate line is itself the defect.

trace.description: The fetchNotification method receives a url parameter from its caller (caller is outside this file). The parameter is of type string with no constraints — no URL format validation, no allowlist, no scheme restriction. The service is designed to fetch system-wide notifications but accepts an arbitrary URL from the caller, creating a trust assumption violation: the caller controls the destination of the request rather than the service itself.

The unvalidated url is passed directly to this.http.get<SystemWideNotificationResponse>(url). No validation, allowlisting, or logging occurs between receiving the URL and making the request. The service can be directed to fetch from any URL the caller provides. There is no logging of the request URL, the response, or any errors — security-relevant events (fetching from arbitrary/unexpected endpoints, failed requests to internal resources) are completely unrecorded.

title: Path injection via unvalidated `id` in URL construction across getById, put, and del methods
description: The `id` parameter is directly interpolated into the request URL path using template literals in `getById`, `put`, and `del` without any validation, sanitization, or encoding. In `getById` (line 26) and `put` (line 35), `id` has no type annotation at all. In `del` (line 39), `id` is typed as `number`, but TypeScript types are compile-time only and do not enforce runtime constraints when the service is called from JavaScript or via injection. An attacker who controls `id` can inject path segments (e.g., `../`, `/`), query parameters (e.g., `?`), or fragments to redirect the HTTP request to a different API endpoint entirely. For example, passing `id = "../Users"` would cause a GET request to `/api/Users` instead of `/api/Addresss/<id>`, enabling unauthorized access to other API resources through path traversal.

trace.description: The `getById(id)` function receives `id` from an outside caller (caller is outside this file). `id` has no type annotation and no validation.
`id` is interpolated directly into the URL via template literal: `${this.host}/${id}`. No encoding (encodeURIComponent), no allow-list, no validation intervenes.
`this.hostServer` is read from `environment.hostServer`, establishing the base URL origin used in every outbound request.
`this.host` is assembled by concatenating `this.hostServer` with the literal string `/api/Addresss`. This is the path prefix that the unvalidated `id` will be appended to.

The constructed URL is passed to `this.http.get(...)`, executing the request. A malicious `id` value such as `../Users` or `1/../../../api/Products` causes the HTTP client to request an unintended endpoint. The same pattern exists in `put` (line 35: `${this.host}/${id}`) and `del` (line 39: `${this.host}/${id}`).

title: Mass assignment — save() and put() forward unfiltered caller params as request body to address API
description: The `save(params)` method (line 30) and `put(id, params)` method (line 35) pass the entire `params` object directly as the HTTP request body to the `/api/Addresss` endpoint without any field allow-list or filtering. There is no explicit property-level authorization — any field the caller includes in `params` is transmitted to the backend API. If the backend model for Address includes sensitive properties (e.g., `UserId`, `isAdmin`, `isDefault`, or other users' address references), a caller can set fields they should not control. The absence of an explicit allow-list means new fields added to the backend model automatically become exposed through this service.

trace.description: The `save(params)` function receives `params` from an outside caller (caller is outside this file). No field filtering or allow-listing is applied.
`params` is passed directly as the request body to `this.http.post(this.host + '/', params)`. Every property in `params` is forwarded to the API unchanged. The same occurs in `put` at line 35.
`this.hostServer` is read from `environment.hostServer`, providing the base URL for the outgoing POST.
`this.host` is assembled by concatenating `this.hostServer` with `/api/Addresss`, forming the target endpoint URL.

The unfiltered body is sent to the `/api/Addresss` POST endpoint. Without an explicit allow-list of permitted fields, any property the caller includes reaches the backend persistence layer. If the backend also lacks property-level authorization, this results in mass assignment of sensitive fields.

title: get() fetches all addresses without pagination or result limits
description: The `get()` method issues an unbounded GET request to `/api/Addresss` with no pagination parameters, page size limits, or result count restrictions. If the backend returns all address records in a single response, a large dataset can cause excessive memory consumption on the client and server, and a single request can pull an unbounded result set. There is no `limit`, `offset`, `page`, or `pageSize` parameter passed to the request.

`this.hostServer` is read from `environment.hostServer`, providing the base URL for the outgoing GET.
`this.host` is assembled by concatenating `this.hostServer` with `/api/Addresss`, forming the endpoint URL. No pagination query parameters are appended.

`this.http.get(this.host)` issues a request to `/api/Addresss` with no query parameters for pagination, page size, or result count limiting. The entire result set is returned and mapped into memory via `.pipe(map((response: any) => response.data))`. An attacker or even a legitimate user with a large number of address records can trigger loading of an unbounded dataset.

title: Path traversal in loadStaticData via unsanitized file parameter
description: The exported function `loadStaticData` accepts a `file` string parameter and directly concatenates it into a filesystem path (`./data/static/' + file + '.yml'`) with no validation, sanitization, or allow-listing. If any caller outside this file passes user-controlled input to this function, an attacker can supply path-traversal sequences (e.g., `../../../config/secrets`) to read arbitrary `.yml` files anywhere on the filesystem. While the `.yml` suffix limits which files can be read, any YAML file on the system becomes accessible. The internal callers in this file pass hardcoded constants ('users', 'challenges', etc.), but the function is exported and the architecture context shows a `handleYamlUpload` route that could route external input into this code path.

trace.description: The exported function `loadStaticData` accepts a `file: string` parameter. The caller is outside this file; the function is a public export, so any module can call it with arbitrary input.

The `file` parameter is concatenated directly into a path string: `path.resolve('./data/static/' + file + '.yml')`. No validation, allow-listing, or sanitization is applied. Path traversal sequences such as `../../` in `file` are not stripped or rejected.

The resolved path is passed to `readFile(filePath, 'utf8')`, which reads the file from disk. An attacker-controlled `file` value like `../../../etc/config` causes the application to read `./data/static/../../../etc/config.yml`, traversing out of the intended directory. This is an injection of path structure into a filesystem operation, and it breaks the access boundary the directory `./data/static/` is meant to enforce.

title: Progress-restoration continue codes passed as URL path parameters, exposing tokens to logging and history
description: The ChallengeService (whose behavior is verified by these tests) sends continue codes — tokens used to restore challenge progress — as URL path segments rather than in the request body or headers. Lines 63, 93, and 123 show the expected requests are PUT http://localhost:3000/rest/continue-code/apply/CODE, /rest/continue-code-findIt/apply/CODE, and /rest/continue-code-fixIt/apply/CODE. A continue code is a progress-restoration token that functions like a session or recovery credential: whoever possesses it can restore a user's challenge progress. Placing this token in the URL path means it will be written to server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and potentially leaked via Referrer headers. This is a token-handling weakness (crypto-auth), a design flaw that places sensitive credentials in a transmission channel that is routinely logged (insecure-design), and it guarantees the token will appear in security-relevant access logs as plaintext (logging-monitoring). An attacker who gains access to server logs, proxy caches, or a shared browser history could replay a captured continue code to restore another user's progress.

trace.description: The test calls service.restoreProgress('CODE') — the caller (ChallengeService.restoreProgress) is outside this file, but this test verifies it receives a continue-code string from the client and embeds it into the request URL.

The test asserts the resulting HTTP request targets 'http://localhost:3000/rest/continue-code/apply/CODE', confirming the continue code is placed directly in the URL path. The same pattern is verified for Find It and Fix It variants at lines 93 and 123.

The same pattern is confirmed for the Find It variant: service.restoreProgressFindIt('CODE') (line 91) produces a request to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/continue-code-findIt/apply/CODE', with the continue code again embedded in the URL path segment.

The same pattern is confirmed a third time for the Fix It variant: service.restoreProgressFixIt('CODE') (line 121) produces a request to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/continue-code-fixIt/apply/CODE'. All three continue-code endpoints — general, Find It, and Fix It — transmit the progress-restoration token as a URL path segment. URLs are routinely recorded by web servers, reverse proxies, CDNs, and browser history, and can leak via Referer headers to third parties. This exposes a progress-restoration credential in channels that are logged in plaintext.

The continue-code token is transmitted as a URL path segment. URLs are routinely recorded by web servers, reverse proxies, CDNs, and browser history, and can leak via Referer headers to third parties. This exposes a progress-restoration credential in channels that are logged in plaintext.

title: Complaint submission endpoint has no client-side rate limiting or throttling
description: The save() method in ComplaintService posts to /api/Complaints/ with no rate limiting, throttling, or debounce mechanism. An attacker (or automated script) can call save() in a tight loop, flooding the backend complaint endpoint with unbounded requests. Each request carries an arbitrary payload (params: any) with no size constraints enforced on the client. While the backend may have its own controls, no client-side protection exists to slow or prevent abuse of the complaint submission workflow. This enables denial-of-service through excessive complaint creation and potential database/storage exhaustion.

The params object is forwarded unchanged into this.http.post(this.host + '/', params). No rate limiter, throttle, queue, or cooldown is applied between successive calls to save().
The target URL originates from environment.hostServer, assigned to this.hostServer. This is a configuration value, not user-controlled, but it defines where the unthrottled requests will be sent.
this.host is constructed as this.hostServer + '/api/Complaints'. The endpoint path is hardcoded; no rate-limiting interceptor or guard wraps this URL construction.

The HTTP POST to /api/Complaints/ is the network sink. There is no per-user, per-IP, or per-session throttling visible in this service, and no payload size cap is enforced before transmission, allowing unbounded request volume and payload size to reach the backend complaint endpoint.

title: Complaint submission accepts unvalidated arbitrary payload with no security event logging
description: The save() method accepts params typed as 'any' and transmits it verbatim to the backend without any client-side validation, schema enforcement, or sanitization. The complaint workflow implicitly trusts that the caller provides well-formed data. If the backend does not independently validate every field, an attacker can inject arbitrary complaint data (e.g., fabricated user IDs, manipulated complaint content, extra fields that the backend may persist). Additionally, there is no logging of complaint submission events — neither success nor failure — within this service, meaning security-relevant events (mass complaint spam, complaint injection, abuse of the complaint system) are not recorded for audit or alerting. The catchError handler on line 21 rethrows errors without logging them, explicitly discarding the opportunity to record failed submission attempts.

The unvalidated params object is passed directly into this.http.post(). No validation, sanitization, or field whitelist is applied. No logging statement records that a complaint submission was attempted, what data was sent, or whether it succeeded or failed.
hostServer is read from environment.hostServer. This is the server address that the unvalidated payload will be sent to; it is not user-controlled but is part of the request path.
this.host is assembled as this.hostServer + '/api/Complaints'. No validation, sanitization, or field whitelist is applied to params at this stage or any prior stage.

The POST request to /api/Complaints/ carries the unvalidated payload to the backend. The design delegates all validation and logging to the server without any compensating client-side control, and no security event is logged at the service layer for this complaint creation operation.

title: Client-controllable challenge completion status in data model
description: The Challenge interface includes a `solved?: boolean` field (line 17) and a `codingChallengeStatus?: 0 | 1 | 2` field (line 21). In a security CTF-style application like Juice Shop, challenge completion status is a security-relevant fact that the server must derive independently (by verifying that the user actually performed the required exploit). The presence of these fields in a client-side data model, marked as optional and mutable, suggests the design allows the client to report its own completion status. If the server accepts a `solved: true` or `codingChallengeStatus: 2` value from the client without independently verifying that the challenge was actually solved, an attacker could mark any challenge as solved by simply sending the boolean or status value. This is a trust assumption violation: the server should decide whether a challenge is solved, not accept the caller's assertion. Because this file is only an interface definition, the exploitation path (how `solved` reaches a server endpoint and whether the server re-derives it) cannot be confirmed from this file alone, but the design surface is visible here.

trace.description: The Challenge interface is exported and defines the shape of challenge data that flows between client and server. Callers outside this file (route handlers, services, API calls) receive and send objects conforming to this interface.

The `solved?: boolean` field is part of the Challenge model. If a client constructs or modifies a Challenge object and sends it to the server (e.g., via a PUT/POST to /api/Challenges or a challenge-solve endpoint), the `solved` field travels as caller-controlled data. The interface imposes no constraint that would prevent a client from setting `solved: true`.

Similarly, `codingChallengeStatus?: 0 | 1 | 2` is a client-facing status field. The type union (0, 1, 2) is enforced by TypeScript at compile time but provides no runtime guarantee on the server side that the value was earned rather than fabricated.

The `id?: number` field is the first property in the interface. Together with `key` (line 11), it identifies which challenge an object refers to. Any client-constructed Challenge object that sets `solved` or `codingChallengeStatus` will also carry an `id` and `key` to tell the server which challenge to mark as solved.

The `key: string` field is a required, non-optional identifier for the challenge. It is the primary way challenges are referenced. A client sending a completion status would pair it with this key. The key is a plain string with no server-derivation constraint in the model.

The `hasCodingChallenge: boolean` field is required (not optional), meaning every Challenge object carries it. This field and `codingChallengeStatus` together form the coding-challenge completion surface: the client knows whether a coding challenge exists and what its status is. If the server trusts the status value the client sends, the `hasCodingChallenge` flag merely tells the attacker which challenges to target.

The closing brace of the interface. At this point the type is complete and exported. Any code that imports this interface and constructs a Challenge object can set every field defined above, including `solved` and `codingChallengeStatus`, with no server-side validation expressed anywhere in this type definition.

The design flaw: the data model allows challenge completion status (`solved`, `codingChallengeStatus`) to be a property of the challenge object that a client can set, rather than a server-derived value. If the server endpoint that receives Challenge objects trusts these fields, an attacker marks challenges as solved without performing the exploit. The caller that would accept this data is outside this file and cannot be inspected here.

title: Private key transmitted over unencrypted HTTP as confirmed by test expectations
description: The test file enforces and verifies that the KeysService.submitKey method sends a user's private key in a POST request body over an unencrypted HTTP connection (http://localhost:3000). Line 66 asserts the request URL uses the http scheme, and line 68 asserts the request body contains { privateKey: 'privateKey' } in plaintext. Private cryptographic keys are highly sensitive credentials; transmitting them over HTTP exposes them to network interception (man-in-the-middle). The test codifies this insecure behavior — if a developer later switched the service to HTTPS, this test would fail because it expects http://. This is a test file, so the actual vulnerability lives in the KeysService implementation, but the test confirms and locks in the insecure transmission pattern.

trace.description: The test calls service.submitKey('privateKey'), passing a private key string into the service method. The actual service implementation and its caller are outside this file.
The test asserts the request body equals { privateKey: 'privateKey' }, confirming the private key is sent as plaintext JSON in the POST body without any client-side encryption or wrapping.

expect(req.request.method).toBe('POST') confirms the request method is POST, meaning the private key is being sent as request payload data rather than via a query string, but still over the unencrypted HTTP channel established by the URL on line 66.

The test asserts the request is sent to http://localhost:3000/rest/web3/submitKey using the http scheme (not https), confirming the private key traverses an unencrypted transport. A network attacker positioned between client and server could capture the private key.

title: Unvalidated key interpolated directly into API URL path enables path traversal to arbitrary endpoints
description: The get() method accepts a caller-supplied 'key' string and interpolates it directly into a URL path template `${this.host}/${key}` without any validation or sanitization. The design never constrains what a valid key looks like — it could be a simple identifier, or it could contain path traversal sequences such as `../../rest/user/whoami`. Because the browser normalizes URL paths before issuing the request, a key containing `../` segments will cause the HTTP client to make a request to an entirely different endpoint on the same server, outside the intended `/snippets` namespace. If the key is derived from user-controllable data (e.g., a route parameter, a query string value, or user selection in the UI), an attacker can craft a key that redirects the request to any endpoint on the host server, potentially accessing sensitive data or triggering privileged operations. The service design should enforce that keys match an expected format (e.g., alphanumeric challenge identifiers) before constructing the URL.

trace.description: The get(key: string) method receives a 'key' parameter from a caller outside this file. The key is an arbitrary string with no type or format constraint enforced at the interface boundary.

The key is directly interpolated into the URL template string `${this.host}/${key}`. No validation, sanitization, or encoding is applied to ensure the key is a safe URL path segment. this.host is environment.hostServer + '/snippets' (lines 27-28), so the resulting URL is e.g. http://server/snippets/<key>.
The base host URL is loaded from environment configuration: `private readonly hostServer = environment.hostServer`. This establishes the trusted server origin that all requests will target.

The intended API namespace is constructed: `private readonly host = this.hostServer + '/snippets'`. This is the only path segment the service is designed to request — all snippet lookups should resolve under /snippets/.

this.http.get<CodeSnippet>() is called with the constructed URL. If key contains '../' sequences, the browser normalizes the URL path before sending, causing the GET request to target an endpoint outside the intended /snippets path — e.g., key='../../rest/user/whoami' produces a request to http://server/rest/user/whoami. The server receives a legitimate-looking request to a different endpoint, and the client-side code processes whatever response comes back.

title: API error handling rethrows without any security logging, leaving no audit trail for failed or anomalous snippet requests
description: The get() method includes a catchError operator that catches HTTP errors and immediately rethrows them (`catchError((err) => { throw err })`). This is functionally a no-op — it provides no logging, no error context capture, and no security event recording. When a snippet request fails — whether due to authorization failure, a 404 from a path-traversal attempt, a server error, or any other security-relevant condition — the error is propagated to the caller with no local audit trail. There is no logging of the key that was requested, the response status, or the error details. This means that if an attacker uses the get() method to probe arbitrary endpoints (via the path traversal design flaw), there would be no client-side log record of the probing activity. While server-side logging may exist, the absence of any client-side error logging for security-relevant API calls represents a gap in the ability to detect and investigate anomalous access patterns.

trace.description: The HTTP GET request to fetch a code snippet may fail for various security-relevant reasons: 401/403 (unauthorized access), 404 (path traversal probe to nonexistent endpoint), 500 (server error from malformed request). The catchError operator on line 31 intercepts all such errors.

The catchError operator is imported from 'rxjs/operators' (`import { catchError, map } from 'rxjs/operators'`). This is the error-handling mechanism the service has chosen to use — it is the only operator in the pipe chain that intercepts errors, and it is where security-relevant logging should occur.

The catchError handler `(err) => { throw err }` catches the error and immediately rethrows it. No console.error, no logging service call, no metric increment — nothing is recorded. The error object (which may contain status codes, URLs, and response data relevant to security investigation) is discarded from any audit perspective. Security-relevant events such as failed API access, path traversal probes, or anomalous response patterns leave no trace.

title: Unvalidated continueCode concatenated directly into URL path in restoreProgress methods
description: The restoreProgress, restoreProgressFindIt, and restoreProgressFixIt methods accept a continueCode string from the caller (which is outside this file) and directly concatenate it into the request URL path without any validation, sanitization, or URL-encoding. The continueCode is a client-supplied value that the server uses to restore challenge progress. The design trusts the client to provide a well-formed, legitimate continue code. An attacker could supply a crafted continueCode containing path traversal sequences (e.g., '../') or query delimiters ('?') to redirect the PUT request to a different endpoint on the same server. Additionally, if the server does not independently validate the continue code's authenticity, an attacker could forge arbitrary progress by supplying any value. The defect is that the service performs no input validation on a value it places into a security-relevant operation (progress restoration).

The continueCode is directly concatenated into the URL path: this.hostServer + '/rest/continue-code/apply/' + continueCode. No encoding or validation occurs between receiving the value and placing it in the URL.
The constructed URL with the unvalidated continueCode is used in an HTTP PUT request to restore challenge progress. The same pattern repeats at lines 47 and 51 for the FindIt and FixIt variants.

title: find() method accepts unbounded params with no enforced pagination limits
description: The find() method accepts an untyped, unconstrained 'params' object (typed as 'any') and passes it directly as query parameters to the backend /api/Challenges/ endpoint. There is no enforcement of pagination limits (e.g., max page size) on the client side. If the backend also does not enforce limits, a single request with a large or absent limit parameter could cause the server to return an unbounded result set, consuming memory and bandwidth. While the actual enforcement must occur server-side, the client service design does not impose any default pagination constraints that would reduce the blast radius of a malicious or malformed request.

The unvalidated params object is passed directly to this.http.get as query parameters. No default pagination, max limit, or result-set cap is enforced before the request is sent.

title: setRetrieveBlueprintChallengeFile accepts arbitrary file path without validation
description: The exported function setRetrieveBlueprintChallengeFile (lines 34-36) accepts any string from an external caller and stores it directly as the module-level variable retrieveBlueprintChallengeFile. There is no path validation, no allowlist of permitted files or directories, no sanitization of traversal sequences, and no restriction on absolute paths. The variable name indicates it is later used to retrieve a file. If any route or handler exposes this setter to user input, an attacker can point the server at arbitrary internal files (e.g., /etc/passwd, environment files, source code) and have them served or processed as a 'blueprint challenge file.' The design trusts the caller to provide a safe path rather than constraining the value server-side.

The target of the assignment is retrieveBlueprintChallengeFile, a module-level variable declared here as a string export. Because it is exported, its mutated state is visible to all importing modules.
The function returns without error, meaning the caller's arbitrary string has been successfully persisted as the server's configured blueprint challenge file path.

The unvalidated string becomes the value of retrieveBlueprintChallengeFile, which by its name is later consumed to retrieve a file. Because the design imposes no constraint on the path, an attacker who can reach the setter can configure the server to retrieve any internal file.

title: No security logging when blueprint challenge file path is changed

There is no log entry recording who changed the path, what the old and new values were, or when the change occurred. If an attacker uses this setter to point the server at a sensitive internal file, there is no audit trail to detect or investigate the incident. The absence of logging for a configuration change that can redirect file access is a security logging and monitoring failure.

title: Security-sensitive collections exported as mutable shared state without access-control encapsulation
description: Lines 15-20 export mutable plain-object references to security-sensitive data collections: users, products, baskets, basketItems, complaints, and feedback. Any module that imports this file obtains a direct reference to these objects and can read, create, modify, or delete any record for any user without passing through an authorization or ownership-check layer. The design provides no encapsulation, no access-control boundary, and no guardrails that would prevent a handler from, for example, modifying another user's basket items directly through the shared basketItems object. While individual route handlers may perform their own authorization checks, the data-layer design itself enforces none, meaning any handler that forgets or misimplements a check operates directly on all users' data with no safety net.

Because basketItems (and all other collections) are exported as mutable references with no access-control wrapper, a handler that imports this file can directly index into and modify any user's basket items (e.g., basketItems[someId].quantity = 999) without any server-side ownership verification at the data layer. The design relies entirely on every caller remembering to enforce authorization, with no structural safeguard.

title: Data export accepts caller-controlled user ID without server-side re-derivation of identity
description: The test confirms that DataSubjectService.dataExport() takes an arbitrary argument (a user ID or object containing an ID) and forwards it directly as the POST body to /rest/user/data-export. The test on line 44 passes the literal value 1 and the test on line 70 passes { id: 1 }. If the server-side handler uses this client-supplied ID to determine whose data to export—rather than deriving the identity from the authenticated session—any caller could request the data export of any user by supplying that user's ID, constituting an IDOR / broken-object-level-authorization defect. This is an insecure-design issue because the design allows the client to control a value (target user identity for data export) that the server should decide based on the authenticated session.

The test asserts req.request.body === 1, confirming that the caller-supplied ID is passed through unmodified as the HTTP request body to the data-export endpoint. No validation, sanitization, or session-derived identity is apparent.

The POST request is sent to http://localhost:3000/rest/user/data-export with the caller-controlled body. If the server uses this body value to select the data subject rather than the authenticated session identity, an attacker can export arbitrary users' data by supplying their ID.

title: Stored XSS: user-controlled conversation text persisted to localStorage without sanitization
description: The `generateTitle` method accepts free-form user text (`firstMessage`) and uses it directly as a conversation title with only a length truncation applied (line 22). The `save` method accepts an entire `StoredConversation` object — including message content and the generated title — and persists it to localStorage via `JSON.stringify` without any HTML sanitization, encoding, or allow-listing (line 44). Since conversation messages and titles are inherently user-controlled free-form text, any downstream component that renders this data using `innerHTML`, `[innerHTML]` binding, or similar unescaped output will execute injected script. The persistence point (this file) introduces the vulnerability; the render sink is outside this file in the chatbot UI components.

`firstMessage` is conditionally truncated to 50 characters via `substring` and concatenated with an ellipsis, but no HTML encoding, sanitization, or allow-listing is applied. The truncated or full string is returned as the title — still raw user text.
`save` calls `this.getAll()` to load the existing conversation collection. The incoming `conversation` object has not been sanitized at this point.
`all.findIndex(c => c.id === conversation.id)` searches for an existing conversation with the same ID. The unsanitized `conversation` object passes through unchanged.
`if (index >= 0)` — conditional branch that determines whether to update an existing conversation or add a new one. No sanitization occurs in either branch.

`all[index] = conversation` — the unsanitized conversation object (containing user-controlled title and message text) is placed directly into the collection array. (Line 42 `all.push(conversation)` is the equivalent path for new conversations.)

`localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(all))` persists the unsanitized user-controlled conversation data (including titles and message content) to localStorage. The data is stored as-is without any HTML encoding or sanitization. If any downstream component renders this data without Angular's auto-escaping (e.g., via `[innerHTML]`), it becomes stored XSS. The render sink is outside this file.

title: Unbounded conversation storage with O(n) read/parse on every operation
description: The service has no limit on the number of conversations stored in localStorage. Every operation — `getAll()` (line 25), `getById()` (line 32, which calls `getAll()`), `save()` (line 36, which calls `getAll()`), and `delete()` (line 47, which calls `getAll()`) — reads and JSON-parses the ENTIRE conversation collection from localStorage into memory. The `save` method then serializes and writes the entire collection back. There is no pagination, no count cap, and no eviction policy. An attacker (or automated interaction with the chatbot) can create thousands of conversations, causing every subsequent operation to load, parse, and re-serialize the full set, degrading client-side performance and potentially causing UI freezes. While localStorage has a browser-imposed size limit (~5-10MB), the lack of any application-level conversation count limit means performance degrades linearly with stored data volume.

trace.description: The `save` method is called from outside this file with a `StoredConversation` object to persist. There is no check on the current number of stored conversations before adding a new one.

`save` calls `this.getAll()` which reads the entire localStorage value (line 26) and JSON-parses it into an in-memory array (line 28). Every conversation ever stored is loaded and parsed on every single save, delete, or getById call.
Inside `getAll()`, `localStorage.getItem(STORAGE_KEY)` reads the entire serialized conversation collection as a single string. No size limit is enforced.
`if (!raw) return []` — early return only if storage is empty. If data exists, the full payload continues to be processed.

`JSON.parse(raw)` deserializes the entire conversation collection into memory at once. With many stored conversations, this is an O(n) parse of all conversation data on every single save, delete, or getById call.
`conversations.sort((a, b) => b.updatedAt - a.updatedAt)` — additionally sorts the entire collection in memory on every read, adding O(n log n) cost per operation.
Back in `save`, `all.findIndex(c => c.id === conversation.id)` linearly scans the full collection to find a match — O(n) per save.
`if (index >= 0)` — conditional branch. In the else-branch (line 42, `all.push(conversation)`) a new conversation is appended to the unbounded array with no count check or eviction of old entries.

`localStorage.setItem(STORAGE_KEY, JSON.stringify(all))` serializes and writes the entire (unbounded) conversation collection back to localStorage on every save or delete operation. No maximum conversation count, no eviction of old conversations, and no size guard exists. Repeated saves with a growing collection cause unbounded linear growth in both memory consumption and CPU time per operation.

title: Non-cryptographic ID generation using Math.random() for conversation identifiers
description: The `generateId` method (line 15-18) constructs conversation IDs using `Date.now()` concatenated with 8 characters selected via `Math.random()`. `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and produces predictable output. The timestamp component (`Date.now()`) is also easily guessable. If conversation IDs are used in any security-relevant context — such as sharing conversation URLs, cross-tab referencing, or any access-control decision — an attacker who knows the approximate creation time can enumerate or predict conversation IDs. The design relies on a weak randomness source where `crypto.getRandomValues()` (the Web Crypto API) is available in the browser and provides cryptographically secure random values. This is a design flaw because the code works as written but uses an inherently unsuitable randomness source.

trace.description: `generateId()` is called from outside this file to create unique identifiers for conversations. The method is an exported public API of the service.
`const chars = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789'` defines the character set for the random portion of the ID. Only 36 characters, meaning each of the 8 positions has only 36 possible values.

`return \`${Date.now()}_${random8}\`` — the final ID combines `Date.now()` (a millisecond-precision timestamp that narrows an attacker's search window dramatically) with the weak random suffix from `Math.random()`. The resulting ID is returned to the caller and used as the conversation's unique identifier. The Web Crypto API (`crypto.getRandomValues()`) is available in browser contexts and should be used for any identifier with security implications.

ID generation uses `Math.random()` — a non-cryptographic PRNG — to select 8 characters from a 36-character alphabet. Combined with `Date.now()` (line 18), the resulting ID space is predictable: the timestamp narrows the search to a small window, and `Math.random()` output can be predicted or brute-forced. The Web Crypto API (`crypto.getRandomValues()`) is available in browser contexts and should be used for any identifier with security implications.

title: Stored XSS: user message content persisted to localStorage without sanitization
description: The test suite confirms that ConversationStorageService.save() accepts and persists conversation objects containing a free-form `content` string in the messages array (line 156: `messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]`). The tests never verify that this content is sanitized, encoded, or validated before storage. Since the content field is arbitrary user-supplied text and it is persisted via JSON.stringify to localStorage (confirmed by the persistence test at lines 165-174), any HTML or script payload in the content field will be stored verbatim. When this content is later rendered by a chatbot UI component (the render sink is outside this file), if the rendering does not apply context-appropriate output encoding, the stored payload executes as script in the browser. This is a stored/persisted XSS vulnerability — the persistence point is confirmed by this file's tests; the render sink is in a different component not shown here.

`service.save(conversation)` is called, forwarding the full object — including any message content — to the storage layer.

title: Predictable conversation ID generation using timestamp prefix with limited entropy
description: The test suite reveals that ConversationStorageService.generateId() produces IDs in the format `timestamp_random8chars` (line 26: regex `/^\d+_[a-z0-9]{8}$/`). The timestamp prefix is derived from `Date.now()` (confirmed by lines 34-41 which verify the prefix falls between before/after timestamps). The suffix is only 8 characters from the set `[a-z0-9]` (36 symbols), yielding approximately 2.8 trillion combinations — but only if a cryptographically secure RNG is used. In typical JavaScript implementations, `Math.random()` is used, which is not cryptographically secure and its output can be predicted if enough outputs are observed. If the timestamp is known or can be approximated (it is exposed in the ID itself), an attacker only needs to guess the 8-character suffix. If conversation IDs are used for any access control decision or as a pseudo-token (e.g., sharing a conversation by ID, or an ID-based lookup that should be unguessable), the predictability of these IDs undermines that assumption. The actual implementation of generateId is outside this file; the tests only confirm the format and behavior.

The test captures `before = Date.now()`, establishing that the timestamp portion of the ID is derived from the current time.
The test calls `id = service.generateId()`, producing the ID whose timestamp prefix is bounded by the before/after timestamps.
The test captures `after = Date.now()`, bracketing the timestamp used in the ID to a narrow window.
The test extracts the timestamp prefix via `parseInt(id.split('_')[0], 10)`, confirming the prefix is a numeric timestamp that is directly exposed in the ID.

The test asserts `timestamp >= before` and (line 40) `timestamp <= after`, confirming the timestamp prefix is `Date.now()` — a predictable value. Combined with only 8 characters of random suffix (line 26), if the random portion uses Math.random() (the default in non-crypto JS code), the ID is predictable. If these IDs are used for security-sensitive lookups, an attacker who knows the approximate creation time can brute-force or predict the ID.

The test asserts the ID matches `/^\d+_[a-z0-9]{8}$/`, confirming a timestamp prefix (predictable, from Date.now() per lines 34-41) and only 8 alphanumeric random characters. If these IDs are used for security-sensitive lookups (e.g., conversation sharing, access control), an attacker who knows the approximate time of creation can brute-force or predict the ID.

title: Mass assignment: save() accepts full conversation object with all fields caller-controlled
description: The test suite confirms that ConversationStorageService.save() accepts a complete StoredConversation object where every field — `id`, `title`, `messages`, `createdAt`, and `updatedAt` — is provided and controlled by the caller (lines 133-135, 144-145, 153, 156). The tests verify that all these fields are persisted as-is to localStorage (lines 165-174 confirm `parsed[0].id` matches the caller-supplied id). There is no field allow-list: the caller can set `createdAt` and `updatedAt` to arbitrary values (e.g., backdating or future-dating conversations to manipulate sort order in getAll(), which sorts by updatedAt descending per lines 91-103), or supply an arbitrary `id` to overwrite another conversation (confirmed by the update test at lines 152-163 where the same id replaces the existing conversation). This is a mass assignment / broken object property level authorization issue: the service trusts the caller to provide all fields rather than deriving security-relevant fields (id, timestamps) server-side or applying an explicit allow-list.

No allow-list or field filtering is tested or expected, confirming mass assignment.

title: Basket operations accept arbitrary resource IDs without ownership context
description: The test specification verifies that BasketService methods (find, get, put, del, checkout, applyCoupon) accept caller-supplied resource identifiers and place them directly into API URLs with no accompanying ownership or authorization context. For example, service.find(1) issues GET /rest/basket/1, service.del(1) issues DELETE /api/BasketItems/1, and service.checkout(1) issues POST /rest/basket/1/checkout. The tests confirm that the only data transmitted is the resource ID itself—no user identity, session-scoped basket ID, or ownership token is passed alongside it. If the backend does not independently verify that the requesting user owns the basket or basket item identified by the supplied ID, any authenticated user can access, modify, delete, or check out another user's basket by substituting the identifier. This is the classic BOLA pattern: authentication without per-resource authorization. The design flaw is that the service trusts a client-provided ID to select the resource rather than deriving it from the authenticated session.

title: GetFromConfig task exposes arbitrary application configuration to callers
description: The `GetFromConfig` Cypress task accepts an arbitrary variable name from the caller (outside this file) and passes it directly to `config.get(variable)`. This allows the caller to retrieve any configuration value, including secrets, database connection strings, API keys, or internal endpoints stored in the application config. The design provides no allow-list or restriction on which configuration keys can be queried. A caller who can invoke this task can enumerate and exfiltrate sensitive configuration data that should remain server-side.

`config.get(variable)` returns the raw configuration value for the requested key. Any configuration entry — including secrets, connection strings, and internal endpoints — is exposed to the caller. The design never establishes which keys are safe to expose; it accepts any key the caller provides.

title: GenerateCoupon task allows caller-controlled discount with no bounds
description: The `GenerateCoupon` task accepts a `discount` value directly from the caller and passes it to `security.generateCoupon(discount)`. The discount amount is entirely client-controlled with no server-side validation, bounds checking, or re-derivation. This means the caller can generate coupons with arbitrary discount values — including 100% or negative discounts — depending on how the downstream coupon system processes the value. The design delegates a business-critical decision (the discount amount) to the client rather than enforcing it server-side.

The caller-controlled `discount` is passed directly to `security.generateCoupon(discount)` with no validation, bounds check, or clamping.

The coupon is generated using the caller-supplied discount. An attacker who can invoke this task can request coupons with arbitrary discount values, creating economic imbalance. The design never establishes bounds on the discount; it accepts whatever the caller provides.

title: GenerateAuthenticator task uses caller-provided secret for OTP generation
description: The `GenerateAuthenticator` task accepts an `inputString` from the caller and uses it as the OTP secret in `generateSync({ secret: inputString })`. In a proper authenticator flow, the secret is a server-derived, user-specific value that the client should never control. By allowing the caller to specify the secret, this design enables an attacker to generate valid OTPs for any account or secret they can guess or obtain, bypassing the intended authentication mechanism.

`generateSync({ secret: inputString })` produces an OTP for whatever secret the caller provided. The design allows the client to control the authentication secret rather than having the server derive it, violating a trust boundary: the server should decide the secret, not accept it from the caller.

title: GetFromMemories task allows arbitrary property enumeration on memory config
description: The `GetFromMemories` task accepts a `property` string from the caller and iterates through all memory configuration entries, returning the value of `memory[property]` for the first match. This allows the caller to probe for any property name on memory config objects, potentially exposing internal data fields that were not intended to be accessible. The design provides no allow-list of retrievable properties, making any config field on a memory object reachable.

title: toggleDeliveryStatus accepts arbitrary client-controlled params instead of enforcing a server-side toggle
description: The method is named `toggleDeliveryStatus`, implying it should flip a binary delivery status (e.g., pending ↔ delivered). However, it accepts an untyped `params` argument from the caller and passes it directly into the PUT request body with no validation, no status constraint, and no derivation of the new state. The client fully controls the delivery status payload. If the backend endpoint trusts this body, an attacker can set arbitrary delivery status values — skipping required workflow steps (e.g., marking an order as delivered before it ships), reverting delivered orders back to pending, or setting invalid status values — all while the operation succeeds normally. This is a trust boundary violation: the server should re-derive the toggle state from the current record, not accept the new state from the client.

description: The streamMessages function parses LLM-generated streaming responses and yields deltaContent (and deltaToolCalls) directly to callers without any sanitization or encoding. Any consuming component that renders this content as HTML (common in chat UIs that support markdown/rich text) will execute attacker-influenced scripts in the browser. The service is the propagation point where untrusted LLM output is packaged and handed off; the DOM sink is in the caller (outside this file), but the absence of any encoding or sanitization layer here means downstream consumers receive raw, potentially executable content.

title: Client-controlled message roles allow system prompt injection
description: The streamMessages function accepts a messages array where each message has a free-form 'role' string (line 31). This is a prompt injection vector (LLM01) enabled by an insecure design (A04) — the client is trusted to construct the full conversation context including system-level instructions, a responsibility that should belong to the server. title: Client-controlled email header sent on every request enables user impersonation
description: The interceptor reads an 'email' value from localStorage and attaches it as an 'X-User-Email' header on every outgoing HTTP request. localStorage is fully controllable by the client (via browser DevTools, JavaScript injection, or a modified client). The server-side handler(s) that receive this header are given an unauthenticated, caller-supplied identity claim alongside (or instead of) the verified Bearer token. If any server-side code resolves the requesting user's identity from the 'X-User-Email' header rather than from the cryptographically verified token, an attacker can impersonate any user simply by setting localStorage 'email' to the victim's email address. This is a design flaw because the client is trusted to report who it is — a fact the server should derive from the authenticated token, never from a client-supplied header. It is an access-control flaw because it permits broken object/function level authorization (User A accesses User B's resources). It is an authentication flaw because it allows the caller to influence the identity the application associates with the request, bypassing the token-based identity decision.

title: Private key transmitted to server in submitKey workflow
description: The submitKey, verifyNFTWallet, and walletAddressSend methods perform security-sensitive operations — submitting a private key and registering wallet addresses — but none of these code paths include any logging or monitoring hooks. When a private key is submitted or a wallet address is registered, there is no client-side audit trail. If an attacker coerces or tricks a user's browser into calling submitKey (e.g., via a CSRF or XSS payload), there will be no client-side telemetry to detect that a key exfiltration occurred. While the primary logging responsibility lies server-side, this service — which is the single chokepoint for all key and wallet operations on the client — instruments nothing. The catchError handlers merely re-throw errors without recording that a security-relevant event was attempted, even on failure.

title: Indefinite caching of security-relevant configuration without invalidation or refresh
description: The ConfigurationService caches the application configuration observable indefinitely once it has been fetched (lines 118-119). The cached observable is returned on every subsequent call without any TTL, invalidation, or refresh mechanism. title: Broken RxJS pipeline: catchError operator silently disabled on admin configuration request
description: On line 121, the `catchError` operator is incorrectly passed as the second argument to `map()` rather than as a separate argument to `pipe()`. In RxJS, `map(project, thisArg)` treats its second parameter as a `this` binding context, not as a pipeline operator. As a result, `catchError((err) => { throw err })` is silently ignored and never executes. The intended error handling for requests to the `/rest/admin/application-configuration` endpoint is completely non-functional. Any HTTP errors (including authentication failures, server errors, or network issues) propagate as unhandled observable errors with no interception. While the intended handler only rethrows, the fact that error handling is silently disabled means any future enhancement to that handler (e.g., logging, fallback config, retry) would also be silently ignored.

The catchError is passed as the second positional argument to map(), which RxJS interprets as thisArg, not as a pipeline operator.

hostServer is read from environment.hostServer. This value flows into the URL used for the admin configuration request.

Because catchError is consumed by map's thisArg parameter, it is never registered as an operator in the pipeline. Any error from the HTTP request to the admin endpoint propagates as an unhandled error. The correct form would be .pipe(map((response) => response.config), catchError((err) => { throw err })).

title: Untrusted backup file restores challenge progress without integrity verification or ownership checks
description: The restore() function accepts a user-provided File, parses it as JSON, and uses the contained continue codes to call server-side progress-restoration endpoints. The only validation is a version-number check (backup.version === this.VERSION). There is no checksum, signature, or any other integrity verification on the file contents. The continue codes are effectively bearer tokens for challenge progress — an attacker can craft or modify a backup file with another user's continue codes (or a stolen code) and restore progress they did not earn. The client-side code performs no authorization check to confirm the continue codes belong to the current user before sending them to the server. This is both an integrity failure (untrusted data modifies application state without verification) and an insecure design (progress is portable via files, making it shareable/stealable). The access-control concern is that the client sends arbitrary continue codes to the restore endpoints without any per-user ownership validation visible in this code; whether the server enforces this cannot be confirmed from this file.

The continue codes extracted from the untrusted file (backup.continueCode, backup.continueCodeFindIt, backup.continueCodeFixIt) are sent directly to server-side restore endpoints via challengeService.restoreProgress(), restoreProgressFindIt(), and restoreProgressFixIt() (lines 81-83). An attacker can craft a backup file containing a stolen or forged continue code to restore another user's challenge progress.

title: Cookies restored from backup file without secure or sameSite flags
description: When restoring a backup, cookies are set via cookieService.put() with only an expiration date in the options object. The secure flag (restricting transmission to HTTPS) and sameSite attribute (providing CSRF protection) are not set. The cookie values originate from an untrusted backup file, making this especially concerning — an attacker-crafted backup file can inject arbitrary values into cookies that lack transport and cross-site protections.

trace.description: restore(backupFile: File) receives a File from outside this file. The file contents are user-controlled.

Cookie values are extracted from the parsed backup object (backup.banners?.welcomeBannerStatus, backup.banners?.cookieConsentStatus, backup.language, backup.continueCode, etc.) on lines 69-74 and passed to restoreCookie().
restoreCookie() receives the cookie name and value from the untrusted backup data.

JSON.parse(backupData) deserialises the raw text into a Backup object. Cookie-related fields (backup.banners, backup.language, backup.continueCode, etc.) are populated from the untrusted parsed data.
The version check (backup.version === this.VERSION) gates all subsequent cookie restoration. Once passed, all cookie values from the untrusted backup are processed without further validation.

const expires = new Date() begins constructing the cookie options. Line 102 sets the expiration one year forward. Only the expires property is populated in the options object.

cookieService.put() is called with options { expires } only. The secure flag and sameSite attribute are absent, meaning cookies will be transmitted over plain HTTP if available and are vulnerable to cross-site request forgery.

title: URL path injection via untyped id parameter in getById
description: The getById method accepts an untyped `id` parameter and interpolates it directly into a URL path using a template literal. Because Angular's HttpClient does not re-encode path segments of an already-constructed URL string, a caller that passes an `id` containing path separators (e.g., `1/../../api/Users`) can cause the request to target a completely different API endpoint than intended. This is a path/URL injection that can bypass the intended endpoint boundary and access other resources on the same origin.

trace.description: The `getById(id)` function receives an `id` parameter from a caller outside this file. The parameter has no type annotation, no validation, and no allow-listing — any string value is accepted.

The untrusted `id` is interpolated directly into the URL path via template literal: `${this.host}/${id}`. No encoding, sanitization, or format check (e.g., numeric-only) is applied before the value is embedded into the request URL.
The base server host is retrieved from the environment configuration and assigned to `this.hostServer`.
The target API path `/api/Cards` is appended to `this.hostServer` to construct the base `this.host` URL.

The constructed URL is passed to `this.http.get(...)`, issuing an HTTP GET. If `id` contains `/` or `..`, the resulting request targets an endpoint other than `/api/Cards/<id>`, e.g., `id = '1/../../api/Users'` normalizes to a request against `/api/Users`.

title: Unfiltered request body in save() enables mass assignment of card properties
description: The save method accepts a `params` object from the caller and posts it verbatim to the `/api/Cards` endpoint without any field allow-list or property filtering. If the backend model auto-binds request body fields to model properties, a caller can include sensitive or unintended fields (e.g., `userId`, `balance`, `isActive`, `cardType`) that the application never intended to expose for client control. The absence of an explicit allow-list in this service means every property on the caller's object is transmitted and potentially persisted by the backend.

The entire `params` object is passed directly as the request body to `this.http.post(this.host + '/', params)`. No properties are stripped, validated, or restricted before the POST.
The base server host is retrieved from the environment configuration and assigned to `this.hostServer`.
The target API path `/api/Cards` is appended to `this.hostServer` to construct the base `this.host` URL.

The unfiltered body is sent to the `/api/Cards` POST endpoint. If the backend persists all submitted fields (a common auto-binding pattern), any caller-supplied field — including sensitive model properties not intended for client control — is written to the data store. The render/persistence sink is on the backend, outside this file.

title: Coupon value interpolated directly into URL path without encoding in applyCoupon
description: The `applyCoupon` method interpolates the caller-supplied `coupon` string directly into the URL path via a template literal: `${this.hostServer}/rest/basket/${id}/coupon/${coupon}`. Angular's HttpClient does not URL-encode path segments, so a coupon value containing path-traversal sequences (e.g., `../`) or other URL-special characters can alter the effective request path. An attacker could supply a crafted coupon string to redirect the PUT request to a different server-side route, potentially reaching administrative or other unintended endpoints.

trace.description: applyCoupon(id?: number, coupon?: string) accepts a caller-supplied coupon string. The caller is outside this file (a component or route handler invoking this service method).

The coupon value is interpolated directly into the URL path string: `${this.hostServer}/rest/basket/${id}/coupon/${coupon}`. No encodeURIComponent, no allow-listing, and no validation of the coupon format occurs before it is embedded in the URL.

The assembled URL is passed to this.http.put(), which issues the request with the unencoded coupon in the path. A crafted coupon value (e.g., `../../admin/settings`) would change the effective route the server receives.

title: Basket and basket-item operations accept arbitrary resource IDs without ownership verification
description: The find, get, put, del, and mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket methods all accept a basket or basket-item identifier and issue HTTP requests against it without any client-side check that the ID belongs to the current user. The basket ID is read from sessionStorage (line 65), which is fully client-controllable — a user can set `bid` to any value. Additionally, mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket accepts a targetBasketId parameter from its caller and fetches/modifies that basket (lines 158–171) without verifying ownership. If the server does not enforce per-resource authorization, User A can read or mutate User B's basket by substituting the identifier.

trace.description: find(id?: number) accepts a basket ID from its caller (outside this file). The ID is not validated against the current user's identity.

updateNumberOfCartItems reads the basket ID from sessionStorage.getItem('bid') — a client-controllable storage location — and passes it to find(). A user can arbitrarily set this value to another user's basket ID.

mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket(targetBasketId: number) receives an arbitrary basket ID from its caller and calls this.find(targetBasketId) to fetch that basket, then modifies it via put() and save() at lines 169–171 — all without any ownership check.
updateNumberOfCartItems() begins execution to refresh the cart item count.
mergeGuestBasketIntoUserBasket(targetBasketId: number) receives an arbitrary basket ID from its caller (outside this file).

The unvalidated basket ID is sent to the server in the URL: GET /rest/basket/${id}. No ownership verification occurs between receiving the ID and issuing the request. The same pattern repeats for get (line 40), put (line 44), and del (line 48) on /api/BasketItems/${id}.

title: PUT and POST basket-item operations accept untyped arbitrary params without field allow-listing
description: The `put` method accepts `params: any` and passes it directly as the request body to the PUT /api/BasketItems/{id} endpoint (line 44). The `save` method similarly accepts `params?: any` and POSTs it directly (line 52). Neither method applies an explicit field allow-list. If the server binds request body fields directly to model properties, a caller could inject sensitive fields (e.g., isAdmin, userId, price) alongside the expected quantity/ProductId fields, leading to mass assignment / privilege escalation.
