The params object is passed directly as the HTTP request body to this.http.put(). No field filtering, allow-listing, or shape validation occurs. The save method at line 52 does the same with this.http.post().
save(params?: any) accepts an untyped, unrestricted params object from its caller (outside this file).

The unfiltered params reach the server as the POST body via this.http.post(). If the server auto-binds body fields to model properties, caller-controlled fields beyond quantity/ProductId would be persisted.

The unfiltered params reach the server as the PUT body. If the server auto-binds body fields to model properties, caller-controlled fields beyond quantity/ProductId would be persisted. The same risk exists for the POST at line 52.

title: Checkout trusts client-supplied payment, address, and delivery method identifiers
description: The `checkout` method sends `orderDetails` — containing `paymentId`, `addressId`, and `deliveryMethodId` — directly from the client to the server in the POST body (line 56). These are trust-sensitive values: the server should derive or validate them rather than accept caller-supplied identifiers. An attacker could substitute another user's paymentId or addressId, or supply an invalid deliveryMethodId to manipulate pricing or routing of the order.

trace.description: checkout(id?: number, couponData?: string, orderDetails?: OrderDetail) accepts orderDetails from its caller (outside this file). OrderDetail contains paymentId, addressId, and deliveryMethodId — all caller-supplied string values.
The orderDetails object is placed directly into the POST body { couponData, orderDetails } without any server-side re-derivation or validation of the payment, address, or delivery method values.

The client-supplied order details are sent to POST /rest/basket/${id}/checkout. If the server trusts these values without re-validating ownership of the paymentId and addressId, an attacker could checkout using another user's payment instrument or shipping address.

title: Socket.IO client connection established without transport security enforcement or authentication configuration
description: The SocketIoService creates a socket connection to `environment.hostServer` (line 26) using the default Socket.IO client options. No `secure` flag, no TLS enforcement, and no authentication token or credentials are passed to the connection. If `environment.hostServer` resolves to an `http://` URL, all real-time communication — including any session-bound or user-specific data exchanged over the socket — travels in plaintext and is susceptible to interception or tampering on the network path. Additionally, the absence of any authentication mechanism (e.g., a JWT in the `auth` option or `query` parameter) means the server cannot cryptographically verify the identity of the connecting client at the transport layer; any client that knows the endpoint URL can establish a socket connection and emit or receive events. The same concern applies to the `window.location.origin` branch (line 22), which inherits whatever protocol the page was loaded with — including `http://` in non-production or misconfigured deployments.

trace.description: The constructor calls `io(environment.hostServer)` with no options object. The caller (environment configuration) is outside this file. No `secure`, ` transports`, `auth`, or credential options are provided, so the connection relies entirely on whatever protocol the hostServer URL uses and carries no client-side authentication material.

The resulting socket is stored in `this._socket`. Because no transport security or authentication options were set, every subsequent message sent or received over this socket inherits the insecure baseline established at connection time.
The `else` block concludes, and control flow exits the conditional.
The callback passed to `this.ngZone.runOutsideAngular` concludes, finalizing the constructor's execution.
The `socket()` method is defined, providing a public accessor to the private `_socket` instance.
The `socket()` method returns `this._socket` to any caller, exposing the unauthenticated, potentially unencrypted socket for arbitrary use throughout the application.

title: Unvalidated arbitrary parameters for sensitive GDPR data-subject operations
description: The DataSubjectService exposes two methods — erase() and dataExport() — that handle GDPR data-subject rights (right to erasure and right to data portability). Both methods accept `params: any` and pass it directly to HTTP POST calls without any validation, type-checking, or structural enforcement on the parameters. This is a trust assumption violation: the client fully controls what parameters are sent for sensitive privacy operations. If the server trusts these parameters (e.g., a user ID, a confirmation token, or a scope of data to export/erase), an attacker could manipulate them to export another user's data, bypass erasure confirmation steps, or alter the scope of the operation. The design never establishes what parameters are legitimate or derives them server-side; it accepts whatever the client sends.

trace.description: The erase() method receives `params: any` from an outside caller (the caller is outside this file). The parameter type `any` means no structure, type, or content constraints are enforced on the input. The same pattern applies to dataExport() at line 26.
The hostServer value is loaded from the environment configuration to establish the base URL for the request.
The full host path is assembled by concatenating hostServer with '/rest/user'.

The unvalidated `params` object is passed directly as the body of an HTTP POST to /rest/user/erasure-request. Line 27 does the same for /rest/user/data-export. No validation, transformation, or server-derived values are introduced between receiving the parameters and sending the request. The client controls the entire request body for operations that should have server-side authority over parameters such as target user identity, confirmation state, and data scope.

title: No security logging for data erasure and data export operations
description: Data erasure (right to be forgotten) and data export (right to data portability) are security- and privacy-relevant events that must be auditable under GDPR and general security best practices. The DataSubjectService handles both operations but contains no logging whatsoever — no audit log of who requested erasure, who requested a data export, when, or with what parameters. There is no correlation ID, no event emission, and no error logging beyond re-throwing exceptions. Without logging these events, the organization cannot detect, investigate, or respond to misuse such as unauthorized data exports or malicious erasure requests.

trace.description: The erase() method initiates a data erasure request — a security-relevant event involving permanent data deletion. The dataExport() method at line 26 initiates a data export — a security-relevant event involving bulk access to personal data. Neither method logs the event.
The hostServer is loaded from the environment to prepare the request endpoint, with no logging setup or audit context initialized.
The host URL is assembled for the privacy-related API endpoints without generating any correlation IDs or logging the intent to call them.

The HTTP POST to /rest/user/erasure-request (line 22) and /rest/user/data-export (line 27) are executed with no logging before, during, or after the call. The catchError handlers (lines 22-23, 27) merely re-throw errors without logging them. There is no audit trail for these sensitive privacy operations anywhere in this service.

title: No rate limiting or throttling on data export and erasure request endpoints
description: The dataExport() method triggers a potentially resource-intensive server-side operation (generating and transmitting a complete export of user data). The erase() method triggers a cascading deletion operation. Neither method implements any client-side rate limiting, throttling, or cooldown mechanism. An attacker can call these methods repeatedly in rapid succession, causing the server to generate multiple concurrent data export archives or process multiple erasure workflows, consuming CPU, memory, disk, and database resources. The absence of any visible throttling control means the only protection would need to exist at the server or infrastructure level, which is not confirmable from this file.

trace.description: The dataExport() method (and similarly erase() at line 21) can be called by an outside caller (outside this file) with no restriction on frequency. There is no rate limiter, debounce, cooldown timer, or request counter.
The hostServer is loaded from the environment configuration to determine where the unthrottled requests will be sent.
The target host path is assembled by concatenating the base host with '/rest/user', readying the unthrottled call.

Each call to dataExport() issues an HTTP POST to /rest/user/data-export, triggering a potentially expensive server-side data generation operation. With no client-side throttling and no visible indication of server-side rate limits, repeated rapid calls can cause excessive resource consumption on the server.

title: Wallet balance update accepts client-controlled amount, enabling balance manipulation
description: The test file reveals that the WalletService's `put` method sends a client-supplied balance value directly to the server's `/rest/wallet/balance` endpoint via HTTP PUT. On line 43, the test calls `service.put(1)` and on line 68 `service.put({ amount: 1 })`, confirming that the client provides the balance amount. In a wallet/payment system, the server should derive the wallet balance from authoritative transaction records, not accept a client-reported balance value. This design permits an attacker to send an arbitrary amount (e.g., `service.put(999999)`) to inflate their own wallet balance. The actual defect is in the WalletService implementation and the server-side handler (both outside this file), but this test file is where the client-controlled balance pattern is visible and confirmed.

trace.description: The test calls `service.put(1)`, passing a raw numeric balance value as an argument to the WalletService. The caller (WalletService.put) is outside this file, but this test confirms the service accepts a client-supplied balance amount.
The test verifies the service issues an HTTP PUT to `http://localhost:3000/rest/wallet/balance`, confirming the client-controlled balance value is sent directly to the server's balance endpoint.
The test flushes a mock response `{ data: 'apiResponse' }` from the expected request, completing the HTTP interaction cycle for the client-supplied balance update.

The test asserts the request method is PUT, confirming the wallet balance is updated via a client-initiated write of a client-supplied value. The server endpoint `/rest/wallet/balance` accepts this value, meaning the wallet balance is client-controlled — a design that allows an attacker to set an arbitrary balance by calling put() with any amount.

title: Password change request transmits credentials via GET query string parameters
description: The changePassword method issues a GET request and places the current password, new password, and repeat password directly into the URL query string. GET requests with sensitive data in query parameters are logged by web servers, proxies, CDNs, and browser history. The passwords will also appear in Referer headers sent to any third-party resources loaded on subsequent pages. Using GET for a state-changing credential operation also violates HTTP semantics. The password values are concatenated without URL encoding, which can additionally cause corruption or truncation of special characters. This design exposes plaintext passwords through multiple logging and caching surfaces that would not capture them in a POST body.

trace.description: changePassword(passwords: Passwords) receives an object containing current, new, and repeat passwords. The caller is outside this file (a component or route handler invoking the service).

The password values are interpolated directly into a URL query string: '...change-password?current=' + passwords.current + '&new=' + passwords.new + '&repeat=' + passwords.repeat. No encoding is applied and the HTTP method is GET.

this.http.get(...) sends the GET request with all three password values embedded in the URL. Any HTTP intermediary (reverse proxy, load balancer, WAF, browser) that logs request URLs will record plaintext passwords in its access logs.

title: Client-side login state set before server authentication completes
description: The login method calls this.isLoggedIn.next(true) synchronously on line 45, BEFORE the HTTP POST authentication request is even sent (line 46). This means any component subscribed to the isLoggedIn observable will treat the user as authenticated before the server has verified credentials. If the server rejects the login (wrong password, locked account, etc.), the client-side application state is already 'logged in', creating a window where UI elements, routes, or features gated on getLoggedInState() may be accessible despite failed authentication. This is a design flaw: authentication state must be derived from the server's authentication response, not set optimistically before it.

trace.description: login(params: any) receives login credentials. The caller is outside this file (a login component).
this.isLoggedIn.next(true) broadcasts an authenticated state to all subscribers immediately, before any server verification. The HTTP POST on line 46 is still pending at this point.

title: OAuth access token sent as unencrypted query parameter to Google userinfo endpoint
description: The oauthLogin method appends the OAuth access token directly as a query parameter in the URL to Google's userinfo endpoint. While the Google API does accept access_token as a query parameter, this approach exposes the bearer token in browser history, server logs, and potentially Referer headers. The recommended approach is to send the token via the Authorization header. An attacker who gains access to proxy or server logs could capture and replay the token to impersonate the user.

trace.description: oauthLogin(accessToken: string) receives an OAuth access token. The caller is outside this file.
The access token is concatenated directly into the URL query string: 'https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v1/userinfo?alt=json&access_token=' + accessToken
this.http.get(...) sends the request with the bearer token embedded in the URL rather than in an Authorization header, exposing it to logging surfaces.

title: Unencoded search criteria interpolated into URL enables query-parameter injection to bypass pagination and result limits
description: The `search` method receives a `criteria` string from its caller (outside this file, ultimately from the search bar) and interpolates it directly into the request URL using template literal string interpolation without calling `encodeURIComponent`. Because the value is not encoded, an attacker can inject additional query parameters by supplying a value like `x&limit=999999` or `x&offset=0&size=10000000`. The resulting URL becomes `.../rest/products/search?q=x&limit=999999`, which the backend will parse as two separate query parameters. If the backend honours a `limit` or `size` parameter to cap result sets, the attacker overrides it, causing the server to return an unbounded result set into memory. Even if the backend has a default limit, the injected parameter can raise it, leading to excessive memory and database resource consumption. This is also an insecure-design flaw: the service constructs a query string by concatenation rather than using the framework's built-in parameter encoding (`HttpParams`), which is the correct mechanism for safely passing user values as query parameters.

trace.description: The `search` method receives `criteria: string` from its caller. The caller is outside this file (likely a component bound to the search bar), and `criteria` originates from user input.

`criteria` is interpolated directly into the URL string: `${this.hostServer}/rest/products/search?q=${criteria}`. No `encodeURIComponent`, no `HttpParams`, no validation is applied — the raw string is placed after `q=`.

The constructed URL is passed to `this.http.get(...)`. An attacker supplying `criteria = 'x&limit=999999'` causes a GET to `.../rest/products/search?q=x&limit=999999`. The backend sees two query parameters (`q=x` and `limit=999999`), allowing the attacker to override pagination limits and trigger unbounded result-set retrieval, consuming server memory and database resources.

title: Product update (PUT) transmits caller-supplied parameters without validating economic fields, enabling trust-assumption violation
description: The `put` method receives an untyped `params` object from its caller (outside this file) and passes it directly as the request body to `PUT /api/Products/:id`. There is no validation, field filtering, or server-side re-derivation of sensitive product fields (such as price, unit, or deleted status). In the Juice Shop domain, products carry price data that the server should authoritatively control. If the caller includes a `price` field in `params` — which nothing in this service prevents — the client is effectively setting the price of a product on the server. The design flaw is that the service treats all product attributes as client-provided values with no distinction between fields the client may legitimately modify (e.g., description) and fields the server must own (e.g., price). A concrete attack: an attacker (or a compromised/manipulated frontend) calls `productService.put(productId, { price: 0.01 })` to set an arbitrary price, and the server accepts it because no server-side price validation is enforced by this design.

trace.description: The `put` method receives `id: number` and `params` (untyped) from its caller. The caller is outside this file. The `params` object is not validated or constrained by any type or schema in this service.

`params` is passed directly as the second argument to `this.http.put(`${this.host}/${id}`, params)` with no field filtering, no allow-listing of modifiable properties, and no server-side re-derivation of economic fields.

The unfiltered `params` object becomes the PUT request body sent to `/api/Products/:id`. If `params` includes a `price` field, the client is setting product pricing — a value the server should derive or validate rather than accept from the caller. This is a trust-assumption violation: the design permits the client to control economic data.

title: Client-controlled author field in review creation allows review impersonation
description: The create() method accepts an 'author' field as part of the review object and passes it directly into the HTTP PUT body sent to the server. The author of a review should be determined server-side from the authenticated session, not accepted from the client. A caller can set 'author' to any value, allowing them to post reviews under another user's identity. This is both a mass assignment issue (a sensitive property exposed to caller control without an allow-list) and an insecure design issue (a trust assumption violation where the client controls a fact the server should decide).

The entire 'review' object — including the caller-controlled 'author' field — is passed verbatim as the PUT request body to `${this.host}/${id}/reviews`. No field allow-listing or server-side author override is applied; the object is spread directly into the request.
The HttpClient instance (`this.http`) is injected here. It is the vehicle that will transport the caller-controlled 'review' object to the server.
The base URL for the request is loaded from the environment configuration, establishing the server target.
The `host` property is initialized by appending '/rest/products' to the base URL, finalizing the target endpoint path for the reviews API.

The patch() method receives a 'review' object with { id: string, message: string }. The caller (outside this file) supplies both the 'id' (which review to modify) and the 'message' (new content). The client fully determines the target resource.

The HTTP PATCH call sends the entire caller-supplied review object, including the 'id', to the server. If the server does not verify that the authenticated user owns the review identified by 'id', an attacker can modify reviews authored by other users.

The HTTP PUT call persists the caller-supplied 'author' field. The server (outside this file) is expected to store it. If the server does not override 'author' with the session user, an attacker can post reviews attributed to any user, enabling impersonation and reputational damage.

title: Unsanitized free-form message field persisted as review text enables stored XSS
description: The create() and patch() methods accept a free-form 'message' string and send it directly to the server for persistence without any sanitization, encoding, or content validation. This message is review text that will be rendered in product review displays. If the server stores it as-is and the frontend renders it without context-appropriate output encoding, an attacker can inject script or markup that executes in other users' browsers. The persistence point is in this file; the render sink is outside this file.

title: Patch method accepts caller-supplied review id without ownership indication
description: The patch() method accepts a review object containing 'id' and 'message' from the caller. The 'id' field determines which review is modified. There is no indication that the caller's authority to edit the review with that id is verified before the request is sent. If the server trusts the client-supplied id without verifying that the requesting user owns the review, any user could edit any other user's review. This is a trust assumption violation: the client controls which resource is modified, and the server-side ownership check (outside this file) is the only barrier.

trace.description: The patch() method receives a 'review' object with { id: string, message: string }. The caller (outside this file) supplies both the 'id' (which review to modify) and the 'message' (new content). The client fully determines the target resource.

The entire review object including the caller-chosen 'id' is passed directly as the PATCH request body to '/rest/products/reviews'. No client-side ownership check is performed (nor should it be), meaning the server is the sole enforcer.

The HTTP PATCH call sends the caller-supplied review id to the server. If the server does not verify that the authenticated user owns the review identified by 'id', an attacker can modify reviews authored by other users, violating data integrity.

title: Unvalidated, untyped address ID accepted from child component without integrity checks
description: The AddressSelectComponent stores an address identifier received via getMessage(id) into the field addressId, which is declared as `any` with no type constraint, no validation, and no bounds checking. The id parameter of getMessage is also completely untyped. This follows the insecure-design pattern of a client-side component accepting and propagating an identity token (an address ID) that the server should independently validate and re-derive. If this addressId is later sent to the server to associate a shipment or order with an address, an attacker could tamper with the value in the browser (e.g., substituting another user's address ID) to redirect deliveries or manipulate order data. The design places trust in the client-supplied addressId without any compensating control visible in this component. The actual exploitability depends on whether the server re-validates the addressId against the authenticated user's owned addresses — which cannot be confirmed from this file alone.

The id parameter is completely untyped; no validation, sanitization, or ownership check is performed.
The unvalidated id is assigned directly to this.addressId, which is declared on line 20 as `any` — no type constraint, no default guard, no integrity check.

addressId (typed as `any`, unvalidated) is stored as component state. This value is the address selection that downstream order/checkout logic will rely on. The design accepts a client-controlled address identifier without any server-side re-derivation or ownership verification visible in this component, creating a trust assumption violation where the client determines which address is used.

title: Feedback comments passed through DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml enabling stored XSS
description:
The test file confirms that AboutComponent.populateSlideshowFromFeedbacks() calls DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml with HTML that embeds raw feedback comment text (line 178 expects '

Great!

'). bypassSecurityTrustHtml is Angular's explicit security-bypass API that marks untrusted HTML as safe for rendering. Feedback comments are user-submitted content retrieved from FeedbackService.find(). By routing them through bypassSecurityTrustHtml without any sanitization, any HTML or script in a comment will be rendered directly in the DOM. An attacker who submits a feedback comment containing malicious script tags or event-handler attributes can achieve stored XSS when any visitor views the About page and the feedback gallery renders. The mock at line 56 shows bypassSecurityTrustHtml as a passthrough, mirroring the real API's behavior of skipping sanitization entirely. The actual sink (the component's HTML rendering) is in about.component.ts, outside this file, but this test file establishes the data flow and confirms the bypass is called with unvalidated user content.

trace.description: FeedbackService.find mock returns feedback objects with a 'comment' field containing free-form text ('Great!'). This simulates user-submitted feedback data arriving from the backend (caller is outside this file). The comment field is attacker-controllable user input.

component.populateSlideshowFromFeedbacks() is called, which processes the feedback array. The test at lines 176-178 verifies that the method constructs an HTML string embedding the raw comment text inside a

element and passes it to sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml().

The mock implementation of bypassSecurityTrustHtml is defined as a passthrough: mockImplementation((value: string) => value). This mirrors the real Angular DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml, which marks the input as trusted and returns it without any sanitization. The HTML string containing the raw comment passes through unchanged.

The mock sanitizer is injected into the component via { provide: DomSanitizer, useValue: sanitizer }, so the component's real call to this.bypassSecurityTrustHtml uses the bypass function that returns the input unmodified.
The actual argument passed to bypassSecurityTrustHtml is captured from mock.calls[0][0] as sanitizedHtml. This is the HTML string constructed by the component from the feedback comment.

The assertion confirms the HTML string contains '

Great!

' — the raw, unescaped comment text is embedded directly inside a

element with no encoding or sanitization applied to it.
The test asserts galleryRef.addImage was called once, confirming that the trusted HTML (containing the raw comment) is forwarded to the gallery's addImage method for DOM rendering.

The test asserts galleryRef.addImage.mock.calls[0][0].src is 'assets/public/images/carousel/1.jpg', confirming the addImage call receives a data object. The HTML from bypassSecurityTrustHtml — which contains the unsanitized feedback comment — is part of this object that gets rendered into the DOM by the gallery component. No sanitization occurs between the user-controlled comment and this rendering sink, enabling stored XSS via malicious feedback comments.

The test asserts sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml is called (toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)) with HTML containing the unsanitized comment. Line 56 shows the mock implementation of bypassSecurityTrustHtml is a passthrough (returns value unchanged), mirroring the real Angular DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml which explicitly bypasses the framework's built-in output sanitization. The resulting trusted HTML is then passed to galleryRef.addImage (line 182) for DOM rendering. No sanitization occurs between the user-controlled comment and the security-bypass sink, enabling stored XSS via malicious feedback comments.

title: Unauthenticated security question retrieval by email enables account takeover reconnaissance
description: The findBy method accepts an arbitrary email string and sends it directly to the /rest/user/security-question endpoint to retrieve the security question for that user's account. There is no authentication check, no rate limiting, and no logging of this security-relevant retrieval. Security questions are intended to serve as a secret recovery factor, but exposing them to any unauthenticated caller who knows (or guesses) an email address defeats their purpose as an authentication mechanism. An attacker can enumerate email addresses, retrieve the corresponding security questions, research the answers (which are often based on public information like mother's maiden name or first pet), and then use those answers to reset passwords and take over accounts. The email parameter is also concatenated directly into the URL without URL-encoding, making it susceptible to query parameter manipulation. The design flaw is that the server-side endpoint is designed to return security questions based solely on an email parameter with no compensating controls (authentication, rate limiting, or audit logging) visible in the calling code.

trace.description: The findBy method receives an email string from a caller outside this file (an Angular component or other service). There is no authentication, authorization, or validation performed on the email parameter before it is used.

The raw email string is concatenated directly into the request URL: this.hostServer + '/' + 'rest/user/security-question?email=' + email. No URL-encoding is applied, and no logging records that a security question lookup is being performed for this email.

The hostServer value is read from the environment configuration object. This base URL is later combined with the user-supplied email to construct the request endpoint. No security check or logging is applied at this configuration-derivation step.

The HTTP GET request is sent to the security-question endpoint, and the response's 'question' field is returned to the caller. Any caller — authenticated or not — can retrieve the security question for any email address, and no audit log entry is generated for this security-relevant event.

title: Security answer save accepts arbitrary unvalidated params with no throttling
description: The `save` method accepts `params: any` and POSTs it directly to `/api/SecurityAnswers/` with no validation of the payload structure, no client-side rate limiting, and no confirmation step. Security answers are part of the password recovery/authentication flow. The `any` type means the service enforces no contract on what fields are sent (e.g., user ID, question ID, answer text). If the backend trusts the frontend payload structure, an attacker could submit security answers for arbitrary users, set malformed answers, or submit excessive payloads. Additionally, there is no throttling on the save call — an attacker can invoke it in a tight loop to flood the endpoint, potentially exhausting backend database connections or memory. The `catchError` on line 23 is a no-op that merely rethrows, providing no error handling or retry backoff that would mitigate rapid repeated calls.

trace.description: The `save` method receives `params: any` from a caller outside this file (an Angular component). No type, structure, or content validation is applied to `params` before it is used in the HTTP request.
The unvalidated `params` object is passed directly as the body of `this.http.post(this.host + '/', params)`. No fields are checked, no size limit is enforced, and no rate limiting wraps the call.

The `map` operator transforms the successful response by extracting `response.data`. This is the success path of the observable — no validation, size check, or throttle is applied to either the request or the response here.

The pipe closes with `)`, returning the observable to the caller. At no point in this chain — from params reception through the HTTP call, through the map and catchError operators, to the returned observable — is there any rate limiting, payload validation, or throttling control. An attacker can call `save` in an unbounded loop.

The `catchError((err) => { throw err })` handler is a no-op — it catches errors and immediately rethrows without logging, backoff, or any throttle. This means failed save attempts produce no observable record and the caller can immediately retry in a tight loop, enabling resource exhaustion against the backend security-answers endpoint.

title: No logging of security answer save operations or failures
description: The `save` method handles the creation of security answers — a security-relevant event in the authentication recovery flow. Neither successful saves nor failed attempts are logged anywhere in this service. The `catchError` operator on line 23 explicitly intercepts errors but only rethrows them without recording the failure. If an attacker manipulates security answers (e.g., setting answers for other users' accounts to enable password reset takeover), there is no client-side audit trail of the attempt. While backend logging may exist, the absence of any logging in the service that handles this security-critical operation is a monitoring gap.

trace.description: The `save` method is the entrypoint for saving security answers. This is a security-relevant operation (password recovery flow). The caller is outside this file.
The HTTP POST to `/api/SecurityAnswers/` executes the save. No logging statement exists before, during, or after this call to record that a security answer save was attempted.

The `map` operator processes the successful response, extracting `response.data`. A successful security answer save — which could indicate account takeover if the user ID was spoofed — is not logged at any point in this success path.

The `catchError` handler receives errors from the save operation but performs no logging — it simply rethrows the error. Failed security answer save attempts (which could indicate brute-force or manipulation attempts) are silently discarded.

title: Client-controlled wallet balance data sent to server without validation
description: The `put` method accepts an arbitrary `params` object from the caller (a component outside this file) and passes it verbatim as the request body to the server's wallet balance endpoint (`PUT /rest/wallet/balance`). No validation, sanitization, or server-derived recomputation is performed in this service. This is a trust assumption violation: the client is supplying wallet balance data (e.g., a balance amount or transaction value) that the server should independently compute or validate. If the server trusts this client-supplied value, an attacker can manipulate their own wallet balance or perform negative-value transactions by crafting the `params` payload directly rather than through the intended UI flow.

trace.description: The `put(params)` method receives an untyped `params` object from a caller outside this file (an Angular component). No type annotation, schema, or validation constrains what `params` contains.
`params` flows directly into `this.http.put(this.host, params)` with no transformation, filtering, or validation. The entire caller-supplied object becomes the PUT request body.
The `http` HttpClient instance — the mechanism that will transmit `params` — is injected via `inject(HttpClient)`. This is the transport over which the unvalidated data will be sent.

`hostServer` is read from `environment.hostServer`, establishing the base URL for the wallet endpoint. This is configuration-derived, not user-controlled, so the destination is fixed — but the body that will be sent there is not.
`host` is constructed as `this.hostServer + '/rest/wallet/balance'`, finalizing the endpoint URL that the unvalidated `params` will be sent to. The URL is trusted; the body is not.

The HTTP PUT request sends the client-controlled body to `/rest/wallet/balance`. The server endpoint receives whatever financial data the client chose to send. If the server does not re-derive the balance independently, the client can set arbitrary wallet balances, creating an economic imbalance.

title: No security logging for wallet balance modifications
description: Wallet balance changes are security-relevant financial events that should be logged for audit and fraud detection. The `put` method performs a balance mutation (PUT to `/rest/wallet/balance`) but contains no logging of the operation, the amount changed, or the user performing it. While this is a frontend service and server-side logging may exist, the service itself provides no client-side observability for this critical financial operation, and any error path (the `catchError` on line 25) also discards the error without logging.

The `catchError` and `map` operators are imported from `rxjs/operators`. These are the operators that will process the response pipeline. Their presence establishes the points where logging could be inserted for either success or error outcomes.

The HTTP PUT is executed and the response (or error) is processed with `catchError((err) => { throw err })`. No logging occurs on either the success or error path. A failed balance modification attempt — which could indicate an attack — is silently re-thrown with no audit trail.

title: Stored XSS via bypassSecurityTrustHtml on feedback comments
description: User-submitted feedback comments are retrieved from the server and passed directly to DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml() without any sanitization. This explicitly disables Angular's built-in output encoding and marks attacker-controlled content as trusted HTML. If a user submits a feedback comment containing <script> tags or event-handler attributes, that markup will be rendered and executed in the browser of any administrator viewing the feedback table. This is a stored/persistent XSS — the payload is persisted via the feedback submission flow (entrypoint outside this file) and rendered here in the administration component.

The subscribe next callback receives the feedbacks array from the server response.

Angular will render this without escaping, enabling execution of any HTML/script contained in the comment. No sanitization, filtering, or encoding is applied between the source and this sink.

The email value is user-controlled (set at registration, entrypoint outside this file) and reaches the bypassSecurityTrustHtml sink without any encoding or sanitization.

title: Unbounded selectedLines array sent to verdict endpoint without size validation
description: The `check` method accepts a `selectedLines: number[]` parameter with no size limit or validation. The array is serialized directly into the POST body and sent to the `/snippets/verdict` endpoint. A caller can pass an extremely large array, producing an unbounded request payload. There is no client-side cap on array length, no request body size limit, and no pagination. If the server processes each element in the array (e.g., matching against vulnerability line sets), this can cause excessive memory or CPU consumption on both the client (constructing and serializing the payload) and the server (processing it).

title: Security-relevant API errors caught and rethrown without any logging
description: The `check` method makes a POST to a security verdict endpoint that validates vulnerability line selections. The `catchError` operator on line 24 intercepts all errors from this call but simply rethrows them without logging any information — not the error status, not the request that caused it, not any correlation identifier. Repeated failures from this endpoint (which could indicate brute-forcing vulnerability answers, probing the verdict system, or an attack on the endpoint) would leave no trace in application logs. The error handler is effectively a no-op pass-through that discards the opportunity to record security-relevant failures.

The error handler body is `(error: any) => { throw error }` — it catches the error and rethrows it immediately without writing any log entry, emitting any metric, or recording any trace. No security-relevant event from this endpoint is logged.

title: Order tracking lookup by raw ID with no design-level access control or verification
description: The TrackOrderService.find() method accepts an arbitrary string as an order identifier and directly queries the server's track-order endpoint by appending it to the URL path. The design of this feature — order lookup by a simple ID — provides no compensating control against enumeration. There is no requirement for a tracking token, no email/ownership verification, no rate-limiting hint, and no format validation that would constrain guessing. If the server endpoint also does not enforce authorization (which cannot be confirmed from this file alone), an attacker can enumerate order IDs to access other users' order details. The design itself — exposing order data through a predictable, unverified identifier — is the defect, regardless of whether the server adds checks after the fact.

The input is URL-encoded with encodeURIComponent, which prevents path traversal and injection but does not validate that the input is a legitimate order ID, enforce any format constraint, or add any verification token.
The base server host is loaded from the environment configuration into this.hostServer, establishing the target for the HTTP request.
The track-order endpoint path is constructed by concatenating the host with '/rest/track-order', defining the route to which the user-supplied ID will be appended.

The encoded value is sent as a path segment in a GET request to /rest/track-order/{params}. The design provides no authentication context, no ownership proof, and no anti-enumeration mechanism — the server is trusted entirely to decide whether the caller may view this order.

title: No logging of order tracking queries or lookup failures
description: The find() method makes HTTP requests to look up orders and uses catchError to handle errors, but the error handler merely rethrows the error without logging any detail. There is no logging of successful order lookups, failed lookups, or repeated queries that could indicate order ID enumeration. Order tracking is a security-relevant event — an attacker enumerating order IDs to discover other users' order information would produce a pattern of failed and successful lookups that should be logged and alertable. The complete absence of any logging mechanism in this service means that enumeration attacks against the track-order endpoint would only be detectable through lower-level infrastructure logs (e.g., web server access logs), with no application-level security event recording.

The catchError handler at line 22 is the point where a failed order lookup should be logged as a security-relevant event (especially repeated failures indicating enumeration). Instead, the error is silently rethrown with no log record created, and successful lookups are also not logged.

title: 2FA can be disabled using only a password, without the second factor
description: The disable() method sends only the user's password to the /rest/2fa/disable endpoint. The function signature accepts a single 'password' parameter and the request body contains only that password. If two-factor authentication is meant to protect accounts whose passwords have been compromised, allowing 2FA to be disabled without providing the current TOTP token defeats the purpose of the second factor entirely. An attacker who has obtained a user's password (via breach, phishing, or brute force) can disable 2FA and then fully compromise the account, bypassing the very protection 2FA was intended to provide. The design of this disable flow should require the TOTP token (or another form of step-up verification) to confirm that the person disabling 2FA is the legitimate account holder who possesses the second factor.

trace.description: The disable() function is an exported service method. Its caller is outside this file. It receives a single parameter: 'password: string'. No TOTP token, no second-factor verification parameter is accepted.
The request body sent to /rest/2fa/disable is constructed as { password } — only the password. No TOTP token or second-factor credential is included in the payload.

The observable is returned with map and catchError. The initial POST on line 57 carries only the password. The design of this flow allows 2FA to be turned off without proving possession of the second factor. An attacker with a stolen password can disable 2FA and take over the account.

The POST to /rest/2fa/disable carries only the password. The design of this flow allows 2FA to be turned off without proving possession of the second factor. An attacker with a stolen password can disable 2FA and take over the account.

title: 2FA secret and setup token exposed via status endpoint response
description: The TwoFactorAuthStatusPayload interface defines 'secret' and 'setupToken' as fields returned by the status() method, which issues a GET request to /rest/2fa/status. The TOTP shared secret is the seed used to generate one-time passwords — if an attacker can obtain it, they can clone the 2FA factor and generate valid TOTP codes indefinitely, completely bypassing the second factor. Exposing the secret via a status-check endpoint (rather than only during a one-time, authenticated setup flow) increases the window for theft. Additionally, GET responses may be cached by browsers or intermediaries, increasing exposure risk for the secret and setupToken. The setupToken, if it is a bearer token that authorizes 2FA setup, is also sensitive and should not be broadly retrievable.

trace.description: The TwoFactorAuthStatusPayload interface is defined with fields 'secret?: string' (line 24) and 'setupToken?: string' (line 25), indicating the status endpoint returns these sensitive values.

The status() method issues an unauthenticated GET (no body, no TOTP) to /rest/2fa/status and maps the response directly to TwoFactorAuthStatusPayload, which includes the TOTP secret and setup token. An attacker who can invoke this endpoint (e.g., via session hijacking or CSRF on the GET) obtains the 2FA secret and can clone the second factor.

title: 2FA temporary authentication token stored in localStorage, accessible to XSS
description: The verify() method reads 'totp_tmp_token' from localStorage to send as the temporary authentication token for 2FA verification. localStorage is synchronous storage accessible to any JavaScript executing on the same origin. Unlike HttpOnly cookies, which are inaccessible to client-side scripts, data in localStorage can be exfiltrated by any XSS payload. If the application has an XSS vulnerability anywhere on the same origin, an attacker can read localStorage.getItem('totp_tmp_token') and use it to complete the 2FA verification step on behalf of the victim, achieving full authentication bypass. The temporary token serves as a bridge between the first-factor (password) verification and the second-factor (TOTP) verification, so stealing it allows the attacker to skip directly to the TOTP verification step.

trace.description: The verify() function is an exported service method. Its caller is outside this file. It accepts a totpToken parameter from the caller.

The temporary authentication token is retrieved from localStorage via localStorage.getItem('totp_tmp_token'). Because localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript on the page, an XSS attack can exfiltrate this token and use it to complete the 2FA verification flow, bypassing the authentication step it is meant to protect.

title: No security logging for 2FA verification, setup, or disable operations
description: The TwoFactorAuthService handles critical security operations — 2FA verification (verify), 2FA setup (setup), and 2FA disable (disable) — but none of these methods log security-relevant events. Failed 2FA verification attempts, 2FA setup, and especially 2FA disablement are high-sensitivity security events that should be logged for audit and incident response. Without logging these events, an attacker who repeatedly attempts TOTP brute force, who disables 2FA on a compromised account, or who sets up 2FA to lock out the legitimate user, leaves no trace detectable by security monitoring. The catchError handlers on each method (lines 40, 45, 53, 58) silently rethrow errors without any logging, meaning failed verification attempts produce no audit trail on the client side.

Each method includes a catchError handler (lines 40, 45, 53, 58) that rethrows errors without logging. No console.warn, no telemetry, no audit logging is performed for any security event — successful or failed.

The catchError handler rethrows the error without logging.

The catchError handler rethrows the error without logging. Failed 2FA setup attempts are silently passed over.

The disable() method (lines 56-59) performs a security-critical operation — turning off 2FA — with no logging of the event. The absence of logging across all 2FA operations means there is no client-side audit trail for 2FA enablement, disablement, or verification failures, hindering detection and investigation of 2FA-based attacks.

title: Security question retrieval by email is unauthenticated, enabling account enumeration and recovery-question harvesting
description: The SecurityQuestionService.findBy() method retrieves a user's security question using only an email address as a query parameter. The test at line 46 confirms that a GET request to /rest/user/security-question?email=x@y.z returns the security question ({ question: 'apiResponse' }) without any authentication or authorization. This is an account-recovery flow that discloses security questions to any caller who knows (or guesses) an email address. An attacker can enumerate valid accounts (the endpoint returns a question for existing emails) and harvest security questions for targeted social engineering or password-reset bypass. The design has no compensating control: no rate limiting is tested, no authentication is required, and the question itself is returned in full rather than only being verified after the user answers it.

The actual HTTP entrypoint (/rest/user/security-question) and route handler are outside this file; the trace begins at the service method invocation that the test exercises.

The test confirms that findBy constructs a GET request to http://localhost:3000/rest/user/security-question?email=x@y.z — the email is passed as a plain query parameter with no authentication token, session, or credential in the request.

expect(req.request.method).toBe('GET') is the only assertion on the request — it confirms the HTTP method but does not check for any authentication token, session cookie, or authorization header, establishing that no credential is required.

expect(res).toBe('apiResponse') confirms the caller received the security question text. This is the account-recovery decision point (crypto-auth playbook item 10) and a design flaw: the server reveals the security question to any unauthenticated caller who supplies an email, with no rate limiting, no identity verification, and no attempt to verify the answer before disclosing the question.

The mock response confirms the endpoint returns { question: 'apiResponse' } — the actual security question text for the given email. This is an account-recovery decision point (crypto-auth playbook item 10) and a design flaw: the server reveals the security question to any unauthenticated caller who supplies an email, with no rate limiting, no identity verification, and no attempt to verify the answer before disclosing the question.

title: Security question retrieval endpoint has no rate limiting, enabling brute-force account enumeration
description: The test for findBy (lines 41-53) confirms that the /rest/user/security-question?email= endpoint accepts arbitrary email values and returns results without any observable rate limiting. An attacker can script rapid requests with different email addresses to enumerate which accounts exist in the system. This is an authentication-adjacent endpoint (it is part of the account recovery flow), and missing throttling here enables both account enumeration and preparation for security-question-based attacks. The test does not exercise or assert any throttling behavior, and the find(null) test at line 31 also shows an unbounded GET of all security questions with no pagination.

title: Security questions list endpoint returns unbounded result set with no pagination
description: The test for find(null) (lines 26-38) confirms that the /api/SecurityQuestions/ endpoint returns all security questions in a single response with no pagination parameters. The test explicitly passes null as the filter and asserts that the request params are empty (line 36), confirming no limit, offset, or page size is sent. An attacker can issue a single GET request to retrieve the entire security-questions table, which could be large in a production system, consuming server memory and bandwidth. This is a missing pagination finding on a public list endpoint.

title: API error responses logged to browser console exposing potential sensitive error details
description: The AddressComponent logs error responses from API calls directly to the browser console via console.log. The test suite explicitly verifies this behavior for both the address retrieval (get) and address deletion (del) API calls. HTTP error objects can contain sensitive information such as internal URLs, response bodies with stack traces, authentication tokens in headers, or internal system details. Logging these to the browser console exposes them to anyone with access to browser developer tools, including in shared or public computing environments, and provides no filtering or redaction of sensitive fields.

title: Client-controlled address ID stored in sessionStorage without server-side ownership verification visible
description: The AddressComponent.chooseAddress() method stores the currently selected addressId into browser sessionStorage. The test at lines 132-137 confirms this: it sets component.addressId = 1, calls chooseAddress(), and verifies sessionStorage.setItem('addressId', 1) was called. The addressId is a client-side value that can be freely modified by the user (via browser dev tools or DOM manipulation). If the server-side checkout or delivery flow trusts this client-stored addressId without re-verifying that the address belongs to the authenticated user, an attacker could substitute another user's address ID and potentially ship orders to or access another user's saved address. This is a trust-assumption violation: the client determines which address is selected, and the server-side ownership check (if any) is not visible in this file.

title: JWT decoded without signature verification in role-based authorization guards
description: AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, and DeluxeGuard all use `jwtDecode()` from the `jwt-decode` library to extract the user's role from the token stored in localStorage. `jwtDecode` only base64-decodes the payload — it does NOT verify the JWT signature. An attacker can craft an arbitrary JWT (e.g., with `{"data":{"role":"admin"}}` in the payload), store it in localStorage under the `token` key, and pass the AdminGuard check. Since these guards control access to admin and accounting routes, this enables privilege escalation to any role by forging a token. The application never independently verifies the token against a trusted signing key on the client side, and if the server-side enforcement is similarly weak or absent, the forged role would be trusted throughout the session.

The decoded (unverified) payload is checked: if payload.data.role === roles.admin, access is granted (line 55). Because the payload came from an unsigned/unverified decode, an attacker who places a forged JWT with role 'admin' in localStorage passes this check.

title: LoginGuard authorizes access based solely on token existence in localStorage without any validation

This means a user can bypass the login requirement entirely by writing any value to the `token` key in localStorage (e.g., via browser devtools or an XSS payload). This is an authentication bypass because the guard treats token existence as proof of authentication without verifying the token's integrity, signature, or expiration.

title: Authorization decisions rely entirely on client-controlled localStorage with no server-side re-derivation of identity or role
description: All guards in this file (LoginGuard, AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, DeluxeGuard) base their authorization decisions on a JWT stored in localStorage — a value fully controllable by the browser user. The role claim is read directly from the token payload without any server-side re-validation of the user's current role or session validity. A user who was once admin but has been demoted, or whose session has been revoked, would still pass these checks as long as the old token remains in localStorage. The design trusts the client to faithfully represent server-side identity state, which it cannot guarantee.

title: Continue code cookie set without Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite attributes

The options object is verified to contain only an `expires` field — no `secure`, `httpOnly`, or `sameSite` attributes are set or checked, confirming the cookie is stored without security controls for a 1-year period.

title: Security-relevant API and service errors logged to browser console.log instead of a monitoring system
description: The tests at lines 162-175 and 392-399 reveal that the component logs errors from the continue code API call and country mapping service failures directly to `console.log`. The tests mock `console.log = vi.fn()` and then assert `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')` and `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('CountryError')`. This confirms the component's actual behavior is to write errors to the browser console. Browser console logs are ephemeral, cannot be aggregated or alerted on, and are not sent to any backend monitoring system. Security-relevant failures — such as a continue code API failure that could indicate tampering with challenge progress, or a country mapping service failure — are therefore undetectable by operators. There is no structured logging, no correlation ID, and no alerting threshold for these failure events.

trace.description: The test mocks challengeService.continueCode to return throwError('Error'), simulating an API failure received from the external ChallengeService. A second entrypoint is at line 394 where countryMappingService.getCountryMapping returns throwError(() => 'CountryError').
The test replaces console.log with a mock fn, establishing that the component's error handling path uses console.log as its logging sink. The same pattern appears at line 395.

The test calls component.saveProgress(), which subscribes to the continueCode observable. When the observable errors, the component's error handler is triggered, forwarding the error value to console.log.
The test calls fixture.detectChanges() to flush any pending async operations and ensure the error handler has executed before asserting on the mock.

The assertion expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error') confirms the component writes the raw error from the continue code API directly to browser console.log with no structured logging, no severity level, and no transmission to a backend monitoring system. The same pattern is confirmed at line 397 for country mapping errors.

title: Challenge progress state (continueCode) stored in client-controlled cookie without server-side validation
description: The test at lines 145-160 reveals the component's saveProgress() method retrieves a continue code from the ChallengeService and stores it in a browser cookie named 'continueCode' with a 1-year expiration. The continue code represents the user's challenge-solving progress. By persisting this value in a client-side cookie, the application's design permits the client to control its own progress state: a user can read, modify, or forge the cookie value to restore or advance progress without server re-validation. The test shows the cookie value ('12345') is stored verbatim from the API response with no additional integrity protection (no signing, no server-side session binding). This is a trust assumption violation — progress state should be server-derived and server-validated, not accepted from a client-controlled storage mechanism.

trace.description: The test mocks challengeService.continueCode to return of('12345'), simulating the component receiving a continue code from the external ChallengeService API.
The test calls component.saveProgress(), which takes the continue code value and stores it in a client-side cookie. The design delegates progress persistence to client-controlled storage.

The test retrieves the actual call arguments via vi.mocked(cookieService.put).mock.lastCall to inspect the exact value and options that were passed, confirming the raw continue code string was stored without transformation.

The test verifies only callArgs[2].expires.getFullYear(), confirming the options object contains date-related expiry but no integrity protection mechanism. An attacker who reads this cookie can replay or modify it to manipulate their challenge progress state, since the client controls the stored value and there is no evidence of server-side re-validation or cryptographic binding on subsequent reads.

The assertion confirms the continue code '12345' is written to a cookie named 'continueCode' with a 1-year expiration and no integrity protection. An attacker who reads this cookie can replay or modify it to manipulate their challenge progress state, since the client controls the stored value and there is no evidence of server-side re-validation on subsequent reads.

title: Client-side computed order total stored in sessionStorage for later checkout use
description: The getBonusPoints method receives a total array from a child component (PurchaseBasketComponent) and stores the first element as 'itemTotal' in sessionStorage (line 48). This is a client-computed financial value persisted in client-accessible storage. The design delegates the calculation of the order total to the client and stores it in a location an attacker can freely modify (sessionStorage is writable via browser DevTools or script injection). If the server-side checkout flow reads and trusts this 'itemTotal' value instead of re-deriving the order total from server-side cart/price data, an attacker can set an arbitrary low total and complete a purchase for a fraction of the real price. This is a trust assumption violation: the server should decide the price, not accept it from the caller.

trace.description: getBonusPoints(total: [number, number]) receives data from outside this file — the caller is the PurchaseBasketComponent child component (output binding). The 'total' parameter is a client-computed [itemTotal, bonusPoints] tuple.
total[0] is converted to a string and stored in sessionStorage under the key 'itemTotal'. No server-side validation or re-derivation occurs before storage.

sessionStorage.setItem('itemTotal', total[0].toString()) persists a client-controlled financial value in client-accessible storage. An attacker can overwrite this value at any time (e.g., sessionStorage.setItem('itemTotal', '0.01')) before the checkout flow consumes it.

title: Checkout gate relies solely on client-side token existence check without validation
description: The checkout() method (line 31) checks only whether localStorage contains a 'token' key — it verifies neither the token's validity, expiry, nor the user's authorization to proceed. Any arbitrary string placed in localStorage (e.g., via browser DevTools: localStorage.setItem('token', 'fake')) bypasses this gate and navigates the user to the address-selection step of the checkout workflow. This is a client-side access control check that can be trivially defeated. While server-side validation of the token should exist independently, the design of this component treats token existence as equivalent to authentication, establishing an insecure-design pattern. If the corresponding server-side endpoints for the checkout workflow do not independently validate the token, this client-side gate becomes the only barrier, creating a broken function-level access control issue where an unauthenticated user can advance through checkout steps.

trace.description: checkout() is a public method invoked by user interaction (button click in the basket template). It is the entry point for the purchase workflow.

localStorage.getItem('token') == null — the only condition checked is whether a token key exists in localStorage. No validation of token content, signature, expiry, or user authorization is performed.

return — this statement would prevent reaching the checkout navigation, but it only executes inside the if-block (lines 32-38) when the token is null. When a fake token exists, the condition on line 31 is false, this return is skipped entirely, and execution falls through to line 40.

If the token existence check passes (which it does for any non-null string in localStorage), the user is navigated to '/address/select', advancing in the checkout workflow. An attacker who sets localStorage.setItem('token', 'anything') reaches this sink and proceeds to address selection without valid authentication.

title: Passwords transmitted as URL query parameters in GET request for password change
description: The test confirms that UserService.changePassword() sends the current password, new password, and repeat password as URL query parameters in a GET request to /rest/user/change-password. Credentials placed in URLs are exposed to server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and Referer headers. Additionally, using GET for a state-changing security operation (password change) violates HTTP semantics and means the credentials could be cached, bookmarked, or replayed. The test at line 94-96 explicitly verifies this insecure behavior, confirming the service constructs the request this way.

trace.description: The test calls service.changePassword({ current: 'foo', new: 'bar', repeat: 'bar' }) which invokes the UserService.changePassword method (implementation in user.service.ts, outside this file). The test confirms the expected API contract.

The test asserts the HTTP request URL is 'http://localhost:3000/rest/user/change-password?current=foo&new=bar&repeat=bar' — the passwords 'foo' and 'bar' are embedded directly in the query string of the URL.
The mock flushes a generic user response, completing the request-response cycle and forwarding the response to the subscriber.

The test confirms the request method is GET (line 99: expect(req.request.method).toBe('GET')). A GET request carrying passwords in query parameters means the credentials will be logged by any HTTP server, reverse proxy, or CDN in the request path, stored in browser history, and potentially leaked via Referer headers. This is both a cryptographic/auth failure (poor credential handling) and a logging-monitoring failure (passwords written to access logs), and an insecure design (GET for a mutating security operation).

title: OAuth access token transmitted as URL query parameter
description: The test confirms that UserService.oauthLogin() sends the Google OAuth access token as a URL query parameter (access_token=at) when calling the Google userinfo endpoint. OAuth tokens in URLs are exposed to server logs, proxy logs, browser history, and Referer headers. An attacker who obtains the token from logs or Referer leakage can impersonate the user against the OAuth provider.

trace.description: The test calls service.oauthLogin('at') where 'at' represents an OAuth access token. This invokes UserService.oauthLogin (implementation in user.service.ts, outside this file).
The test asserts the HTTP request URL is 'https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v1/userinfo?alt=json&access_token=at' — the OAuth access token is embedded directly in the query string.

The access token is passed in the URL query string rather than in an Authorization header. This exposes the token to logging in proxy/server access logs and potential Referer header leakage. The token grants access to the user's Google account info; compromise of the token from logs enables account impersonation.

title: Endpoint exposing all users' authentication details appears accessible without per-user authorization
description: The test confirms that UserService.find() makes a GET request to /rest/user/authentication-details/ which, based on the endpoint name, returns authentication details for all users. The test does not indicate any authorization scoping — it simply calls find() and expects a response. If this endpoint is reachable by any authenticated user and returns authentication-sensitive data (password hashes, security answers, tokens) for all users rather than just the caller, it represents a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability. The caller is outside this file (UserService.find in user.service.ts); this test confirms the API contract.

trace.description: The test calls service.find() with no parameters — no user ID, no filter, no role specification. This invokes UserService.find() (implementation in user.service.ts, outside this file).

The test asserts the HTTP request is a GET to 'http://localhost:3000/rest/user/authentication-details/' — an endpoint whose name implies it returns authentication details. The test expects params to be empty (line 37: expect(req.request.params.toString()).toBeFalsy()), meaning no filtering or scoping parameters are sent.

The test flushes a generic response and verifies it is returned (line 38). There is no indication of per-resource ownership verification — the endpoint appears to return authentication details for all users to any caller that reaches it. If a standard authenticated user can call this endpoint and receive other users' authentication data, that is a BOLA/access control violation.

title: Checkout proceeds based on token existence in localStorage, not token validity
description: The test suite reveals that BasketComponent.checkout() determines authentication state solely by whether Storage.getItem() returns a non-null value. The test at line 137 mocks getItem to return the arbitrary string 'valid-token' and the test asserts that the user is navigated to '/address/select' (line 140), proceeding with checkout. There is no token validation, signature verification, or server-side session check — any string placed in localStorage by an attacker (e.g., via browser devtools) satisfies the check and grants access to the checkout flow. This is both a broken access control (authentication confused with authorization) and an identification/authentication failure (identity is never verified), and it stems from an insecure design that trusts client-side storage for authentication state.

The test mocks Storage.prototype.getItem to return the arbitrary string 'valid-token'. This simulates any non-null value in localStorage — not a validated or signed token. The component treats this as proof of authentication.
The Router is injected from TestBed. This is the navigation target that the checkout flow will use once the token check passes.
A spy is placed on router.navigate to capture where checkout redirects the user. The spy resolves successfully, simulating that navigation proceeds without error.

Because the mock returns 'valid-token' (a truthy non-null string), the authentication check passes and checkout proceeds to the navigation step. There is no intermediate validation, signature check, or server round-trip — the string 'valid-token' could be any arbitrary string an attacker places in localStorage.

The test asserts navigation to '/address/select', confirming that checkout proceeds when any string is present in storage. An attacker can set localStorage.setItem('token', 'anything') in the browser console to bypass the login gate and reach the checkout/address-selection flow without authenticating.

title: Item total (pricing data) stored in client-side sessionStorage and controlled by the client
description: The test at lines 82-86 reveals that getBonusPoints() writes 'itemTotal' into sessionStorage via Storage.setItem. The value stored is derived from the bonus points array passed to the component (the first element, '1' in the test). SessionStorage is fully client-controlled — an attacker can modify or set itemTotal to any value before checkout. If the server later reads or trusts this client-stored total (e.g., during order confirmation or payment), the attacker can manipulate the price. Even if the server recalculates, storing pricing data in client-side storage is an insecure design that creates a trust boundary violation: the client should never own authoritative pricing state.

A spy is placed on Storage.prototype.setItem to capture what the component writes to sessionStorage. This spy will intercept the call that persists the itemTotal value.

It extracts the first element (1) as the itemTotal and calls Storage.setItem('itemTotal', '1'). The value originates from a client-supplied array and is written directly to client-controlled storage with no server-side derivation or validation.

The test asserts that setItem was called with ('itemTotal', '1'), confirming that a pricing-related value derived from client-received bonus points is persisted in client-controlled sessionStorage. An attacker can overwrite this value at any time via the browser console or DOM storage APIs.

title: Continue code cookie set without secure or sameSite attributes
description: The component stores the user's progress continue code in a browser cookie via `cookieService.put()`. The options object passed includes only an `expires` date and omits `secure: true` and `sameSite` directives. Without `secure`, the cookie can be transmitted over plaintext HTTP connections, exposing the continue code to network eavesdropping. Without `sameSite`, the cookie is vulnerable to cross-site request inclusion. The continue code represents the user's challenge-solving progress and could be used to impersonate or share progress.

trace.description: saveProgress() calls challengeService.continueCode() to obtain a continue code from the server.
The continue code is stored in a cookie with options object { expires }, which sets the expiry but omits security-relevant flags.
The subscribe callback's next handler receives continueCode as its parameter.
A falsy check on continueCode: if (!continueCode) throws an error. If truthy, execution continues.
The throw path for invalid continue codes — execution only reaches the cookie write when this guard is passed.

expires.setFullYear(expires.getFullYear() + 1) — the expiry is set to one year in the future.

cookieService.put('continueCode', continueCode, { expires }) — the cookie is set without `secure: true` or `sameSite: 'strict'|'lax'`, allowing transmission over insecure channels and cross-site inclusion.

title: Unsanitized socket event data flows into notification message text
description: Data received from a socket.io 'challenge solved' event includes a `challenge` name field that is interpolated into a translated message string and pushed into the notifications array without any sanitization or encoding. If the HTML template (outside this file) renders this message via `[innerHTML]` binding or similar unescaped output, an attacker who can control the challenge name — by injecting it server-side or via a compromised socket connection — can achieve stored XSS. The persistence point is in this file; the render sink is in the template which is not visible here.

The render sink is outside this file.

title: Challenge progress state stored in client-accessible cookie enables progress sharing and manipulation
description: The saveProgress() method retrieves a continue code from the server and stores it in a client-side cookie. This design allows any user to read the continue code from the cookie, share it with others, or submit a modified/forged continue code to restore an arbitrary progress state. The continue code is the sole mechanism for tracking which challenges a user has solved, and storing it in a client-readable and client-writable location means the server cannot trust the progress state. An attacker can copy a continue code from one account to another to inherit all solved challenges, or craft a modified code to unlock progress they did not earn.

saveProgress() requests a continue code from the server via challengeService.continueCode().
