The continue code is stored in a browser cookie (cookieService.put('continueCode', ...)). The cookie is client-readable and client-writable. The design trusts the client to hold and re-submit progress state, meaning progress can be shared, copied between accounts, or forged. The server must re-validate the continue code on use, but the design places trust in client-held state.

title: Chat message content passed via URL query parameter causes plaintext logging in access logs and browser history
description: The onMessageSent method places the user's initial chat message into a URL query parameter (initialMessage) when navigating to the conversation route. URL query parameters are routinely recorded in plaintext by web server access logs (nginx, Apache, cloud load balancers), stored in browser history, and can leak via Referer headers to third-party resources. Chat messages can contain sensitive information (PII, credentials, personal disclosures). The design choice to route message content through the URL rather than through a POST body or a client-side state mechanism directly causes user communications to be written to access logs in plaintext. This is a design flaw because the data flow—message to URL to navigation—works exactly as designed, and that design inherently exposes the message to logging systems.

trace.description: onMessageSent receives the user's chat message as the 'message' parameter from an external caller (the ChatWelcomeScreenComponent's messageSent event, which is outside this file).

The message is placed directly into queryParams as { initialMessage: message } and passed to router.navigate. This embeds the full plaintext message into the URL of the conversation route, making it part of the URL that the browser requests from the server.

The URL containing the plaintext message is navigated to. Standard web infrastructure (reverse proxies, load balancers, web servers) logs full URLs including query strings by default. The message content will appear in plaintext in access logs, browser history, and any analytics/monitoring pipeline that captures URLs. This is both an insecure design flaw (the data flow is designed to put messages in URLs) and a logging-monitoring failure (sensitive user communications are written to access logs in plaintext).

title: Conversation ID accepted from client without validation before navigation
description: The onConversationSelected method accepts a conversation ID string from the welcome screen's conversationSelected event and navigates directly to the conversation route without any validation. While client-side access control is inherently limited, the complete absence of any format validation, ownership check, or sanitization on the ID before it is used in navigation means the component trusts whatever value the caller provides. If the server-side route handler does not independently verify that the requesting user owns or has access to the conversation identified by this ID, this design permits IDOR — an attacker could enumerate or guess conversation IDs to access other users' chat histories. The design flaw is that the component treats an externally-supplied identifier as trusted without establishing any constraint on its provenance or format.

trace.description: onConversationSelected receives an 'id' string from an external caller (the ChatWelcomeScreenComponent's conversationSelected event, which is outside this file). The origin and validation of this ID is not controlled by this component.

The received id is passed directly to router.navigate as a route parameter without any validation, format checking, or ownership verification. There is no guard that the ID matches an expected format or that the current user is authorized to access the conversation it references.

The unvalidated ID is used to navigate to '/chatbot/conversation/<id>'. If the server-side handler for this route does not enforce authorization, an attacker who controls the conversationSelected event (or manipulates the welcome screen's conversation list) can navigate to arbitrary conversation IDs, potentially accessing other users' conversations.

title: Client-side price and quantity clamping can be bypassed; server trusts client-determined values
description: The accounting component allows modification of product price and quantity from client-side input fields. The component performs client-side clamping of negative values to zero (tested at lines 253-261), but this control exists only in the browser. The actual values sent to the API (via productService.put and quantityService.put) are entirely client-determined, as shown by tests that pass arbitrary values like 100 directly. An attacker can bypass the client-side clamping by calling the underlying service methods directly or by intercepting the HTTP request, sending negative prices or arbitrary quantities. The design relies on the client to enforce value constraints rather than validating on the server, which is a trust-boundary violation: price and quantity are economic values that the server should independently derive or validate.

Test confirms modifyQuantity(1, -10) clamps negative quantity to 0 — again, client-side only.
Assertion confirms productService.put was called with (1, { price: 0 }) — the clamped value is what gets sent to the API, but the clamping decision was made entirely on the client.
Assertion confirms quantityService.put was called with (1, { quantity: 0 }) — again the clamped value sent to the API, but the control lives only in the browser.
Price and quantity inputs are selected from the DOM as HTMLInputElement nodes — the values are raw DOM strings, not validated numbers.
Price input value is read as the string '1.99' from the DOM. No type coercion or validation is performed before passing it onward.
Buttons are selected from the DOM; clicking them will trigger the modify handlers with whatever values the inputs currently hold.

Test 'should modify price of a product' confirms productService.put is called with client-determined values (e.g., price 100) with no server-side validation visible. The same pattern holds for quantityService.put at line 200. The server accepts whatever price/quantity the client sends, making the client-side clamping the sole control — a control that can be trivially bypassed.

title: API error objects logged directly to browser console without sanitization or structured logging
description: The accounting component logs full API error objects to the browser console via console.log instead of routing them through a structured logging service. Multiple tests confirm this behavior: product search errors, order history errors, quantity errors, delivery status toggle errors, and price/quantity modification errors all flow to console.log with the raw error object. This exposes internal error details (including server error structures) in the browser console, where they can be read by anyone with devtools access. More critically, the absence of any structured client-side logging service means security-relevant events — failed data modifications, delivery status changes, API errors — are not captured in a centralized, queryable log. There is no correlation ID or request tracing, making it impossible to reconstruct an attack timeline from client-side logs.

title: Chat input has no length or content bounds — unbounded user message emission
description: The ChatInputBoxComponent is the entry point for user-supplied chat messages in the chatbot interface. The send() method trims the message and checks only for emptiness and a client-side disabled flag, but the design never establishes any bound on message length or content. An attacker can submit arbitrarily large messages through this component. If the server-side handler does not independently enforce length limits (which cannot be confirmed from this file), this permits resource exhaustion attacks — flooding the chatbot backend with very large payloads that consume memory, storage, or processing time. The design flaw is that the component responsible for receiving user text input establishes no constraints on the quantity of data it accepts and forwards.

trace.description: The 'message' model (line 28) is bound to a textarea in the template and receives arbitrary user input. The caller is outside this file — the user types into the textarea element referenced at line 31.
In send(), the message is retrieved via this.message() and trimmed, but no length validation, rate limiting, or content filtering is applied. The only guard is an emptiness check (line 47).
The only guard check (!content || this.disabled()) permits the message to continue as long as it is non-empty and the component is not disabled. No upper bound on message size is enforced here.

The unbounded content is emitted via this.messageSent.emit(content), forwarding it to the parent component and ultimately to the chatbot backend with no established design limit on message size or frequency.

title: Rate limiting on chat message submission relies solely on a client-side disabled flag
description: The only mechanism preventing rapid or repeated message submission is the 'disabled' input property (line 29), which is set by the parent component. The send() method checks this flag at line 47, but this is a client-side control that can be bypassed by manipulating the Angular model or DOM directly. An attacker can call send() repeatedly regardless of the disabled state by modifying the model value, enabling message flooding through the chatbot interface. The design establishes no server-side or independent rate-limiting mechanism — it trusts the client-side disabled flag as the sole guard against message flooding.

send() checks only two conditions: content is non-empty and disabled() is false. The disabled flag (line 29) is a client-side input property that an attacker can override by manipulating the Angular component state.
The event is cast to KeyboardEvent as 'keyEvent', preserving all attacker-controlled properties of the original event.
The shiftKey property is checked. If false (normal Enter press), execution continues to line 40-41. This is the only branching logic before send() is invoked.
event.preventDefault() is called, but this only suppresses default browser behavior (e.g., newline insertion); it does not impose any rate limit on send() invocations.

title: No security logging of chatbot message submissions
description: The ChatInputBoxComponent handles the submission of user messages to the chatbot but performs no logging of message-sent events. Chatbot inputs are security-relevant because they are a channel for injecting malicious payloads (XSS, prompt injection, command injection) into the application. Without logging at the point of message emission, there is no client-side audit trail for reconstructing what a user submitted through the chatbot. While server-side logging may exist outside this file, the component that is the direct entry point for user chat input records nothing about what was sent, when, or by whom.

The message content is retrieved and trimmed. This is the point at which the final user-submitted text is materialized into the 'content' variable — a security-relevant value that should be logged.
The guard check passes the content through to emission if it is non-empty and the component is not disabled. No logging of the accepted message occurs at this decision point.

title: LoginGuard authenticates based on token presence, not validity — any string in localStorage grants access
description: The test at line 32 sets localStorage 'token' to 'TOKEN' — a plain string that is not a JWT — and asserts that LoginGuard.canActivate() returns true (line 33). Conversely, removing the token (line 39) causes canActivate to return false (line 40). This demonstrates that the LoginGuard only checks for the existence of a token in localStorage, not whether the token is a valid, signed, non-expired JWT. An attacker can bypass authentication entirely by setting localStorage.setItem('token', 'anything') in the browser console. This is an authentication bypass: the application treats token presence as proof of identity without any cryptographic or structural validation of the token itself. The consequence is that any route protected only by LoginGuard is accessible to unauthenticated users who can set an arbitrary localStorage value.

title: Role-based access control trusts unverified JWT role claims — attacker can forge admin/accounting/deluxe roles
description: The AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, and DeluxeGuard all derive the user's role from tokenDecode() — which decodes the JWT payload (lines 43-51) without signature verification (the test names say 'decoding', and the invalid-JWT test at line 57 only checks for malformed format returning null, not signature failures). The guards then grant or deny access based on the role claim in that decoded payload (e.g., AdminGuard checks for role: 'admin' at line 100, AccountingGuard checks for role: 'accounting' at line 160, DeluxeGuard checks for role: 'deluxe' at line 219). Since the JWT is never signature-verified, an attacker can craft an unsigned or self-signed JWT with { data: { role: 'admin' } } in the payload, store it in localStorage, and gain admin access to all admin-gated routes. This is both a broken function-level authorization (access-control) and a cryptographic failure (no signature verification, crypto-auth).

title: All access control enforcement is client-side only — guards can be bypassed by manipulating localStorage
description: All four guards (LoginGuard, AdminGuard, AccountingGuard, DeluxeGuard) are Angular route guards that run entirely in the browser. They read tokens and role claims from localStorage (line 32) and from client-decoded JWT payloads (lines 100, 160, 219). localStorage is fully under the user's control — it can be modified via the browser console or developer tools at any time. The entire authorization model depends on the client honestly reporting its own identity and role. This is an insecure design: the server delegates identity and authorization decisions to the client, which is the trusted-boundary violation. Even if the JWT were signature-verified, the client-side guard can be bypassed by directly navigating to routes or intercepting the router. The correct design is server-side authorization checks on every API request.

title: Challenge verdict accepted from caller without server-side proof of solution; errors only console-logged
description: The handleVerdict function receives a `verdict` boolean from its caller (outside this file) and, when it is true, requests a continue code from the server via `continueCodeFindIt()` or `continueCodeFixIt()`. Critically, these methods are called with NO arguments — no solution token, no proof-of-work, no challenge answer is sent to the server. The server is expected to issue a continue code purely based on the fact that the client called the endpoint, with the client's own `verdict` being the only gate. An attacker who calls handleVerdict with `verdict: true` (or directly hits the continue-code endpoint) receives the continue code without solving the challenge, bypassing the entire challenge workflow. This is a trust assumption violation: the client controls the completion status. Additionally, when the server call errors, the error is only written to `console.log` (line 37) — there is no security-relevant logging of challenge completion or failure events, making it impossible to detect or investigate abuse of this flow from server-side logs.

If the continue code is falsy, an error is thrown. If it is present, the flow proceeds to store it — the attacker has obtained the continue code.

The continue code is stored in a cookie, completing the bypass. An attacker who called this flow with verdict=true (or hit the endpoint directly) now has a valid continue code without solving the challenge.

On error, the handler only calls `console.log(err)`. There is no security-relevant logging of the challenge-completion event, failed attempts, or server communication failures. This makes detection of challenge-bypass abuse impossible from application logs.

title: Continue code stored in cookie without secure or sameSite flags

The continue code represents challenge progress and potentially game-state integrity. Without the `secure` flag, the token can be intercepted over HTTP. Without `sameSite`, the cookie is sent on cross-origin requests, widening the attack surface.

title: Client-side fetch of arbitrary configurable notification URL without validation
description: The component retrieves a notification URL from application configuration (line 31) and immediately uses it to fetch data (line 39) with no validation of the URL scheme, host, or origin. If an attacker can influence the configuration (the configuration source is outside this file), they can redirect all clients to fetch from an attacker-controlled or internal URL. This enables data exfiltration (the notification service receives each user's IP and can serve malicious content), SSRF from user browsers to internal endpoints, and the display of untrusted content as system-wide notifications. The design flaw is that the server should proxy or validate the notification endpoint rather than broadcasting an arbitrary URL to clients.

title: Address fetched by ID from client-controlled sessionStorage without visible ownership verification
description: On line 48, the component reads 'addressId' from sessionStorage and passes it directly to addressService.getById(). sessionStorage is fully client-controllable — a user can write any value into it. If the backend getAddressById endpoint does not verify that the address belongs to the currently authenticated user, this is a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) pattern: User A can set sessionStorage.addressId to User B's address ID and retrieve another user's address data. The component itself performs no ownership check before the lookup; it trusts the client-supplied identifier entirely.

next: (address) => { — the subscription's success callback receives the fetched address object. If the backend did not enforce ownership, this is another user's address data.

this.address = address — the fetched address (potentially belonging to another user) is stored on the component instance, making it available to the template for rendering. A user can substitute another user's addressId in sessionStorage to retrieve and view that address.

addressService.getById(sessionStorage.getItem('addressId')) performs a resource lookup using the client-controlled address ID. No per-resource ownership check is visible in this component between reading the ID and fetching the resource. A user can substitute another user's addressId in sessionStorage to retrieve that address.

title: Security-relevant password change failures logged via console.log instead of proper security logging
description: The spec confirms that when a password change operation fails, the production component logs the error to the browser console via console.log rather than using a structured security logging mechanism. Failed password changes are security-relevant events (potential brute-force attempts, credential stuffing) that must be captured through centralized, server-side security logging with proper correlation and alerting. Using console.log means: (1) events are only visible in the client browser, not to security monitoring; (2) error details may be exposed in the browser console where they can be inspected; (3) no audit trail exists for investigating password-change-related attacks. The spec at line 111 mocks console.log and at line 118 asserts it was called with the raw error value, actively enforcing and documenting this insecure logging behavior.

trace.description: Test 'should clear form and gracefully handle error on password change' begins by configuring the mock UserService to return an error on password change, simulating a failed password change operation — a security-relevant event.

The test replaces console.log with a vi.fn() mock, confirming that the production component under test calls console.log during error handling. This establishes that the component's error path routes through console.log.
userService.changePassword.mockReturnValue(throwError('Error')) — the mock is configured to throw the error value 'Error'. This is the origin of the error value that will flow to console.log.
vi.spyOn(component, 'resetPasswords') — spy is set up on the component's resetPasswords method, confirming the test expects the error path to call resetPasswords as part of its handling.
component.passwordControl.setValue('old') — the current password form field is populated, enabling the changePassword() call to proceed past form validation.
component.newPasswordControl.setValue('foobar') — the new password form field is populated, further satisfying the form's required-field validation so changePassword() can execute.

component.repeatNewPasswordControl.setValue('fooabar') — the repeat password field is set (note: deliberately mismatched with the new password), completing the form inputs that trigger the changePassword() call.

component.changePassword() — this call triggers the component's internal flow: it calls userService.changePassword(), which throws 'Error', and the component's catch handler routes that error to console.log. This is the propagation point where the error value flows from the service into the logging sink.

expect(component.error).toBe('Error') — assertion confirms the raw error value 'Error' was assigned to component.error, showing the error value propagated untransformed through the component's error handler.

The test asserts expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error'), confirming that the raw error from a failed password change is written to the browser console. This is the security sink: a security-relevant event (failed password change) is logged via console.log with the raw error value, providing no server-side audit trail, no alerting capability, and no incident investigation support.

title: Password policy relies solely on length validation (5-40 chars) with no complexity requirements
description: The spec tests for the new password control reveal that the only validation enforced on new passwords is length (5-40 characters). There are no tests for — and by the spec's own assertions, no requirements for — character complexity, mixed case, digits, special characters, or checks against common/breached passwords. The design never establishes a password complexity rule. This permits users to set trivially weak passwords like 'aaaaa' or '12345', undermining the security purpose of the password change workflow. The test at line 64 confirms 'new password' (all lowercase, no digits, no special chars) is accepted as valid, and line 66 confirms an even longer all-lowercase-no-complexity string is also valid.

trace.description: The test 'length of new password must be 5-40 characters' is the entry point — it defines and enforces the expectation that the new password control's only validation is length-based. The caller (the component's form initialization) is outside this file, but the spec confirms what validation rules exist.

The test sets component.newPasswordControl.setValue('new password') and asserts it is valid (line 65). This password has no uppercase, no digits, no special characters, and no complexity — yet the validation accepts it. The design establishes no complexity rule, so an attacker who gains access to the change-password flow can set a trivially guessable new password.

title: Privileged account password policy is advisory-only and does not block weak passwords
description: The changePassword() method includes a check (lines 78-86) that detects when a privileged support account is setting a new password that does not meet the corporate policy for privileged accounts (12-30 chars with upper, lower, digit, and special). However, this check only emits a console.error and does NOT prevent the password change from proceeding. The call to userService.changePassword() on line 87 executes unconditionally, regardless of whether the policy check passed or failed. This is a design flaw: a security-critical control (enforcing strong passwords for privileged accounts) is implemented as a non-blocking advisory rather than an enforcement gate. An attacker who has access to a support account can set a weak password that violates the corporate policy, and the application will accept it. Additionally, the privileged-account determination itself relies on localStorage.getItem('email') (line 78), which is client-controlled storage — an attacker can tamper with localStorage to change the email value and skip even the advisory warning.

trace.description: changePassword() is the public method invoked when the user submits the password change form. The caller (template/button handler) is outside this file.

The method reads the user's email from localStorage and checks whether it matches a privileged support account pattern (/support@.*/), then checks whether the new password meets the privileged-account policy regex. Both the email source (client-controlled localStorage) and the policy check are client-side only.

Regardless of whether the privileged-account policy check on lines 78-86 passed or failed, this.userService.changePassword() is called with the new password. The console.error on line 83 is the only consequence of a policy violation — no return, no exception, no flag is set to prevent the change. The design permits a privileged account to set a policy-violating password.

title: Privileged account password policy violation logged only to browser console — no server-side security event
description: When a privileged support account attempts to set a password that violates the corporate policy for privileged accounts (lines 78-86), the only logging is a console.error on lines 83-85. The browser console is not a security monitoring channel: it is visible to the end user, not collected by any SIEM or monitoring system, and cannot be used to detect or respond to security incidents. A security-relevant event — a privileged account setting a weak password — produces no server-side audit log, no alert, and no monitoring trail. Additionally, line 107 logs the raw error object from a failed password change attempt via console.log(error), which may expose internal error details or sensitive response data in the browser console.

The method determines whether the current user is a privileged support account and whether the new password violates the privileged-account password policy.
The if condition begins, evaluating whether the current user is privileged and whether the new password violates policy.
this.newPasswordControl.value is matched against the privileged-account password policy regex. A match failure here means the password violates the policy.

The policy violation is logged only via console.error() to the browser console. No server-side security event, audit log entry, or alert is generated. This security-relevant event (privileged account setting a weak password) is invisible to any security monitoring infrastructure. Separately, line 107 uses console.log(error) to dump the raw error from a failed password change, potentially exposing internal error details.

title: Client-side trust assumption: privileged account identity derived from tamperable localStorage
description: On line 78, the application determines whether the current user is a privileged support account by reading localStorage.getItem('email') and matching it against the pattern /support@.*/. localStorage is fully client-controlled storage — an attacker can modify it at will using browser developer tools or script injection. This means the privileged-account check is trivially bypassable: an attacker can change the stored email to a non-support value to skip the advisory policy check entirely, or conversely, the check provides no reliable server-side guarantee about who the user actually is. Trusting client-side storage to determine account privilege level is a design flaw — the server should make this determination based on the authenticated session, not on a client-supplied and client-modifiable value.

trace.description: localStorage.getItem('email') reads the user's email from client-controlled browser storage. This value was set elsewhere (outside this file) and is freely modifiable by the user via developer tools or script.
The if condition closes. The decision of whether to apply the privileged-account policy has been made entirely based on the client-controlled email value.
The only consequence when the policy check does fire is console.error — an advisory message with no enforcement. When the check is bypassed via localStorage tampering, even this advisory is skipped.

this.userService.changePassword() is called regardless. The server receives no indication of the client-side privilege determination and presumably has no equivalent enforcement (given that the check here is only advisory). The client-controlled identity check provides no real security boundary.

The client-controlled email value is matched against /support@.*/ to determine whether the privileged-account password policy should apply. Since the source is client-controlled, this determination can be bypassed by tampering with localStorage. The server receives no indication of this client-side check and presumably has no equivalent enforcement (given that the check here is only advisory per finding 1).

title: Raw error object from failed password change logged to browser console, potentially exposing sensitive internals
description: On line 107, the error handler for a failed password change attempt calls console.log(error), dumping the raw error object to the browser console. This error object originates from the server's response to the password change request and may contain sensitive internal details such as stack traces, database error messages, authentication internals, or other information that should not be exposed to the end user. Additionally, this is a security-relevant event (failed password change, which could indicate an account takeover attempt) that is logged only to the browser console rather than to any server-side monitoring system, making it invisible to security operations.

this.userService.changePassword() initiates the password change request to the server, returning an observable.
.subscribe() registers both a 'next' handler (line 94) and an 'error' handler (line 106) for the observable returned by the service call.

The error handler receives the raw error object from the failed password change HTTP response. This object may contain server-side error details, stack traces, or other sensitive internal information.

console.log(error) dumps the raw error object to the browser console. This may expose sensitive internal details to the end user and does not generate any server-side security log or alert for the failed password change event.

title: Sensitive routes missing authentication guards — change-password, data-export, 2FA, wallet, order-history, payment, and last-login-ip are reachable without any client-side auth check
description: The routing configuration applies LoginGuard to address routes (lines 94, 99, 104) and AdminGuard/AccountingGuard to admin/accounting routes (lines 80, 85), but fails to guard numerous sensitive routes. The entire `privacy-security` subtree (lines 204-228) — which contains `change-password` (line 212), `two-factor-authentication` (line 216), `data-export` (line 220), and `last-login-ip` (line 224) — has no canActivate guard on the parent or any child. Similarly, `wallet` (line 157), `order-history` (line 149), `order-summary` (line 145), `payment/:entity` (line 153), and `saved-payment-methods` (line 121) are unguarded. While client-side guards are not the sole security boundary (server-side enforcement is needed), the inconsistency shows that the developer intended to protect some routes but missed these. If the backend does not independently enforce authentication for each corresponding API call, an unauthenticated user can directly load these components and interact with sensitive functionality. The `privacy-security/change-password` route being unguarded is particularly dangerous — a user could navigate to the password change UI without any authentication context, and if the component trusts the session without re-verifying, the password could be changed.

The caller (Angular router) is outside this file; this file is the authoritative source for which guards apply to which routes.
The `administration` route applies `canActivate: [AdminGuard]` — establishing the pattern that sensitive routes are expected to have guards.
The `address/select` route applies `canActivate: [LoginGuard]` — establishing that user-facing sensitive routes are expected to require authentication.
The `deluxe-membership` route applies `canActivate: [LoginGuard]` — another user route correctly guarded, reinforcing that the absence of guards on similar routes is an omission, not a design choice.
The `saved-payment-methods` route (lines 120-123) has no `canActivate` property. Payment method data is sensitive; the guard is absent.
The `order-summary` route (lines 144-147) has no `canActivate` property. Order data is user-specific and sensitive.
The `order-history` route (lines 148-151) has no `canActivate` property. Order history exposes purchase records and PII.
The `payment/:entity` route (lines 152-155) has no `canActivate` property. This route handles payment processing and accepts a dynamic `:entity` parameter.
The `change-password` child route (lines 211-214) has no `canActivate` property. This is a password-change UI reachable without any authentication gate.
The `two-factor-authentication` child route (lines 215-218) has no `canActivate` property. MFA configuration UI is reachable without authentication.
The `data-export` child route (lines 219-222) has no `canActivate` property. Data export exposes all user-held PII.
The `last-login-ip` child route (lines 223-226) has no `canActivate` property. Last login IP is security-relevant metadata.

All routes are registered via `RouterModule.forRoot(routes, { useHash: true })`. Every unguarded route in the array — including change-password, data-export, 2FA, wallet, order-history, payment, saved-payment-methods, and last-login-ip — is now live. An unauthenticated user navigates directly to e.g. `/#/privacy-security/change-password` or `/#/wallet` and the component renders without any authentication gate.

Additional sensitive routes lack guards: `wallet` (line 157), `order-history` (line 149), `order-summary` (line 145), `payment/:entity` (line 153), `saved-payment-methods` (line 121). Compare with `address/select` (line 94) which correctly uses `canActivate: [LoginGuard]`. The inconsistency demonstrates these omissions are defects, not intentional public routes. An unauthenticated user navigates directly to e.g. `/#/privacy-security/change-password` or `/#/wallet` and the component renders without any authentication gate.

title: OAuth access token extracted from URL fragment and passed as route data
description: On line 255, the OAuth route configuration extracts the raw URL fragment (containing `#access_token=...`) from `window.location.href` and passes it as route `data`. This implements the OAuth implicit grant flow where the access token is placed in the URL fragment. Access tokens in URLs are a known weakness: they can be leaked via browser history, HTTP Referer headers when the page loads external resources, proxy logs, and browser extensions. The token is not validated, sanitized, or immediately exchanged — it is stored in the Angular route data object, making it accessible to any component or service that reads route data. Additionally, the `oauthMatcher` (line 278) checks `window.location.href` for `#access_token=` to decide whether to route to the OAuth component, meaning the mere presence of a token in the URL triggers the component. There is no verification that the token came from a legitimate OAuth provider — an attacker could craft a URL with a malicious token to influence the OAuth component's behavior.

trace.description: The OAuth route's `data` property extracts the URL fragment via `(window.location.href).substr(window.location.href.indexOf('#'))`. The URL (and its fragment) comes from the browser's address bar, which is attacker-influenceable. The full fragment — including the access token — is stored as route data.
The route declares `matcher: oauthMatcher`, meaning the Angular router will call the custom `oauthMatcher` function to determine whether this route should activate for the current URL.
`component: OAuthComponent` — the OAuthComponent is the component that will render. It receives the route data containing the raw, unvalidated access token extracted from the URL fragment.
The `oauthMatcher` function is defined. It receives `url: UrlSegment[]` from the Angular router (caller outside this file).

Inside `oauthMatcher`, `const path = window.location.href` reads the full browser URL directly, bypassing Angular's URL segment abstraction. This is the same `window.location.href` value that line 255 reads for the `data` property.

`if (path.includes('#access_token='))` checks for the literal substring `#access_token=` in the URL. There is no validation of the token issuer, no state parameter check, no PKCE verification — any URL containing this substring triggers the route.

`return ({ consumed: url })` — when the substring is found, the matcher returns a match result, causing the Angular router to activate this route. The route's `data` property (line 255) is then evaluated, passing the raw fragment (including the token) into the route data object.

The routes are registered via `RouterModule.forRoot(routes, { useHash: true })`. The `useHash: true` configuration means all routing uses URL fragments, so the OAuth token sits alongside routing fragments in the same URL. The OAuthComponent (line 256) receives the raw token data with no signature verification, no origin validation, and no sanitization — any value placed in the fragment is accepted.

title: Hidden TokenSale route protected only by obfuscated string matching — security through obscurity
description: The `tokenMatcher` function (lines 290-300) gates access to the TokenSaleComponent using a path that must match a string constructed by two obfuscation functions (`token1` and `token2`, lines 302-316). These functions perform arithmetic on numeric arrays to derive character codes, producing a hidden string that the URL path must match. This is security through obscurity: the 'protection' for the token sale page is that its path is hard to guess, not that access is authorized. The obfuscation is trivially reversible by anyone who reads the source (which is shipped to the client in an Angular application), and the functions `token1` and `token2` are even exported, making them easy to call from the browser console to reconstruct the hidden path. There is no authentication or authorization check — the only barrier is knowing the obfuscated string.

trace.description: The `tokenMatcher` function is the gatekeeper for the TokenSaleComponent route (line 260). It receives URL segments from the Angular router (caller outside this file). The matcher checks whether the path matches a string built by `token1(25, 184, 174, 179, 182, 186)` concatenated with `(36669).toString(36).toLowerCase()` concatenated with `token2(13, 144, 87, 152, 139, 144, 83, 138)` concatenated with `(10).toString(36).toLowerCase()`.
The route object declares `matcher: tokenMatcher`, linking the matcher function to this route entry in the routes array.
`component: TokenSaleComponent` — the TokenSaleComponent renders when the matcher succeeds. There is no `canActivate` guard on this route object.

`RouterModule.forRoot(routes, { useHash: true })` registers all routes including the token-sale route. The route is now live, protected only by the obscurity of the obfuscated path string. Any user who reads this client-side source code — which is shipped to the browser in an Angular application — can call the exported `token1` and `token2` functions to reconstruct the hidden path and navigate directly to the TokenSaleComponent.
`if (url.length === 0)` checks for an empty URL segment array. If empty, the function returns `null` (no match). This is the only validation before the path is checked.
`const path = url[0].toString()` extracts the first URL segment as a string. This is the user-controlled path value that will be matched against the obfuscated string.

`return ({ consumed: url })` — when the obfuscated string matches, the matcher returns a match result. The Angular router activates the route. No authentication or authorization is checked at any point in this path.

`token1` function is defined and exported. It is called on line 296 with arguments `(25, 184, 174, 179, 182, 186)` to produce the first segment of the hidden path. Because it is exported, any user can call it from the browser console.

Inside `token1`, `L.reverse().map(function (C, A) { return String.fromCharCode(C - D - 45 - A) }).join('')` performs simple arithmetic subtraction on the numeric arguments to derive ASCII character codes. This is trivially reversible: an attacker reads the source, calls `token1(25, 184, 174, 179, 182, 186)` in the console, and obtains the first segment of the hidden path.

`token2` function is defined and exported. It is called on line 296 with arguments `(13, 144, 87, 152, 139, 144, 83, 138)` to produce the third segment of the hidden path. Also exported, so callable from the console.
Inside `token2`, `T.reverse().map(function (m, H) { return String.fromCharCode(m - M - 24 - H) }).join('')` performs the same style of arithmetic obfuscation as `token1`, equally trivial to reverse.

If the obfuscated path matches, the route returns `{ consumed: url }` and the TokenSaleComponent renders (line 261). There is no `canActivate` guard, no role check, no authentication verification. The only access control is the obscurity of the constructed string. Since this code ships to the client, any user can open browser dev tools, call `token1(25, 184, 174, 179, 182, 186)` and `token2(13, 144, 87, 152, 139, 144, 83, 138)` directly, and discover the hidden path.

title: Prompt injection via initialMessage query parameter sent directly to LLM
description: The component reads an `initialMessage` value from the URL query parameters and passes it directly to `sendMessage()`, which sends it to the LLM as a user message without any sanitization, fencing, or separation from system instructions. An attacker can craft a URL (e.g., `/chat/<id>?initialMessage=<prompt injection payload>`) and deliver it to a victim. When the victim opens the link, the injected content is automatically submitted to the LLM as the user's first message. This enables the attacker to control the victim's LLM session — causing the model to reveal sensitive information, perform unintended tool calls, or produce manipulated output — all within the victim's authenticated context.

The raw `initialMessage` string is passed directly to `void this.sendMessage(initialMessage)` with no validation, sanitization, or fencing applied.
Inside `sendMessage`, the content is added to the messages array as a user-role message: `this.messages.update(prev => [...prev, { role: 'user', content }])`.
Conditional check `if (initialMessage)` — lets the value continue if it is truthy.
The `sendMessage` method receives the value as its `content` parameter.
Guard `if (!content || this.isLoading()) return` — checks only for empty content or concurrent loading; does not validate or sanitize the content.
The messages array is read into `apiMessages`: `const apiMessages = this.messages()`.
The array is sliced to exclude the last (empty assistant placeholder) message: `.slice(0, -1)`.
Error messages are filtered out: `.filter(m => !m.error)`. The injected user message passes this filter.
Messages are mapped to API format: `.map(m => ({ role: m.role, content: m.content }))`. The injected content is copied verbatim into the `content` field.

The messages (including the injected `initialMessage`) are sent to the LLM via `this.chatService.streamMessages(apiMessages)`. No prompt fencing, instruction separation, or content validation is applied between the URL query param and the LLM call. The attacker's injected content is interpreted as a user instruction by the model, enabling prompt injection attacks against the victim's session.

title: LLM-generated content persisted without sanitization enables stored XSS
description: The component accumulates LLM response content from stream chunks into message objects and persists them to conversation storage without any HTML sanitization or output encoding. Since the LLM's output is influenced by user input (including the prompt-injection vector above), an attacker can cause the LLM to emit HTML/script markup. This content is stored via `conversationStorage.save()` and will be rendered when the conversation is reloaded (line 72-74 sets messages from storage). The render sink is in the template file (outside this file), but if it uses `innerHTML` or bypasses Angular's auto-escaping, the stored content executes as script in the victim's browser. The persistence point — where the unsanitized content is written to storage — is in this file.

The messages (including unsanitized LLM content) are read: `const msgs = this.messages()`.

The unsanitized messages are assigned to the conversation object: `messages: msgs`.

`this.messages.update(prev => {` begins the update callback that will modify the assistant message.
The array is shallow-copied: `const updated = [...prev]`.
The assistant message at `assistantIndex` is targeted for replacement: `updated[assistantIndex] = {`.

After the stream loop ends, `this.persistConversation()` is called to save the messages.

When the conversation is later loaded (line 72-74: `this.messages.set(existing.messages)`), this content is rendered. The actual DOM render sink is in the template file (`chat-conversation.component.html`, outside this file), but the persistence of unsanitized free-form content occurs here. This is the stored XSS persistence point.

title: No rate limiting or message count cap on client-side LLM message sending
description: The `sendMessage` method has no rate limiting, no maximum message count per conversation, and no cooldown between messages. Combined with the `initialMessage` query parameter that auto-triggers a message send, an attacker could craft a URL that repeatedly triggers LLM calls (e.g., by causing navigation with new initialMessage values), or a user could spam messages without throttling. This enables unbounded LLM API consumption (token costs, API rate limit exhaustion) from a single client session. The design lacks any client-side throttling or step cap that would limit the blast radius of automated or scripted message submission.

trace.description: The `sendMessage` method is the entrypoint for sending messages to the LLM. It is called from user input (chat input box, outside this file) and from the `initialMessage` query parameter handler (line 80).

The only guard is `if (!content || this.isLoading()) return` — this prevents concurrent sends while a response is streaming, but does not prevent rapid sequential sends, does not limit total messages per session, and does not enforce any cooldown period.
The message is added to the messages array: `this.messages.update(prev => [...prev, { role: 'user', content }])`. No count check is performed.
Loading state is set: `this.isLoading.set(true)`. This only prevents concurrent calls, not sequential rapid calls.
Messages are read into `apiMessages`: `const apiMessages = this.messages()`. No cap on array length is enforced.
The array is sliced: `.slice(0, -1)`. No message-count limit is applied.
Error messages are filtered: `.filter(m => !m.error)`. No throttling logic is present.
Messages are mapped to API format: `.map(m => ({ role: m.role, content: m.content }))`. No rate-limit check or message-count cap intervenes.

Every call reaches `this.chatService.streamMessages(apiMessages)` which invokes the LLM API. There is no cap on the number of LLM calls, no rate limiting, and no maximum conversation length enforced before this call. The design permits unbounded resource consumption of LLM API tokens and backend processing.

title: Service errors logged directly to browser console exposing internal error details to end users
description: The unit tests at lines 87-98 explicitly verify that the DeliveryMethodComponent logs raw error objects from both AddressService (getById) and DeliveryService (get) directly to the browser console via console.log. Since these tests pass, the component's production behavior is to write service error details — which may include internal server error messages, stack traces, endpoint paths, or database error information — to the client-side console. Any user who opens browser developer tools can read these errors, gaining insight into backend internals, service structure, and potentially sensitive data. This is both a logging-monitoring failure (internal error data exposed to untrusted clients instead of being handled and logged server-side) and a misconfiguration (debug/diagnostic output exposed in a production-facing component).

This confirms the component catches service errors and passes them to console.log.

An identical test at lines 94-99 verifies the same behavior for DeliveryService.get — the error is logged verbatim to the browser console. Two independent service error paths are confirmed to use console.log for error output.
In the beforeEach block, the addressService mock object is created with a getById method, setting up the service that will later be injected into the component.

title: Unvalidated error key from query parameters reflected as error message without whitelist
description: The ErrorPageComponent reads an 'error' query parameter from the route and passes it directly to ngx-translate's get() method. When the translation key is not found (which is the expected case for any attacker-supplied string that isn't a registered translation key), the error callback sets this.error to the raw translationId — which is the attacker-controlled query parameter value verbatim. The design never validates, sanitizes, or whitelists acceptable error keys. This allows an attacker to craft a URL such as '/error?error=Your+session+expired.+Please+re-enter+your+credentials+at+http://evil.com' that will display an arbitrary attacker-chosen message in the application's trusted error page UI. This creates a phishing/social-engineering vector where the application lends its own visual trust (branding, styling, domain) to attacker-controlled content. A correct design would restrict displayed errors to a fixed set of known error codes and reject or default any unrecognised key.

The if (errorKey) conditional is the only check applied. It tests truthiness only — any non-empty string passes. There is no validation that errorKey is a member of a known set of application error codes.

When ngx-translate cannot find a translation for the given key, it invokes the error callback, passing back the original key string as translationId. This is the expected path for any attacker-supplied string that is not a registered translation key.

In the error callback, this.error is set to translationId — which ngx-translate returns as the original key string when no translation is found. This means any arbitrary user-supplied string that is not a registered translation key is reflected verbatim into this.error and rendered to the user. The design provides no whitelist, validation, or default fallback for unrecognised error keys.

title: Notification endpoint URL configured with HTTP instead of HTTPS — transport security not enforced
description: The test fixtures for the CTF system-wide notification component configure the notification polling endpoint using an insecure HTTP URL ('http://example.com/notify'). title: File upload accepts dangerous file types (XML, YAML, ZIP) without integrity verification
description: The FileUploader configuration explicitly allows XML, YAML, and ZIP MIME types. XML files can enable XXE attacks if parsed with external entity resolution enabled on the server. The allowedMimeType is a client-side check that can be bypassed, but its presence indicates the server endpoint at /file-upload is designed to accept these dangerous file types. The actual processing vulnerability is server-side (outside this file), but this file is the entry point that sends dangerous file types to the server.

title: Forgotten test parameter 'testDecal' allows path traversal and unsanitized server-side emission

title: Challenge success state set before continue code is confirmed — error leaves inconsistent state
description: The test suite reveals a design flaw in the verdict workflow: on a true verdict, the result is set to ResultState.Right (tested at line 65) and the continue code is fetched asynchronously (tested at lines 80, 95). This means the user-visible state remains 'Right' (challenge solved) even though the continue code was never obtained or stored. This is a state transition inconsistency: the system transitions to a 'solved' state without completing all required steps of the workflow. An attacker who can induce a network error (or who controls network conditions) could see a challenge marked as solved without the corresponding continue code being persisted, creating an integrity gap in the challenge progression system.

title: Private key transmitted to server instead of requiring a signature proof
description: The NFT unlock workflow requires users to paste their actual blockchain private key into a form field and transmit it to the server via keysService.submitKey(). This is a fundamental design flaw: private keys should never leave the user's control. The correct design is for the server to send a challenge and the client to respond with a signature, proving key ownership without revealing the key. By accepting the raw private key, the design guarantees that the server (and any attacker who compromises it, logs it, or performs MITM) can capture and use the user's private key to drain their wallet. This is an insecure design because the flaw exists in the intended workflow itself, not in a missing validation check.

title: OAuth login derives a predictable password from the user's email, allowing OAuth bypass
description: When an OAuth login succeeds, the component derives the user's password by Base64-encoding the reversed email address: `btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))`. Since the email is the only input and Base64/reverse are trivially invertible, anyone who knows a user's email address can compute their password and authenticate directly via the standard login endpoint — completely bypassing OAuth. This defeats the purpose of OAuth as an authentication mechanism and enables account takeover for any user whose email is known.

Even without spoofing, the design assumes the email from the OAuth profile is authoritative for account ownership, and combines this with a password that is publicly derivable — meaning the account created via OAuth is permanently accessible without OAuth.

The only logging present is `console.log(err)` for basket merge errors (line 110) and OAuth redirect URI mismatch (line 86), neither of which captures authentication events.

trace.description: The `login()` method is the primary authentication entrypoint. The caller is outside this file (triggered by the login form submission).
`this.userService.login(this.user).subscribe({...})` initiates the authentication request and subscribes to both success and error callbacks.

The `next` callback (lines 99-116) processes a successful authentication — storing tokens, merging baskets, completing login — but performs no security logging of the successful login event (no user identifier, no timestamp, no IP is recorded).

The error handler (lines 118-131) processes failed login attempts and TOTP challenges but performs no security logging of the event — no user identifier, no timestamp, no failure reason is recorded. The success handler (lines 99-116) likewise logs nothing about the successful authentication. Security events (login success, login failure, MFA challenge) pass through this code with no audit trail.

title: API error responses logged to browser console in production
description: The tests verify that the OrderCompletionComponent logs backend API errors directly to the browser console via console.log. When getApplicationConfiguration or trackOrderService.find throws an error, the component catches it and writes the raw error object to console.log. In a production environment, this exposes internal error details—potentially including server-side stack traces, database error messages, or other sensitive internal information—to any user who can open the browser developer console. This is both a logging-monitoring failure (sensitive data written to an insecure log channel) and a misconfiguration (debug/diagnostic output exposed in production). The test file confirms this behavior exists: the tests at lines 152-157 and 160-165 explicitly assert that console.log is called with the raw error string 'Error'.

trace.description: The test mocks configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration to throw an error, simulating a real backend API failure. The component under test (outside this file) receives this error via its ngOnInit lifecycle hook.

component.ngOnInit() is called, which triggers the API calls that throw errors. The component (implementation outside this file) catches these errors. A second test at lines 160-165 confirms the same pattern for trackOrderService.find errors.

The test asserts that console.log was called with 'Error', confirming the component logs raw API errors to the browser console. Line 164 shows the identical pattern for order detail API errors. In production, these console.log calls expose internal error details to end users via the browser developer console, which can contain server-side internals, stack traces, or sensitive data from error responses.

title: Open redirect via unvalidated redirectUrl query parameter after login
description: The test at lines 297-305 confirms that the LoginComponent reads a redirectUrl from the route's query parameters and, after a successful login, navigates directly to that URL via router.navigateByUrl. The test substitutes an arbitrary value ('/profile') into the query param and verifies the component blindly forwards to it. There is no indication in the test that the redirect URL is validated against an allowlist of internal paths before navigation. An attacker can craft a phishing URL like /login?redirectUrl=https://evil.com, and after the victim authenticates, they are redirected to the attacker's site — potentially leaking the freshly minted session token via referer headers or enabling credential theft through a fake login page. This is an insecure design flaw because the trust boundary for post-login navigation is placed entirely in client-controlled query parameters without server-side or client-side allowlisting.

trace.description: The test injects a mock route snapshot whose queryParamMap.get returns an arbitrary string '/profile' as the redirectUrl. This simulates an attacker-controlled query parameter reaching the LoginComponent. The actual entrypoint (the route handler serving /login?redirectUrl=...) is outside this file.

The test triggers component.login() which performs authentication via userService.login. After successful authentication, the component is expected to use the redirectUrl from the query parameter for navigation.
The test spies on router.navigateByUrl, confirming that the component calls this method to perform the redirect. The navigation target is derived from the attacker-controllable query parameter.
component.login() is called, which processes the authentication, and upon success reads the redirectUrl from the query parameters and calls router.navigateByUrl with it.
await fixture.whenStable() waits for the asynchronous login and navigation flow to complete, ensuring the redirect has been executed.

The assertion expects(navSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/profile') confirms the component passes the unvalidated redirectUrl directly to router.navigateByUrl. No validation, sanitization, or allowlist check is performed on the redirect target. An attacker can substitute any URL (e.g., https://evil.com) to achieve open redirect after victim authentication.

title: TOTP temporary authentication token stored in localStorage, vulnerable to XSS exfiltration
description: The test at lines 317-328 confirms that when the server indicates a TOTP token is required for two-factor authentication, the LoginComponent stores the returned temporary token (tmpToken) in localStorage under the key 'totp_tmp_token'. localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript running on the page, including malicious scripts injected via cross-site scripting (XSS). An attacker who finds an XSS vulnerability anywhere in the application can steal the TOTP temporary token, potentially bypassing the second factor of authentication. This is a session management weakness: authentication tokens should be stored in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies rather than localStorage. The test confirms this insecure storage pattern is the actual production behavior.

trace.description: The test simulates a login response requiring TOTP by having userService.login return an error with status 'totp_token_required' and a data.tmpToken of 'tmp'. This represents server-provided authentication state reaching the component.
component.login() is called, which processes the TOTP-required response and stores the temporary token.
The test sets up a spy on router.navigate, establishing that the component redirects to the 2FA page. The actual entrypoint (the login form submission) is outside this file.

The assertion expect(localStorage.getItem('totp_tmp_token')).toBe('tmp') confirms the component writes the TOTP temporary authentication token to localStorage. This storage location is accessible to any JavaScript on the page, making it exfiltrable via XSS. The token grants access to the 2FA verification step, so stealing it enables authentication bypass.

title: Authentication token stored in localStorage after successful login
description: The test at lines 152-156 confirms that the LoginComponent stores the authentication token returned by the login service directly in localStorage under the key 'token'. Like the TOTP token finding, storing the primary session/authentication token in localStorage exposes it to theft via any XSS vulnerability in the application. HttpOnly cookies would prevent JavaScript access to the token. The test confirms this is the actual production behavior — the component writes the token to localStorage on every successful login.

trace.description: The test mocks userService.login to return an object containing { token: 'token' }, simulating the server's authentication response reaching the LoginComponent.
component.login() is called, which processes the successful login response and stores the token.

The assertion expect(localStorage.getItem('token')).toBe('token') confirms the component writes the authentication token to localStorage. This makes the session token accessible to any JavaScript on the page, including attacker-injected scripts via XSS, enabling session hijacking.

title: Error responses from authentication and basket operations logged to console without redaction
description: Multiple tests (lines 271-293, 307-315) confirm that the LoginComponent logs raw error objects to the console via console.log. The test at lines 307-315 specifically confirms that when merging a guest basket fails, the raw error ('mergeErr') is logged. Similarly, lines 288-293 confirm that configuration loading errors are logged to console. In a production environment, console output may be visible in browser developer tools and could expose internal error details, stack traces, or sensitive information about the application's backend structure. More critically, the tests confirm there is no structured security logging of failed login attempts — the test at lines 164-175 shows that failed login only sets a component error flag and returns the error message to the client, with no indication of security event logging for failed authentication attempts.

The test assigns console.log = vi.fn(), establishing that the component uses console.log for error output. The actual entrypoint (the login flow triggering the basket merge) is outside this file.

await fixture.whenStable() waits for the asynchronous login and basket merge flow to complete, ensuring the error handler has executed and logged the error.

The assertion expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('mergeErr') confirms the component logs the raw error object to the console without redaction or structured security logging. Similarly, the failed-login tests (lines 164-175) show no security event logging — only a component error flag is set and the raw server error message is surfaced to the client.

title: Test enshrines console.log as the error-logging mechanism for configuration failures
description: The test on lines 62-67 verifies that when the application configuration fetch fails, the component logs the error via `console.log`. By asserting `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')`, this test actively enforces and locks in the practice of routing error information through the browser console rather than a structured, server-side, or centralized logging system. Configuration-fetch failures can be security-relevant (e.g., a misconfigured or tampered configuration endpoint), and console.log output is ephemeral, unstructured, visible to any user with devtools, and not forwarded to any monitoring or alerting pipeline. If a developer later replaced console.log with a proper logging service, this test would break, actively preventing the improvement of security logging.

The test replaces console.log with a vi.fn() spy, confirming that the component's error path (triggered by ngOnInit on line 65) is expected to route through console.log rather than any structured logging service.

component.ngOnInit() is called, which subscribes to getApplicationConfiguration, receives the mocked error, and executes its error-handling logic — the path the test is validating.

The assertion `expect(console.log).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Error')` enshrines console.log as the accepted error-logging sink. Security-relevant configuration errors are logged to the browser console only — no structured logging, no server-side forwarding, no alerting, and the test prevents migration to a better mechanism.

title: Production error logging to browser console exposes internal details from configuration service
description: When the call to getApplicationConfiguration() fails, the error object is logged directly to the browser console via console.log(err) (line 40). In a production deployment, this exposes internal error details — potentially including backend configuration paths, network error messages, or service endpoint information — to any user who opens the browser developer tools. This is both a misconfiguration (debug/diagnostic output left active in production) and a logging-monitoring concern (sensitive internal error data written to a client-accessible log channel). The error handler should either suppress the output in production or log only a sanitized, user-facing message without internal details.

The error callback receives the raw error object `err` from the failed configuration fetch. No sanitization or filtering is applied before it is passed to the logging call.

Angular's framework lifecycle calls ngOnInit() on this component. The caller (Angular framework) is outside this file. This is the entry point that initiates the configuration fetch and error-handling flow.

console.log(err) writes the full error object to the browser console in all environments, including production. The raw error may contain internal service URLs, stack traces, or configuration details that should not be exposed to end users. This serves as both an insecure default (debug output enabled in production) and an inadequate logging practice (sensitive internal data written to an uncontrolled, client-side log channel).

title: Error details logged to browser console exposing potential backend information
description: The test on lines 88-96 explicitly verifies that the ProductReviewEditComponent logs raw error objects to the browser console via console.log when a backend API call fails. HTTP error responses can carry sensitive backend details such as internal paths, database error messages, stack traces, or API structure information. Logging these to the browser console exposes them to any user who opens developer tools, creating an information disclosure risk. The test confirms this is intentional, expected behavior of the component.

description: The OrderHistoryComponent logs errors from order history and product API calls directly to the browser console via console.log. In a production environment, this exposes internal server error details, potential stack traces, authentication token information, or other sensitive backend details to anyone who can open the browser developer console. Security-relevant errors (e.g., unauthorized access attempts, server failures) should be handled with proper error reporting mechanisms, not dumped to the client-side console where they can be inspected by attackers or leaked via browser extensions.

title: Order confirmation PDFs served over insecure HTTP from exposed /ftp/ path with unvalidated order ID
description: The openConfirmationPDF method constructs a URL by concatenating a host server base URL with '/ftp/order_' + orderId + '.pdf' and opens it in a new browser tab. The test at line 163 reveals three issues: (1) the host server uses HTTP not HTTPS, meaning order confirmation documents (which contain PII, financial details, order information) are transmitted without transport-layer encryption; (2) the PDFs are served from an '/ftp/' directory path, suggesting an exposed internal file-serving resource that should be restricted; (3) the order ID is directly interpolated into the URL path without validation or sanitization, allowing path traversal or arbitrary file access within the /ftp/ directory. An attacker who can influence the order ID parameter could construct requests to access other files served from the /ftp/ endpoint.

trace.description: Test calls component.openConfirmationPDF('abc123') — the order ID parameter originates from caller code outside this file (the component's template or a method call). The test demonstrates that an arbitrary string is accepted as the order ID.

basketService is configured with hostServer: 'http://host.example' — an insecure HTTP base URL. The component uses this host server value to construct the PDF URL, meaning order confirmations are fetched over unencrypted HTTP.

vi.spyOn(window, 'open') intercepts the window.open call. The spy is set up before openConfirmationPDF is invoked, confirming the test's intent to verify the exact URL and target passed to the browser's window.open.

The test asserts window.open is called with 'http://host.example/ftp/order_abc123.pdf' and '_blank'. The URL is constructed by interpolating the order ID directly into a path under /ftp/. This reveals: HTTP transport for sensitive documents (misconfiguration), an exposed /ftp/ file path (misconfiguration), and no validation of the order ID before URL construction (insecure design — the server should validate the order ID belongs to the requesting user and the client should not construct file paths from raw input).

title: Faucet withdrawal amount is entirely client-controlled with no validation
description: The `withdrawAmount` field is bound to a user-controlled form input (line 55) and flows directly into `contract.withdraw(amount)` (line 235) with no validation of its value — no maximum cap, no positivity check, no server-side re-derivation. A faucet's core business rule is to limit how many tokens each user can withdraw; this code enforces no such limit at the application level. The only pre-withdrawal check is whether the user has enough ETH for gas (line 226), which is unrelated to the disbursement amount. An attacker can set `withdrawAmount` to any value (including values exceeding the faucet's balance or crafted to exploit smart-contract edge cases) and the application will submit the transaction without objection. Whether the smart contract itself enforces a cap is not visible from this file; the application layer provides no compensating control.

trace.description: `withdrawAmount: number = null` is a public component field bound to a form input (via FormsModule import at line 41), making it user-controlled.
`extractBEETokens(amount = this.withdrawAmount)` receives the user-controlled value as its default parameter.
The only validation before withdrawal checks ETH balance for gas (`balanceEth < '0.001'`), not the withdrawal amount itself. No bound, positivity check, or per-user limit is applied to `amount`.
The guard `if (!this.session)` checks only a client-side boolean and returns early if false; it does not validate the `amount` parameter.
The `try {` block begins the core withdrawal logic, receiving `amount` without any prior validation.
`const balanceBigNumber = await provider.getBalance(userAddress)` fetches the user's ETH balance for gas checking, bypassing any validation of the token withdrawal amount.
`const balanceEth = ethers.utils.formatEther(balanceBigNumber)` formats the ETH balance for comparison, still without touching `amount`.
`const contract = new ethers.Contract(...)` instantiates the faucet contract, preparing to forward the unvalidated `amount` to the blockchain.

`const tx = await contract.withdraw(amount)` submits the unvalidated amount to the BeeFaucet smart contract. The application never enforces a maximum withdrawal or validates the amount is within allowed faucet limits.

title: No rate limiting or cooldown on faucet withdrawals allows repeated draining
description: The `extractBEETokens` method (line 211) can be invoked repeatedly with no cooldown, per-user throttle, or rate limit of any kind. Each invocation creates a blockchain transaction that withdraws tokens from the faucet contract. Combined with the absence of amount validation (separate finding), an attacker can call `extractBEETokens` in a loop to drain the faucet's token balance. The method checks only `this.session` (a client-side boolean set at line 200) and ETH gas balance — neither constitutes a rate limit. No timestamp tracking, no per-address withdrawal count, and no backend-enforced throttle is visible anywhere in the component.

trace.description: `extractBEETokens` is a public async method callable from the template (the component is the faucet UI). The caller is outside this file (template button binding).
The guard checks only `this.session` (client-side boolean) — there is no rate limit, no cooldown timer, no per-user withdrawal counter, and no check against a last-withdrawal timestamp.

`contract.withdraw(amount)` executes the withdrawal transaction. After completion, the method refreshes balances (lines 239-240) and returns with no state that would prevent an immediate subsequent call. An attacker can invoke this in a loop to exhaust the faucet contract's token supply.

title: Security-relevant faucet operations logged only to browser console with no structured security logging
description: Token withdrawals (`extractBEETokens`), NFT minting (`mintNFT`), and wallet authentication (`handleAuth`) are security-relevant events in a crypto faucet application. These events are logged exclusively via `console.log`/`console.error` (lines 225, 238, 277, 283, 306, 207) with no structured security logging, no correlation IDs, and no server-side audit trail visible from this component. While some backend logging may exist in the services called, the component itself provides no security event instrumentation. Additionally, sensitive financial data (ETH balances at line 225, token balances at lines 120/146, transaction details at lines 277/283) is written to the browser console, which could be accessible to browser extensions or other scripts. The absence of structured security logging for withdrawal and mint operations means the application cannot reconstruct an attack timeline from these events.

After a successful withdrawal, the only logging is `console.log('BEE tokens extracted successfully')` — no structured security log, no user identifier, no amount, no correlation ID. The same pattern applies to NFT minting (line 306) and wallet auth (line 204).
