`const balanceEth = ethers.utils.formatEther(balanceBigNumber)` converts the balance to a readable string, leading directly to a console log statement.
`const contract = new ethers.Contract(...)` prepares the contract call, bypassing any structured security event logging for the pending withdrawal.
`const tx = await contract.withdraw(amount)` executes the withdrawal transaction, a critical security event, with no audit log generated at this step.
`await tx.wait()` confirms the transaction on the blockchain, finalizing the security-relevant state change without recording it in a monitoring system.

`console.log('ETH balance:', balanceEth, typeof balanceEth)` writes the user's ETH balance to the browser console. Sensitive financial data (balances, transaction hashes) is exposed in console output at lines 120, 146, 225, 238, 277, 283 without any security event being logged to a proper audit system.

title: Client-side-only password strength evaluation with no enforcement mechanism
description: The PasswordStrengthComponent calculates password strength entirely on the client side using a simplistic checklist approach (lines 30-40). The component receives the password via an @Input binding and computes a strength score by counting how many of five regex-based criteria are met, then divides by five to produce a percentage. There is no enforcement of any minimum strength threshold — the component is purely advisory (it sets a progress bar color). If the server-side password-change or registration flow relies on this client-side check to enforce password policy (which cannot be confirmed from this file alone), an attacker can bypass the strength requirement entirely by submitting the form directly with a weak password. Additionally, the algorithm itself is gameable: a password like 'Aa1!!!!!!' satisfies all five checks and scores 100% ('high') despite being trivially crackable, giving users a false sense of security. The minLength property (line 20) is declared but unused — the actual check on line 47 hardcodes 8 rather than referencing the property, indicating the design never established a configurable, enforceable policy.

trace.description: The component receives a password string from an external caller via @Input() password = ''. The caller (a parent Angular component or template) is outside this file. This is the trust boundary where untrusted input enters the component.

ngOnChanges receives the changed password value and calls calculatePasswordStrength() on line 26. No validation, threshold enforcement, or server-side check is invoked — the password is used directly in client-side regex checks.
if (changes.password) gates execution — the strength calculation only runs when the password input has actually changed, but no validation or threshold check is performed here.

this.passwordStrength = this.calculatePasswordStrength() invokes the private calculation method and stores the numeric result. The result is later consumed only by the progressColor getter (lines 42-43) for UI coloring — no enforcement gate, no server-side call, no submission block.

private calculatePasswordStrength(): number begins the strength computation. The method builds an array of five getter references (lines 31-37) that each read this.password: containAtLeastMinChars (line 47, hardcoded length >= 8), containAtLeastOneLowerCaseLetter (line 51), containAtLeastOneUpperCaseLetter (line 55), containAtLeastOneDigit (line 59), containAtLeastOneSpecialChar (line 63). The minLength property declared on line 20 is never referenced.

const checks = [ ... ] builds the array of getter references (lines 31-37). These getters are not yet evaluated — they are property accessors on this that will be invoked when .filter() iterates the array on the next line. Each getter reads this.password directly via regex .test() calls or .length comparison.

calculatePasswordStrength() returns a percentage based on 5 simple regex checks (lines 31-37). The result is stored in passwordStrength (line 26) and used only to set a progress bar color (lines 42-44). There is no enforcement gate — the component never blocks submission, never calls a server-side validation endpoint, and never enforces a minimum acceptable strength. The design assumes the client-side advisory check is sufficient for password policy, with no compensating server-side control visible in this file.

title: Authentication and UI access gating based solely on unvalidated localStorage token presence
description: The test suite confirms that the PhotoWallComponent's `isLoggedIn()` method returns the raw string stored under the 'token' key in localStorage without performing any validation — no signature verification, no expiration check, no format validation. Any arbitrary string (e.g., 'abc') placed in localStorage causes the component to report the user as authenticated. The share-a-memory form and submit button are rendered based solely on this check (tested in the template rendering block), meaning the client-side access control for submitting memories is bypassable by setting any value in localStorage. While server-side enforcement may exist separately, the client-side authentication decision is meaningless and reveals the application's auth model relies on token presence rather than token validity.

The actual component being tested (PhotoWallComponent, outside this file) implements isLoggedIn() which reads localStorage directly.

The test then asserts expect(component.isLoggedIn()).toBe('abc'), confirming the component returns the raw token value without any cryptographic validation, signature check, or expiration verification.

expect(component.isLoggedIn()).toBeNull() confirms that when no token is in localStorage, the component reports the user as not logged in (null). This establishes that the component's auth check is purely a presence check on the 'token' key — there is no server-side validation call or token verification step in between.

expect(component.isLoggedIn()).toBe('abc') confirms the component returns the raw token value without any cryptographic validation, signature check, expiration verification, or format parsing. The crypto-auth weakness is established here: the authentication decision is based entirely on the existence of a localStorage key, not on the validity of its contents.
localStorage.removeItem('token') cleans up after the first test, but the vulnerability has been demonstrated: any value placed in the 'token' key is treated as proof of authentication.

The template rendering test 'should render the share-a-memory form only when a token is stored' begins by removing the token, confirming the form is not rendered without one (line 283 asserts null). This links the isLoggedIn() check to UI-level access control.

Line 288 further confirms the submit button is rendered. The client-side access control for submitting memories is bypassable by setting any value in localStorage, establishing the access-control defect: the UI gates a privileged action (memory submission) on an unvalidated, attacker-controllable client-side value.

The template rendering test at lines 280-290 confirms that the share-a-memory form ('.share-memory-section') and submit button ('#submitButton') are rendered based solely on the presence of a token string in localStorage (localStorage.setItem('token', 'token')). An attacker can bypass this client-side access control by setting any arbitrary value in localStorage, gaining access to the memory submission form without legitimate authentication.

title: API error details logged directly to browser console via console.log
description: The test suite confirms that the PhotoWallComponent logs raw error responses from multiple API calls (get memories, addMemory, getApplicationConfiguration) directly to the browser console using console.log. In a production environment, these error objects may contain sensitive information such as internal endpoint paths, stack traces, authentication details, or backend error messages. Exposing this information in the browser console makes it accessible to anyone who can open browser developer tools, potentially aiding attackers in understanding the application's internal structure and identifying further attack vectors. The tests explicitly assert that the error value is passed to console.log, confirming this is intentional behavior rather than accidental.

title: Errors logged directly to browser console exposing internal error details
description: The test suite verifies that the ProductDetailsComponent logs raw error objects directly to the browser console via console.log. This occurs both when retrieving user information (whoAmI) and when posting a product review. Logging unhandled error objects to the client-side console exposes internal application error details, stack traces, and potentially sensitive information to any user who opens browser developer tools. This is a security logging failure because it leaks internal error information to end users rather than handling errors with generic user-facing messages while logging details server-side.

title: Service errors logged directly to browser console may expose sensitive data
description: The OrderSummaryComponent intentionally catches errors from AddressService and PaymentService and logs them directly to the browser console via console.log. In production, these error objects may contain sensitive information such as payment card details, address PII, API tokens, internal endpoint paths, or server-side stack traces. Browser console output is accessible to anyone with dev tools open and can be captured by browser extensions or injected scripts. The tests explicitly verify this behavior, confirming it is by design rather than accidental. Security-relevant errors should be handled with sanitized user-facing messages, with full details sent to a controlled server-side logging pipeline rather than the client console.

title: Client-controlled pricing and discount values trusted by the order summary component
description: The test at lines 155-161 reveals that getMessage receives an array [itemTotal, bonus] from an external source and stores these values directly as component state. Separately, the promotional discount (couponDiscount) is read from sessionStorage (line 156), which is fully client-controllable. A user can modify sessionStorage to set an arbitrary couponDiscount value (e.g., 70, 99, or even a negative number) before placing an order. If the server trusts or re-uses these client-side values during checkout rather than independently recomputing prices and discounts, this enables price manipulation. The test confirms the component's design accepts these values without server-side re-derivation. Additionally, paymentId and addressId stored in sessionStorage (lines 123, 143, 150) are used to look up payment and address records via getById calls — if the server does not verify ownership of these IDs, this establishes a BOLA vector where a user can substitute another user's paymentId or addressId.

This value is fully controllable by the user. component.getMessage([100, 1]) is called, and the test verifies that itemTotal is set to 100 and bonus to 1. The pricing data arrives via a message mechanism and is trusted directly by the component without server-side re-derivation.

The test confirms component.promotionalDiscount is set to 70 — the value from sessionStorage. The component trusts client-side sessionStorage for the discount amount. If this value flows to the checkout (basketService.checkout at line 164), the server must independently recompute the discount. The test at line 164 shows checkout is called, but there is no evidence in this file of server-side price validation.

title: Sensitive identifiers (paymentId, addressId) stored in sessionStorage without protection
description: The tests reveal that paymentId, addressId, and deliveryMethodId are stored in sessionStorage (lines 123, 143, 150, 167-171). sessionStorage is accessible to any JavaScript running on the same origin, including third-party scripts and XSS payloads. Storing resource identifiers that grant access to payment methods and addresses in sessionStorage means a successful XSS can trivially exfiltrate these IDs and use them to access the user's payment and address records. While sessionStorage is cleared on tab close, it provides no protection during an active session. The test at lines 163-172 confirms these values are cleaned up after checkout, but they remain exposed for the duration of the ordering flow.

paymentService.getById is called using the paymentId from sessionStorage. The test at line 167 confirms paymentId is later removed, but it is exposed in sessionStorage throughout the ordering flow.

The test verifies that paymentId, addressId, deliveryMethodId, couponDetails, and couponDiscount are all removed from sessionStorage after placeOrder(). This confirms all these sensitive values were stored in sessionStorage — accessible to any same-origin script — during the entire ordering process.

title: Authentication token stored in localStorage, vulnerable to XSS-based theft
description: The component stores the authentication token returned from the upgradeToDeluxe API call into localStorage (and a cookie). localStorage is accessible to any JavaScript executing on the page, so if an XSS vulnerability exists anywhere in the application, an attacker can exfiltrate the token and impersonate the user. This is a well-known identification and authentication failure: tokens should be stored in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies that are not accessible to client-side JavaScript. The test confirms this is the component's real behavior, not just a mock artifact.

Without knowing the cookie options (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), the cookie storage may or may not be safe, but the localStorage write at line 354 is definitively vulnerable.

The test asserts setItemSpy was called with ('token', 'tokenValue'), confirming the component writes the authentication token into localStorage. Line 355 confirms the token is also placed in a cookie via cookieService.put. localStorage-stored tokens are readable by any JavaScript on the page, making them stealable via XSS.

title: Backend error objects logged to browser console and surfaced to users, exposing internal details
description: Multiple test cases confirm that the component logs raw backend error responses to console.log and displays raw error messages to end users via snack bars. The test at line 512-517 shows a backend error object { error: { message: 'Wallet down' } } being both logged to console and surfaced directly in the UI. In production, these errors could contain stack traces, internal endpoint paths, database errors, or other sensitive internal information. Additionally, console.log of error objects in a production client is a misconfiguration (debug/diagnostic output left active). The tests verify this behavior across at least four distinct code paths, confirming it is the component's designed behavior rather than an incidental occurrence.

title: Discount percentage and payment ID stored client-side in session storage, trust boundary violation
description: The component stores the coupon discount percentage in sessionStorage (lines 246-251) and the payment ID in sessionStorage (lines 315-329). SessionStorage is fully controllable by the client. If the backend later trusts these client-stored values to determine the discount applied to an order or the payment method chosen, an attacker can modify them to apply arbitrary discounts or forge payment selections. The discount value is particularly critical: the test at line 249 shows showConfirmation(70) stores 70 as the coupon discount, but this value originates from a client-side call and is stored in client-accessible storage. The server should independently re-derive the discount from the coupon code rather than trusting a client-stored percentage. This is a trust assumption violation where the client controls a value the server should validate.

title: Delete payment method accepts arbitrary card ID without ownership verification
description: The delete() method receives a card ID from the template (caller outside this file) and passes it directly to paymentService.del() without verifying that the ID corresponds to one of the current user's stored cards. The component loads the user's cards into this.storedCards via load() (called from ngOnInit), but never checks whether the ID passed to delete() is present in that collection. If the backend API similarly fails to enforce per-user ownership (BOLA), an attacker can supply another user's card ID and delete it. Even on the frontend, the absence of a client-side guard means the component will dutifully send any ID the DOM provides to the deletion endpoint.

The id is passed directly to this.paymentService.del(id) with no check against this.storedCards (loaded at line 68) to confirm the ID belongs to the current user's cards.

The load() method is defined here; it fetches the current user's stored cards via the payment service.

The fetched cards are assigned to this.storedCards. This is the collection that delete() should check the id against to verify ownership, but it never does.

The deletion service call is invoked with an unverified card ID. No ownership or authorization check exists between the entrypoint and this sink. An attacker who can invoke delete() with an arbitrary ID (e.g., via DOM manipulation or direct API call mirroring this request) can delete another user's payment method if the backend also lacks BOLA enforcement.

title: Credit card validation relies solely on client-side numeric range check with no Luhn or format verification
description: The save() method builds a card object from Angular form controls and sends it to the payment service. The only validation on the card number is a numeric range check (Validators.min(1000000000000000), Validators.max(9999999999999999)) which merely ensures the value is a 16-digit integer. There is no Luhn checksum validation, no card network format validation, and critically, all validation is client-side only. The expiry month and year controls (lines 43-44) have only Validators.required with no range or logical checks (e.g., expired date detection). If the server trusts this client-side validation as authoritative, an attacker can bypass it entirely by crafting direct API requests with invalid or malformed card data, potentially storing garbage data or probing the system.

The save() method copies form control values directly into this.card: fullName from nameControl (line 76), cardNum from numberControl (line 77), expMonth from monthControl (line 78), expYear from yearControl (line 79). Month and year controls (lines 43-44) only have Validators.required — no range or expiry logic.

The yearControl is defined with only Validators.required — no range check, no expiry logic (e.g., rejecting past years). The yearRange at line 51 starts at 2080 but this is only used for the dropdown options, not enforced as a validator.

this.yearControl.value is copied into this.card.expYear — only validated by Validators.required, no expiry logic.

this.paymentService.save(this.card) sends the card object with only client-side validation to the backend. All validation is bypassable by an attacker who crafts a direct request. The design assumes the client will validate, but the server should be the authority for payment data validation.

title: Security-relevant errors during card loading and deletion are only logged to browser console with no application-level security logging
description: Both the load() and delete() methods handle errors by calling console.log(err) — writing error details to the browser console only. For the delete() operation in particular (line 106), a failed deletion attempt could indicate an access control violation or an attack (attempting to delete another user's card). There is no application-level security logging, alerting, or audit trail for these payment-related security events. This means that if an attacker attempts to delete cards they don't own or triggers errors during card operations, there is no server-side or application-level log record to detect or investigate the incident.

The same pattern appears in the load() error handler: console.log(err) at line 71 for card loading errors. Both security-relevant error paths (load failure and delete failure) route only to the browser console, which is inaccessible to security operators and provides no audit trail for incident investigation.

The 'next' callback handles successful deletion by calling this.load() to refresh the card list — no security logging of the successful deletion event either.

On error, the only action is console.log(err) — writing to the browser console. No application-level security logging, no audit trail, no alerting for failed deletion attempts that could indicate unauthorized access attempts. The same pattern appears at line 71 for card loading errors.

title: OAuth account creation uses deterministic, publicly-derivable password (base64 of reversed email)
description: The test suite documents that when a user logs in via OAuth for the first time, the OAuthComponent creates a regular account whose password is the base64 encoding of the reversed email address. For email 'test@test.com', the expected password is 'bW9jLnRzZXRAdHNldA==' which decodes to 'moc.tset@tset' (the email reversed). This password derivation is entirely deterministic and computable by anyone who knows the user's email address, which is typically public information. An attacker who knows a victim's email can compute the password and log in directly through the regular login endpoint, completely bypassing the OAuth flow and any OAuth provider's authentication. The test at line 94-98 further confirms this same derived password is then used for subsequent regular logins, cementing that this predictable credential is the user's actual account password.

This is a deterministic, publicly-derivable password: anyone who knows the email can compute the account password and bypass OAuth entirely. Line 98 confirms the same password is used for regular login: userService.login is called with { email: 'test@test.com', password: 'bW9jLnRzZXRAdHNldA==', oauth: true }.

title: OAuth login proceeds with regular credential login even after account creation failure, using predictable password
description: The test at lines 94-98 demonstrates that when account creation fails (e.g., account already exists), the OAuthComponent catches the error and falls through to a regular login using the same email-derived predictable password. This means the predictable password scheme is not just used for initial account creation—it is the persistent credential used for all subsequent authentications of OAuth-originated accounts. An attacker can compute the password for any email known to have been used with OAuth and authenticate directly, without needing the OAuth provider at all.

The component catches the save error and proceeds to authenticate via the regular login endpoint using the email-derived base64-reversed-email password. This confirms the predictable password is the persistent credential for the account, and the fallback login path means an attacker never needs to interact with the OAuth provider to gain access—just the email.

title: OAuth access token received via URL query parameter (implicit grant flow)
description: The test configuration at line 61 provides an ActivatedRoute snapshot with params containing '?alt=json&access_token=TEST'. This documents that the OAuthComponent is designed to receive OAuth access tokens directly in URL query parameters — the deprecated implicit grant flow. Access tokens in URLs are exposed to browser history, referrer headers, server access logs, proxy logs, and the Referer header on subsequent navigations. Any party with access to these artifacts can steal the token and impersonate the user. The secure alternative is the authorization code flow with PKCE, where the token is exchanged server-side via a POST request and never appears in a URL.

This reflects the production design: the component reads access tokens from the URL rather than exchanging an authorization code server-side.

The component reads the access_token from the ActivatedRoute snapshot's URL params and uses it to call userService.oauthLogin. The token has already been exposed in the URL at this point — it is in the browser history, the page URL, and potentially in referrer headers and server/proxy logs. The processing of the URL-exposed token for authentication confirms the implicit grant flow design.

title: Review message persisted without sanitization — stored XSS at persistence point
description: The editReview method sends the user-controlled review message directly to productReviewService.patch() without any HTML sanitization or content validation beyond length. The form control validators (line 39) only enforce required, minLength(1), and maxLength(160) — none of which prevent script or markup injection. This is the persistence point for a stored XSS vulnerability: the message is written to the datastore as free-form text, and if any downstream rendering template displays it without Angular's default escaping (e.g., via [innerHTML] binding or server-side rendering), the injected content executes in a victim's browser. The render sink is outside this file.

The raw, unsanitized user input (this.editReviewControl.value) is sent as the message field to be persisted. No encoding, sanitization, or allow-listing intervenes between the form control value and the persistence call. The render sink where this stored content is displayed is outside this file.

description: When the review patch API call fails, the full error object is logged to the browser console via console.log(err) on line 52. API error responses frequently contain internal details such as stack traces, database error messages, internal endpoint paths, or request correlation data. Exposing these in the client-side console makes them accessible to anyone inspecting the browser, including attackers who deliberately trigger error conditions to enumerate internal architecture. Additionally, the error object is also assigned to this.error (line 53) and may be rendered to the user, compounding the exposure.

title: Review edit patch sent with only review ID — no ownership verification in the component
description: The editReview method patches a review using this.data.reviewData._id as the sole identifier. The component does not verify that the currently authenticated user is the author of the review being edited. The _id arrives via MAT_DIALOG_DATA injection (line 32-34), which is populated by whatever caller opens the dialog. An attacker who can manipulate the dialog data or call the productReviewService directly could supply any review _id and attempt to overwrite another user's review message. While the definitive access-control enforcement must occur on the backend, this component performs no client-side ownership check and passes only {id, message} with no user-identity context, meaning the backend receives no indication of who is making the request from this code path.

editReview() calls this.productReviewService.patch({ id: this.data.reviewData._id, message: this.editReviewControl.value }). The review _id from the injected dialog data is used directly as the patch target. No ownership check, user-identity assertion, or authorization token is attached to the request payload from this component.

title: Unsanitized orderId interpolated into URL path enables path traversal and arbitrary file access
description: The `openConfirmationPDF` method accepts an `orderId` parameter and interpolates it directly into a URL using a template literal at line 114. No validation, encoding, or sanitization is applied to `orderId` before it is embedded into the URL path. An attacker who can influence the `orderId` value can inject path traversal sequences (e.g., `../`) to escape the `/ftp/` directory, or inject URL fragment characters (`#`) to truncate the `.pdf` suffix, enabling access to arbitrary files or paths on the server. The resulting URL is then opened via `window.open` at line 115. Because the `orderId` is embedded in a URL path rather than passed as a bound query parameter, the browser will normalize `../` sequences and interpret URL metacharacters, making this exploitable.

trace.description: The public method `openConfirmationPDF(orderId: string)` receives `orderId` from outside this file (called from the component template with order data). The parameter has no type constraint beyond `string` and no validation is performed.

`orderId` is interpolated directly into a URL via template literal: `const redirectUrl = \`${this.basketService.hostServer}/ftp/order_${orderId}.pdf\``. No encoding, sanitization, or allow-listing is applied to `orderId` before interpolation. Path traversal sequences (`../`), URL fragments (`#`), or query separators (`?`) in `orderId` will be interpreted by the browser when the URL is opened.

`window.open(redirectUrl, '_blank')` opens the constructed URL. Because `orderId` was embedded unsanitized, an attacker-controlled `orderId` such as `../acquisitionsb2b%23` would produce a URL that, after browser normalization, resolves to `https://host/acquisitionsb2b` — accessing an arbitrary file outside the intended `/ftp/order_*.pdf` path. This is both a path traversal injection (user input interpreted as URL structure) and an SSRF-class defect (caller-controlled destination opened as a request to a server resource).

title: Order confirmation PDFs served from publicly accessible /ftp/ directory without authorization
description: The URL construction at line 114 reveals that order confirmation PDFs are served from a `/ftp/` directory on the server. In the Juice Shop application, the `/ftp/` directory is a known misconfiguration where sensitive files (backups, configuration files, internal documents) are served without authentication. Additionally, the URL pattern `/ftp/order_${orderId}.pdf` is entirely predictable from the `orderId` alone — no session token, signed URL, or authorization parameter is included. Any user who can guess or enumerate an `orderId` can construct the URL to access another user's order confirmation PDF. The client-side code performs no ownership check before constructing and opening the URL, and the URL design itself contains no access-control mechanism.

trace.description: The public method `openConfirmationPDF(orderId: string)` is callable from outside this file (the component template). It accepts any `orderId` value without verifying that the current user owns the corresponding order.

The URL is constructed as `${this.basketService.hostServer}/ftp/order_${orderId}.pdf`. Two issues are visible: (1) the `/ftp/` path indicates files are served from an FTP-style directory, which in the Juice Shop context is a misconfiguration exposing sensitive files without authentication; (2) the URL contains no authorization token, signature, or user-scoping — the only variable is `orderId`, making the resource accessible to anyone who knows or guesses the identifier.

`window.open(redirectUrl, '_blank')` navigates the browser to the constructed URL. Because the URL pattern is predictable and unauthenticated, User A can substitute User B's `orderId` to access User B's order confirmation PDF. No ownership or authorization check intervenes between receiving `orderId` and opening the resource.

title: Order tracking navigation accepts untyped orderId without validation
description: The `trackOrder` method accepts an `orderId` parameter with no type annotation (line 118) and passes it directly as a query parameter to the router navigation (line 121). The lack of type safety and validation on `orderId` means any string value can be injected into the tracking flow. While the immediate impact depends on how the `/track-result` route handles the `id` query parameter (which is outside this file), the design defect is that the client trusts an unvalidated, untyped identifier to reference a server-side resource without establishing any invariant about its format or the user's authority to access it.

The navigation completes with the unvalidated `orderId` as the `id` query parameter. The tracking result page (outside this file) will receive this value and use it to fetch tracking data. The client-side design establishes no rule about what constitutes a valid `orderId` or whether the current user is authorized to track the referenced order, deferring all safety to the server without any client-side invariant.

title: Client-controlled UserId sent to backend in recycle save payload
description: The test reveals that the RecycleComponent constructs a recycle object on the client side that includes a `UserId` field derived from the `whoAmI()` API response, and passes the entire object to `recycleService.save()`. The server receives and presumably persists this client-supplied UserId. This is a trust assumption violation — the server should derive the user identity from the authenticated session, not accept it from the client. An attacker could modify the UserId in the request body to create recycle records attributed to another user, or manipulate the quantity/date fields to abuse the recycling workflow. The test at lines 157-160 explicitly verifies that the save payload includes `UserId: undefined`, and lines 176-179 verify it includes `UserId` alongside `isPickUp`, `date`, `AddressId`, and `quantity`. There is no indication of an allow-list restricting which fields the backend accepts, making this also a mass-assignment risk.

The test constructs the expected recycle payload as { UserId: undefined, AddressId: '1', quantity: 100 }, confirming that UserId is a field included in the object the component sends to the backend.

A second test variant confirms the full payload shape: { isPickUp: true, date: '10/7/2018', UserId: undefined, AddressId: '1', quantity: 100 }. All fields are client-constructed with no server-side derivation visible.

The test asserts component.recycle.UserId equals 42, confirming that the UserId from whoAmI() is stored directly on the recycle model object that will later be sent to the backend.

The test asserts that recycleService.save() is called with the client-constructed recycle object (line 160: mock.calls[0][0] equals the recycle object). The save call sends the UserId and all other fields to the backend. Since the server accepts and persists these client-supplied fields without deriving UserId from the session, an attacker can set an arbitrary UserId to impersonate another user in the recycling system.

title: Security-relevant errors logged via console.log instead of structured security logging
description: The test verifies that both backend API errors (lines 199-204) and user retrieval errors (lines 206-211) are logged using `console.log`. Using console.log for error handling means security-relevant events — such as backend failures that could indicate an attack, or user-service communication failures — are written to the browser's developer console rather than to a structured, server-side logging pipeline. These logs are not persistent, not correlated with request IDs, and are invisible to security monitoring. The test explicitly mocks `console.log` and asserts it is called with the raw error, confirming this is the production behavior being validated.

title: Client-controlled author field in review submission allows impersonation
description: The review object built in addReview() sets the author field from a client-side variable (this.author), which is derived from a whoAmI() API call result. This value is then sent to the server as part of the review creation payload. The server should derive the author identity from the authenticated session token, not accept it from the request body. An attacker can intercept the HTTP request and change the author field to any value, posting reviews attributed to another user. This is a trust assumption violation — the client controls who the review appears to be from, and the server has no opportunity in this code path to reject a spoofed author.

title: Unsanitized free-form review text persisted to backend enables stored XSS
description: The review message is taken directly from a textarea value (textPut.value) and placed into the review object sent to productReviewService.create() with no sanitization or encoding. The only validation applied (line 49, Validators.maxLength(160)) is a length constraint on an Angular FormControl, but addReview reads the value directly from the DOM element (textPut.value), bypassing the form control entirely. When the review is later fetched and rendered (lines 53/78 via productReviewService.get()), if the template does not escape, the stored script executes in viewers' browsers.

title: Client-side points calculation from price allows value manipulation
description: The component calculates product points on the client side as Math.round(price / 10) and stores the result back into the product data object (this.data.productData.points). If this points value is later sent to the server (e.g., when a purchase awards loyalty points), the server would accept a client-derived value rather than re-deriving it from the authoritative price. An attacker can modify the points value in the object before it reaches any subsequent server operation, awarding themselves arbitrary points. Even if the current flow does not send points back, the design places a server-decided value under client control.

title: Authentication token stored in localStorage is accessible to XSS
description: The isLoggedIn() method reads the authentication token from localStorage. Storing session tokens in localStorage makes them accessible to any JavaScript running on the page, including malicious scripts injected via XSS. If an XSS vulnerability exists (such as the stored XSS in review messages described above), an attacker can trivially exfiltrate the token via localStorage.getItem('token'). The secure alternative is to store session tokens in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, which are not accessible to JavaScript.

title: Weak password policy — minimum length of only 5 characters
description: The registration component's password validation accepts passwords as short as 5 characters, as confirmed by the test at lines 109-114. A 5-character minimum is far below modern recommendations (NIST SP 800-63B recommends a minimum of 8 characters). This weakens the authentication mechanism by allowing users to choose trivially guessable or brute-forceable passwords, making the application more susceptible to credential attacks. The test file itself does not define this policy — it verifies the component's behavior — so the actual validation logic resides in RegisterComponent, but this test confirms the weak policy is in effect.

title: Security-relevant errors logged to console.log potentially exposing sensitive data
description: The tests at lines 179-184 and 186-191 confirm that the RegisterComponent logs backend API errors via console.log. During user registration, the error objects passed to console.log may contain sensitive information such as user credentials, email addresses, or internal server details. In a browser environment, console.log output is accessible to any scripts running on the page and to browser extensions. Additionally, using console.log for error handling is not a proper security logging mechanism — it provides no structured logging, no alerting, and no tamper resistance. The test verifies this behavior exists in the component; the actual logging call is in RegisterComponent.

description: The NavbarComponent logs raw error objects directly to the browser console when backend API calls fail (application version, user identity, application configuration, and score board status). These tests confirm the production behavior: errors from backend services are passed verbatim to console.log(). In a production environment this exposes internal error messages, potential stack traces, backend structure details, and possibly sensitive data to any user or attacker who opens browser developer tools. Security-relevant events such as authentication failures and configuration retrieval failures should not be surfaced to end users in raw form.

title: Authentication state determined solely by token presence in localStorage without validation
description: The isLoggedIn() method returns the raw token string from localStorage without any validation of its contents, structure, expiration, or signature. The test at line 503-504 demonstrates that setting an arbitrary string 'abc' as the token causes isLoggedIn() to return 'abc' (truthy), meaning the component treats any non-empty localStorage entry as a valid authenticated session. This enables an attacker to forge an authenticated state by placing any arbitrary value in localStorage, potentially unlocking authenticated-only UI elements and client-side behaviors. While the backend may independently validate tokens, the client-side authentication state is trivially spoofable.

title: Client-side role-based access control via decoded token without server-side verification
description: The isAccounting() method determines the user's role by decoding the authentication token client-side and checking the 'role' field. The tests at lines 508-521 confirm this behavior: when the decoded token contains data.role='accounting', isAccounting() returns true. Client-side role checks are inherently bypassable because an attacker can modify the localStorage token, intercept the tokenDecode function, or manipulate the client-side state to assume any role. This is a Broken Function Level Authorization pattern where the frontend grants access to accounting features based on a client-decoded role claim that can be tampered with. The server should independently verify the user's role before serving accounting-related data or allowing accounting operations.

An attacker who controls the token in localStorage (as shown in the isLoggedIn test at line 503) can craft a token with role='accounting' to bypass this client-side access control check.

title: MIME type validation relies solely on 4-byte magic number check, trivially bypassable
description: The validator reads only the first 4 bytes of an uploaded file (lines 20-25) and compares them against a hardcoded list of PNG and JPEG magic numbers (lines 26-40). An attacker can prepend valid magic bytes (e.g., `89 50 4e 47` for PNG) to any arbitrary file content — such as an HTML file with JavaScript, a polyglot file, or a file with an embedded payload — and this validator will accept it as a valid image (line 41-42). The design never validates the full file structure, does not check file extensions against content, and does not verify that the remainder of the file is a well-formed image. If this client-side validator is the only check (or if the server trusts the client's validation result), an attacker can upload arbitrary content disguised as a permitted image type. Even as a purely client-side convenience check, the 4-byte-only approach gives a false sense of security because it cannot distinguish a real image from a spoofed header on arbitrary data.

The 4-byte header is compared against known PNG and JPEG magic numbers. A match sets isValid=true regardless of what the rest of the file contains.

The function checks `typeof (control.value) === 'string'`. For File objects this is false, so execution continues to the magic-number check path. (The string path at line 13 is a separate bypass, covered in another finding.)
The attacker-controlled value is cast to `File` and bound to the `file` variable.
A `FileReader` is instantiated to read the file contents.
An Observable is created wrapping the asynchronous file-reading and validation logic.
A `loadend` event listener is registered on the FileReader. When the file finishes loading, the callback runs the validation logic.
A `header` string is initialized empty, to be populated with the hex representation of the 4 bytes.
`isValid` is initialized to false. It will only be set true if the 4-byte header matches a known image magic number.
A for-of loop begins iterating over the 4-byte array.
Each byte is converted to a hex string and appended to `header`. After the loop, `header` contains the 8-character hex representation of the first 4 bytes.
Case '89504e47' (PNG magic) sets isValid=true. An attacker who prepends these 4 bytes to any payload matches this case.
JPEG magic number cases (ffd8ffe0 through ffd8ffe8) also set isValid=true. Same spoofing technique applies.
The default case sets isValid=false for any header not matching the hardcoded list. This is the only rejection path.

The function returns `of(null)` immediately, which Angular treats as 'no validation error.' All MIME type checking is skipped. The string value — whatever it contains — passes validation as if it were a valid image.

When isValid is true, observer.next(null) is called, signaling the form that the file is valid. An attacker who prepends e.g. '89504e47' to any payload passes validation. No full-file-structure validation, no extension cross-check, and no server-side re-validation is invoked from this code path.

The complete absence of any logging in this validator means there is no audit trail for upload validation failures. If the server-side handler also lacks logging (which cannot be confirmed from this file), there is no way to detect or reconstruct an attack timeline involving malicious file upload attempts. This is a frontend validator, so the more critical gap would be server-side; however, the file presents no logging whatsoever on the rejection path.
