title: Progress restoration trusts client-controlled cookie values without integrity verification
description: The component reads 'continueCode', 'continueCodeFindIt', and 'continueCodeFixIt' from cookies and sends them directly to backend restore-progress endpoints. These codes represent the user's earned hacking progress (solved challenges). The client performs no integrity check on these values — they are read from an unprotected cookie, URL-encoded, and submitted. If the backend accepts a continueCode without cryptographic verification (e.g., signature, HMAC), an attacker can forge a code to restore progress for challenges they never solved, gaining credit and potentially bypassing the challenge-solving workflow entirely. Even if the server does validate, the client-side design stores progress-restoration credentials in cookies without any visible security attributes or integrity protection, making them trivially readable and modifiable by the user or any XSS payload. The automatic restoration on every 'server started' event means a forged cookie will be submitted without any user interaction.

The raw cookie value is URL-encoded and passed to challengeService.restoreProgress(). The continueCode functions as an authentication credential for progress restoration — it proves (or should prove) that the user legitimately earned the progress being restored. The identical pattern applies to restoreProgressFindIt (line 68) and restoreProgressFixIt (line 77).

The if (continueCode) conditional is the only gate before the value is sent to the backend. It checks only for presence/truthiness — it does not verify origin, signature, format, or integrity. A forged cookie value passes this check identically to a legitimate one.

The client-controlled, integrity-unverified continueCode is sent to the backend as the sole basis for restoring solved-challenge progress. The design places complete trust in a client-editable cookie value. If the backend does not cryptographically verify the code (the file provides no evidence of signing or MAC verification on the client side), an attacker can forge a continueCode cookie with arbitrary challenge-solving claims, submit it via this automatic restore flow, and receive credit for unsolved challenges. This is an insecure-design issue (trusting client-controlled state for a server-side decision about earned progress) and, if the code is unsigned, a crypto-auth issue (missing integrity protection on a credential used for authentication of progress).

RouterModule.forChild(routes) registers the unguarded route. If no parent-level or global guard protects this path, the Web3SandboxComponent is accessible without authentication, allowing unauthenticated access to Web3/blockchain sandbox functionality.

title: CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA disables Angular's strict element validation
description: The module declares schemas: [CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA], which instructs Angular to silently accept any unknown element tag in templates without error. While this is a legitimate Angular feature for integrating Web Components, it also means Angular will not flag unexpected or potentially malicious elements injected into the DOM. This is a permissive configuration that trades safety checking for flexibility. The impact is limited since this is client-side, but it weakens the framework's built-in validation that could catch template injection or unexpected element rendering.

trace.description: The @NgModule decorator begins the module configuration. The caller (Angular's module system) is outside this file.
schemas: [CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA] is declared, disabling Angular's strict element-name validation for all templates in this module. Any element name will be accepted without warning.

title: Client-controlled wallet amount stored in sessionStorage and trusted by payment flow
description: The wallet component allows the user to enter an amount (validated only client-side with min=10, max=1000) and then stores that raw client-supplied value directly into sessionStorage under the key 'walletTotal' before navigating to the payment route. sessionStorage is fully controlled by the client — an attacker can call sessionStorage.setItem('walletTotal', '999999') from the browser console and bypass the Angular Validators entirely. If the subsequent payment flow (outside this file) trusts this sessionStorage value as the amount to charge or credit, the design permits the client to dictate a financial quantity that the server should derive or validate. This is a trust-assumption violation: the server-side balance and transaction logic should re-derive the wallet amount rather than accepting a client-stored value.

trace.description: balanceControl is an UntypedFormControl with only client-side Angular Validators (min 10, max 1000). These validators run in the browser and are trivially bypassed by directly manipulating sessionStorage or the form control value.
The continue() method reads this.balanceControl.value — the raw, user-entered amount — without any server-side re-validation of the value against the actual wallet balance.

this.balanceControl.value is stored directly into sessionStorage as 'walletTotal' and the user is navigated to /payment/wallet. Since sessionStorage is entirely client-controlled, an attacker can set an arbitrary walletTotal value (e.g., '999999') before or after this call, bypassing the min/max validators. The payment flow that receives this value is outside this file, but this component is where the client-controlled financial amount enters the flow.

title: Wallet balance fetch failure logged to browser console instead of application security log
description: When the walletService.get() call fails (line 33-40), the error is written only to the browser console via console.log(err). This is a client-side component, so this logging is not a server-side security log. If a user tampers with requests or if an access-control violation occurs on the wallet endpoint (e.g., another user's wallet is accessed), there is no security-relevant logging visible in this component. While this is a frontend component and server-side logging may exist elsewhere, the error handler here swallows failures without any structured error handling or user-facing feedback, making it harder to detect or investigate anomalous wallet access patterns from the client perspective.

trace.description: walletService.get() is called on component initialization to fetch the user's wallet balance. If this call fails, it could indicate an access-control violation, a tampered request, or an anomalous condition.

The error callback is defined: error: (err) => { ... }. The error object from the failed wallet fetch is received here as the parameter 'err' — this is the point where the component decides what to do with the failure.

The error handler simply calls console.log(err), logging to the browser developer console. No structured security event is generated, no alert is surfaced, and no correlation ID or user context is captured. Failed wallet access attempts are effectively invisible to security monitoring from this component's perspective.

title: Wallet balance fetch has no visible ownership/authorization scoping in this component
description: The walletService.get() call on line 33 fetches a wallet balance without any visible parameter indicating which user's wallet is being requested. If the underlying service or API endpoint (outside this file) accepts a user identifier from the request rather than deriving it from the authenticated session, a user could potentially access another user's wallet balance (BOLA). From this file alone we cannot confirm whether the backend properly scopes the query to the current user — the call passes no resource identifier, which is ambiguous. If the backend derives the user from the session, this is safe; if it accepts a user ID from headers/params, this is exploitable. This finding is flagged at low confidence because the authorization check, if any, exists in a different file.

trace.description: this.walletService.get() is called with no arguments — no user ID, no wallet ID, no ownership token. The caller (this component) provides no resource identifier and no authorization context. Whether the backend correctly scopes the result to the authenticated user cannot be determined from this file.

The next callback receives the returned balance as its parameter: next: (balance) => { ... }. The balance value arrives here from the service call without any ownership verification having occurred in this component.

The returned balance is directly assigned to this.balance and rendered to the user. If the backend service does not verify ownership, any authenticated user could receive another user's wallet balance. The ownership check, if it exists, is entirely in the WalletService or backend (outside this file).

title: Raw error object logged to browser console in production code
description: The component fetches user details (potentially including PII such as email, name, and other profile data) via userService.get(), but there is no security-relevant logging on either the success or error path. On success (line 34), the user data is simply assigned to this.user with no audit log of who accessed whose profile. On error (line 36), only a console.log is used, which is client-side only and not persisted or monitored. If a user can fetch arbitrary users' details (as noted in the IDOR finding above), there is no server-side audit trail to detect or investigate unauthorized access to user PII. The absence of logging for a data-access operation on potentially sensitive user records means security incidents involving unauthorized profile viewing cannot be detected or reconstructed.

title: User detail fetch uses client-supplied ID without server-side authorization enforcement visible in this component
description: The component receives an ID from MAT_DIALOG_DATA (injected dialog data, line 26) and passes it directly to userService.get() (line 32) without any validation or authorization check within this component. The dialog data is provided by whatever component opens this dialog — the caller is outside this file. An attacker who can influence the dialog data (e.g., by manipulating client-side state, modifying the Angular component's inputs through browser dev tools, or crafting the dialog-opening call) can substitute an arbitrary user ID and retrieve details for any user. The design assumes the client will always pass the correct, authorized user ID, rather than enforcing on the server that the requesting user is permitted to view the requested user's details. While the server may enforce this separately, the component's design provides no compensating control and trusts client-provided input for access scoping.

this.user = user stores the fetched user details, which are then rendered in the component's template. The design trusts the client to supply the correct ID rather than deriving it server-side from the authenticated session.

The only 'logging' is console.log(err) on the error path — a browser-only, non-persistent, non-monitored output. On the success path (line 34), there is no logging at all. Neither path creates a security audit record of user detail access.

title: Backend API errors logged to browser console exposing internal error details
description: The WalletComponent logs raw errors from the backend wallet balance API directly to the browser console via console.log. The test on lines 103-108 confirms this is by design: it mocks the wallet service to return an error and then asserts that console.log was called with the error value. The browser console is an exposed log surface accessible to any user with browser developer tools. API errors can contain sensitive internal details such as stack traces, database error messages, internal endpoint paths, or authentication-related information. This creates an information disclosure risk where an attacker can trigger API errors and inspect the console to learn about backend internals. Additionally, if the error object contains sensitive user data (e.g., balance information, account identifiers), that data would be written in plaintext to the browser console.

title: Wallet balance amount validated only on client side without evidence of server-side enforcement
description: The tests on lines 80-94 verify that the WalletComponent's balanceControl enforces a required value and a range of [10, 1000]. This is client-side validation only, performed in the Angular reactive form. The design pattern revealed here — where the client enforces amount bounds and the server presumably receives the already-validated value — is a classic trust boundary violation. An attacker can bypass the client-side form validation by crafting a direct API request to the wallet endpoint with an amount outside the [10, 1000] range (e.g., a negative amount that could increase balance, or an extremely large amount). Without server-side re-validation, the client-controlled amount becomes the source of truth for a financial operation. This test file only proves client-side validation exists; it does not test or confirm any server-side equivalent, which is exactly the gap an insecure design creates.

The test sets balanceControl.setValue(-1) and expects it to be invalid (line 87), then sets 10000000000 and expects invalid (line 89). This confirms validation is performed entirely within the client-side reactive form before any submission to the backend.

walletService.put is mocked here, representing the backend submission path that would receive the amount. Since only client-side validation is verified in this test suite and no server-side re-validation is evident, an attacker can bypass the client form and submit arbitrary amounts directly to this backend interface, demonstrating a trust boundary violation and insecure design.
The WalletComponent instance is created from TestBed. This component contains the reactive form and balanceControl that performs the client-side validation being tested.

The test confirms that only values 10 (line 90) and 1000 (line 92) are accepted by the form. However, this validation is client-side only. The walletService.put (mocked at line 36) would carry the amount to the backend, and there is no evidence in this test suite that the server independently re-validates the amount. An attacker bypassing the client form can submit arbitrary amounts directly to the API, potentially creating economic imbalances (negative amounts, over-limit credits).

title: Authentication token stored in cookie without secure, httpOnly, or sameSite flags
description: The 2FA token is validated client-side using Angular form validators (minLength 6, maxLength 6, required, pattern matching 6 digits) on line 43. The verify() method then passes this.client-validated token directly to the service. While the service call is outside this file, the component design trusts that the form validation is sufficient and provides no additional defense. A client can bypass the form validators entirely by calling twoFactorAuthService.verify() directly with any value, enabling brute-force attempts with arbitrary token formats or rapid submissions. The component also shows no rate-limiting or lockout mechanism on failed attempts (the error handler just resets the error flag after 5 seconds), which permits unlimited 2FA brute-force attempts. This is an insecure design (no compensating control for a risky operation — MFA verification) and an authentication weakness (bypassable MFA enforcement).

The token is first stored in localStorage, making it accessible to any JavaScript running in the page origin (XSS-accessible).
The verify() method is the entrypoint. It is called from the component's template (outside this file) when the user submits the 6-digit token.
The form values are extracted into fields: TokenEnterFormFields = this.twoFactorForm.value, making the user-entered token available as fields.token.
The next callback (authentication) => { ... } receives the authentication response containing authentication.token and authentication.bid.

token: new UntypedFormControl('', [Validators.minLength(6), Validators.maxLength(6), Validators.required, Validators.pattern('^[\\d]{6}$')]) configures the token field with client-side validators only. These validators run in the browser DOM and are trivially bypassable by calling verify() programmatically or by modifying the form value directly.

The error callback: (error) => { ... } handles verification failure. This is the path taken on every incorrect token guess. There is no counter increment, no exponential backoff, no lockout — the callback simply sets a UI flag.

this.errored = true is the only consequence of a failed attempt. Combined with the setTimeout on line 65 that resets it after 5 seconds, the component is immediately ready to accept another guess. There is no rate limiting, no lockout, and no attempt counter — the design permits unlimited brute-force attempts against the 2FA token.

The token is also written to a cookie with this.cookieService.put('token', authentication.token, { expires }) — the options object specifies only 'expires' and omits 'secure', 'sameSite', and 'httpOnly'. The auth token is therefore transmittable over cleartext HTTP and readable by client-side scripts.

title: No security logging of 2FA verification success or failure
description: The verify() method handles both successful and failed 2FA token verification but logs neither event. Failed 2FA attempts are a critical security signal — they may indicate an attacker who has stolen the password attempting to brute-force the second factor. The error handler (lines 63-69) simply sets a UI error flag and clears it after 5 seconds with no logging. The success handler (lines 52-61) stores tokens and redirects with no logging. Without logging these events, the application cannot detect or investigate brute-force attacks against 2FA, credential stuffing that has progressed past the password stage, or account takeover attempts.

The token is sent to twoFactorAuthService.verify(). Both the 'next' (success) and 'error' (failure) callbacks are defined.
const fields: TokenEnterFormFields = this.twoFactorForm.value extracts the token from the form for submission.
The success path: next: (authentication) => { ... } receives the authentication response. This is a successful 2FA verification — a security-relevant event — but no logging is performed.
this.userService.isLoggedIn.next(true) changes the application's login state to authenticated. This privilege/state transition occurs without any audit log entry.
await this.router.navigate(['/search']) redirects the now-authenticated user. The successful 2FA login completes with no security event recorded anywhere in this flow.
this.errored = true is the only action taken on failure — a UI display flag is set. No log entry, no counter, no alert.

setTimeout(() => { this.errored = false }, 5 * 1000) schedules the error flag to clear after 5 seconds. The failed 2FA attempt is silently discarded with no security event recorded, making brute-force attacks undetectable in logs.

The error callback (lines 63-69) handles failed 2FA verification by setting this.errored = true and scheduling its reset — no logging of the failed attempt, no counter increment, no alerting. The success callback (lines 52-61) similarly lacks any logging of the successful authentication event.

title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials in source code
description: The file embeds a valid email/password credential pair in plaintext: 'testing@juice-sh.op' (line 54) and 'IamUsedForTesting' (line 60). These are real authentication credentials for the application (the Exposed Credentials challenge asks users to find them in client-side bundles). Because they appear in source code that ships to or is accessible from the frontend, anyone who reads this file — or the compiled client-side bundle that includes it — obtains valid credentials and can authenticate without any brute-forcing or credential theft. This is both a cryptographic/authentication failure (hardcoded credentials enable authentication bypass) and a misconfiguration (secrets hardcoded in source code rather than loaded from a secure secret store or environment).

trace.description: The file exports `ExposedCredentialsInstruction`, a challenge instruction object that is part of the frontend bundle. The caller that mounts or renders this instruction is outside this file.
The instruction's `resolved` callback checks that the user has typed the email 'testing@juice-sh.op' into the #email input field, embedding the credential value directly in source.
The exported object's `hints` array holds the sequence of instruction steps. The credential literals are embedded inside two of these hint objects, making them part of the exported value.

The sixth hint object (the 'email field' step) is where the first credential value is introduced. Its `resolved` property on line 54 calls `waitForInputToHaveValue` with the hardcoded email address 'testing@juice-sh.op'.

The seventh hint object (the 'password field' step) is where the second credential value is introduced. Its `resolved` property on line 60 calls `waitForInputToHaveValue` with the hardcoded password 'IamUsedForTesting'.

The instruction's `resolved` callback checks that the user has typed the password 'IamUsedForTesting' into the #password input field. Together with the email on line 54, a complete, valid credential pair is hardcoded in plaintext in client-side source code. Anyone with access to the source or the compiled bundle can extract these credentials and authenticate to the application.

title: Hardcoded user password in frontend source code
description: Jim's plaintext password (`ncc-1701`) is embedded directly in a frontend TypeScript instruction file that gets compiled into the client-side JavaScript bundle. Any user who inspects the browser's downloaded assets (View Source, DevTools, or the compiled JS bundle) can extract this real credential and authenticate as Jim without any SQL injection or other attack. Hardcoding credentials in source code is a security misconfiguration (OWASP A05), and exposing a user's password in client-accessible code is an authentication failure (OWASP A02/A07) because it allows an attacker to bypass the authentication mechanism entirely by simply reading the password from the shipped code.

trace.description: The module exports `LoginJimInstruction`, a configuration object that is part of the frontend bundle shipped to every client browser. This object contains challenge hint data including embedded credential values.

The hint instruction for the password field calls `waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty('#password', 'ncc-1701')`. The second argument — the string literal `'ncc-1701'` — is Jim's actual plaintext password, hardcoded as a comparison value in the instruction configuration.
The exported object's `hints` property is an array of hint instruction objects. The credential value is carried inside one of these array elements, which will be serialized into the client bundle.
The hint element at this position in the `hints` array is the object whose `resolved` property will carry the hardcoded password. This is the object that instructs the user on the password field.

The `resolved` property of this hint object is set to the return value of the helper call on the next line. The resolved property is the control decision that determines when the hint is satisfied, and its argument carries the plaintext password.

The password `ncc-1701` is present in the compiled frontend JavaScript bundle. An attacker opens browser DevTools, searches the JS sources for password-like strings, finds `ncc-1701`, and uses it (along with Jim's email `jim@juice-sh.op` also visible on lines 67 and 90) to authenticate as Jim via the normal login flow — no injection or exploit required.

title: TOTP shared secret exposed in the DOM via data attribute
description: The spec asserts that the component renders the TOTP shared secret into a data attribute (`data-test-totp-secret`) on the initial-token input element. A TOTP shared secret is the seed from which all one-time codes are derived; exposing it in the DOM makes it readable by any JavaScript running in the page context — including browser extensions, third-party scripts, or the payload of an XSS. An attacker who reads this secret can clone the user's 2FA factor and generate valid codes independently, fully bypassing the second factor. The secret should never be present in the DOM; the QR code image itself is the intended delivery channel for the secret.

trace.description: The test mocks the 2FA status service to return `secret: 'super-secret'` when 2FA is not yet set up. The caller (the component's updateStatus method) is outside this file.
The test calls `component.updateStatus()`, which populates `component.totpSecret` from the service response. The test then calls `fixture.detectChanges()` to render the template.
The test calls `fixture.detectChanges()`, triggering Angular's change detection and causing the template to re-render with the now-populated `totpSecret` value.
The test queries the rendered DOM for the `#initialToken` input element, the element on which the secret is exposed via a data attribute.

The test asserts `input.getAttribute('data-test-totp-secret')` equals `'super-secret'`, confirming the component writes the TOTP shared secret into a DOM data attribute on the initial-token input element. This is the component under test exposing the secret in the rendered DOM.

title: TOTP secret delivered to client and used to construct otpauth URL in the browser
description: The spec reveals that the 2FA status API response includes the raw TOTP `secret` field, and that the component constructs the `otpauth://` provisioning URL entirely client-side using that secret. Delivering the shared secret as a raw value to the browser (as opposed to having the server generate and return only the QR code image or a signed provisioning URL) increases the attack surface: the secret is present in JavaScript memory, in network responses accessible via dev tools or MITM, and available for interception by any script in the page. This is an insecure design choice for 2FA provisioning — the server should retain control of secret generation and delivery.

The test calls `component.updateStatus()`, which stores the secret from the response into component state (`totpSecret`, `totpUrl`).

The test mocks `configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration` to return `{ application: { name: 'Test App' } }`, providing the application name that will later be embedded in the otpauth URL as the issuer and label.
The test asserts `component.setupStatus` is `false`, confirming that the component recognized 2FA is not yet configured and proceeded down the setup path that populates the TOTP secret and URL.

The test asserts `component.totpUrl` equals `'otpauth://totp/Test%20App:email?secret=secret&issuer=Test%20App'`, confirming the component constructs the full provisioning URL client-side using the raw secret received from the API.

title: Security-relevant 2FA status failure logged only via console.log
description: The spec asserts that when fetching the 2FA status fails, the component calls `console.log('Failed to fetch 2fa status')`. Using `console.log` for a security-relevant event means the failure is only visible in the browser's developer console — it is not sent to any server-side logging, monitoring, or alerting system. Failures in 2FA status retrieval could indicate tampering attempts, service disruption, or unauthorized access attempts, and the absence of server-side logging means security teams cannot detect or investigate such events. The event also lacks contextual detail (user identity, error details, correlation IDs).

The test replaces `console.log` with a spy (`console.log = vi.fn()`), indicating the component under test uses `console.log` as its logging mechanism for this error path.

The test calls `component.updateStatus()`, which subscribes to the status observable. The subscription's error handler (in the component, outside this file) receives the thrown error and invokes `console.log` with the failure message.

The test asserts `console.log` was called with the string `'Failed to fetch 2fa status'`. This confirms the component logs a security-relevant event (2FA status fetch failure) solely to the browser console with no structured logging, no error details, and no server-side reporting.

title: Wallet authentication sends address without cryptographic proof of ownership
description: The handleAuth() method connects to a MetaMask wallet, reads the account address, and sends it to the backend via keysService.walletAddressSend(). At no point does the code request the user to sign a challenge message or otherwise prove they control the private key for that address. The wallet address alone is sent as an authentication credential. Since the address is a public value visible on-chain and to anyone, an attacker can submit any wallet address to the backend endpoint and authenticate as that wallet's owner without possessing the private key. This bypasses identity verification entirely — the application trusts a self-reported public identifier as proof of identity.

trace.description: handleAuth() is the authentication entrypoint, called from ngOnInit() on component load and on chain change events.
The connected wallet address is read from provider.account and stored in this.metamaskAddress. This is a public identifier — it does not prove private key ownership.
const { isConnected } = getAccount() checks the current connection state from the wagmi client.
if (isConnected) conditional — if already connected, the flow proceeds to disconnect first, clearing any prior session.
await disconnect() tears down any existing connection before proceeding to re-authenticate.

const provider = await connect({ connector: new InjectedConnector() }) connects to the injected wallet (MetaMask). This returns a provider whose .account field is the wallet's public address — a value that is public and observable by anyone on-chain, not a secret.

this.keysService.walletAddressSend(this.metamaskAddress) sends the raw wallet address to the backend as an authentication credential. No signature challenge, no message signing, no proof-of-ownership step occurs anywhere in this flow. The backend (caller outside this file) receives only a public address and must decide identity from it. An attacker can call this same service with any victim's wallet address and impersonate them.

title: Transaction amount not validated before deposit and withdrawal operations
description: The depositETH() and withdrawETH() methods accept this.inputAmount directly from user form input without any validation. There is no check that the amount is positive, non-zero, within the user's balance, or bounded to a reasonable range. The value is parsed with ethers.utils.parseEther() and passed directly to the smart contract. A negative inputAmount would produce a negative BigInt value passed to the contract's ethdeposit or withdraw function. Depending on the contract logic, this could enable economic exploitation (e.g., depositing a negative amount that credits balance, or withdrawing a negative amount). Even if the contract rejects negative values, the absence of client-side validation for financial transactions is a design flaw that delegates safety entirely to the contract layer.

trace.description: inputAmount is declared as a nullable number bound to a form input via FormsModule. It accepts any numeric value from the user including negative, zero, or extremely large values.
In depositETH(), inputAmount is converted to a string: const depositAmount = this.inputAmount.toString(). No validation occurs — no positivity check, no upper bound, no balance comparison.
depositETH() is the method called to initiate a deposit transaction. It reads this.inputAmount directly.
const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum) creates the Web3 provider for signing the transaction.
const contract = new ethers.Contract(BankAddress, web3WalletABI, signer) instantiates the contract interface that will receive the unvalidated amount.

The unvalidated amount is passed to ethers.utils.parseEther(depositAmount) and then to contract.ethdeposit(this.metamaskAddress, { value: ... }). The same pattern repeats in withdrawETH() at line 84-87 where withdrawalAmount is also unvalidated before being passed to contract.withdraw(ethers.utils.parseEther(withdrawalAmount)).

title: Sensitive error objects logged to browser console
description: The handleAuth() method catches errors and logs the full error object to the console via console.log(err) at line 169, and the wallet address submission error handler logs via console.error(error) at line 132. In a Web3 context, error objects from ethers.js and MetaMask interactions can contain sensitive details such as wallet addresses, transaction hashes, RPC responses, and internal provider state. Console logging of these objects exposes sensitive information in the browser's developer console, which could be accessible to browser extensions or other scripts running on the page. Additionally, there is no structured security logging of authentication events (successful or failed wallet connections) for audit purposes — the only logging is ad-hoc console output.

trace.description: handleAuth() is the authentication flow entrypoint. Security-relevant events occur here: wallet connection, address submission to backend, chain switching.
const provider = await connect({ connector: new InjectedConnector() }) — the connect call can throw errors that propagate to the catch block.
this.metamaskAddress = provider.account — uses the provider result; if provider is malformed, this can throw.
this.keysService.walletAddressSend(this.metamaskAddress).subscribe(...) initiates the backend authentication call.
if (response.success) — the success path is handled silently: successResponse is set at line 127, but no security audit log of the successful authentication event is emitted.
error: (error) => { — the error handler for the walletAddressSend subscription is reached when the backend authentication call fails.
console.error(error) logs the full error object from the backend authentication call to the browser console. This can contain sensitive request/response details.
await ethereum.request({ method: 'wallet_addEthereumChain', ... }) — this MetaMask RPC call can also throw, and any error propagates to the catch block at line 168.

In the catch block, console.log(err) logs the full error object. Similarly at line 132, console.error(error) logs the error from the walletAddressSend subscription. No structured security logging occurs for successful authentication (line 126-129) or failed authentication. The authentication outcome at line 127 (response.success) is handled silently without any security audit log.

title: Authentication token stored in localStorage, accessible to XSS
description: The application stores the user's authentication token in localStorage (lines 67, 90, 95) and also in a cookie (line 96). Tokens in localStorage are fully accessible to any JavaScript running on the page, meaning a single cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability anywhere in the application or its third-party dependencies allows an attacker to exfiltrate the token and impersonate the user. Unlike HttpOnly cookies, localStorage provides no isolation barrier between the token and client-side script. The token is read directly on line 67 to determine if the user is logged in, and on line 90 in isLoggedIn(). This is a session management design flaw: the authentication token should be stored in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so it cannot be read by JavaScript.

trace.description: ngOnInit reads the authentication token directly from localStorage to decide whether to fetch user details. The caller is outside this file (Angular lifecycle), but the token retrieval and trust decision are here.
isLoggedIn() returns the raw localStorage token value as the sole indicator of authentication state.
If the token exists, getUserDetails() is called, propagating the authenticated state derived from the localStorage token.
getUserDetails() function definition, entered as a result of the token check.
this.userService.whoAmI(['email']) is called, which relies on the localStorage token being implicitly attached by an HTTP interceptor to authenticate the request.

logout() removes the token from localStorage and a cookie, confirming the token is the session credential. Because it lives in localStorage, any XSS can read and exfiltrate it, enabling session hijacking.

title: Client-side role check for accounting features relies on token decode without server-side enforcement visible
description: The isAccounting() method (lines 156-159) decodes the JWT token on the client side via loginGuard.tokenDecode() and checks whether the role claim equals the accounting role. This is a client-side authorization decision: the UI shows or hides accounting-related navigation items based on a value decoded from a token that the user controls. A user can modify their own token (or craft one) to include the accounting role, causing the client to display and potentially navigate to accounting features. If the server-side endpoints backing those features do not independently verify the caller's role, this is Broken Function Level Authorization. Even if the server does enforce, the client-side decode without signature verification (visible in the call to tokenDecode which returns data the code trusts) means an attacker can manipulate the displayed UI to discover accounting endpoints. The real risk is that this client-side check is the only authorization gate visible in this file.

trace.description: isAccounting() is called to gate UI access to accounting features. The caller is outside this file (Angular template binding), but the authorization decision is made here.
loginGuard.tokenDecode() decodes the JWT payload client-side. No signature verification is visible in this file; the decoded payload is treated as trusted.

The role claim from the decoded token is compared to roles.accounting. Because the token is user-controlled and decoded without visible verification, an attacker can set an arbitrary role claim to pass this check and access accounting UI features.

title: Error objects logged to console in production code
description: Multiple error handlers throughout the component call console.log(err) with the full error object (lines 62, 94, 122, 131, 152). In a production Angular build, console output is still visible in browser developer tools. These error objects can contain sensitive information such as internal API URLs, server-side stack traces, authentication details, and internal service names. Additionally, logging errors only to the browser console means security-relevant failures (e.g., failed version fetch, failed user detail fetch, failed configuration fetch) are not reported to any server-side monitoring system, leaving security teams unable to detect or investigate incidents. The logout handler (line 94) logs errors from saveLastLoginIp() to console rather than to a security logging pipeline.

trace.description: Error handler for getApplicationVersion() calls console.log(err), logging the full error object. Similar patterns repeat on lines 94, 122, 131, and 152.
The logout() method's saveLastLoginIp error handler also logs to console.log(err), potentially exposing details about the IP-tracking endpoint and any server errors.
this.administrationService.getApplicationVersion().subscribe({ initiates the version fetch which can fail.
The subscribe handler awaits the next value, but if an error occurs it goes to the error callback.
this.challengeService.find({ name: 'Score Board' }).subscribe({ initiates the challenge fetch.
error: (err) => { console.log(err) } logs the challenge fetch error to the console.
this.userService.whoAmI(['email']).subscribe({ initiates the user details fetch.
error: (err) => { console.log(err) } logs the user details fetch error to the console.
this.configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration().subscribe({ initiates the config fetch.

getApplicationDetails() error handler logs configuration fetch errors to console. Configuration errors may reveal internal service structure. All five console.log(err) instances (lines 62, 94, 122, 131, 152) expose error details in production and fail to route security-relevant failures to a monitoring system.

title: Security-relevant events (logout, login state change) lack security logging
description: The logout() method (lines 93-102) performs security-relevant actions — removing the authentication token, clearing session storage, and updating the login state — but does not log the logout event to any server-side security log. The only server interaction is saveLastLoginIp(), which records the last login IP but does not log the logout itself. Similarly, the login state subscription (lines 73-79) reacts to login/logout state changes but does not report these transitions to a security monitoring system. Without logging security events like logins and logouts, the application cannot maintain an audit trail for incident investigation or detect suspicious session activity (e.g., rapid login/logout cycles, concurrent sessions).

trace.description: logout() is the entrypoint for user-initiated session termination. The caller is outside this file (template event binding), but the logout logic is here.
this.userService.saveLastLoginIp().subscribe(... is called, which interacts with the server but only logs IP, not the logout event.
localStorage.removeItem('token') clears the token locally.
this.cookieService.remove('token') clears the cookie.
sessionStorage.removeItem('bid') clears session data.
sessionStorage.removeItem('itemTotal') clears more session data.
sessionStorage.removeItem('guestBasket') clears the final session data.

The logout flow clears tokens and session state (lines 95-99) and updates the login observable (line 100) but never reports the logout event to a server-side security log. The saveLastLoginIp call on line 94 records IP but not the logout action itself, leaving a gap in the security audit trail.

title: Hardcoded user password exposed in client-side source code
description: The instruction definition embeds what appears to be Bender's actual application password — 'OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!' — directly in the frontend source code on line 84. This value is passed as an argument to waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty, which waits for the password field to contain something other than this known value. Because this file ships in the client-side JavaScript bundle, any user who inspects the browser source or devtools can extract the credential and authenticate as Bender directly, bypassing the intended SQL injection challenge entirely. Hardcoding credentials in source code is both an authentication failure (credential exposure enabling direct login) and a security misconfiguration (secret material committed to source and shipped to clients).

trace.description: LoginBenderInstruction is an exported ChallengeInstruction object. As part of the frontend bundle, all of its string literals — including the one on line 84 — are visible to any user who inspects the client-side JavaScript in the browser.

The string literal 'OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!' is passed as the second argument to waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty('#password', ...). This value is Bender's real password, used here as the sentinel that the password field must NOT equal — confirming the tutorial author knows this is the valid credential.

hints: [ — the hints array property of LoginBenderInstruction. The hint containing the hardcoded password is an element of this array, so the password value is nested inside the exported object via this property.
{ — the opening of the specific hint object that targets the password input field. This object contains the resolved property on line 84 where the password literal is embedded.

fixture: '#password' — this hint is associated with the password input element, establishing that the resolved callback on the next line operates in the context of the password field, where the real credential is about to be referenced.

The hardcoded credential is shipped to every client in the JavaScript bundle. An attacker need only read the source to obtain 'OhG0dPlease1nsertLiquor!' and log in as bender@juice-sh.op directly at the login form, bypassing authentication without any SQL injection. This is both a hardcoded-secret misconfiguration and an authentication failure: the secret that should prove identity is publicly exposed.

title: Basket loaded using client-controlled basket ID from sessionStorage without ownership verification
description: The `load()` method reads a basket ID (`bid`) directly from `sessionStorage` and passes it to `basketService.find()` to fetch the user's basket. No check is performed to verify that the basket identified by this client-supplied ID belongs to the currently authenticated user. An attacker can modify the `bid` value in sessionStorage to an arbitrary integer and the component will fetch and display another user's basket contents (products, quantities, prices). Similarly, the `delete(id)` and `addToQuantity(id, value)` methods accept item IDs from the template (caller outside this file) and perform mutations — `basketService.del(id)` and `basketService.put(id, { quantity: newQuantity })` — without any per-resource ownership check. If the server-side API does not independently verify that the requesting user owns the basket or basket item identified by these IDs, this is a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability. The design flaw is that the basket identifier is client-controlled state rather than being derived server-side from the authenticated session.

trace.description: The `load()` method reads `sessionStorage.getItem('bid')`, a client-controlled value, parses it as an integer, and passes it as the resource identifier to `basketService.find()`. The caller (ngOnInit at line 52) is inside this file, but the `bid` value originates from client-side storage that an attacker can freely modify.

`parseInt(sessionStorage.getItem('bid'), 10)` produces an arbitrary integer controlled by the client. This value is passed directly to `this.basketService.find(...)` which issues a server request to retrieve the basket by that ID.

The response (`basket.Products`) is assigned to `this.dataSource` and rendered. No ownership check occurs between the lookup (line 77) and the use of the returned data. The same pattern applies to `delete(id)` at line 143 and `addToQuantity(id, value)` at lines 172 and 176, where item IDs received from the template are used for mutations without verifying the authenticated user owns those items.

The `next: (basket) => {` subscribe callback receives the basket object returned by the server. At this point the server has already returned data for whatever basket ID the client supplied, with no indication that ownership was verified. The basket object flows into the callback body for further processing.

`if (this.isDeluxe())` is a conditional branch that gates whether deluxe pricing is applied. This check is about the current user's membership tier, not about whether the user owns the basket. It does not constitute an ownership verification — it operates on data that was already fetched without authorization.

`basket.Products.forEach(product => { product.price = product.deluxePrice })` modifies the price field on each product in the fetched basket. This loop processes the unauthorized basket data, iterating over products that may belong to another user's basket.

`this.basketService.find(parseInt(sessionStorage.getItem('bid'), 10))` fetches a basket by a client-controlled ID with no ownership verification. An attacker substitutes another user's basket ID in sessionStorage to view their basket. Likewise, `this.basketService.del(id)` (line 143) and `this.basketService.put(id, ...)` (line 176) mutate basket items by caller-supplied ID without per-resource authorization.

title: Basket item mutations (delete, quantity change) accept arbitrary item IDs without ownership checks
description: The `delete(id)`, `inc(id)`, `dec(id)`, and `addToQuantity(id, value)` methods accept an item ID from the caller (the Angular template, outside this file) and perform server-side mutations — deletion and quantity updates — on that item. Neither method verifies that the item ID belongs to the current user's basket before issuing the request. An attacker who knows or guesses another user's basket item IDs could delete items from or modify quantities in another user's basket by invoking these functions with the victim's item IDs.

trace.description: `delete(id)` receives an `id` parameter from the template (caller outside this file). The parameter is a basket item identifier with no validation or ownership context attached.

The `id` is passed directly to `this.basketService.del(id)` which issues a DELETE request. No check verifies the authenticated user owns this basket item. The same pattern exists in `addToQuantity` (line 160) where `id` flows to `this.basketService.get(id)` (line 172) and `this.basketService.put(id, { quantity: newQuantity })` (line 176) without ownership verification.

`if (localStorage.getItem('token') == null)` checks only whether the user is authenticated (has a token). This is an authentication gate, not an authorization check — it verifies that a token exists but does not verify that the user owns the basket item identified by `id`. The authenticated path continues to line 143.
`addToQuantity(id, value)` shows the same pattern for quantity mutations. It receives an `id` from the caller (template, outside this file) with no ownership context.
`if (localStorage.getItem('token') == null)` in `addToQuantity` is again only an authentication check — it gates the authenticated path but does not verify ownership of the basket item.

`this.basketService.get(id).subscribe(...)` fetches the basket item by the caller-supplied `id`. The server returns the item data without any indication that ownership was verified — the same BOLA pattern as the basket fetch.

`const newQuantity = basketItem.quantity + value` computes a new quantity from the fetched item data. The item was retrieved using a caller-supplied ID with no ownership check, so this quantity applies to a potentially unauthorized item.

`this.basketService.put(id, { quantity: newQuantity < 1 ? 1 : newQuantity })` issues a PUT request to update the quantity of the basket item identified by the caller-supplied `id`. The quantity is clamped to a minimum of 1, but no ownership check is performed on the item ID.

`this.basketService.del(id)` deletes a basket item by caller-supplied ID. If the server does not verify ownership, an attacker can delete or modify items in another user's basket by supplying the victim's item ID. The `put` call at line 176 has the same issue for quantity modifications.

title: Full error objects logged to console in multiple error handlers
description: Multiple error handlers throughout the component log the complete error object via `console.log(err)`. HTTP error responses can contain sensitive server-side information including internal paths, stack traces, database error details, or authentication-related data. In a browser environment, console output is accessible to any script running on the page and to browser extensions. While this is client-side logging, the error objects originate from server responses (via the basket, user, and product services) and may leak server internals. The pattern repeats at lines 66, 91, 132, 148, 183, and 187.

trace.description: Error handler in `userService.whoAmI` subscription logs the full error: `console.log(err)`. The same pattern appears at lines 91, 132, 148, 183, and 187. These errors are HTTP response objects from server API calls that may contain sensitive server-side details.

`this.userService.whoAmI(['email']).subscribe({...})` initiates the server API call whose error response becomes the `err` object. The subscription sets up the success and error callbacks that will receive the server's response.

`error: (err) => {` defines the error callback that receives the full HTTP error response object from the server. This `err` object may contain server-side stack traces, internal paths, database error messages, or other sensitive details embedded in the response body and headers.

`console.log(err)` writes the complete error object — including potentially sensitive server response data — to the browser console. Lines 91, 132, 148, 183, and 187 repeat this pattern across basket loading, guest basket loading, deletion, and quantity update operations.

title: Feedback form exposes a client-controllable userId field, enabling feedback forgery
description: This challenge-instruction file confirms that the application's Customer Feedback form renders a hidden `userId` input field in the DOM (accessed at lines 59 and 61 via `document.getElementById('userId')`). The very existence of this field means the server accepts a client-provided user identity when recording feedback authorship, rather than deriving the author from the authenticated session on the server side. An attacker can open DevTools, change the hidden `userId` value to another user's ID, and submit feedback that is attributed to that other user. This is a trust assumption violation: the client controls a value (the author identity) that the server should independently determine from the session token. The file explicitly walks through this attack (lines 53-73), confirming the design flaw is exploitable. The actual vulnerable implementation lives in the feedback form component and the backend feedback API, which are outside this file; this file interacts with the DOM element and thereby confirms the field is present and mutable.

trace.description: The file reads `document.getElementById('userId')` from the feedback form DOM. This field originates outside this file — it is rendered by the application's feedback form component. The presence of a `userId` DOM element in the feedback form indicates the application places a client-controllable user-identity field into the form.

The code checks whether the `userId` field's `.value` has changed from its original value, confirming the field is freely mutable by the user in the browser. This establishes that the client can arbitrarily set the author identity before form submission.

The code enters a `while (true)` polling loop. This loop is the control mechanism that watches the `userId` DOM element for any modification made by the user in the browser. No validation is performed on what the new value might be — any change at all is accepted.

The `break` statement exits the polling loop once any change to `userId` is detected. This is the control decision that lets the flow proceed: the code accepts an arbitrary client-supplied user identity and moves on to instruct the user to submit the form.

The `await sleep(100)` call is the polling interval inside the loop body. While not directly manipulating the value, it is part of the control-flow path the mutated `userId` passes through — the loop repeatedly re-reads the DOM value every 100ms until the change is detected.

The instruction tells the user to submit the form (`waitForElementToGetClicked('#submitButton')`), which sends the manipulated `userId` to the server. The server's feedback endpoint (outside this file) accepts this client-supplied `userId` and records the feedback as authored by the impersonated user, completing the forgery.

title: Hardcoded weak admin credentials embedded in client-side source code
description: This file is a client-side tutorial ('hacking instructor') that walks a user through logging in as the administrator. In doing so, it hardcodes the administrator's email address and password directly in the source code. On line 43 the admin email 'admin@juice-sh.op' is embedded as the expected input value. On lines 55, 61, 67, and 73 the password is progressively revealed, building from 'admin' to 'admin1' to 'admin12' to 'admin123'. These are not placeholder values — they are the actual administrative credentials for the application, and any user who can read this source file (which ships to the browser in a frontend bundle) obtains full admin credentials without any exploitation at all. From a misconfiguration standpoint, hardcoded credentials in source code are always a finding regardless of usage context. From a crypto-auth standpoint, the admin account uses an extremely weak, trivially guessable password ('admin123') for an administrative account, and that credential is furthermore exposed in plaintext in source code delivered to every client.

trace.description: The exported object PasswordStrengthInstruction is a client-side instruction definition that ships in the frontend bundle. Any user can inspect the bundled JavaScript to read its contents.
The admin email address 'admin@juice-sh.op' is hardcoded as the expected value for the email input field, exposing the administrative account's username in client-accessible source.
The hints array contains all tutorial steps, including those that embed the admin email and progressively reveal the admin password.
The hint object beginning at this line is the one that will contain the admin email address as its expected input value.
The hint object beginning at this line starts the password progression, telling the user to try any password and then providing feedback that guides them toward the correct one.
The first password fragment 'admin' is hardcoded as the expected value via waitForInputToHaveValue('#password', 'admin'), beginning the progressive exposure of the admin password.
The hint object beginning at this line continues the password progression, telling the user to add non-letter characters.
The second password fragment 'admin1' is hardcoded as the expected value via waitForInputToHaveValue('#password', 'admin1'), further narrowing the password.
The hint object beginning at this line continues the password progression, telling the user to add more numbers.
The third password fragment 'admin12' is hardcoded as the expected value via waitForInputToHaveValue('#password', 'admin12'), further narrowing the password.
The hint object beginning at this line continues the password progression, telling the user to add one more digit.

The admin password 'admin123' is hardcoded as the expected value for the password input field (built up progressively through lines 55 'admin', 61 'admin1', 67 'admin12', and 73 'admin123'). This exposes the complete administrative credentials — both email and password — in plaintext in client-side source code. An attacker who reads the bundle obtains admin login credentials directly, bypassing all authentication.

title: Stored XSS via configuration-controlled welcome banner message
description:
The `message` property is initialized with raw HTML (line 28) and then overwritten with data from an external configuration source (line 39). The `ConfigurationService.getApplicationConfiguration()` call fetches application configuration that includes `welcomeBanner.message`. Since the message contains HTML markup (`

`, ``, `` tags), it is almost certainly rendered via `innerHTML` or a similar binding in the template file (outside this file). If the configuration endpoint allows any user or admin to modify the welcome banner message — which in Juice Shop's architecture is a known attack surface — an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript that will execute in the browser of every user who sees the welcome banner. The persistence point is in this file (line 39); the render sink is in the template, which is outside this file.

trace.description: ngOnInit() calls this.configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration(), receiving external configuration data. The caller (ConfigurationService) is outside this file; this is where outside data enters the component.

config.application.welcomeBanner.message is assigned directly to this.message with no sanitization, encoding, or validation. The property is typed as a plain string but its initial value on line 28 demonstrates it is expected to contain raw HTML markup.
next: (config) => { — the subscribe callback receives the config object. The full configuration object is now available inside the component.

if (config?.application?.welcomeBanner) { — conditional check that gates whether the external message value continues to be assigned. If welcomeBanner exists in config, the flow proceeds; there is no validation of the message content here.

this.message is initialized with raw HTML containing

, , and tags, confirming it is rendered as HTML (not plain text) in the template. The actual rendering sink (innerHTML binding or similar) is in welcome-banner.component.html, which is outside this file. Configuration-controlled HTML content rendered without sanitization is a stored XSS vector: an attacker who can modify the application configuration injects script that executes for all users viewing the welcome banner.

title: Cookie set without Secure, SameSite, or path attributes
description: The `closeWelcome()` method sets the `welcomebanner_status` cookie with only an `expires` option. No `secure: true` flag is set, meaning the cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. No `sameSite` attribute is set, leaving the cookie with the browser default (which varies) and potentially allowing cross-site request inclusion. While this cookie only stores 'dismiss' and carries no sensitive data, the absence of security flags is a misconfiguration pattern that should be corrected, particularly the lack of a SameSite attribute which provides defense-in-depth against CSRF scenarios.

trace.description: closeWelcome() is a public method that sets a cookie. It is called from startHackingInstructor() (line 53) and is also invokable from the template (dismiss button).
private readonly welcomeBannerStatusCookieKey = 'welcomebanner_status' — the cookie key is defined as a class field. This constant is the first argument passed to cookieService.put().

const expires = new Date() — begins constructing the options object that will be passed to the cookie setter. Only an expiry date is being prepared; no secure, sameSite, or path attributes are introduced at this point.
expires.setFullYear(expires.getFullYear() + 1) — sets the expiry to one year in the future. The options object now contains only the expires field. No security-related cookie attributes are added.

this.cookieService.put() is called with the cookie key 'welcomebanner_status', value 'dismiss', and an options object containing only { expires }. No secure, sameSite, or path attributes are specified. The cookie is set without transport security constraints (no Secure flag) and without cross-site protection (no SameSite attribute).

title: Tutorial-first restriction enforced only client-side
description: When `restrictToTutorialsFirst` and `showHackingInstructor` are both enabled in the configuration, the component disables the dialog close button and hides the dismiss button (lines 44-45). This restriction is enforced entirely on the client side. A user can bypass it by: (1) calling `closeWelcome()` directly from the browser console, which sets the cookie and closes the dialog; (2) manually setting the `welcomebanner_status` cookie to 'dismiss' and reloading; or (3) manipulating the DOM to re-enable the close button. The design relies on client-side UI state to enforce a workflow ordering constraint (tutorials must be completed first), but the server has no corresponding enforcement. The `closeWelcome()` method is public and unguarded — any caller can invoke it regardless of the restriction state.

trace.description: ngOnInit() checks config.challenges.restrictToTutorialsFirst and config.hackingInstructor.isEnabled. When both are true, it sets this.dialogRef.disableClose = true and this.showDismissBtn = false to prevent the user from dismissing the welcome banner before completing tutorials. This is the only enforcement of the tutorial-first constraint.
ngOnInit (): void { — the component lifecycle hook where the tutorial-first restriction is established. This is where external configuration data enters the component to set up the restriction.
this.configurationService.getApplicationConfiguration().subscribe({ — fetches external configuration that includes the restrictToTutorialsFirst and hackingInstructor flags.
next: (config) => { — the subscribe callback receives the config object containing the flags that determine whether the tutorial-first restriction should be enforced.
this.showHackingInstructor = config?.hackingInstructor?.isEnabled — reads the hackingInstructor isEnabled flag from configuration and stores it as component state.
this.dialogRef.disableClose = true — enforces the restriction by disabling the dialog's close button. This is a client-side UI control only.
this.showDismissBtn = false — hides the dismiss button as a second client-side enforcement mechanism. Both enforcement mechanisms are UI-state-only.

startHackingInstructor () { — a public method that calls this.closeWelcome() on line 53. This demonstrates that closeWelcome() is callable from within the component's own public API. More importantly, closeWelcome() itself is a public method callable from the Angular component instance, bypassing the UI restrictions.
this.closeWelcome() — calls the closeWelcome method directly, which unconditionally closes the dialog and sets the dismissal cookie. This call site does not check restrictToTutorialsFirst.

closeWelcome() is a public method (no access modifier, line 52 shows the same pattern with startHackingInstructor being public) that unconditionally closes the dialog and sets the dismissal cookie. It performs no check of the restrictToTutorialsFirst flag or the showHackingInstructor state. Any user can invoke this method directly from the console (e.g., via Angular's component reference) to bypass the tutorial-first restriction. The design places a workflow-ordering constraint in client-side UI state with no server-side enforcement, and the bypass method is publicly callable.

title: Bootstrap errors logged only to browser console without monitoring integration or production sanitization
description: The application's bootstrap promise rejection handler on line 130 calls `console.log(err)` to handle bootstrap failures. In production, this writes the full Error object — potentially including stack traces, internal module paths, and configuration details — to the browser console where it is visible to any user with devtools open. Simultaneously, no error is forwarded to any remote logging, monitoring, or observability service (e.g., Sentry, a custom logging endpoint). This means the development and security teams have no visibility into client-side bootstrap failures, including failures that could result from security-relevant issues such as corrupted configuration, failed authentication module initialization, or tampered assets. title: Logger uses format without timestamps, preventing attack timeline reconstruction
description: The winston logger is configured with `winston.format.simple()` on line 12. The `simple` format outputs only `level: message` — it omits timestamps entirely. For security logging and incident response, timestamps are essential to reconstruct the sequence and timing of events during an attack (e.g., correlating a series of failed login attempts with a subsequent successful one, or determining the order of privilege escalation steps). Without timestamps in the log output, any security events logged through this logger cannot be placed on a timeline, severely limiting the ability to detect, investigate, and respond to security incidents. This is a logging-monitoring design defect in the logger configuration itself — every log entry produced by this logger will lack a timestamp regardless of what callers log.

This is both a logging-monitoring defect (sensitive data exposure in logs) and a misconfiguration defect (the dangerous default of no redaction left active on a logger that handles application-wide logging).

title: Unencoded email interpolated into otpauth URL allows URL parameter injection
description: On line 77, the TOTP URL is constructed using template interpolation. While `encodedAppName` is properly URL-encoded via `encodeURIComponent`, the `email` value and the `secret` value are interpolated directly into the URL without any encoding. If the email contains URL-significant characters such as `&`, `#`, `?`, or `=`, an attacker can inject additional parameters into the otpauth URL or truncate/alter its structure. Since the email is typically user-controlled (users set their own email address during registration or profile updates), this is a URL injection that flows into the QR code rendered for 2FA setup. A malicious email like `attacker@evil.com&issuer=Evil` would override the issuer parameter, and an email containing `#` would truncate subsequent parameters such as `secret`.

title: Stored XSS via HTML entity decode after sanitizeHtml in challenge notification
description: The sendNotification function constructs a notification string that includes the challenge description. It first passes the description through sanitizeHtml with no allowed tags (stripping all HTML), but then immediately pipes the result through entities.decode(), which converts HTML entities back to their literal characters. This defeats the sanitization: an input like '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>' contains no actual HTML tags for sanitizeHtml to strip, but entities.decode converts it to '', producing live HTML in the notification string. This notification is then emitted to all connected Socket.IO clients via io.emit. If the client renders the 'challenge' field as HTML (e.g., via innerHTML), the decoded markup executes in the victim's browser. The challenge description is persisted through the POST /api/Challenges route (outside this file), making this a stored XSS where the persistence point and rendering sink are both outside this file, but the defective decode-after-sanitize logic is here.

trace.description: sendNotification receives a ChallengeModel object whose .description field originates from stored data (persisted via POST /api/Challenges, outside this file). The caller is outside this file.

The notification's 'challenge' field is assembled by concatenating challenge.name with entities.decode(sanitizeHtml(challenge.description, { allowedTags: [], allowedAttributes: {} })). sanitizeHtml strips all HTML tags, but entities.decode then converts HTML entities like < and > back to literal < and >, re-introducing active HTML that sanitizeHtml was meant to remove.

notSolved(challenge) is checked as a gate; if the challenge has not been solved, the function returns early at line 49 and no notification is built. Only a solved challenge proceeds to notification construction.
The notification object literal begins construction. The 'challenge' field will be assigned on line 65.
notifications.push(notification) stores the notification object (with the decoded HTML in its 'challenge' field) into the in-memory notifications array.

The emit is gated by: if (globalWithSocketIO.io && (isRestore || !wasPreviouslyShown)). If the socket server exists and either this is a restore or the notification hasn't been shown before, the emit proceeds.

globalWithSocketIO.io.emit('challenge solved', notification) sends the notification object containing the decoded HTML to all connected Socket.IO clients. The rendering sink (client-side browser) is outside this file, but the defective decode-after-sanitize that produces injectable markup is at line 65.

title: Anti-cheat score influenced by caller-supplied isCheating flag
description: The solveIf function accepts an isCheating parameter from its caller and passes it through to solve(), which in turn passes it to antiCheat.calculateCheatScore(). The isCheating value is a trust assumption: the server should independently determine whether cheating occurred, not accept a caller-provided boolean. If any route handler passes a client-influenced value as isCheating (e.g., defaulting to false, or accepting it from request context without server-side verification), an attacker could solve challenges while suppressing their cheat score. The design relies on every caller to correctly set this flag rather than having the anti-cheat system derive it independently.
