solveIf passes isCheating directly to solve(challenge, isRestore, isCheating) with no validation or server-side re-derivation.

if (notSolved(challenge) && criteria()) — the isCheating value is not examined here; this gate only checks whether the challenge is unsolved and the criteria function returns truthy. If the gate passes, isCheating flows onward.
solve receives isCheating as its third parameter, with no validation or re-derivation at the function boundary.
challenge.solved = true is set, and on line 31 the challenge is saved. Neither operation touches isCheating; it is simply held in scope.
if (!isRestore) — the anti-cheat path is only entered for non-restore solves. isCheating is still unmodified and will be passed through.

solve passes isCheating to antiCheat.calculateCheatScore(challenge, isCheating). The cheat score calculation trusts this caller-supplied value rather than independently determining whether the solve was legitimate.

title: File deletion operations are not logged — no audit trail of removed FTP files
description: The cleanupFtpFolder function deletes every PDF file found in the ftp/ directory (line 15) but only logs when an error occurs (line 18). Successful deletions produce no log entry at all. If the ftp folder is writable by users (as it is in Juice Shop, where file-upload routes exist), an attacker who places files there and triggers or waits for a startup cleanup cannot determine from logs what was deleted, when, or how many files were removed. This eliminates the audit trail for a security-relevant file-destruction event, preventing incident investigation and reconstruction of an attack timeline.

trace.description: cleanupFtpFolder is an exported async function. Its caller is outside this file (it is a startup routine in lib/startup/). The function receives no parameters; it operates on the hardcoded ftp/ directory.
glob('ftp/*.pdf', ...) enumerates all PDF files in the ftp folder. The matched file list is stored in `files`.

The function opens a try block. This control structure governs the entire success path: if anything inside throws, execution jumps to the catch block on line 17. As long as the operations succeed, no logging occurs within this block.
The for...of loop iterates over each filename in the matched list, exposing each file path to the deletion operation in the loop body.

Each matched file is deleted via fs.remove(filename) inside the loop (lines 14-16). No log statement records the deletion — not the filename, not the count, not the fact that deletion occurred. The only logging is in the catch block (line 18) for errors. Successful file deletions are entirely unlogged, eliminating the audit trail for a destructive file operation.

title: Unbounded file enumeration and deletion in FTP folder cleanup
description: The glob pattern 'ftp/*.pdf' (line 13) can match an arbitrary number of files, and the loop on lines 14-16 processes every match sequentially with no cap on count, no batching, and no timeout. If an attacker can write PDF files into the ftp/ directory (Juice Shop exposes file-upload routes that can place files there), they could pre-fill the directory with thousands or millions of PDF files. When the cleanup runs — either at startup or if triggered by a re-import — the function will enumerate and attempt to delete all of them, consuming disk I/O, memory (the full file list is held in memory via glob's returned array), and CPU time. There is no limit on the number of files processed, no pagination, and no timeout on the operation as a whole.

trace.description: cleanupFtpFolder is an exported async function invoked during startup. Its caller is outside this file. The ftp/ directory it operates on is writable by users through file-upload routes elsewhere in the application.

glob('ftp/*.pdf', { windowsPathsNoEscape: true }) returns an array of all matching file paths. There is no limit option passed to glob (e.g., no maxResults or similar), so the returned array can grow unboundedly based on how many PDF files exist in the directory. An attacker who can upload PDF files to the ftp folder controls the size of this array.
The try block opens, defining the scope for the unbounded file operations that follow. There is no guard or limit applied before the enumeration begins.

The for...of loop iterates over every matched file in the array. There is no check on the total iteration count or any early exit mechanism; the loop will run as many times as there are files in the array.

The for...of loop iterates over every matched file and calls fs.remove(filename) for each. There is no cap on iteration count, no timeout, and no batching. With a sufficiently large number of files placed by an attacker, this loop consumes excessive memory (holding the full file list), disk I/O (stat + unlink for each file), and time, potentially blocking startup or degrading service.

title: Admin role check via unverified JWT decode in waitForAdminLogIn
description: The waitForAdminLogIn function reads a JWT from localStorage and uses jwtDecode() to extract the user's role, then checks if role === 'admin'. jwtDecode() only base64-decodes the JWT payload — it does NOT verify the cryptographic signature. An attacker can craft an arbitrary JWT with { data: { role: 'admin' } } in its payload, store it in localStorage, and satisfy this admin check. While this is a client-side helper for the hacking-instructor feature, any downstream logic that trusts the outcome of waitForAdminLogIn for gating admin-level instructional content can be bypassed by token forgery. The use of a decode-without-verify function for an authentication decision is the core defect: the code trusts an unsigned, unverified claim to determine identity/role.

trace.description: waitForAdminLogIn is an exported function; its caller is outside this file. It polls localStorage for a token and determines whether the current user is an admin.
The JWT is read from localStorage.getItem('token') — a value fully controllable by the user in the browser.
jwtDecode(token) is called. The jwt-decode library only decodes the payload; it performs no signature verification, no expiration check, and no issuer validation.
The function returns an async closure that will be invoked by the caller to begin polling.
The closure enters a while(true) loop — it will poll indefinitely until an admin role is detected.
role is initialized to an empty string, establishing the default non-admin state for each iteration.
A try block begins — any failure in token retrieval or decoding will be silently caught, leaving role as ''.
The decoded token is cast to `any` as payload, removing any type-level constraint on what fields are expected.
role is assigned from payload.data.role — the attacker-controlled, unverified claim from the JWT payload.
The catch block begins — if jwtDecode throws (e.g., malformed token), execution falls through without setting role.
On error, a console.log is emitted but no other action is taken — the function does not abort or signal failure.
End of catch block — control resumes after the try/catch with role either set from the unverified payload or still ''.

The decoded (unverified) payload's data.role field is compared to 'admin' to make an authorization decision. An attacker who crafts a JWT with role:'admin' in localStorage bypasses this check entirely, since the signature is never validated.

title: Admin application-configuration endpoint fetched without authentication credentials
description: Two functions in this file — waitForInputToHaveValue (line 42) and waitInMs (line 149) — fetch the endpoint /rest/admin/application-configuration via fetch() without attaching any Authorization header or auth token. In Juice Shop, authentication is typically JWT-based via a Bearer token from localStorage. The fetch call here sends no credentials beyond what the browser automatically includes (cookies). If the server-side handler for /rest/admin/application-configuration does not enforce authentication, any unauthenticated user can retrieve the full application configuration, which may include sensitive settings, internal endpoints, or feature flags. Even if the server does enforce auth, the client-side code demonstrates that no token is explicitly forwarded, which means the endpoint is either publicly accessible or relies solely on cookie-based session auth that may not be present for all users.

trace.description: waitForInputToHaveValue is an exported function called from outside this file. When options.replacement is provided, it needs server configuration data.
The function returns an async closure that will be invoked by the caller at runtime.
The code checks whether options.replacement has exactly two elements — this is the gate that determines whether the configuration fetch path is entered at all.
The code checks whether the module-level config variable is falsy — the fetch only happens once (lazy initialization), after which the cached config is reused.

fetch('/rest/admin/application-configuration') is called with no headers, no Authorization token, and no credentials option beyond defaults. The same pattern appears at line 149 in waitInMs. The endpoint name indicates it is an admin-level resource, yet no authentication is attached to the request. If the server does not independently enforce auth on this route, the configuration is exposed to unauthenticated callers.

title: Unbounded polling loops with no timeout in waitFor* functions
description: Every waitFor* function in this file (waitForInputToHaveValue, waitForInputToNotHaveValue, waitForInputToNotHaveValueAndNotBeEmpty, waitForInputToNotBeEmpty, waitForElementToGetClicked, waitForElementsInnerHtmlToBe, waitForAngularRouteToBeVisited, waitForLogIn, waitForAdminLogIn, waitForLogOut, waitForDevTools, waitForSelectToHaveValue, waitForSelectToNotHaveValue, waitForRightUriQueryParamPair) uses a while(true) loop with a 100ms sleep and no maximum iteration count or timeout. If the awaited condition is never met — for example because the DOM selector changes, the route is never visited, or the token is never set — the loop runs indefinitely. This is an insecure design choice: there is no fail-safe, no timeout, and no way for the application to recover. In a browser context this causes the affected tab to consume CPU continuously, degrading the user's experience and potentially making the application unresponsive. While the direct attack surface is limited (these are instructional helpers), the design itself permits indefinite resource consumption with no compensating control.

trace.description: Exported waitFor* functions are called from outside this file (the hacking-instructor orchestration layer). Each returns an async function that begins polling.
The returned async function enters a while(true) loop. This pattern is repeated identically at lines 71, 88, 107, 133, 161, 172, 183, 203, 220, 235, 250, and 261.
The function returns an async closure — the polling logic is deferred until the caller invokes it.

Inside the closure, document.querySelector(inputSelector) retrieves the DOM element to monitor. If the selector does not match, this returns null and the subsequent .value access would throw — but the while loop structure means execution will retry.

The options.replacement check determines whether a server configuration fetch occurs before polling begins. This is an optional pre-step that itself contains an unbounded dependency (the fetch and config traversal), but the primary concern is the polling loop that follows.

The condition check evaluates whether the input element's value matches the expected value (case-insensitive when options.ignoreCase is true). If it does not match, control falls through to the sleep.
If the condition is satisfied, break exits the loop. But if it is not, execution continues to line 60.
The else-if branch checks the case-sensitive comparison path. If this also fails, control falls through to the sleep with no exit.
The break inside the else-if only fires when the case-sensitive match succeeds. When neither condition matches, no break occurs.

Each loop iteration calls await sleep(100) and re-checks the condition. There is no iteration counter, no timeout, and no abort mechanism. If the condition is never satisfied, the loop runs forever, continuously performing DOM queries (document.querySelector) or localStorage reads every 100ms with no upper bound on duration or resource usage.

title: Unsafe YAML deserialization via yaml.load() without explicit safe schema
description: The script calls yaml.load() on line 22 to parse YAML configuration files without specifying a safe schema. In js-yaml versions prior to 4.0, yaml.load() defaults to DEFAULT_FULL_SCHEMA, which supports types like !!js/function and !!js/undefined that can instantiate arbitrary JavaScript objects and execute code during parsing. Even in js-yaml v4+ where load() is safe by default, the absence of an explicit schema means the safety of this call depends entirely on which version of js-yaml is installed — a downgrade or dependency conflict would silently re-enable code execution during parse. The schema validation on line 28 occurs AFTER deserialization, so it cannot prevent code execution that happens during the yaml.load() call itself. If an attacker can influence the contents of any .yml file in the config directory (e.g., through the application's YAML file upload route), they could inject malicious YAML tags that execute arbitrary code when this linter runs. The attack would be: upload a malicious YAML config file containing !!js/function tags, then trigger or wait for the lint:config script to run, achieving remote code execution.

trace.description: The validateFile function receives a file path string. The caller is outside this file (the main function on line 42 reads directory entries from a fixed config directory, but the broader application has a POST /file-upload → handleYamlUpload route that could place attacker-controlled YAML files into the config directory).

The file contents are read with readFile(file, 'utf8') and passed directly to yaml.load() without any schema restriction. No { schema: yaml.DEFAULT_SAFE_SCHEMA } or equivalent option is provided, so the call relies on whatever default the installed js-yaml version provides.

The main function calls readdir(configDir) to list all entries in the config directory. The caller is outside this file — this is a CLI entry point invoked via npm run lint:config. The config directory is fixed at line 17, but file contents within it may be influenced by external sources such as the application's POST /file-upload → handleYamlUpload route.
Entries are filtered to those ending with .yml, sorted, and each name is joined with configDir via path.join to produce full file paths. No content inspection or path validation occurs at this stage.
A for...of loop iterates over every .yml file path in the array, passing each one to validateFile.
validateFile(file) is called with the file path string. The result is AND-ed with the running success flag, but no validation or sanitization of the file path itself occurs before the call.

yaml.load() deserializes the YAML content. In js-yaml v3 (or v4 with DEFAULT_FULL_SCHEMA explicitly set), this can instantiate arbitrary objects and execute embedded JavaScript via tags like !!js/function. The subsequent schema validation on line 28 (ValidationSchema.safeParse) runs after parsing is complete and cannot prevent code execution that occurred during the yaml.load() call.

title: Unbounded file read without size limits on config files
description: The validateFile function reads entire YAML files into memory using readFile(file, 'utf8') on line 22 without any size limit or streaming. While the config directory path is fixed (line 17), if an attacker can place large files into the config directory (e.g., via the application's file upload functionality), a single very large .yml file could exhaust server memory. The directory listing on line 43 also processes all .yml files without any count limit, so many files could amplify the effect. This is a CLI script, so the impact is limited to the process running the linter rather than the web server itself, but in CI/CD pipelines or automated environments this could cause resource exhaustion.

trace.description: The main function reads all entries from the config directory. The caller is outside this file — this is a CLI entry point invoked via npm run lint:config. The config directory is fixed at line 17, but file contents within it may be influenced by external sources such as the application's YAML file upload route.
The validateFile function receives the file path as its parameter. No size check or file stat is performed before the read.
Entries are filtered to .yml files, sorted, and mapped to full paths. There is no limit on the number of files selected — every .yml file in the directory will be processed.
The for...of loop iterates over every file in the array with no cap on iteration count, meaning an unbounded number of files will each be fully read into memory.
validateFile(file) is called for each file path, forwarding it to the function that performs the unbounded read.

Each file in the directory is processed in sequence (line 47-49) with no cap on the number of files, so an attacker who can populate the config directory with many large .yml files can cause unbounded memory consumption.

title: XML External Entity (XXE) injection via dangerously configured XML parser
description: The parseXmlString function accepts untrusted XML data (from a caller outside this file) and parses it with external entity substitution (XML_PARSE_NOENT) and DTD loading (XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD) explicitly enabled. Additionally, xmlRegisterFsInputProviders() is called during library initialization to grant the WASM sandbox host filesystem access, so that external entities like file:///etc/passwd resolve against the real filesystem. An attacker who can supply XML to this function can inject DOCTYPE declarations with external entity references to read arbitrary local files, perform SSRF via HTTP/HTTPS entity references, or cause denial of service via entity expansion (mitigated only partially by the vm timeout). The vm.runInContext call is not the injection vector — the code string is static — but the user-controlled `data` flows into libxml2's parser which interprets entity definitions embedded in that data, making this an injection class vulnerability where the interpreter is the XML parser.

trace.description: The exported function parseXmlString accepts a `data` parameter of type string. The caller is outside this file (a route handler or other service passing user-supplied XML). This is the entrypoint for untrusted input.
The untrusted `data` is placed into the vm sandbox object alongside the parser options, making it available as a variable to the XML parsing call.

Parser options explicitly enable XML_PARSE_NOENT (entity substitution — entities are replaced with their resolved values) and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD (external DTD loading). Combined with xmlRegisterFsInputProviders() called at lines 21-22 during initialization, this configuration allows external entity references such as file:///etc/passwd to resolve against the host filesystem. This is the misconfiguration: dangerous parser defaults are deliberately enabled.
Inside loadLibxml2's initialization IIFE, dynamicImport('libxml2-wasm/lib/nodejs.mjs') loads the Node.js integration module that provides filesystem input providers for the WASM sandbox.

xmlRegisterFsInputProviders() is called, granting the WASM sandbox host filesystem access so external entities like file:///etc/passwd resolve. This is the first misconfiguration: filesystem access is deliberately enabled for the XML parser.

loadLibxml2() is called, returning the libxml2 instance. On first invocation this triggers the async initialization block inside loadLibxml2 (lines 15-27) where the dangerous filesystem access is granted.
vm.createContext(sandbox) turns the sandbox object into an isolated execution context, preparing the environment for the parsing call.

xmlDoc.toString() serializes the parsed document. Because XML_PARSE_NOENT caused entity substitution, any resolved external entity values (e.g., file contents from file:///etc/passwd) are now embedded in the output string.
xmlDoc.dispose() cleans up the parsed document object in WASM memory. The resolved entity values have already been extracted into xmlString by this point.
The function returns the resolved XML string (containing exfiltrated file contents or other entity-resolved data) to the caller, completing the data exfiltration path.

vm.runInContext executes the static code string 'libxml2.XmlDocument.fromString(data, { option })' in the sandbox. The user-controlled `data` variable is passed to libxml2's XmlDocument.fromString, which parses the XML with the dangerous options. Because XML_PARSE_NOENT and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD are active and filesystem input providers are registered, any DOCTYPE/external entity declarations in the attacker-supplied XML are interpreted and resolved, achieving XXE injection. The design itself (documented in comments at lines 29-31 as 'intentionally vulnerable to XXE') makes this an insecure-design finding: the architecture deliberately enables external entity resolution with no input validation or entity allow-listing, relying only on a vm timeout to mitigate expansion bombs.

title: No security logging for XML parsing operations vulnerable to XXE
description: The parseXmlString function performs a security-sensitive operation — parsing untrusted XML with external entity loading enabled — yet logs nothing. Parse failures, entity resolution attempts, timeouts from entity-expansion bombs, and successful parses containing DOCTYPE declarations are all security-relevant events in the context of XXE. The absence of any logging in this function means that if an attacker exploits the XXE vulnerability to exfiltrate files, there is no audit trail in this code path to detect or investigate the attack. While library functions often delegate logging to callers, the deliberate enabling of dangerous parser features here creates a heightened duty to at minimum log anomalous parse results (timeouts, entity-related errors). This is a secondary finding; the primary defect is the XXE itself.

trace.description: parseXmlString receives untrusted XML data from a caller outside this file. This is a security-sensitive entrypoint for XML parsing with known-dangerous configuration.

The XML is parsed in a vm context with a timeout. If the timeout fires (entity-expansion bomb) or if parsing succeeds with external entities resolved, no log entry is produced. The function catches nothing, logs nothing, and returns the parsed string directly.
loadLibxml2() is called to obtain the configured parser instance. No logging occurs at this step — the library load and its dangerous filesystem-access configuration are silently completed.
Parser options with dangerous flags (XML_PARSE_NOENT, XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD) are assembled. No logging records that these risky options are being applied to untrusted input.
The sandbox object is constructed with the user-controlled `data`. No logging records what data is about to be parsed.
vm.createContext(sandbox) creates the execution context. No logging.
xmlDoc.toString() extracts the serialized result. No logging of the parse output or any indicators of entity resolution.
xmlDoc.dispose() performs cleanup. No logging.

The function returns the parsed XML string to the caller. Throughout the entire function body (lines 33-42) there is no console, logger, or telemetry call. Security-relevant events — XXE attempts, timeout-triggered entity bombs, successful external entity resolution — are completely unlogged at this layer.

title: PrivacyRequestModel exposes sensitive fields (UserId, deletionRequested) without property-level authorization or field restrictions
description: The PrivacyRequestModel defines two sensitive fields — UserId and deletionRequested — with no field-level protection. UserId is a plain integer that maps a privacy request to a user account; deletionRequested is a boolean flag controlling whether account deletion has been requested. In Sequelize, all model fields are mass-assignable by default unless explicitly excluded. If any route handler (outside this file) spreads a request body into PrivacyRequestModel.create() or .update(), an attacker could set deletionRequested: true to trigger a deletion request without going through the intended workflow, or set UserId to another user's ID to file a deletion request on behalf of another user. The deletionRequested flag is a server-determined state that should never be caller-controlled, yet the model design permits direct assignment with no constraint beyond a defaultValue.

trace.description: PrivacyRequestModel is defined as a Sequelize Model class. It is exported (line 46) and available for use by route handlers outside this file that may bind request body fields directly into create/update calls.

UserId is declared as a plain DataTypes.INTEGER field (lines 31-33) with no foreign key enforcement, no allow-list, and no indication that it should be derived from the session rather than accepted from the request body. Any caller-supplied value for UserId would be persisted if spread into a create/update call.
The class declares UserId as a public property, allowing it to be read and set freely by Sequelize operations.
The class declares deletionRequested as a public property, exposing this sensitive state flag to direct manipulation.

PrivacyRequestModel.init() is called to register the model schema with Sequelize. No field restrictions (such as `allowNull: false` combined with session-derived defaults, or custom setters) are passed to restrict mass assignment.

deletionRequested is declared as a DataTypes.BOOLEAN with defaultValue: false (lines 34-37) but with no restriction preventing it from being set to true by a caller. This is a sensitive state flag: if mass-assigned from a request body, an attacker can directly request account deletion without any verification workflow. The model design treats a security-significant state transition as a simple settable property rather than a server-governed process.

title: noUpdate constraint bypassed when previous field value is null or undefined
description: The `makeKeyNonUpdatable` function is intended to enforce property-level authorization: a designated column should never be updated after creation. However, the guard at lines 35-38 only blocks the update when `instance._previousDataValues[fieldName]` is neither `undefined` nor `null`. This means that if the protected field's previous (stored) value is null or undefined, the constraint is silently skipped and the field becomes updatable. An attacker who can influence a record while the protected column is still null (e.g., a newly created record, a record created before the column was populated, or a record where the column was nulled out) can set the supposedly-immutable field to an arbitrary value. If this control is used to protect sensitive fields like role/isAdmin flags or identity keys, the bypass enables privilege escalation or data integrity violations. The design assumes a non-null prior value always exists, which is not guaranteed.

trace.description: The exported function `makeKeyNonUpdatable(model, column)` is the entrypoint. The caller is outside this file (a model definition invoking this to protect a column). It registers a `beforeValidate` hook on the given Sequelize model that is supposed to block updates to `column`.

For every changed field, the hook looks up the field definition and the previous data value via `instance.rawAttributes[fieldName]` (line 33) and `instance._previousDataValues[fieldName]` (line 36), preparing to decide whether to block the change.

The guard condition at lines 35-38 requires `instance._previousDataValues[fieldName] !== undefined && instance._previousDataValues[fieldName] !== null` before it will push a validation error. When the previous stored value is null or undefined, the condition short-circuits to false, the matching `if` body (lines 40-51) is skipped, and no `ValidationErrorItem` is created for that field.

`model.addHook('beforeValidate', ...)` registers the hook callback that will fire before any validation pass on instances of this model, giving the hook the opportunity to inspect and block field changes.
`if (!options.validate) return` — the hook exits early if validation is not being performed. When validation IS being performed, execution continues into the field-change inspection logic.
`if (instance.isNewRecord) return` — the hook skips new records (creation), so the constraint is intended to apply only to updates of existing records.
`const changedKeys: unknown[] = []` initializes the array that will collect the names of all fields whose values have changed on this instance.
`const instanceChanged = Array.from(instance._changed)` extracts the set of changed field names from the Sequelize instance's internal `_changed` collection into an iterable array.
`instanceChanged.forEach((value) => changedKeys.push(value))` copies every changed field name into the `changedKeys` array, building the complete list of fields the caller attempted to modify.
`if (changedKeys.length === 0) return` — if no fields changed, the hook exits; otherwise it proceeds to check each changed field against the non-update constraint.

`const validationErrors: ValidationErrorItem[] = []` initializes the array that will collect validation errors for any protected field that was modified. If this array stays empty, the update will proceed.

`const fieldDefinition = instance.rawAttributes[fieldName]` looks up the Sequelize model definition for the changed field, which is used later to check whether the field name matches the protected `column`.

`instance._previousDataValues[fieldName] !== undefined &&` — first sub-condition: the previous stored value of this field must not be `undefined`. If the field was never set (undefined), this is false and the entire guard short-circuits, skipping the error push. This is one half of the bypass.

`instance._previousDataValues[fieldName] !== null &&` — second sub-condition: the previous stored value must not be `null`. If the field's prior value was `null`, the guard short-circuits to false, no `ValidationErrorItem` is pushed for this field, and the supposedly non-updatable column can be changed. This is the core of the bypass: the design assumes a non-null prior value always exists, which is not guaranteed for newly created records, records where the column was nulled, or columns with no default.

`(fieldDefinition.fieldName === column)` — third sub-condition: confirms the changed field matches the protected column name. This check is correct in isolation but is never reached when the previous value was null or undefined, so it provides no protection in those cases.

`validationErrors.push(new ValidationErrorItem(...))` — this line (40-51) is the error-creation block that should execute for every protected-field change. When the guard at lines 36-37 short-circuits due to a null/undefined prior value, this block is skipped entirely and no error is recorded for the protected field.

`})` closes the `changedKeys.forEach` callback. After this point, the `validationErrors` array is either empty (if all protected fields had null/undefined prior values) or contains errors only for fields that passed the full guard.

Because no validation error was pushed for the protected field when its prior value was null/undefined, `validationErrors.length` remains 0 (or excludes that field), no `ValidationError` is thrown, and the update proceeds. The non-updatable constraint is thereby bypassed: a caller can mutate the protected column whenever its previous value was null or undefined, defeating the property-level authorization this function is meant to enforce.

title: Config schema accepts arbitrary strings for security-critical URLs, enabling SSRF and OAuth redirect hijacking via config upload
description: The validation schema defines URL fields such as `llmApiUrl`, `authorizedRedirects[].uri`, and `authorizedRedirects[].proxy` as plain `z.string()` without any URL format validation, HTTPS enforcement, or allowlisting. The application architecture includes a YAML upload endpoint (POST /file-upload → handleYamlUpload), and this schema (ValidationSchema) is the gatekeeper for validating uploaded custom configs. Because the schema imposes no constraints on URL values, an attacker who can upload a custom YAML config can set `llmApiUrl` to an attacker-controlled server, causing all chatbot API requests (which may contain user prompts and contextual data) to be sent to the attacker. Similarly, an attacker can add arbitrary entries to `authorizedRedirects` with a malicious `uri` and `proxy`, allowing interception of OAuth authorization codes. The design flaw is that the schema — which is the sole validation layer for config data — never establishes that URLs must be well-formed, HTTPS, or within an allowlist, so the attack succeeds even when the schema validation passes.

Any arbitrary string — including an attacker-controlled URL — passes validation. This is a misconfiguration: the schema should enforce z.string().url() at minimum, and ideally restrict to HTTPS.

GoogleOauthSchema.authorizedRedirects accepts an array of objects where both `uri` and `proxy` are z.string() with no validation. An attacker can inject arbitrary redirect URIs and proxy URLs that pass schema validation. The design never enforces that redirect URIs must be HTTPS or belong to trusted origins, so OAuth code interception is possible through valid config.

ApplicationSchema.googleOauth is typed as GoogleOauthSchema (line 102). This links the application config to the GoogleOauthSchema definition.

In the ValidationSchema, googleOauth is overridden as GoogleOauthSchema.partial().optional(). A custom config can supply a partial googleOauth object containing only authorizedRedirects, and it will pass validation.

title: Security question answers accepted and stored as plaintext strings in MemorySchema
description: The MemorySchema defines fields `geoStalkingMetaSecurityAnswer` and `geoStalkingVisualSecurityAnswer` as plain `z.string()` with no hashing or encryption transformation. Security question answers are authentication-adjacent secrets — they are used for account recovery and identity verification. Storing them as plaintext strings means anyone with read access to the memories data (including through API endpoints like GET /api/Recycles or data leak challenges) can directly read the answers. The design flaw is that the schema never establishes that security answers must be hashed or protected; it treats them identically to display fields like `caption`. The attack: an attacker who can read memory records (e.g., through an IDOR or data exposure vulnerability) obtains plaintext security answers and uses them to reset victim accounts.

trace.description: MemorySchema is exported and used both in AppConfigSchema (line 173, for seed data) and in ValidationSchema (line 210, for uploaded custom configs). The caller is outside this file — memory records are created and stored via API routes such as POST /rest/memories → addMemory.

geoStalkingMetaSecurityAnswer is defined as z.string().optional() with no transformation. Line 149 defines geoStalkingVisualSecurityAnswer identically. Both accept and preserve plaintext security answers. The schema design treats security answers as ordinary display strings, establishing no protection for these authentication-adjacent secrets. Any data store populated through this schema will contain plaintext security answers.

title: Dependency validation crashes unsafely when checker throws, instead of failing closed
description: The validateDependencies function catches errors from the dependency checker (lines 16-18) but does not return or re-throw. Execution continues to line 20, where dependencies.depsWereOk is undefined (dependencies is still the empty object from line 13), so the else branch is taken. Line 25 then attempts to iterate dependencies.error, which is undefined, causing an unhandled TypeError ('undefined is not iterable'). The function is responsible for enforcing that dependencies are satisfied — a fact the server must decide at startup. When the checker itself fails (e.g., corrupted package.json, filesystem error, or a bug in check-dependencies), the design should fail safely by returning a clear failure result. Instead, it crashes with an unhandled exception. If the caller catches that crash, the application proceeds with no validation result at all — a missing compensating control for an inherently risky operation (running with unvalidated dependencies).

dependencies is initialized to an empty object {} as the default value before the try block.
If dependencyChecker (line 15) throws, the catch block on line 16-18 logs a warning but does NOT return, re-throw, or set dependencies to a safe shape. dependencies remains {}.
The try block begins, enclosing the dependency checker call so that thrown errors are caught.

A warning is logged with the error message. The function does not set dependencies to a safe shape or return a failure result — execution falls through.
The catch block closes. Normal execution resumes with dependencies still equal to the empty object {} from line 13.
The condition dependencies.depsWasOk === true is evaluated on the empty object. The property does not exist, so it is undefined; the strict equality is false.
Because the condition was false, the else branch is entered.
A warning is logged stating dependencies are not rightly satisfied. Execution continues to the for-loop.

After the catch block, dependencies.depsWereOk is undefined ({} has no such property), so the else branch is entered. Line 25 executes 'for (const err of dependencies.error)' where dependencies.error is undefined, throwing an unhandled TypeError. The validation function crashes instead of returning a safe failure indication, leaving the application's dependency state unvalidated.

title: Dependency validation scope excludes devDependencies, allowing vulnerable dev tools to go undetected
description: The check-dependencies call on line 15 is configured with scopeList: ['dependencies'], which intentionally excludes devDependencies from validation. Development dependencies (build tools, test frameworks, linters) can contain vulnerabilities or version mismatches that affect the build pipeline and supply chain. By excluding them from the startup validation check, the configuration allows mismatched or tampered dev dependencies to pass without any warning. This is a dangerous default — a comprehensive dependency validation should include all dependency scopes to ensure the integrity of the entire dependency tree at startup.

dependencies is initialized to an empty object {} before the try block. This variable will hold the result of the dependency check, including which scopes were validated.
The try block begins, enclosing the dependency checker call.

dependencyChecker is invoked with scopeList: ['dependencies'], configuring the checker to only validate the 'dependencies' scope and explicitly excluding 'devDependencies'. Any version mismatch or missing package in devDependencies will not be reported, leaving a gap in dependency integrity validation.

title: WebSocket CORS origin hardcoded to development localhost URL
description: The Socket.IO server is initialized with `cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' }` on line 20. This hardcodes a development origin into the WebSocket configuration. In a production deployment, this either breaks legitimate cross-origin WebSocket communication or, if the application is reverse-proxied on the same host, silently exposes the WebSocket endpoint to any page served from that origin. The origin should be sourced from configuration or environment variables, not hardcoded to a localhost development port.

The Socket.IO server is constructed with `cors: { origin: 'http://localhost:4200' }`, a hardcoded development-origin CORS policy that is not driven by environment or application configuration.

title: Unauthenticated WebSocket clients can connect, receive all notifications, and delete notifications from the global array
description: The WebSocket connection handler (line 23) performs no authentication or authorization check. Any client that can reach the WebSocket endpoint is accepted. On connection, the handler immediately emits every notification in the global `notifications` array to the newly connected socket (lines 29-31), leaking all challenge-solved notifications to unauthenticated clients. Furthermore, the `notification received` event handler (lines 33-38) trusts client-supplied `data` to locate and splice entries out of the shared global `notifications` array without verifying that the client is authenticated or authorized to dismiss notifications. An unauthenticated attacker can connect, harvest all notification flags, then send `notification received` events for each flag to drain the notification array, disrupting the notification system for all other users. There is also no rate limiting on connections or events, so an attacker can open many sockets or send many events without throttling.

trace.description: io.on('connection', ...) accepts any incoming WebSocket connection. There is no authentication middleware, no token check, and no rate limit on new connections. The caller that exposes this server is outside this file.

On every new connection, the handler iterates over the global `notifications` array and emits each notification to the connecting socket via `socket.emit('challenge solved', notification)`, disclosing all stored notifications to any client.

The `if (firstConnectedSocket === null)` conditional on line 24 gates only the 'server started' emission and the assignment of `firstConnectedSocket` on line 26. The notification emission on lines 29-31 runs unconditionally for every connection, regardless of this check — it is outside the if-block.

`socket.emit('challenge solved', notification)` sends each notification object — including its `flag` field — to the connecting socket. This is the data-disclosure sink: all challenge-solved notifications are emitted to any client that connects.

`const i = notifications.findIndex(({ flag }: any) => flag === data)` uses the untrusted client-supplied `data` value directly to locate a matching notification by its `flag` field in the global `notifications` array. There is no validation of `data` and no authorization check — any connected client can search for any flag value.

`if (i > -1)` is the only conditional guarding the splice. It checks only whether a match was found — it does not check whether the client is authorized to delete this notification. Any match found allows execution to continue to the splice.

`notifications.splice(i, 1)` removes the matched notification from the shared global `notifications` array. Because `notifications` is a module-level reference imported from `../../data/datacache` (line 9), this mutation affects all connected clients. An unauthenticated attacker can drain the entire notification array by sending `notification received` events for each flag value harvested from the emission on line 30.

The `notification received` handler accepts unauthenticated client-supplied `data`, uses it to find a matching notification by flag (line 34), and splices it from the global `notifications` array (line 36). Any connected client can delete any or all notifications.

title: No security logging for WebSocket connections, notification manipulation, or challenge verification events
description: The file registers handlers for security-relevant events — new WebSocket connections, challenge-solved notifications being emitted and deleted, and three challenge verification attempts (`verifyLocalXssChallenge`, `verifySvgInjectionChallenge`, `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge`) — but logs none of them. There is no log entry for connection establishment, no log for notification creation or deletion, and no log for challenge verification attempts. An attacker who connects to drain notifications or attempts challenge verification would leave no trace in application logs, making detection and investigation of abuse impossible.

The `notifications.forEach` loop emits all challenge-solved notifications to the connecting socket. This is a data-disclosure event — sensitive challenge flags are sent to an unauthenticated client — and no log entry records that the emission occurred or to whom.

The `socket.on('notification received', ...)` handler accepts client input that will mutate global state. No log entry records that a notification-dismissal request was received, which socket sent it, or what data it contained.
`notifications.findIndex` uses the client-supplied `data` to search the global notification array. The lookup result — whether a match was found or not — is not logged.
The `if (i > -1)` conditional determines whether a mutation will occur. Neither the true nor the false branch logs the outcome.

The `notifications.splice(i, 1)` call mutates the global notification array based on unauthenticated client input, and neither this mutation nor any other security-relevant action in the file is logged. The absence of any logging call in the entire file is the finding.

title: Challenge verification handlers accept client data but perform no verification
description: Three event handlers — `verifyLocalXssChallenge` (line 40), `verifySvgInjectionChallenge` (line 43), and `verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge` (line 46) — accept a `data` argument from the client but have empty bodies. If the challenge system relies on these handlers to perform server-side verification of challenge completion, the absence of any verification logic means the design trusts the client to report its own challenge status. Even if these are placeholders, accepting client-supplied data for a verification flow with no server-side check is an insecure design: the server should independently verify challenge completion rather than accepting a client-reported event.

trace.description: socket.on('verifyLocalXssChallenge', (data: any) => { }) registers a handler that accepts client-supplied data for a challenge verification event but has an empty body. Lines 43 and 46 show the same pattern for two additional challenge verification handlers.

The handler body is empty — no verification logic executes. The server accepts a verification event from the client but performs no server-side check, meaning the verification step is entirely absent by design.

title: UserId field exposed without property-level authorization on auto-generated CRUD, enabling mass assignment and BOLA
description: The Card model defines `UserId` (line 29-31) as a plain INTEGER column with no special protection, no field exclusion, and no allow-listing. The file's auto-generated CRUD surface (`/api/Cards` POST and `/api/Cards/:id` PUT) typically binds request body fields directly to model attributes. This means a caller can supply `UserId` in the request body to any value, associating a card with an arbitrary user account. This is both a mass assignment vulnerability (Broken Object Property Level Authorization — the caller controls the ownership field) and a BOLA enabler (cards can be created under or reassigned to other users). Additionally, the auto-generated GET `/api/Cards/:id` endpoint performs a primary-key lookup with no ownership check, so any authenticated user who substitutes another user's card ID receives that card's details.

trace.description: The Card model declares `UserId` as a plain DataTypes.INTEGER field (lines 29-31) with no indication that it should be server-derived, excluded from mass binding, or protected from caller control. The auto-generated CRUD surface for this model (POST /api/Cards, PUT /api/Cards/:id, GET /api/Cards/:id) is the entrypoint; the caller is outside this file.

All fields — UserId, fullName, cardNum, expMonth, expYear — are declared as simple model attributes (lines 29-61) with no Sequelize-level field exclusion, no `readOnly` flag, and no allow-list separating user-settable fields from server-controlled fields. Sequelize's auto-generated CRUD binds every declared field from the request body by default.

Card.init() is called, which registers every field in the attributes object (lines 28-62) as a bindable, persistable column. Sequelize's auto-generated CRUD will accept any of these fields from a request body.
The type is set to DataTypes.INTEGER with no additional options such as `set`, `get`, or a custom setter that would sanitize or derive the value server-side. The field is a raw, bindable integer.

The options object passed to Card.init (lines 63-66) contains only `tableName` and `sequelize` — no `defaultScope` restricting fields, no hooks that would override or validate `UserId`, and no paranoid/timestamps configuration that would add server-side guards.
The tableName 'Cards' is set but no field-level security, scope, or access control is configured in the model options.

The sequelize instance is passed in, completing the model registration. At this point all fields including UserId are registered as fully bindable, persistable columns with no property-level authorization.

The CardModel and CardModelInit are exported, making the model available to the rest of the application including the auto-generated CRUD endpoints that bind request body fields directly to model attributes.

Because `UserId` is a directly bindable model attribute with no property-level authorization, an attacker calling POST /api/Cards with `{"UserId": <victim_id>, "fullName": "...", "cardNum": ..., ...}` creates a card record owned by the victim. Similarly, GET /api/Cards/:id with any id returns that card without an ownership check. The model provides no per-resource authorization constraint — no scope, no hook, no field guard.

title: Full payment card number (PAN) stored in plaintext as an integer, violating PCI DSS design requirements
description: The `cardNum` field (lines 38-44) stores the full 16-digit Primary Account Number as a plaintext INTEGER. The validation enforces that the value is a 16-digit number (min 1000000000000000, max 9999999999999998), confirming that the complete PAN is persisted. PCI DSS requirement 3.4 mandates that PAN be rendered unreadable anywhere it is stored — through tokenization, truncation, or strong cryptography. Storing the full PAN as a plaintext integer means any database compromise exposes all stored card numbers in immediately usable form. This is a design-level defect: the model's design itself permits the storage of sensitive cardholder data without any compensating control, and no amount of correct implementation of this design closes the gap.

The options object (lines 63-66) contains no `hooks` that would encrypt the PAN before saving, no `defaultScope` that would mask it on retrieval, and no other compensating control.

The CardModel and CardModelInit are exported (line 70), making the plaintext-PAN-storing model available to the entire application. Any route that creates or retrieves Card records will persist or expose the full PAN without any model-level protection.

The validation (lines 40-44) confirms the intent to store full PANs: it requires the value to be between 1000000000000000 and 9999999999999998 — exactly the range of 16-digit card numbers. No masking, hashing, or tokenization is applied at any point in the model definition. A database breach directly exposes all stored card numbers.

title: ChallengeDependency model exposes sensitive fields without property-level authorization
description: The ChallengeDependency Sequelize model defines a `key` field (line 44-46) and a `missing` boolean flag (lines 47-49) as plain STRING and BOOLEAN types with no field-level access restrictions. In Sequelize, all fields are mass-assignable by default unless explicitly excluded or an allow-list is enforced at the controller level. If a route handler spreads a request body directly into a create or update call for this model (the caller is outside this file), an attacker could set the `key` field — which may be a cryptographic key, API key, or other secret — or toggle the `missing` flag to alter dependency state. The architecture context shows auto-generated-style CRUD endpoints for other Sequelize models (e.g., POST /api/Products, POST /api/Challenges), suggesting ChallengeDependency may be exposed similarly. There is no explicit allow-list or exclude-list defined in the model to prevent caller-controlled binding of these fields.

The `missing` property is declared on the model class as `declare missing: boolean` with no access modifier or guard. This establishes missing as a publicly settable attribute on model instances.

Both the ChallengeDependency model class and the ChallengeDependencyModelInit function are exported, making them available to external callers. Any route handler or service that imports this model and passes an unfiltered request body into a Sequelize create/update operation will persist caller-controlled values into the key and missing fields.

The model is initialized via ChallengeDependency.init() with all five data fields (ChallengeId, name, documentation, key, missing) declared as mass-assignable columns. Any caller that passes an unfiltered request body into a Sequelize create/update operation for this model will persist caller-controlled values into the `key` and `missing` fields, achieving property-level authorization bypass.

title: Captcha answer stored in plaintext with no field-level protection
description: The Captcha model stores the captcha answer as a plaintext DataTypes.STRING (line 30) with no serialization restrictions, default scope exclusions, or field-level guards. A captcha is a security control whose entire purpose is to present a challenge that only a human can solve — the answer is the secret. The model design provides no mechanism to prevent the `answer` field from being exposed through CRUD operations or API responses. The architecture context shows auto-generated CRUD endpoints for other models (e.g., GET /api/Users, POST /api/Products), and if a similar GET /api/Captchas or similar endpoint exists, an attacker can read the answer directly from the API response, completely bypassing the captcha verification. Even in a create/update context, the lack of any field allow-list means a caller could set the `answer` field directly via mass assignment. The design flaw is that the model treats the captcha answer as an ordinary string field with no elevated protection, when it is the core secret of a security control.

trace.description: The Captcha model class is exported as CaptchaModel (line 39). Callers outside this file — route handlers, auto-generated CRUD controllers, or services — will interact with this model to create, read, update, or delete captcha records. The entrypoint for data flow is the model itself and its field definitions.

The `answer` field is declared as `answer: DataTypes.STRING` with no additional constraints — no `primaryKey`, no `defaultValue`, no `validate`, and critically no serialization exclusion or default scope. Sequelize models expose all defined fields by default in toJSON() serialization unless explicitly excluded. This means any controller that returns a Captcha instance or collection will include the `answer` field in the JSON response.
The `answer` attribute is declared on the class as a string property (`declare answer: string`). This TypeScript declaration sets up the property on the model instance.
The `CaptchaModelInit` function is defined, receiving the Sequelize instance from a caller outside this file. This function is responsible for binding the model attributes to the database schema.
The `Captcha.init()` method is called to initialize the model with its schema configuration. The attribute definitions passed here dictate how fields are serialized and validated.

The `answer` field reaches the sink — API exposure — through the model's default serialization behavior. With no `exclude` list, no `defaultScope` with `attributes: { exclude: ['answer'] }`, and no field-level authorization, the captcha answer is treated as an ordinary data field. If the caller (outside this file) uses auto-generated CRUD or a generic model endpoint pattern (as seen for Users, Products, Complaints, etc. in the architecture), the answer is directly readable. An attacker can request captcha records from the API, read the `answer` field, and submit it — defeating the captcha security control entirely. Additionally, during create/update operations, the lack of a field allow-list means a caller could set `answer` directly via mass assignment, bypassing the challenge entirely.

title: captchaId missing primaryKey configuration
description: The `captchaId` field is defined as DataTypes.INTEGER (lines 26-28) but lacks the `primaryKey: true` property. By naming convention and intent, `captchaId` is the identifier field for the Captcha model. Without `primaryKey: true`, Sequelize will auto-generate a separate `id` primary key column, leaving `captchaId` as an unindexed, unconstrained integer field. This can lead to duplicate captcha records, unpredictable query behavior when code assumes `captchaId` is the unique identifier, and potential issues with record lookups and updates. The misconfiguration is the absence of the primary key designation on a field that is clearly meant to be the model's unique identifier.

trace.description: CaptchaModelInit is an exported function (line 39) that receives a Sequelize instance from a caller outside this file. This is where the model's schema is configured.

The `captchaId` field is defined inside Captcha.init() as `{ type: DataTypes.INTEGER }` (lines 26-28). The field configuration object contains only `type` and omits `primaryKey: true`, `autoIncrement: true`, and `allowNull: false` — all of which would be expected for a primary key identifier field.
The `Captcha.init()` method is called to initialize the model. The first argument is an object defining the model's attributes.
The attribute configuration object for `captchaId` contains `type: DataTypes.INTEGER`.

The misconfigured schema reaches the database at model synchronization time. Sequelize, finding no field marked as primaryKey, will inject its own auto-generated `id` primary key. The `captchaId` field becomes an ordinary nullable, non-unique integer column. Any code that later relies on `captchaId` as the unique identifier — lookups by `captchaId`, updates, deletes — will operate on a non-unique column, allowing duplicate records and potentially returning the wrong captcha record, which could cause a user to be validated against the wrong captcha answer or cause data integrity issues.

title: Missing foreign key constraint on SecurityAnswerModel → UserModel relationship
description: SecurityAnswerModel.belongsTo(UserModel) at line 124-128 is defined without `constraints: true` or `foreignKeyConstraint: true`, unlike the vast majority of other user-associated models in this file (AddressModel, BasketModel, CardModel, ComplaintModel, MemoryModel, PrivacyRequestModel, RecycleModel, WalletModel all explicitly enable FK constraints). Security answers are part of the account recovery / password reset flow — a security-critical path. The absence of a database-level referential integrity constraint means security answer records can reference non-existent users, or survive after a user is deleted, creating orphaned recovery data. This is both a misconfiguration (missing security-relevant database constraint that other models in the same file have) and an insecure design issue (the recovery flow's integrity is not enforced at the data layer, relying instead on application logic that may not compensate). The FeedbackModel at line 65-69 also lacks FK constraints but explicitly comments this as intentional ('no FK constraint to allow anonymous feedback posts'); SecurityAnswerModel has no such justification, and its security role makes the omission dangerous.

trace.description: SecurityAnswerModel.belongsTo(UserModel, { foreignKey: { name: 'UserId' } }) — the relation is established without constraints. The caller (relationsInit) is invoked from outside this file during Sequelize initialization.

Unlike all other security-relevant models (e.g., WalletModel at line 137-143, RecycleModel at line 109-115), this association omits `constraints: true` and `foreignKeyConstraint: true`. The SecurityAnswerModel does have FK constraints to SecurityQuestionModel (line 129-135) but not to UserModel, making the omission inconsistent and likely unintentional.

The options object for the belongsTo call is opened with `foreignKey:` but does not include `constraints: true` or `foreignKeyConstraint: true`. This is the configuration decision point: every other UserModel association that needs integrity (e.g., WalletModel at line 137-143) sets these flags. Their absence here means Sequelize will not emit a DDL-level FK constraint for UserId on the SecurityAnswers table.

The `foreignKey` sub-object is defined, naming the column. This is where `constraints` and `foreignKeyConstraint` would also appear if present — they do not. Compare with line 130-131 where the very next association (SecurityAnswerModel → SecurityQuestionModel) explicitly sets both `constraints: true` and `foreignKeyConstraint: true`.

The column name 'UserId' is specified. This is the foreign key column that will lack a referential integrity constraint to the Users table. The configuration decision made at line 125 (no constraint flags) propagates through this column definition.

Immediately after, SecurityAnswerModel.belongsTo(SecurityQuestionModel, { ... }) begins — this association DOES set `constraints: true` (line 130) and `foreignKeyConstraint: true` (line 131). The contrast between the two consecutive calls on the same model makes the omission on line 124-128 inconsistent and likely unintentional rather than a deliberate design choice.

Without the FK constraint, the database enforces no referential integrity between security answers and users. An attacker who can manipulate the SecurityAnswer table (directly or through an application path that doesn't validate user existence) can create orphaned security answer records. In a password-reset flow, this could allow recovery attempts against dangling answer records or bypass the intended 1:1 user-to-answer relationship, undermining the account recovery security control.

title: Regex injection via unescaped challengeKey interpolation into RegExp
description: The challengeKey is extracted from file content (comment markers in source files) and then interpolated directly into RegExp constructors on lines 59, 76, and 78 without any escaping of regex metacharacters. If an attacker can place a crafted file containing malicious `vuln-code-snippet` comment markers into one of the SNIPPET_PATHS directories (e.g., via the file-upload endpoint that exists in the application), the challengeKey string becomes a regex fragment. This enables two attacks: (1) regex injection — the attacker alters matching semantics to extract unintended content or bypass boundary checks, and (2) ReDoS — a crafted challengeKey like `(a+)+` or `(a|a)*` interpolated into the complex pattern on line 59 (which already contains nested quantifiers via `.*` and `([^])*`) can cause catastrophic backtracking, hanging the Node.js event loop and denying service to all users.

title: Unbounded file reading without size limits in recursive directory traversal
description: findFilesWithCodeChallenges recursively traverses directories and reads every file entirely into memory via fs.readFile without any size cap. If an attacker can place large files in one of the SNIPPET_PATHS directories (e.g., via the file-upload endpoint), each call to getCodeChallenges will attempt to read all of them into memory. Since getCodeChallenges caches results in a module-level Map (line 96-99) and only populates it once, a large number of files or very large files could exhaust memory. Additionally, the regex operations on lines 59, 76, and 78 are applied to the full file content with no input size guard, compounding the resource consumption risk.

title: Mass assignment of `unlocked` field via auto-generated CRUD allows bypassing hint visibility controls
description: The Hint model defines an `unlocked` boolean field (line 47) that controls whether a hint is visible to users. The model's init (lines 27-53) imposes no field-level restrictions or allow-lists — every column is implicitly writable. The architecture context confirms an auto-generated CRUD surface at POST /api/Hints and PUT /api/Hints/:id, which will bind all request body fields to model columns. An attacker can include `"unlocked": true` in a POST or PUT request to unlock hints that should remain locked, bypassing the intended hint-progression mechanic. This is both a mass assignment vulnerability (no explicit allow-list; all fields including the sensitive `unlocked` flag are caller-settable) and an insecure design flaw (the server should derive unlock status from challenge-completion state rather than accepting it as a client-supplied mutable field).

Hint.init() defines all columns (ChallengeId, text, order, unlocked) without any field exclusion or allow-list. Sequelize's auto-generated CRUD binds any matching request body property to a column. There is no `fields` option or equivalent restriction on the init or model.

The opening brace of the attributes object. Every property inside this object — ChallengeId, id, text, order, unlocked — is registered as a writable column. There is no per-field `set`, `readOnly`, or equivalent restriction on any attribute.
The closing brace of the attributes object. The object is passed as the first argument to init (line 27) with no field exclusion list applied between the attributes definition and the init call.

The `unlocked` boolean reaches persistence with no server-side derivation. An attacker who sends {"text": "...", "unlocked": true} to POST /api/Hints creates a hint that is immediately unlocked, or via PUT /api/Hints/:id flips an existing hint's locked state. The unlock decision should be made by the server based on challenge progress, not accepted from the caller.

title: Stored XSS: `text` field accepts unsanitized free-form string with no encoding or validation

Hint text is user-influenced data that will be stored and later rendered in the Juice Shop frontend. Because no encoding or sanitization is applied at the persistence layer, an attacker who can create or modify a hint (via the auto-generated CRUD at /api/Hints) can inject HTML/script content. When the hint text is rendered in a browser without context-appropriate output encoding, this becomes a stored XSS vulnerability. The render sink is outside this file, but the absence of any sanitization at the model level is where the stored XSS defect is introduced.

The rendering of this field occurs outside this file (frontend template), but the model introduces no encoding, sanitization, or validation that would prevent script content from being stored. A field typed as free-form text with no sanitization hook is the persistence point of a stored XSS vulnerability.

title: Auto-generated CRUD exposes all hints by ID without per-resource authorization
description: The Hint model is exposed via auto-generated CRUD at /api/Hints and /api/Hints/:id (per architecture context). The model defines an `unlocked` boolean (line 47), indicating that some hints are intended to be locked and not accessible to all users. However, the GET /api/Hints/:id endpoint performs a lookup by primary key with no ownership or authorization check — any authenticated user can retrieve any hint by substituting the ID, including hints whose `unlocked` flag is false. The model itself provides no authorization scoping (e.g., a default scope filtering by `unlocked: true`), and the auto-generated route handler will not add one. This is a BOLA pattern: authentication (is the user logged in?) without authorization (is this user allowed to see this hint?).

The auto-generated GET /api/Hints/:id route (outside this file) accepts this ID as a path parameter and performs a primary-key lookup on the Hints table. The model defines no default scope or authorization filter that would restrict which hints are returned.

The `unlocked` boolean field indicates access control is conceptually needed — some hints are locked. Yet the model provides no mechanism (no scope, no hook, no access filter) to enforce that only unlocked hints are returned to unauthorized users. The lookup by ID returns the record regardless of the `unlocked` value.
The options object for Hint.init() opens with `{`. This is where Sequelize model-level configuration like `defaultScope` would be placed to restrict which records are returned by default queries.

The model is initialized with only tableName and sequelize options (lines 49-52). No defaultScope, no authorization hook, no access-control middleware is configured. The auto-generated CRUD handler will return any hint by ID without checking the `unlocked` flag or the requesting user's entitlements.

title: Stored XSS via Product description setter that conditionally skips sanitization
description: The Product model's `description` field has a custom Sequelize setter (lines 44-50). When `challenges.restfulXssChallenge` is enabled, the setter's if-branch is an empty block — it performs NO sanitization and falls through to `this.setDataValue('description', description)` with the raw, caller-supplied value. When the challenge is disabled, `security.sanitizeSecure(description)` is called. This means that whenever the challenge flag is active, any text a caller supplies for the product description is persisted verbatim. Because the description field is free-form text (DataTypes.STRING) reachable through the auto-generated CRUD surface at /api/Products (POST and PUT), an attacker can inject script markup or HTML into the description. The rendering sink is outside this file (likely a frontend template or HTML response), but the defect — absence of sanitization at the persistence point — is introduced here. The design flaw is that a security control (sanitization) is conditionally disabled by a challenge toggle, meaning the model's own design permits unsanitized storage.

trace.description: The `set(description: string)` custom setter on the `description` field receives caller-supplied text. The caller is outside this file — the data arrives via the auto-generated CRUD surface at POST /api/Products or PUT /api/Products/:id, where Sequelize binds request body fields to model attributes.

The setter checks `utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.restfulXssChallenge)`. When true, the if-body (line 46) is an empty block — no sanitization, no encoding, no allow-listing is applied to `description`.

When the challenge is enabled, the if-body is an empty block — no sanitization, no encoding, no allow-listing is applied to `description`. The raw caller-supplied value passes through untouched. This empty branch is the design flaw: a security control is conditionally disabled.

When the challenge is disabled, the else branch would execute `description = security.sanitizeSecure(description)`. This is the stronger control that sits beside the empty if-branch. The code shows the developer knew sanitization was needed but chose to disable it conditionally.

`this.setDataValue('description', description)` persists the raw, unsanitized user input into the model's description attribute. This is the persistence point for stored XSS. The render sink (where the stored value is interpolated into HTML) is outside this file, but the absence of sanitization at this storage point is the defect.

title: Mass assignment of price and deluxePrice fields via auto-generated CRUD exposes economic fields to caller control
description: The Product model declares `price` (line 52) and `deluxePrice` (line 53) as plain DECIMAL fields with no field-level access restrictions, no exclude lists, and no server-side re-derivation. The architecture context confirms an auto-generated CRUD surface at /api/Products (POST and /api/Products/:id PUT). Auto-generated Sequelize CRUD endpoints typically bind all model fields from the request body. This means a caller can set `price` and `deluxePrice` to arbitrary values — for example, setting a product's price to 0.01 or a negative value. The server should derive or validate pricing, not accept it from the client. The model definition provides no field allow-list or property-level authorization, and the auto-generated CRUD inherits this permissive surface.

trace.description: The `price` field is declared as `DataTypes.DECIMAL` with no access restriction. The caller is outside this file — data arrives via the auto-generated POST /api/Products or PUT /api/Products/:id endpoint, which binds request body fields to model attributes.

The `deluxePrice` field is similarly declared as `DataTypes.DECIMAL` with no access restriction. Neither field has a custom setter, validation, or any mechanism to prevent caller-controlled values from being persisted.

Both `price` and `deluxePrice` are part of the fields object passed as the first argument to `Product.init(...)`. This object defines the complete set of writable model attributes. There is no `fields` allow-list or per-field `allowNull`/`validate` configuration that would restrict which fields the auto-generated CRUD surface accepts.

The options object passed as the second argument to `Product.init` (lines 56-60) configures `tableName`, `sequelize`, and `paranoid`, but includes no `defaultScope`, no field exclusion, and no access-control configuration that would prevent `price` or `deluxePrice` from being bound by the auto-generated CRUD handlers. The server never re-derives price — it trusts the client-supplied value, which is an insecure design choice for economic fields.

`Product.init(...)` registers all fields including `price` and `deluxePrice` as writable model attributes. The auto-generated CRUD surface inherits this schema, allowing any caller who can reach POST /api/Products or PUT /api/Products/:id to set pricing fields directly. The server never re-derives price — it trusts the client-supplied value, which is an insecure design choice for economic fields.

title: SSRF via unvalidated URL download in retrieveCustomFile
description: The retrieveCustomFile function checks if a configuration value is a URL (via utils.isUrl) and, if so, downloads the content to the local filesystem using utils.downloadToFile. The destination URL is taken directly from application configuration with no allow-listing, no internal-range blocking, and no scheme restriction beyond what isUrl may enforce. If an attacker can influence configuration values (through environment variables, a config-administration endpoint, or config file injection — node-config reads environment variable overrides), they can force the server to make outbound requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., 169.254.169.254), or other restricted network resources. The downloaded content is written to disk and in some cases copied or referenced by the frontend, compounding the impact.

The actual external data is the config value itself, read at line 74 via config.get<string>(sourceProperty). The config module (node-config) supports environment variable overrides, so these values can originate from outside the application code.
utils.isUrl(file) checks whether the config value looks like a URL. If true, the code enters the download branch — there is no allow-list or destination validation.
let file = config.get<string>(sourceProperty) — the untrusted config value is loaded into the local variable `file`. No validation has been applied yet.
const filePath = file — the full, unvalidated URL is preserved verbatim in `filePath`, ready to be passed to the download function.
file = utils.extractFilename(file) — `file` is reassigned to just the extracted filename for use in the local destination path. The original URL remains untouched in `filePath`.

await utils.downloadToFile(filePath, destinationFolder + '/' + file) — the full, unvalidated URL from config is passed directly as the download target. No origin allow-list, no private-IP/loopback blocking, no metadata-endpoint filtering is applied. An attacker who controls the config value can direct the server to fetch from internal services.

title: Stored XSS via unencoded config values injected into index.html
description: Multiple customization functions read values from application configuration and inject them directly into frontend/dist/frontend/index.html using the 'replace' module's regex replacement. None of the values are HTML-encoded or sanitized before insertion. customizeTitle wraps the config value in <title> tags; customizeTheme inserts it into an HTML class attribute; customizeFavicon inserts a filename into an href attribute; customizeCookieConsentBanner concatenates four config values into a JSON-in-HTML structure. Because index.html is served to every user, any script or markup injected through these config values becomes persistent stored XSS affecting all visitors. If an attacker can influence any of these config values (e.g., application.name, application.theme, application.cookieConsent.message, etc.) through environment variables or a config-management interface, they can execute arbitrary JavaScript in every user's browser.

No HTML encoding is applied. The caller (customizeApplication at line 14) is within this file, but the config value originates from external configuration (node-config, which reads config files and environment variables).

The unencoded title string is passed as the 'replacement' argument to replace(), which performs a regex-based substitution in frontend/dist/frontend/index.html. The same unencoded-injection pattern appears in customizeTheme (line 95, class attribute), customizeFavicon (line 58, href attribute), and customizeCookieConsentBanner (line 106, JSON-in-HTML with four unescaped config values concatenated into a string).
