The same unencoded-injection pattern appears in customizeTheme (line 95→98, class attribute), customizeFavicon (line 58, href attribute), and customizeCookieConsentBanner (line 106→109, JSON-in-HTML with four unescaped config values).

The replacement writes the unencoded config value into index.html, which is served to all users. A config value like '</title><script>alert(document.cookie)</script>' would execute JavaScript in every visitor's browser. The render sink (browser rendering of index.html) is outside this file, but the injection point — where unencoded data is written into HTML markup — is here. For customizeCookieConsentBanner (line 106), a config value containing a double-quote also breaks out of the JSON string context, enabling arbitrary script injection through the JSON-in-HTML boundary.

title: Fragile string-concatenation of config values into JSON structure without escaping
description: customizeCookieConsentBanner constructs a JSON object string by concatenating four separate config values (message, dismissText, linkText, linkUrl) into a template with hardcoded double-quotes. No JSON string escaping is applied to any value. A config value containing a double-quote character breaks the JSON structure, which can corrupt the page's JavaScript or enable injection. This is a design flaw: the code should parse, modify, and re-serialize the JSON rather than building it by string concatenation. The same design flaw exists in the use of regex replacement to modify structured HTML — the code treats markup as a flat string rather than parsing the DOM, making it fragile to content that matches or breaks the regex patterns.

The replace() call is initiated. The concatenated `contentProperty` string containing four unescaped config values is about to be passed as the replacement.

It is a fragile regex that assumes the existing content matches exactly; it does not validate or sanitize the replacement value.

The design assumes all four config values are safe JSON string contents — no escaping of quotes, backslashes, or control characters is performed. If any value contains a double-quote, the JSON structure is broken, potentially corrupting the page's JavaScript context. The design choice to build JSON by string concatenation rather than JSON.parse/modify/stringify is the root flaw — the code works correctly only when all inputs are benign, and the design provides no defense when they are not.

title: UserId field on Address model is caller-controllable via auto-generated CRUD, enabling cross-user address creation and BOLA
description: The Address model defines a `UserId` field (line 33-35) as a plain INTEGER with no validation, no default derived from session, and no field-level access restriction. The architecture context confirms this model is exposed through an auto-generated CRUD surface at `/api/Addresss` (POST) and `/api/Addresss/:id` (PUT). Auto-generated CRUD endpoints typically bind all request body fields directly to the model. A caller can therefore include `UserId` in the request body and create or update an address record that belongs to another user. This is a mass assignment / broken object property level authorization issue (API3) because the sensitive ownership field `UserId` is not on an allow-list of server-controlled fields. It is also a BOLA issue (API1) because once an address is created under another user's ID, the `/api/Addresss/:id` lookup by primary key would return it to anyone who knows the ID without verifying ownership. From an insecure-design perspective, the server should derive `UserId` from the authenticated session, not accept it as a client-supplied value — the design never establishes that rule.

The caller is outside this file — the auto-generated CRUD endpoint at POST /api/Addresss and PUT /api/Addresss/:id receives the request body and passes it into Sequelize model create/update.

UserId has only a type constraint (DataTypes.INTEGER) and no validation rule that restricts its value, no default that derives it from the session, and no indication it is excluded from mass assignment. All other fields (fullName, mobileNum, zipCode, streetAddress, city, state, country) have validations (lines 41-66) but UserId has none.

Address.init (line 31) registers the model with Sequelize. The auto-generated CRUD layer will call Address.create(req.body) / Address.update(req.body, ...) binding all fields including UserId. A caller can POST to /api/Addresss with {"UserId": <victim_id>, "fullName": "...", ...} and create an address under another user's account. On PUT /api/Addresss/:id, they can reassign ownership. The model provides no field allow-list, no server-side UserId derivation, and no ownership scoping.

title: Free-form text fields on Address model stored without sanitization enable stored XSS

No sanitization, encoding, or content allow-listing is applied. These are conventional display fields (names, addresses) that will be rendered in an address book or checkout UI. If any rendering context outputs these values without HTML encoding, a stored XSS payload (e.g., `` in `fullName`) will execute in the victim's browser. The render sink is outside this file, but the persistence point — where unvalidated text is accepted into the datastore — is here.

title: systemWideNotifications URL validated for presence but not for scheme or destination, enabling SSRF
description: The `checkForIllogicalCombos` function validates that if `ctf.systemWideNotifications.url` is set, a `pollFrequencySeconds` value must also exist and be positive. However, the URL itself is never validated for scheme (http/https only), destination host, or against any allow-list. If the configuration is user-controllable — which is plausible given the application's `POST /file-upload → handleYamlUpload` route that accepts YAML configuration — an attacker could set this URL to an internal service address (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or an internal admin endpoint). The application would then make periodic outbound requests to that URL, enabling server-side request forgery. The validation function's job is to validate configuration before it is used, and it validates every other aspect of the notifications config except the URL destination.

The function reads `configuration.ctf?.systemWideNotifications` and checks `notifications?.url` for truthiness (presence) only.

`success = checkConfigSchema() && success` — the Zod schema validation runs first (on the default config object, see line 54). If the schema permits arbitrary URL strings for systemWideNotifications.url, the URL passes this gate without scheme or destination validation.

First illogical-combo check (restrictToTutorialsFirst vs hackingInstructor). The function proceeds through its checks sequentially; this gate does not touch the URL but confirms the validation flow continues.

After the truthiness check on the URL, the only subsequent validation targets `pollFrequencySeconds` (must be a positive number). The URL itself is never re-examined. The function returns `success` at line 184, and the validated URL is consumed elsewhere in the application to make outbound polling requests — creating an SSRF vector where an attacker-controlled URL pointing to internal services or cloud metadata endpoints passes validation.

The only validation applied to `notifications.url` is a truthiness check. The URL scheme, host, port, and destination are never validated. No allow-listing, no origin comparison, no scheme restriction is performed. title: Schema validation and content validation operate on different data sources, allowing injected products/memories to bypass schema validation
description: In `validateConfig`, `checkConfigSchema()` is called at line 31 with no arguments, so it validates the default configuration object (`config.util.toObject()`). However, the subsequent checks (lines 32–39) validate the `products` and `memories` parameters that were passed into `validateConfig` — which may have been supplied by a caller outside this file (e.g., from a YAML upload). This means the passed-in products and memories are never subjected to the Zod schema validation (`ValidationSchema.safeParse`). The individual check functions only verify specific conditions (minimum count, uniqueness of special products, required keys), but they do not validate the overall structure, type, or content of the product/memory objects. Malicious content — dangerous URLs, script payloads, or unexpected types in product fields — would pass all checks in this file. This is a design flaw because the validation pipeline assumes the schema check covers the same data that the content checks examine, but it does not.

title: pollFrequencySeconds validated as positive but with no minimum bound, enabling excessive polling
description: The `checkForIllogicalCombos` function validates that `pollFrequencySeconds` is a number greater than zero (line 179), but imposes no minimum practical bound. If the application uses this value to schedule periodic HTTP requests to `systemWideNotifications.url`, an attacker who controls the configuration (e.g., via YAML upload) could set an extremely small polling interval, causing the application to make rapid, repeated outbound requests. title: SSRF via downloadToFile — arbitrary URL fetched without destination validation
description: The exported `downloadToFile` function accepts a URL parameter and passes it directly to the `download()` HTTP client without any validation of the destination. There is no parsing of the URL origin, no allow-list of permitted hosts, no check for internal IP ranges (loopback, private networks, cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254), and no scheme restriction beyond what the `download` library defaults to. Any caller that passes user-controlled input as the `url` argument creates a Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability. The route listing shows `POST /profile/image/url -> profileImageUrlUpload()` with `auth: none`, which is a strong candidate caller for this function. An attacker could supply `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or `http://localhost:3000/api/Users` to access internal services and cloud metadata.

Per the SSRF playbook, a destination is only validated if the check parses the URL and compares the origin (scheme + host + port) against an allow-list; a simple prefix check does not constitute validation.

title: HMAC-SHA1 used for CTF flag generation — deprecated hash algorithm
description: The `ctfFlag` function uses `crypto.createHmac('sha1', getCtfKey())` to generate CTF flags. SHA-1 is a deprecated cryptographic hash algorithm (NIST SP 800-131A disallows SHA-1 for digital signatures and HMAC applications requiring collision resistance after 2013). While HMAC-SHA1 is not as catastrophically broken as raw SHA-1, modern guidance recommends SHA-256 or stronger. If the CTF key is used for any security-relevant purpose beyond display flags, or if flag forgery is a concern, this is exploitable. The key is sourced from either an environment variable (`CTF_KEY`) or a file (`ctf.key`) with no enforcement of key length or entropy.

title: Recycle model exposes UserId for mass assignment via auto-generated CRUD
description: The Recycle model defines `UserId` as a plain INTEGER column with no field-level protection, no default hook, and no beforeCreate/beforeUpdate enforcement that ties it to the authenticated session. Because the application auto-generates CRUD endpoints at POST /api/Recycles and PUT /api/Recycles/:id with automatic field binding, a caller can supply `UserId` in the request body to create or update a Recycle record under any arbitrary user's identity. This is broken object property level authorization (mass assignment): the caller controls a field (the owning user) that the server should derive from the session. The impact is impersonation — an attacker can create recycle records attributed to other users, or reassign existing records to different users via PUT. The model design itself is insecure because it never establishes a server-side invariant that UserId must match the authenticated user.

The attacker sets UserId to another user's ID, creating or reassigning a recycle record under that user's identity — a mass assignment privilege escalation with no compensating control in the model.

title: Unvalidated webhook URL passed directly to fetch() enables SSRF
description: The `notify` function accepts a `webhook` parameter (defaulting to an environment variable) and passes it directly to `fetch()` on line 18 without any URL validation. title: Monetary fields use FLOAT type, enabling precision-based economic imbalance
description: The `price` and `deluxePrice` fields (lines 36-37) are declared as DataTypes.FLOAT. Floating-point representation cannot exactly represent many decimal currency values, which creates a class of economic-imbalance defects: rounding errors accumulate across transactions, and an attacker who can perform repeated operations (e.g., split a delivery into sub-transactions, or exploit refund/cancellation logic) may cause the server to compute a different total than the intended price. The correct design for monetary values is DECIMAL/NUMERIC with fixed precision. This is a design flaw — the model works exactly as declared, and the declared type permits precision-based abuse.

Both fields represent monetary values but use a floating-point type, which cannot guarantee exact decimal precision. This design choice permits rounding discrepancies that an attacker could exploit to achieve economic imbalance — for example, by engineering transactions where accumulated floating-point error causes the server to accept a lower total than the sum of the intended prices.

title: Reflected XSS via error message constructed with unencoded request URL
description: The serveAngularClient middleware extracts the request URL and, when the URL starts with '/api' or '/rest', passes it into an Error message via string concatenation: `next(new Error('Unexpected path: ' + url))`. The URL is user-controlled and URL-decoded by Express before reaching this handler. An attacker can craft a request such as `/api/<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` (or its URL-encoded form). Because the URL starts with '/api', it enters the else branch and the raw decoded value is interpolated into the error message with no encoding. If Express's default (or a custom) error handler renders the error message in an HTML response — which Express does in development mode and many custom handlers do in production — the attacker's markup executes in the victim's browser. This is a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability.

The caller (an Express route registration outside this file) passes every request through this handler. The url value is fully user-controlled and URL-decoded by Express before it arrives here.

The url is tested with utils.startsWith(url, '/api') and utils.startsWith(url, '/rest'). Any URL beginning with '/api' or '/rest' (e.g., '/api/') falls into the else branch on line 16. The check does not sanitize or encode the url; it only decides the branch.
The else branch is entered because the url did start with '/api' or '/rest' (negated by the ! operators on line 13). Control flow falls through to line 16, carrying the unmodified url value forward.

The unencoded url is concatenated into an Error message: next(new Error('Unexpected path: ' + url)). The error object (carrying the attacker-controlled string in its .message) is passed to Express's next(), handing it to the error-handling middleware chain. Express's default error handler renders error.message inside an HTML response in development mode, and custom error handlers commonly do the same in production. There is no output encoding applied to url at any point between the request and this sink, so any HTML/script content in the URL is reflected verbatim into the error document.

title: Hardcoded database credentials in Sequelize initialization
description: The createSequelize function constructs the database connection with hardcoded literal values for the database name ('database'), username ('username'), and password ('password') on line 33. While the current dialect is SQLite (which ignores these credentials), these hardcoded values are embedded in source code and represent a dangerous default configuration pattern. If the dialect or storage backend were changed, these default credentials would be used without further configuration. Per the misconfiguration playbook, hardcoded secrets in source code are always findings regardless of whether they are currently used in production. The resulting instance propagates through the module: it is returned from createSequelize (line 44), assigned to the module-level `sequelize` variable (line 30), used to initialize every application model (line 75), and exported for external callers (line 77).

No security-relevant database events — authentication lookups, data access, privilege changes — will be logged at the database layer.

title: Database query logging disabled

This means no database-level audit trail exists for security-relevant operations such as authentication queries, privilege changes, data exports, or suspicious query patterns. In the event of a security incident, investigators cannot reconstruct which database operations were performed. The complete absence of SQL logging is both a logging-monitoring failure (inability to detect or investigate database-level attacks) and a misconfiguration (a dangerous default where security-relevant observability is turned off).

title: Captcha answer stored in plaintext enables captcha bypass on any data exposure
description: The ImageCaptcha model stores the captcha `answer` as a plain `DataTypes.STRING` (line 35). Captcha answers are secrets that must be hashed before persistence — the server needs to verify a user's response, but must never be able to return the expected answer itself. Storing the answer in plaintext means that any endpoint that serializes or returns an ImageCaptcha record (a BOLA, an overly broad API response, a debug endpoint, an error trace) immediately defeats the captcha. An attacker who can read the record gets the correct answer and can submit it. This is a design-level defect: the model works as written, but the design of storing a verification secret in cleartext is inherently insecure and creates a single point of failure where any unrelated data-exposure bug becomes a complete captcha bypass.

The model also stores `image` as a plain STRING (line 34). Together, `image` and `answer` form a complete captcha challenge-solution pair. Any read of this row exposes both the image and its solution.

`class ImageCaptcha extends Model<...>` — the class inherits Sequelize's Model base class, which means all declared attributes are automatically mapped to database columns and persisted as-is unless hooks or setters intervene.

`declare answer: string` — the TypeScript property declaration confirms the answer is a plain string type. There is no wrapper type, no branded type, and no indication that this value should be treated as a secret requiring one-way transformation.

`const ImageCaptchaModelInit = (sequelize: Sequelize) => {` — the initialization function receives the Sequelize connection. This is the function a caller (outside this file) invokes to register the model with the database, and it contains no pre-processing of the answer field.

`ImageCaptcha.init(` — the init call registers the column definitions (lines 29–37) with Sequelize. At this point the schema is finalized: `answer` is a plain STRING column with no `set` hook, no `get` hook, and no custom field type that would hash on write.

The options object `{` begins here, containing only `tableName: 'ImageCaptchas'` (line 40) and `sequelize` (line 41). There are no `hooks` (e.g., `beforeCreate` to hash the answer), no `setterMethods`, and no `defaultScope` that would hide the answer from serialization. The absence of any transformation mechanism here is what allows the plaintext answer to reach the database unchanged.

The plaintext `answer` column is the sink. The design flaw is that no hashing or one-way transformation is applied — the answer is persisted exactly as the server generated it. Any downstream read of an ImageCaptcha record (the caller is outside this file) returns the correct answer, defeating the captcha.

title: Mass assignment risk: captcha answer field is a writable model property with no field-level restriction
description: The ImageCaptcha model defines `answer` as a standard writable Sequelize attribute (line 35) with no exclude mechanism, no default, and no read-only guard. Sequelize models are writable on all declared fields by default. If any route handler elsewhere in the application performs automatic or semi-automatic field binding — e.g., `ImageCaptcha.create(req.body)` or spreading the request body into a create/update call — a caller could supply their own `answer` value, creating a captcha record with a known solution. This would let the attacker solve their own captcha challenges trivially, bypassing the anti-automation control. The model provides no field-level authorization (no `allowNull` constraint combined with a server-set default, no field exclusion from mass assignment) to prevent caller-controlled `answer` values from being persisted.

`ImageCaptcha.init()` (line 27) registers all four fields — `image`, `answer`, `UserId`, `createdAt` — as model attributes. Sequelize treats all of these as writable by default. There is no field allow-list or deny-list configured in the model options (lines 39-42) to restrict which fields can be set via `create()` or `update()`.

`class ImageCaptcha extends Model<...>` — the class inherits Sequelize's Model base class. By Sequelize convention, all attributes declared in `init()` are writable via `create()`, `update()`, `build()`, and `set()` unless explicitly restricted. There is no read-only or computed-field marker on the class.

`declare answer: string` — the TypeScript property declaration has no `readonly` modifier. The model's type system permits assignment to `answer` at any time, consistent with Sequelize's default writable behavior.

`UserId: { type: DataTypes.INTEGER }` — this is another sensitive field that is also freely writable. An attacker who can mass-assign could set `UserId` to any value, associating a captcha record with a different user. This confirms the pattern: every field in this model is exposed to caller-controlled writes with no per-field authorization.

The options object `{` begins here, containing only `tableName` (line 40) and `sequelize` (line 41). There is no `readonlyAttributes` array, no `createOnly` list, and no Sequelize hook that would override caller-supplied values for sensitive fields. The model explicitly opts out of field-level protection.

The sink is the `answer` field itself: any `ImageCaptcha.create(callerControlledObject)` or `instance.update(callerControlledObject)` call (the caller is outside this file) would persist a caller-supplied `answer` value without objection from the model layer.

title: Admin application-configuration endpoint exposes full config without authentication
description: The handler `retrieveAppConfiguration` is registered at `GET /rest/admin/application-configuration` with no authentication middleware (`auth: none`). The route name indicates this is an admin-only endpoint, but no authorization check exists in the handler either. Every other configuration value — potentially including database connection strings, internal service URLs, API keys, secrets, and other sensitive settings — is returned to any unauthenticated caller. This is a Broken Function Level Authorization failure (an admin endpoint reachable without auth) and a security misconfiguration (full internal configuration exposure with incomplete scrubbing of secrets).

An attacker simply sends `GET /rest/admin/application-configuration` to obtain internal configuration details.

title: Mass assignment of UserId on Complaint model via auto-generated CRUD
description: The Complaint model defines UserId as a plain INTEGER field with no restrictions, no default value, and no server-side derivation from the session. title: Stored XSS: free-form message and file fields persisted without sanitization
description: The Complaint model defines message (STRING(4096)) and file (STRING) as free-form text fields with no sanitization, encoding, or content-type validation. These fields accept arbitrary user-supplied strings that are persisted to the database. The message field is a natural candidate for stored XSS — if rendered in an HTML context without proper output encoding downstream (outside this file), attacker-supplied script will execute in victims' browsers. The file field is especially dangerous: it stores a path or URL with no scheme validation, so a javascript: or data: URI could be persisted and later rendered as a clickable link.

title: UserId is a caller-controlled field with no server-side derivation or referential integrity
description: The Complaint model's design treats UserId as an ordinary data field rather than a server-derived ownership attribute. There is no Sequelize association (belongsTo User), no foreign key constraint, and no hook that sets UserId from the authenticated session. The design delegates the user-complaint linkage entirely to the caller, which means the server never independently establishes who filed a complaint. This permits a user to file complaints attributed to arbitrary users, break referential integrity by referencing non-existent users, and complicate accountability for abuse reports. The fix is a design change: derive UserId server-side from the session, not from the request body.

title: Exported fetch-based functions perform outbound HTTP requests to caller-supplied URLs without destination validation or allow-listing
description: The exported function `checkIfDomainReachable` accepts an arbitrary URL string and passes it directly to `fetch()` with no validation of the scheme, host, port, or IP range. The exported function `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` similarly accepts a URL and fetches `${url}/models`. Neither function checks whether the destination is an internal address, loopback, cloud metadata endpoint, or private network range. While the visible callers in this file pass configuration-derived values (which are not end-user-controlled), both functions are exported and could be invoked from other files with user-controlled input. The functions also lack any retry or concurrency caps, meaning a caller passing many distinct URLs could trigger many simultaneous outbound requests each holding a connection for up to 5 seconds.

The `domain` parameter is passed directly to `fetch(domain, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })` with no URL parsing, scheme validation, host allow-listing, or internal-IP range check.

The exported function `checkIfLlmModelAvailable(llmApiUrl: string)` also receives a URL string from its caller. The only visible internal caller is at line 84, which passes the config-derived `llmApiUrl`; external callers may pass user-controlled values.
`const model = config.get<string>('application.chatBot.model')` retrieves the model name from config. No validation is applied to the `llmApiUrl` parameter.
A `try` block begins. The `llmApiUrl` parameter has not been parsed, validated, or checked against any allow-list.

`fetch(`${llmApiUrl}/models`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })` concatenates the caller-supplied URL with `/models` via template literal and passes it directly to fetch without destination validation. An attacker-controlled `llmApiUrl` could target internal services.

The `fetch()` call makes an outbound HTTP request to whatever URL was supplied. If a caller passes a user-controlled URL (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` or `http://localhost:8080/admin`), the server will make the request and log whether it succeeded, effectively acting as an SSRF oracle. The same pattern exists in `checkIfLlmModelAvailable` at line 236 where `fetch(`${llmApiUrl}/models`)` is called.

title: API key requirement for LLM API bypassed based on weak URL pattern matching instead of explicit configuration flag
description: The function `isOllamaUrl` determines whether an LLM API endpoint should require an API key by matching the URL's port (11434), hostname ('ollama'), or path prefix ('/ollama'). This is a design flaw: the decision to skip credential validation is based on superficial URL pattern matching rather than an explicit configuration property. Any service running on port 11434, any hostname resolving to 'ollama', or any API path starting with '/ollama' will cause the application to skip the `LLM_API_KEY` environment variable check entirely. An attacker who can influence the `application.chatBot.llmApiUrl` configuration value (e.g., through environment variable manipulation or config file injection) could point the LLM API URL to an internal service on port 11434 to bypass the API key precondition, or point it at an attacker-controlled endpoint that mimics the Ollama API shape to intercept or manipulate LLM traffic.

None of these checks verify that the endpoint is actually an Ollama instance or that it is trusted.

`const llmApiReachable = await checkIfDomainReachable(llmApiUrl)` uses the config URL to check reachability. The result gates entry into the block at line 82.

`return parsed.port === '11434' || parsed.hostname === 'ollama' || parsed.pathname.startsWith('/ollama')` performs three weak pattern checks. Any URL on port 11434, any hostname equal to 'ollama', or any path starting with '/ollama' is classified as an Ollama instance, regardless of whether it actually is one.

When `isOllamaUrl` returns true, `checkIfEnvironmentVariableExists('LLM_API_KEY')` at line 97 is never called, and `preconditionResults.LLM_API_KEY` is never set. The application proceeds without any API key validation for the LLM endpoint, relying solely on the URL matching one of three superficial patterns.

title: Unvalidated external URL download into application frontend assets directory
description: The customizeEasterEgg function reads an overlayMap value from configuration. When this value is a URL, the code downloads its contents directly into the application's frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/ directory without validating the URL scheme, verifying content type, checking file integrity, or restricting the destination path. An attacker who can influence the application configuration (e.g., through environment variables, a config injection, or a compromised admin interface) can cause the application to fetch arbitrary content from any URL — including internal network addresses (SSRF) — and place it into the application's public asset directory. This downloaded content is then referenced by the threejs-demo.html page, meaning the attacker can serve arbitrary JavaScript/HTML to application users through a trusted application path.

title: HTML/JavaScript injection via unsanitized config values interpolated into HTML
description: Two configuration values — easterEggPlanet.overlayMap and easterEggPlanet.name — are directly interpolated into HTML content without any sanitization or escaping. The overlay value is inserted into a JavaScript statement within threejs-demo.html (line 27), and the name value is inserted into a <title> tag (line 38). If an attacker can control these configuration values, they can inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript into the threejs-demo.html page, which is served to users from the application's own assets directory. Because the injection point is inside a <script> context (line 27) and a <title> context (line 38), even simple payloads like closing the current tag or string would achieve script execution. The design never establishes sanitization of these values before they reach the HTML template.

title: File modification operations executed with silent mode suppressing all error output and logging
description: Both replace operations that modify threejs-demo.html are invoked with `silent: true`, which suppresses all console output, warnings, and errors from the replacement library. Since these operations modify application assets based on external configuration values — including downloading and placing external content — the lack of any logging makes it impossible to detect or investigate a compromise of the easter egg customization pipeline. title: Address queries scoped by client-controllable req.body.UserId instead of server-derived identity
description: All three handlers (getAddress, getAddressById, delAddressById) scope their database lookups by `req.body.UserId`. The route is protected only by `security.appendUserId()` middleware, whose name suggests it appends the user identity into the body — but the handler itself never reads from a server-trusted source like `req.user` or `req.session`. If the middleware only sets `req.body.UserId` when absent, or if a client can supply a body on a GET request that survives the middleware, an authenticated attacker can substitute another user's UserId and read or delete that user's addresses. Even if the middleware overwrites the value, the design is fragile: the authorization decision is anchored to a value that lives in the request body namespace (client-controlled territory) rather than in a server-side session object. A GET endpoint reading identity from `req.body` is itself a red flag, since GET bodies are unconventional and may bypass middleware that only parses bodies for state-changing methods. The impact is cross-user address disclosure (BOLA) and potential deletion of other users' address records. Because a defect in identity resolution changes who the application believes the caller is, this also establishes the crypto-auth/authentication class.

No server-side identity extraction (e.g., req.user, req.session) occurs at this line or anywhere in the handler.

The full set of matching addresses (potentially another user's) is serialized and returned to the caller via res.status(200).json({ status: 'success', data: addresses }). If req.body.UserId is not definitively overwritten by the middleware, an attacker supplies VictimUserId in the request body and receives all of the victim's addresses. Proof-of-concept: User A sends GET /api/Addresss with body { "UserId": <User B's id> } and receives User B's addresses. The same BOLA pattern in getAddressById (line 18→20) returns a single victim address, and in delAddressById (line 29→31) deletes the victim's address.

title: getAddress returns unbounded result set with no pagination or limit
description: The getAddress handler calls AddressModel.findAll with only a UserId filter and no limit, offset, or pagination parameters. While the architecture summary notes the auto-generated CRUD surface applies pagination, this hand-written route does not. If a user (or an attacker exploiting the BOLA above with a victim who has a large address book) has many address records, a single request loads the entire collection into memory. Repeated requests can amplify memory consumption. Even scoped by UserId, there is no upper bound on how many records a single user may have, and no server-side cap on the returned set.

description: The Memory model defines `caption` (line 36) and `imagePath` (line 37) as plain `DataTypes.STRING` with no validation, sanitization, or URL scheme allow-list. title: Insecure design: `imagePath` accepts arbitrary URL schemes with no server-side validation of what constitutes a valid image URL
description: The design of the Memory model permits any string value for `imagePath` (line 37). There is no design-level rule enforcing that imagePath must be an HTTP(S) URL pointing to an actual image resource, no scheme allow-list, and no content-type validation. The application has a `POST /profile/image/url` route (outside this file) that stores user-provided URLs into this field. The design flaw is that the server never re-derives or validates the nature of the stored path — it accepts whatever the client provides. An attacker can store `javascript:alert(1)//` as an imagePath, and the design provides no control to prevent it. The fix is not a single validation call but a design decision to enforce URL scheme and content-type constraints that the model currently does not encode.

The password-reset flow (outside this file) will present attacker-injected questions to users as if they were official, enabling social engineering and credential theft.

title: Basket retrieval endpoint has no authentication or per-resource authorization (BOLA)
description: The GET /rest/basket/:id route is registered with no authentication middleware (auth: none). The handler retrieveBasket() accepts an arbitrary basket ID from the path parameter and performs a direct lookup via BasketModel.findOne({ where: { id } }) without any ownership or authorization check. Any unauthenticated caller can retrieve any user's shopping basket by supplying or guessing the basket ID. This is a textbook Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability: authentication is absent entirely, and there is no per-resource ownership verification between the lookup and the response. The basket data, including associated products, is returned directly to the caller.

BasketModel.findOne({ where: { id } }) performs a lookup by the caller-supplied ID. The query is not scoped to any user — there is no WHERE clause involving a user_id or session-derived owner. The ORM parameterizes the value (no injection), but the query has no authorization constraint.

The async handler function receives the Request object. No middleware has populated req with a user identity or any authorization context, because auth: none means no auth middleware runs before this handler.
The try block opens. There is no authorization guard at the top of the handler — no check for req.user, no session validation, no role verification.

The returned basket object is accessed: basket.Products is checked for null. At this point the basket has already been fetched for an unverified caller. No authorization check is performed on the basket or its owner before its contents are read.

Each product name is translated via req.__(basket.Products[i].name). The basket data is being actively transformed for return, confirming the handler intends to deliver this data to the caller.

Between the lookup (line 19) and this response, no ownership or authorization check occurs. An attacker can call GET /rest/basket/1, GET /rest/basket/2, etc., and retrieve every user's basket without any credentials.

title: Unauthenticated basket endpoint with no rate limiting or result size cap
description: The GET /rest/basket/:id endpoint is reachable without authentication (auth: none) and performs a database query on every request. There is no visible rate limiting, no request throttling, and no cap on the number of products returned in the basket (the include pulls all associated ProductModel rows). An attacker can flood this endpoint with requests using sequential IDs, causing repeated database queries and large JSON responses, degrading database and application performance. The unauthenticated nature means the attacker needs no credentials to sustain the attack.

title: Hardcoded Hashids salts enable forging of continue codes for challenge progress
description: All three exported functions create Hashids instances with hardcoded salt values (lines 13, 25, 38). Hashids is a reversible encoding library, not a cryptographic primitive — its salt is the only secret preventing decoding and forgery. Because the salts are hardcoded in source code (and this is an open-source project), they are publicly known. An attacker who knows the salt can encode arbitrary challenge IDs to produce a forged continue code that claims any desired set of challenges as solved. The continue code is used downstream as a trust token to restore challenge-solving progress, so this forgery bypasses the entire challenge workflow. The design flaw is that a reversible, non-cryptographic encoding is used as an integrity-protected progress token; the crypto-auth flaw is that the signing secret is hardcoded and publicly exposed.

Solved challenge IDs are encoded with hashids.encode(ids) to produce the continueCode. This encoding is fully reversible by anyone who knows the salt.
The function returns an Express request handler closure that captures the hashids instance with the hardcoded salt.
Inside the handler, an empty ids array is initialized to collect solved challenge IDs.
The handler iterates over all challenges from the global datacache, entering a loop that checks each challenge.
For each challenge, challenge.solved is checked; if true, challenge.id is pushed into the ids array. These IDs are the values that will be encoded.
The loop over challenges ends; the ids array now holds all solved challenge IDs.

The continueCode is returned in the JSON response. Because the salt is hardcoded and public, an attacker can forge a continueCode encoding any challenge IDs (including all of them) and submit it to the progress-restore endpoint to claim credit for challenges they never solved. The same pattern repeats at lines 25/32 and 38/45 with different but equally hardcoded salts.

title: Unauthenticated endpoints expose server-side challenge progress state

Any unauthenticated user can retrieve this information, which reveals the server's current challenge-progress state. If these endpoints were intended to be per-session or per-user, the lack of authentication would also enable cross-user information disclosure.

title: Private asset served without authentication on unauthenticated route

title: BasketId authorization check uses first array element but item creation uses last, enabling cross-user basket manipulation
description: In addBasketItem, the raw body is parsed as an array of key-value pairs and all BasketId values are collected into the basketIds array. The authorization check on line 37 validates only basketIds[0] against the authenticated user's basket ID (user.bid). However, the actual basket item object on line 42 is constructed using basketIds[basketIds.length - 1] — the last element. The authorization check passes because it inspects basketIds[0], but the item is persisted with the victim's BasketId from basketIds[last]. This allows adding items to any user's basket.

title: Unauthenticated basket coupon modification — Broken Object Level Authorization
description: The PUT /rest/basket/:id/coupon/:coupon endpoint has no authentication middleware (auth: none) and the handler performs BasketModel.findByPk(id) without any ownership or authorization check. Any caller — including unauthenticated users — can apply or change the coupon on any basket by supplying an arbitrary basket ID. The basket lookup at line 18 is not scoped to a user (e.g., WHERE user_id = ? AND id = ?); it fetches purely by primary key. This means User A (or an anonymous attacker) can modify User B's basket by substituting the basket ID in the URL. Because the endpoint performs a state-changing write operation (basket.update at line 24) with zero authentication, it is both a BOLA finding and an authentication bypass — the application never verifies who the caller is before mutating a user-owned resource.

return res.status(404).send('Invalid coupon.') — for invalid coupons, a 404 response is returned. The differential between lines 26 and 28 creates an oracle. An attacker can send thousands of requests with different coupon values to discover valid coupons. No rate limit, throttle, or lockout is present in this handler. Because no authentication or authorization was performed, any user (or anonymous attacker) can modify any basket's coupon by substituting the ID in the URL. title: User-controlled `fields` parameter bypasses sensitive-field exclusion, allowing extraction of password hash and other protected properties
description: The handler for GET /rest/user/whoami normally returns a curated subset of user fields that explicitly excludes the password (comment on line 35 says 'not password field'). This is a Broken Object Property Level Authorization (API3) defect: the caller controls which properties are returned, and the default exclusion of sensitive fields is trivially bypassed.

`response = { user: baseUser }` — the attacker-extracted fields are packaged into the response object that will be sent to the caller.

title: JSONP callback on authenticated cookie-based endpoint enables cross-origin theft of user data
description: When the `callback` query parameter is present, the handler responds using `res.jsonp()` (line 55) instead of `res.json()`. This endpoint authenticates via a cookie (`req.cookies.token`, line 17-18). JSONP responses are loaded as `<script>` tags by the browser, and cookie-based requests include the victim's cookies automatically. A malicious website can embed `<script src="http://victim/rest/user/whoami?callback=exfil&fields=password,email">` — the victim's browser sends their auth cookie, the server returns the sensitive user data wrapped in the attacker's callback function, and the attacker's JavaScript receives and exfiltrates the data. This breaks the Same-Origin Policy for an endpoint that returns authenticated, sensitive data. Combined with the `fields` parameter vulnerability, the attacker can steal the victim's password hash and other sensitive fields cross-origin. The design flaw is that JSONP is offered at all on an authenticated, cookie-based endpoint without CSRF protection or origin validation.

`response = { user: baseUser }` — the authenticated user data is packaged into the response object. At this point the response contains sensitive, per-user data tied to the cookie-authenticated identity.

`res.jsonp(response)` returns the authenticated user data as a JSONP-wrapped script. Because authentication is cookie-based and JSONP is loaded via `<script>` tags (which send cookies cross-origin), any third-party site can embed this endpoint with an attacker-chosen callback name and read the victim's full user data, including any sensitive fields requested via the `fields` parameter. There is no CSRF token check, no Origin/Referer validation, and no restriction on cross-origin JSONP access.

title: MD5 used for hashing sensitive data
description: The `hash` function on line 41 uses MD5 (`crypto.createHash('md5')`), a cryptographically broken hash algorithm. MD5 is vulnerable to collision and preimage attacks and provides no key stretching. If this function is used for password hashing, integrity verification, or any security-sensitive purpose, an attacker can leverage precomputed rainbow tables or collision attacks to forge or recover hashed values. No salt is applied either, making rainbow-table lookups trivial. The function is a single-line self-contained operation: the input string flows directly into `createHash('md5')`, then `.update(data)`, then `.digest('hex')` — all on line 41 with no intervening transformation or salt.

`crypto.createHash('md5').update(data).digest('hex')` — MD5 is a deprecated, broken hash algorithm. Any security-sensitive data passed to this function (passwords, tokens, integrity checks) is unprotected.

title: Hardcoded HMAC secret in source code
description: The `hmac` function on line 42 uses a hardcoded secret string `'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'` directly in source code. If this HMAC is used for token generation, integrity verification, or any authentication purpose, an attacker who learns the secret can forge valid HMACs and bypass security controls.

trace.description: The exported `hmac` function accepts a string and computes an HMAC-SHA256 using a hardcoded secret embedded in source code. Callers are outside this file.
`crypto.createHmac('sha256', 'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj')` — the HMAC secret is hardcoded in source, visible to anyone with code access, and cannot be rotated without a code change.

title: Hardcoded RSA private key in source code
description: Line 21 contains a hardcoded RSA private key used for signing JWTs. The private key is a module-level constant assigned directly from a string literal. This key is used by `authorize` (line 54) to sign JWT tokens and by `deluxeToken` (line 148) as an HMAC secret. Anyone with access to the source can extract this key and forge arbitrary JWT tokens, achieving complete authentication bypass. Using an RSA private key as an HMAC secret (line 148) is also a separate cryptographic misuse — RSA key material is not designed for use as a symmetric HMAC key.

trace.description: The `privateKey` constant is assigned a hardcoded RSA private key string in source code.

`crypto.createHmac('sha256', privateKey)` — the same hardcoded RSA private key is also misused as an HMAC secret for `deluxeToken`. RSA private key material is not appropriate for use as a symmetric HMAC key, compounding the cryptographic misuse.

`jwt.sign(user, privateKey, ...)` — the hardcoded private key is used to sign JWT authentication tokens. An attacker with source access can extract this key and forge arbitrary JWT tokens, achieving complete authentication bypass.

title: Open redirect allowlist bypass via substring matching
description: The `isRedirectAllowed` function on line 132 validates redirect URLs by checking if the user-supplied URL *includes* any allowlisted URL as a substring (line 135: `url.includes(allowedUrl)`). Substring matching is not origin matching. An attacker can craft a URL like `https://evil.com/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` which contains the allowlisted URL as a substring in the query string, bypassing the check entirely. This enables open redirect to arbitrary attacker-controlled destinations. The allowlist itself (lines 121-130) contains legitimate URLs, but the matching logic on line 135 defeats its purpose.

trace.description: The exported `isRedirectAllowed` function accepts a URL string from the caller (outside this file) and checks it against an allowlist.

The check `url.includes(allowedUrl)` performs substring matching rather than parsing the URL and comparing the origin (scheme + host + port). A URL like `https://evil.com/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop` passes this check because the allowlisted string appears in the query parameter.
`let allowed = false` — initializes the result flag to false. The function will set this to true if any allowlisted URL matches.
`for (const allowedUrl of redirectAllowlist)` — iterates over the allowlist Set defined on lines 121-130, which contains hardcoded legitimate URLs like `https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop`.
Returns `true` for the attacker-crafted URL, allowing an open redirect to an arbitrary external destination. The caller (outside this file) will redirect the user to the attacker-controlled URL.

title: User identity derived from client-controlled X-User-Email header
description: The `userEmailFrom` function on line 93 extracts a user's email from the `x-user-email` HTTP request header. HTTP headers are fully controlled by the client. If any downstream code uses this email to identify or authenticate the user — rather than deriving identity from a verified JWT token — an attacker can spoof any user's identity by setting an arbitrary `x-user-email` header value, achieving complete authentication bypass. The function destructures the request object to access `headers` and returns the raw header value with no verification.

trace.description: The exported `userEmailFrom` function reads the `x-user-email` header directly from the request object. The request headers are entirely client-controlled. The caller is outside this file.

Returns `headers['x-user-email']` as the user's email identity. Any code that trusts this value for authorization decisions will allow an attacker to impersonate any user by setting an arbitrary email in the header.

title: JWT verification skips expiration check, enabling use of expired tokens
description: The `verify` function on line 55 uses `jws.verify(token, publicKey)` which only checks the JWT signature — it does not validate the `exp` (expiration) claim. The `decode` function on line 56 extracts the payload via `jws.decode(token)?.payload` without any claim validation. The role-checking functions `isAccounting` (line 154), `isDeluxe` (line 164), and `isCustomer` (line 169) all chain `verify()` && `decode()` and then check role claims from the decoded payload. Since `verify` never checks expiration, a token that has expired but retains a valid signature will pass these checks, granting the associated role privileges beyond the intended 6-hour window (set by `authorize` on line 54 with `expiresIn: '6h'`).

trace.description: The exported `verify` function accepts a JWT token string and is used by role-checking middleware. The caller is outside this file.
`jws.verify(token, publicKey)` only verifies the cryptographic signature. It does not parse or validate the `exp` claim, so an expired token still passes verification.

`export const decode = (token: string) => { return jws.decode(token)?.payload }` — extracts the JWT payload via `jws.decode`. No claim validation (expiration, issuer, audience) is performed during decoding. The raw payload is returned.

`if (decodedToken?.data?.role === roles.accounting) { next() }` — grants accounting-level access based on the role claim from an expired-but-validly-signed token. The same pattern appears in `isDeluxe` (line 165) and `isCustomer` (line 170).

`isAccounting` (and similarly `isDeluxe` at line 164, `isCustomer` at line 169) calls `verify(utils.jwtFrom(req)) && decode(utils.jwtFrom(req))` — a token that has expired but retains a valid signature will pass this check, granting the associated role privileges beyond the intended 6-hour window.

title: Weak regex-based HTML sanitization bypassable for stored XSS
description: The `sanitizeLegacy` function on line 59 attempts to sanitize HTML by removing tags using the regex `/<(?:\w+)\W+?[\w]/gi`. This regex is not a valid HTML sanitizer — it matches only a narrow pattern (`<` + word characters + non-word + word character) and fails to handle many XSS vectors including encoded payloads, malformed tags, and event handlers in attributes. The proper `sanitizeHtml` function on line 58 uses the `sanitize-html` library, proving the codebase knows the correct approach. If `sanitizeLegacy` is used to sanitize user input that is later rendered as HTML, it permits stored XSS. The render sink is outside this file.

trace.description: The exported `sanitizeLegacy` function accepts a free-form string and applies a weak regex-based sanitization. The caller is outside this file.

`input.replace(/<(?:\w+)\W+?[\w]/gi, '')` — this regex is not a valid HTML sanitizer. It fails to remove many XSS payloads. If the output is stored and later rendered as HTML (render sink outside this file), stored XSS results. Compare with the proper `sanitizeHtml` function on line 58 which uses a real sanitization library — the existence of this weaker alternative alongside it is itself the defect.

title: denyAll middleware uses non-cryptographic random as JWT secret
description: The `denyAll` function on line 53 creates an `expressJwt` middleware with a secret of `'' + Math.random()`. The intent is to deny all requests by using a secret that no valid token could match. However, `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and its output space is limited. Each call to `denyAll()` generates a new secret, so if the function is called at module load time, the secret is fixed for the process lifetime and potentially predictable. An attacker who can predict or brute-force `Math.random()` output could forge a JWT that passes this check, bypassing the intended deny-all enforcement on protected routes (e.g., `DELETE /api/Products/:id`, `POST /api/Challenges`).

trace.description: The exported `denyAll` function creates an expressJwt middleware with a secret derived from `Math.random()`. This middleware is applied to routes like `DELETE /api/Products/:id`, `POST /api/Challenges`, and `POST /api/Hints` per the route listing.

`expressJwt({ secret: '' + Math.random() })` — `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure. The intent is to create an unguessable secret to deny all access, but using a predictable PRNG undermines this guarantee. If the secret is predictable, an attacker could forge a valid JWT and access denyAll-protected endpoints.

title: Coupon discount value trusted from client without server-side issuance verification
description: The coupon system uses z85 encoding (not signing or encryption) to create discount coupons. `generateCoupon` (line 97) encodes a date and discount value, and `discountFromCoupon` (line 102) decodes a client-supplied coupon and returns the embedded discount via `parseInt`. The only validation is a format regex (line 118) that accepts any two-digit discount (00-99) and a date check (line 110). Since z85 is reversible and the coupon is not cryptographically signed, an attacker can craft their own coupon with the current month/year and a 99% discount, bypassing the server's intended discount limits. The server trusts the client-supplied coupon to determine the discount amount without verifying the coupon was actually issued by the server.

trace.description: `export const discountFromCoupon = (coupon?: string) => {` — the function accepts a coupon string from the client (caller outside this file). This coupon is entirely attacker-controlled.

`const decoded = z85.decode(coupon)` — reversibly decodes the client-supplied coupon. z85 is an encoding scheme, not encryption — anyone can encode and decode freely. Compare with `generateCoupon` (line 99: `z85.encode(coupon)`) which shows the server creates coupons by mere encoding, with no signing or MAC.

`if (decoded && (hasValidFormat(decoded.toString()) != null))` — validates only the format pattern. The regex (line 118) accepts any month abbreviation + two digits + `-` + two-digit discount (e.g., `JAN25-99`). It does not verify the coupon was issued by the server.
`const parts = decoded.toString().split('-')` — splits the decoded string to extract the validity date and discount value. Both values are attacker-controlled.
`if (utils.toMMMYY(new Date()) === validity)` — checks only that the date portion matches the current month/year. An attacker who knows the current date can trivially satisfy this check.

`return parseInt(discount)` — returns the attacker-controlled discount value (up to 99) to the caller. The server has trusted a client-crafted coupon to determine the discount amount without verifying server-side issuance, enabling an attacker to obtain arbitrary discounts.

title: Wallet balance field exposed as directly settable model property without property-level authorization or value constraints
description: The Wallet model defines `balance` (lines 35-41) as a standard integer field with only type validation (`isInt: true`) and a default value of 0. Sequelize models accept all defined fields in `create()` and `update()` calls by default. Because `balance` is a sensitive financial property — it represents the amount of money in a user's wallet — allowing it to be set directly by a caller through standard ORM operations constitutes a Broken Object Property Level Authorization (mass assignment) vulnerability. Any route handler that spreads a request body into `Wallet.create()` or `Wallet.update()` would let a caller set an arbitrary balance, including very large positive values (free money) or negative values. The validation layer (`isInt`) only checks type, not authorization — validation is not authorization. Furthermore, the design itself is insecure: a wallet balance should be derived from a ledger of transactions, not stored as a directly mutable scalar. The model also lacks a minimum value constraint (`min: 0`), so negative balances are permitted by the schema. Even if route handlers elsewhere attempt to guard this field with an allow-list, the model design makes any new field added to the model automatically exposed (implicit-allow pattern), and the absence of server-side derivation of balance means the server trusts the client to report financial state.

trace.description: The Wallet Sequelize model class is exported (line 50) and used by route handlers outside this file. The model definition at lines 15-22 declares `balance` as a settable attribute. Callers outside this file interact with this model through Sequelize's create/update/build methods, which accept field values from request bodies.

The `balance` field is defined at lines 35-41 with `type: DataTypes.INTEGER`, a `validate.isInt: true` check, and `defaultValue: 0`. There is no `allowNull: false`, no `min` validation, and no field-level write protection. Sequelize will accept `balance` in any `create()` or `update()` payload because it is a declared model attribute. The `isInt` validator only rejects non-integer values; it does not prevent a caller from setting balance to 99999999 or -1000.

The TypeScript class declares `balance: CreationOptional<number>` as a model property. This property declaration establishes that `balance` is part of the Wallet model's attribute set and will be accepted by Sequelize when building, creating, or updating Wallet records.

The `WalletModelInit` function is defined, receiving a `sequelize: Sequelize` instance. This is the initialization entry point that callers outside this file invoke to register the model schema with a database connection.

`Wallet.init(...)` is called, registering the model's attribute definitions and options with Sequelize. After this call, Sequelize knows `balance` is a column on the `Wallets` table and will accept it in all create/update/build operations.
`type: DataTypes.INTEGER` sets the column type to integer. This constrains the storage format but does not restrict which callers may write to the field or what range of values is acceptable.
The `validate` object begins, which would be the place to add range constraints (e.g., `min: 0`) or custom authorization validators. Only one validator is present.

`isInt: true` is the sole validation rule. This is a type check — it rejects non-integer values — but it is not a property-level authorization control. It does not prevent a caller from setting balance to 99999999 (free money) or -1000 (negative balance). There is no `min` constraint, no `max` constraint, and no custom validator that checks whether the caller is authorized to modify this field.
`defaultValue: 0` sets the initial balance for new records. This is a sensible default but does not protect against direct writes; a caller can still override it to any integer via create/update.

The export statement `export { Wallet as WalletModel, WalletModelInit }` makes the Wallet model class available to route handlers and controllers outside this file. Any caller that imports `WalletModel` can invoke `WalletModel.create()` or `wallet.update()` with a `balance` field in the payload, and Sequelize will persist it without property-level authorization.

The TypeScript class declares `UserId: number` as a model property. This property declaration establishes that `UserId` is part of the Wallet model's attribute set and will be accepted by Sequelize when building, creating, or updating Wallet records.

The `UserId` field configuration object begins within the attributes definition passed to `Wallet.init`. This is where the field's database-level properties would be specified — including foreign-key references, associations, and validation — but none are present.

`type: DataTypes.INTEGER` is the only property set for `UserId`. There is no `references` key linking it to a Users table, no `onDelete` cascade, no Sequelize association definition, and no validation. The field is a bare integer column with no constraint tying it to the authenticated user's session. Sequelize will accept any integer value for `UserId` in create/update payloads.

The `balance` field definition is the sink: it is a sensitive financial property persisted to the `Wallets` table with no property-level authorization restricting which callers may write to it, no minimum-value constraint, and no server-side derivation from transaction records. Any route handler that binds request body fields to this model (direct spread, `Wallet.create(req.body)`, `wallet.update(req.body)`, etc.) will persist a caller-supplied balance value. The security impact is direct financial manipulation: an attacker sets their own wallet balance to an arbitrary positive integer, obtaining free store credit, or sets another user's balance to a negative value.

title: Wallet UserId field accepts arbitrary values without foreign-key or ownership constraint, enabling cross-user wallet manipulation
description: The `UserId` field (lines 27-29) is defined as a bare `DataTypes.INTEGER` with no foreign-key association, no validation, and no constraint linking it to an authenticated session. Sequelize will accept `UserId` in create/update payloads. If a route handler binds request body fields to the model, a caller could set `UserId` to another user's ID — creating a wallet for or associating a wallet with an arbitrary user. This is a mass assignment risk on an ownership/identity field. Unlike `balance`, `UserId` should never be caller-settable; it must be derived from the authenticated session on the server side. The model provides no mechanism to enforce this.

trace.description: The Wallet model is exported at line 50 and used by route handlers outside this file. The model accepts `UserId` as a declared attribute, meaning Sequelize will bind it from any create/update payload that includes it.

The `UserId` field is defined at lines 27-29 as `type: DataTypes.INTEGER` with no `references`, no `onDelete` cascade, no association definition, and no validation. There is nothing in the model that constrains `UserId` to the currently authenticated user.

The `UserId` field definition is the sink: it is an ownership/identity field persisted without any property-level authorization. Any route handler that spreads a request body into `Wallet.create()` or `Wallet.update()` will let a caller set `UserId` to any integer, potentially creating or modifying wallets belonging to other users. The security impact is cross-user wallet manipulation — an attacker could create a wallet with their own `balance` value under another user's `UserId`, or re-associate a wallet to a different user.

title: Poison null byte bypasses file-type allow-list enabling arbitrary file access from ftp/ directory
description: The servePublicFiles handler validates that the requested filename ends with an allowlisted extension (.md or .pdf) on line 27. However, it then passes the filename through security.cutOffPoisonNullByte() (line 28) which truncates the string at the first null byte (\0). An attacker can supply a filename like 'secret.txt\0.md' — this passes the extension check because it appears to end in '.md', but after the null-byte cut-off the file resolved and served becomes 'secret.txt'. This is a classic poison null byte injection: user-controlled input containing a null byte alters the file path that the runtime ultimately opens, bypassing the intended access restriction. The design flaw is structural: the validation (extension check) occurs before the transformation (null-byte truncation), so the transformation invalidates the guarantee the validation was supposed to provide. Any file in the ftp/ directory — regardless of extension — can be served, including sensitive files like the KeePass database 'incident-support.kdbx' (which is separately allowlisted, suggesting it is sensitive) or any other file stored there.

trace.description: The exported handler servePublicFiles() receives outside data via params.file from the request. The caller (route registration) is outside this file.

The file parameter is checked with endsWithAllowlistedFileType(), which returns true if the name ends with '.md' or '.pdf'. A crafted input like 'target.txt\0.md' passes this check because it appears to end in '.md'.

The validated filename is then passed through security.cutOffPoisonNullByte(file), which truncates the string at the first null byte. The validation on line 27 happened BEFORE this transformation, so the guarantee it provided no longer holds. This ordering is the design flaw: the server transforms the input after validating it, invalidating the result of validation.
The request parameter is assigned to a local variable: const file = params.file. From this point the tainted filename flows through the rest of the handler as 'file'.

A conditional check gates the flow: if (!file.includes('/')). A filename without a forward slash passes this gate and continues; one containing a slash is rejected with a 403. A crafted payload like 'target.txt\0.md' contains no slash and passes this check.
The file variable is forwarded into the verify() helper: verify(file, res, next). This is the internal call that carries the tainted value into the validation-and-serve code path.

res.sendFile(path.resolve('ftp/', file)) serves the now-truncated filename. The attacker-controlled null byte has injected a path-separator/terminator effect into the resolution, causing a different file than the one validated to be served. The access control (extension allow-list) is bypassed.

title: Poison null byte exploit detection function is empty — no logging of security event
description: The function verifySuccessfulPoisonNullByteExploit is defined (lines 39-41) and is called on the code path where a file request reaches the serveFile sink (line 30). The function name and call site indicate it is intended to detect and log a successful poison null byte exploit — a security-relevant event indicating an active attack on the file server. However, the function body is completely empty. There is no logging, no alerting, and no detection logic. This means a successful exploitation of the null byte bypass (described in the companion finding) produces no security event record, preventing detection, investigation, and response.

Inside verify(), the file parameter passes the endsWithAllowlistedFileType() check because the crafted payload appears to end in '.md'. The flow continues into the body that calls cutOffPoisonNullByte and then verifySuccessfulPoisonNullByteExploit.

The function verifySuccessfulPoisonNullByteExploit has an empty body (lines 39-41). No security log entry is written, no alert is triggered, and no detection occurs for this security-relevant event.

title: Unauthenticated retrieval of all user records with full data exposure
description: The retrieveUserList function calls UserModel.findAll() (line 12) without any check that the requester is authenticated or authorized to view user data. It then returns every user's data. On line 25, the response spreads ...user.dataValues, which exposes ALL model fields to the caller. Only 'password' and 'totpSecret' are explicitly masked (lines 26-27); any other sensitive field present on the User model (e.g., email, role, security question answers, API keys, internal flags) is returned in cleartext. Because the spread is an implicit allow-list (allow-all-except-two), any new sensitive field added to the model in the future is automatically exposed. The function receives req (line 10) but never inspects it for an authentication token, session, or role claim. The route registration that maps an HTTP endpoint to this handler is outside this file, but the function itself performs zero access control. Any caller who can reach this handler receives the complete user database.

title: JWT token decoded without signature verification
description: On line 20, the function uses jwt.decode() to read the payload of the user's authentication token. The jsonwebtoken decode() function does NOT verify the token's signature — it simply base64-decodes the payload. While the token here is retrieved from an internal store (security.authenticatedUsers.tokenOf) rather than from the request, the use of decode instead of verify is a crypto-auth weakness. If any code path ever passes an attacker-controlled token through this function (or if the token store is polluted with forged tokens), the forged token's claims would be accepted without verification. The correct function to establish trust in the token's contents is jwt.verify() with the proper secret/public key.

title: Unbounded database query returns all users without pagination or limit
description: The retrieveUserList function calls UserModel.findAll() (line 12) with no limit, offset, pagination, or filtering. This query loads every user record from the database into memory at once. For each user, it then decodes a JWT token and constructs a response object (lines 16-30). On a system with a large user base, a single request to this endpoint consumes unbounded memory and CPU. There is no rate limiting or throttling visible in this function. The route registration (which may or may not add rate limiting) is outside this file. An attacker can trigger this query repeatedly to exhaust server memory or degrade database performance.

The function only has a try/catch that forwards errors to next() (lines 32-34), with no logging on the success path.

title: Unbounded Solidity compilation with no size limits or rate throttling
description: The compileAndFetchContracts method accepts arbitrary-length Solidity source code from the editor with no size cap, complexity check, or rate limiting before passing it to the solidityCompiler. Solidity compilation is computationally expensive (AST parsing, type-checking, code generation). A user can submit extremely large or complex contracts repeatedly, causing excessive CPU and memory consumption in the browser, potentially freezing or crashing the tab. Additionally, the deploy and invoke paths have no throttling, allowing rapid sequential blockchain transactions.

title: Unbounded transaction value (commonGweiValue) with no upper-limit validation
description: The commonGweiValue property (initialized to 0 at line 69) is user-controlled via the template and directly used to set the transaction value in both contract deployment (lines 168-173) and function invocation (lines 236-241). The value is parsed via ethers.utils.parseUnits with no upper bound validation. While MetaMask shows a confirmation dialog, the application itself imposes no limit — a user could enter an extremely large gwei value that could drain their wallet if confirmed, or could be socially engineered into confirming. The design lacks a compensating control (max value cap, warning threshold, or confirmation for large amounts).

title: Solidity compiler binary fetched from external CDN without integrity verification
description: The compileAndFetchContracts method passes a URL to the solidityCompiler that points to https://binaries.soliditylang.org/bin/{selectedVersion}. While the version string comes from a hardcoded allow-list (compilerReleases), the compiler binary itself is fetched without any integrity check — no checksum, no SRI hash, no signature verification. If the CDN is compromised or a MITM attack occurs, a malicious compiler binary could be served that injects backdoors into the compiled bytecode, which is then deployed to the blockchain. The lack of integrity verification on a critical supply chain component is an A08 finding.

title: Default Ethereum provider and autoConnect enabled at module load
description: The wagmi client is created at module scope with getDefaultProvider() (no arguments), which falls back to public, rate-limited, and potentially unreliable RPC endpoints. Additionally, autoConnect: true causes the application to automatically attempt reconnection to a previously connected wallet on page load without explicit user action. This can leak the user's wallet address to the application before the user has explicitly consented to connect, and the default provider exposes all transaction data to third-party RPC providers without the user's knowledge.

title: Unsanitized contract output and error messages stored for template rendering
description: The invokeFunction method stores raw transaction output (line 253: transaction[0].toString()) and raw error messages (line 273: error.message) into the outputValue property of contract function objects. If the template renders outputValue using Angular's [innerHTML] binding or any other bypass of default escaping, this would result in stored XSS. Angular's default interpolation ({{ }}) auto-escapes, but without seeing the template, the rendering context cannot be confirmed. The data shape (free-form text stored without sanitization) is the carrier; the render sink is outside this file.

title: Client-side session flag gates blockchain operations without server-side enforcement
description: The `session` property (line 63, default false) is the sole gate controlling access to deploySelectedContract (line 143) and invokeFunction (line 212). It is set to true at line 329 purely based on a client-side chain ID check against the Sepolia network. An attacker can trivially set this.session = true via browser devtools or Angular inspection, bypassing the wallet connection and chain validation requirements entirely. While MetaMask would still prompt for transaction signing, the chain restriction (Sepolia only) is bypassed — an attacker could interact with contracts on any chain their wallet is connected to. The application trusts a client-set boolean to enforce what should be a server-side or contract-level access control decision.

title: BOLA: Data export uses client-supplied UserId to fetch another user's memories
description: The dataExport handler authenticates the caller via the Bearer token (line 18) and verifies the session user has an email and id (line 19). It correctly derives the email from the authenticated session for orders (line 33) and reviews (line 40). However, for memories it uses `req.body.UserId` (line 26) — a value entirely controlled by the caller — instead of `loggedInUser.data.id`. Any authenticated user can supply another user's UserId in the request body and receive that user's memories (image URLs and captions) in the export. The server should derive the UserId from the trusted session, not accept it from the client. This is both a Broken Object Level Authorization flaw (authentication is present but per-resource authorization is absent for the memories query) and an insecure design flaw (the server delegates identity scoping to the client for a value it already holds in the session).

The handler logs blocked unauthorized attempts on line 109, but when a data export succeeds (line 107), no audit log entry is written. There is no record of who exported data, when, or what was included. This prevents detection of abuse (e.g., repeated exports, exports triggered by a BOLA exploit) and prevents investigation of data exfiltration incidents. The empty loop on lines 105-106 and the unused emailHash on line 104 suggest incomplete implementation where logging may have been intended but was never completed.

A successful data export is sent to the client with res.status(200).send(...). The response includes the user's orders, reviews, and memories. No logging statement precedes or accompanies this response.
