The empty for-loop on lines 105-106 and unused emailHash on line 104 suggest logging was intended but never implemented.

title: Data export endpoint has no rate limiting and performs multiple unbounded database queries
description: The data export handler performs three separate database queries (memories on line 26, orders on line 33, reviews on line 40), all without any pagination or result-size limits. The results are loaded entirely into memory and serialized into a JSON string (line 107). There is no rate limiting visible in the handler. An authenticated user can repeatedly call this endpoint to trigger expensive multi-query operations, and because the memories query accepts req.body.UserId (line 26), an attacker can target users with large datasets, amplifying the resource consumption per request. Combined with the BOLA, an attacker could enumerate and export many users' data while consuming server resources on each request.

title: Current password verification is optional and can be bypassed by omitting the parameter
description: The password-change handler only verifies the user's current password when the `current` query parameter is truthy (line 39: `if (currentPassword && ...)`). If an attacker who has obtained a valid session token (e.g., via XSS, leaked logs, or a man-in-the-middle attack) simply omits the `current` query parameter, the entire current-password check is skipped, and the password is changed on line 51 without any proof of knowledge of the existing credential. This defeats a core authentication control: a password change should always require re-authentication with the current password. The design makes this check conditional on caller input rather than enforcing it unconditionally, which is both an authentication failure and an insecure design flaw.

title: Passwords transmitted via URL query parameters in a GET request
description: The password-change endpoint is registered as a GET handler and extracts the current, new, and repeat passwords from `query` (lines 14-17). GET request query strings are logged by web servers, proxies, and CDNs in access logs; they are stored in browser history and bookmarks; and they are leaked via the Referer header to any third-party resources loaded by the page. This exposes plaintext credentials in multiple persistent stores outside the application's control. Using GET for a credential-bearing, state-changing operation is a fundamental design and configuration error.

title: No rate limiting on password-change endpoint enables brute-force of current password

An attacker with a valid session token can send unlimited requests to brute-force the `current` password field. Each attempt invokes `security.hash()` and a comparison, consuming CPU on every request. This enables both credential brute-force (authentication failure) and resource consumption via repeated hashing operations.

This typically includes sensitive fields such as the password hash, any role/permission flags (e.g., isAdmin), and internal fields. The response has no field-level filtering — no allow-list of properties to return. An attacker who changes a password (especially via the bypass in Finding 1) receives the full user record, exposing the password hash for offline cracking and any privilege-related fields for further exploitation.

title: Hardcoded BIP39 mnemonic in source derives the private key used for challenge verification
description: The checkKeys handler derives an Ethereum wallet's private key from a BIP39 mnemonic that is hardcoded directly in the source code on line 10. The mnemonic is the root secret for the entire key hierarchy — anyone with access to the source (or the deployed binary) can reproduce the exact same private key by running HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase with the same phrase. This defeats the entire purpose of the challenge: the 'secret' the user must guess is not secret at all. The handler compares req.body.privateKey against the key derived from this hardcoded mnemonic (line 15), so an attacker who reads the source simply copies the mnemonic, derives the key, and submits it. This is both a cryptographic failure (hardcoded key material) and a security misconfiguration (secret embedded in source code).

HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase(mnemonic) deterministically derives the full key hierarchy from the hardcoded mnemonic. The private key, public key, and address are all derived from this (lines 12-14).

req.body.privateKey is compared against the derived privateKey. Because the mnemonic is hardcoded in source, an attacker who can read the source can reproduce the exact private key and pass this check, solving the challenge without any cryptographic attack.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint performs expensive BIP39 key derivation on every request with no rate limiting
description: The POST /rest/web3/submitKey endpoint has no authentication middleware (auth: none) and no rate limiting. On every single request, the handler dynamically imports the ethers library and performs HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase(), which executes BIP39 mnemonic-to-seed conversion using PBKDF2 with 2048 iterations of HMAC-SHA512 — a deliberately expensive key-stretching operation. An attacker can flood this endpoint with arbitrary POST bodies, each triggering the full cryptographic derivation, to exhaust server CPU and cause denial of service. The expensive operation runs before any input validation or early-exit logic, so even requests with empty or invalid bodies incur the full cost.

title: Challenge verification design trusts a server-held secret that is embedded in the same source the attacker can inspect
description: The design of the NFT unlock challenge requires the user to submit the correct Ethereum private key. However, the private key is not independently generated or stored in a secret manager — it is deterministically derived from a mnemonic hardcoded in the same source file that defines the verification logic. The design assumes the private key remains unknown to the attacker, but provides no mechanism to keep it secret: it is plaintext in the source. A correct implementation of this design (as written) still permits the attack, because the secret is structurally embedded in the code rather than separated from it. The fix is not a code patch but a design change: the secret must originate from outside the source code.

The mnemonic — the root secret for the entire challenge — is a string literal in the source code. The design places the secret in the same artifact that defines the verification logic, with no separation between secret material and verification code.
The returned async handler is the Express route handler — the design's verification logic begins executing here on each request.
The try block opens the verification path; there is no design-level gate (e.g., a prerequisite step, a session state check, or a proof-of-work) before the secret comparison logic proceeds.
The ethers library is imported — the design relies on client-side-available tooling (ethers) for derivation, meaning the same library an attacker uses is what the server uses.
HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase(mnemonic) derives the wallet from the hardcoded mnemonic; the design uses deterministic derivation that any attacker can replay with the same mnemonic.
The privateKey is extracted from the derived wallet — the design treats this as the secret to compare against, but it is fully reproducible from the source-visible mnemonic.

The verification check compares the submitted key against the key derived from the hardcoded mnemonic. The design as implemented guarantees that anyone who can read the source can solve the challenge. The trust boundary the design relies on (the private key is secret) is violated by the design itself.

title: CAPTCHA answer returned to client in API response, trivially bypassable
description: The GET /rest/captcha handler builds a captcha object that includes the plaintext `answer` field (lines 24-28) and returns the entire object via `res.json(captcha)` on line 31. This means every client that requests a CAPTCHA receives both the challenge expression and its solution. The CAPTCHA mechanism is therefore completely defeated — an attacker simply reads the `answer` from the response and submits it. The design returns the secret the server is supposed to keep, making the verification step on POST /api/Feedbacks (verifyCaptcha) meaningless.

title: Predictable sequential CAPTCHA IDs enable captcha enumeration and replay

Combined with the fact that captchas are never deleted or invalidated after use (verifyCaptcha on line 37-38 only checks but does not remove the record), an attacker who observes a single captcha ID can enumerate all other captcha IDs, look them up in the verifyCaptcha endpoint, and reuse already-solved captchas indefinitely. This undermines the CAPTCHA as an authentication/verification control.

title: CAPTCHA never invalidated after successful verification, allowing indefinite replay
description: The `verifyCaptcha` middleware (lines 35-46) looks up a captcha record by ID and checks whether the submitted answer matches. On success it calls `next()` but never deletes, expires, or marks the captcha record as used. This means a single solved captcha (captchaId + answer pair) can be submitted an unlimited number of times to bypass the CAPTCHA gate on POST /api/Feedbacks. The CAPTCHA's purpose — proving a human solved a fresh challenge for each submission — is subverted. An attacker solves one captcha and reuses it forever.

No flag is set, no timestamp is recorded, no deletion is queued. The loose `==` operator is used rather than strict `===`, but the critical gap is the absence of any invalidation logic.

There is no rate limiting, no cap on the number of captchas generated, and no cleanup of old records visible in this file. An attacker can send a high volume of GET /rest/captcha requests, each of which performs a database write, causing unbounded growth of the captcha table and consuming database storage and memory until service degrades or fails.

title: Local File Inclusion via layout parameter spread into template render context
description: The POST / handler spreads the entire request body (`...req.body`) into the `res.render()` call. Express template engines (e.g., EJS with layout support) interpret a `layout` property in the render context as a file path to include as the layout template. An attacker can set `req.body.layout` to an arbitrary file path. The only protection is a weak substring denylist (line 105) that blocks paths containing 'ftp', 'ctf.key', or 'encryptionkeys' — any other file on the filesystem that doesn't match those substrings can be loaded as a template. Even though the response is truncated to 100 characters (line 114), this still leaks file contents. The `...req.body` spread also constitutes mass assignment: all caller-supplied fields (email, securityAnswer, layout, and any other arbitrary fields) are passed directly into the template context without an allow-list, allowing override of internal template variables.

title: Security answers stored with HMAC instead of a password hashing algorithm
description: Security answers are secrets used in account-recovery/password-reset authentication flows. They must be protected like passwords: salted and hashed with a slow key-stretching algorithm (bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt). Instead, the setter on line 44-46 applies `security.hmac(answer)`, which is a fast keyed hash with no salt and no work factor. HMAC is deterministic—identical answers from different users produce identical hashes, enabling cross-user rainbow-table attacks. Because HMAC is designed for performance, an attacker who obtains the hashes can brute-force candidate answers at high speed. If the HMAC key (likely a single application-wide secret from the `insecurity` library) is compromised, all security answers can be verified offline, enabling mass account takeover via the password-reset flow. This is both a cryptographic failure (wrong algorithm for secret storage) and an authentication failure (weak protection of a credential used in account recovery).

title: Security-answer model design permits pre-population attack on account recovery
description: The SecurityAnswer model enforces a single security answer per user via `unique: true` on UserId (line 31), but the model design does not distinguish between 'user setting their own answer' and 'arbitrary caller creating an answer record.' The design relies on the caller to supply UserId honestly rather than deriving it server-side from the authenticated identity.

description: The handler performs a data mutation (inserting a product review) on a route with auth: none, yet there is no logging of who created the review, what product was reviewed, or even that the operation occurred. Since the author field is caller-controlled (line 22) and no authentication is enforced, there is no way to reconstruct from logs who posted a review or detect abuse such as review spam or impersonation. The complete absence of security-relevant logging for this write operation means incidents involving malicious or spoofed reviews cannot be investigated.

The handler returns a 201 success response after the insert at line 19. title: Unauthenticated review creation endpoint with no rate limiting allows unbounded review spam and database exhaustion
description: The PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews endpoint has auth: none and performs a database insert on every request. There is no rate limiting visible in the handler, no validation of request body size, and no limit on the number of reviews per product or per author. Since no authentication is required, an attacker can send an unlimited number of requests to create reviews, each inserting a document into the reviewsCollection. This can exhaust database storage, degrade query performance on the reviews collection, and flood product pages with spam content.

title: Path traversal via insufficient path validation in log file serving
description: The `serveLogFiles` handler reads a filename from `params.file` and passes it to `res.sendFile(path.resolve('logs/', file))` after only checking that the value does not contain a forward slash (`/`). This check is trivially bypassable on Windows where the backslash `\` is also a path separator — an attacker can supply values like `..\..\..\windows\win.ini` to read arbitrary files outside the `logs/` directory. Even on Linux, the approach of denylisting a single character is fundamentally unsound: the code never verifies that the resolved path remains within the `logs/` directory after `path.resolve` expands `..` segments. A correct fix would resolve the path and then confirm it starts with the intended base directory, rather than checking the raw input string for a single separator character.

The only validation applied to `file` is `!file.includes('/')` — a single-character denylist that blocks forward slashes but permits backslashes, `..` segments, and any other path metacharacters.

`res.sendFile(path.resolve('logs/', file))` serves the resolved path to the client. Because the check on line 13 does not prevent backslash-based traversal (Windows) and never verifies that the resolved path is contained within `logs/`, an attacker can read arbitrary files on the filesystem by supplying a crafted `file` parameter.

title: Log files served without authentication or authorization
description: The `serveLogFiles` handler serves files from the `logs/` directory with no authentication or authorization check whatsoever. Application log files frequently contain sensitive data — stack traces, error messages, user identifiers, request details, and sometimes credentials or tokens leaked into logs. Exposing them through an unauthenticated endpoint means any caller who can reach the route can download the full contents of every log file in the directory. The handler does not verify the caller's identity, role, or session, nor does it restrict which log files are accessible. Even if authentication middleware is applied at the router level (outside this file), the handler itself performs no per-resource authorization, meaning any authenticated user — regardless of role — can read all log files, not just administrators.

trace.description: The exported middleware function receives `({ params }, res, next)` — a standard Express handler. No authentication context (user object, session, role) is destructured or referenced anywhere in the function body. The caller that registers this route is outside this file, but the handler itself contains no access-control logic.

The conditional only checks whether the filename contains a `/` character. There is no check of the request's authentication state, user role, or authorization to view log files. The code proceeds to serve the file to any caller whose `file` parameter passes the trivial slash check.

`const file = params.file` extracts the requested filename. At this point there is no check of who is requesting the file — the variable is populated purely from the request parameter with no identity context consulted.

`res.sendFile(path.resolve('logs/', file))` transmits the entire contents of the requested log file to the client. No authorization gate, role check, or audit log entry precedes this response. Any log file in the `logs/` directory — which may contain sensitive operational data, error traces, or leaked credentials — is served to the caller without restriction.

title: Remote Code Execution via eval of user-controlled order data on unauthenticated endpoint
description: The b2bOrder handler extracts `body.orderLinesData` directly from the request body and passes it to `safeEval` (the `eval` function from the `notevil` library) inside a `vm.runInContext` call. Despite the name 'safeEval', the `notevil` library has known bypass techniques that allow escaping its sandbox, and Node.js `vm` module is explicitly documented as not a security boundary. An attacker can craft malicious JavaScript in the `orderLinesData` field to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server. Critically, the route is registered with `auth: none` — no authentication is required to reach this code execution sink. The design of evaluating user-supplied order-line data as code is itself an insecure design: order data should be parsed as structured data, never executed as code.

vm.runInContext('safeEval(orderLinesData)', sandbox, { timeout: 2000 }) executes the user-controlled string as JavaScript code via notevil's eval inside a VM context. The notevil library has known sandbox-escape techniques, and Node.js vm is not a security boundary per official documentation. This is a remote code execution sink reachable by unauthenticated callers.

title: No rate limiting on endpoint performing VM-based code evaluation
description: The b2bOrder endpoint executes user-supplied code inside a VM with a 2-second timeout. While the timeout prevents a single request from running indefinitely, there is no rate limiting or throttling on the endpoint itself (and the route is unauthenticated). An attacker can send a flood of requests with computationally expensive payloads, each consuming up to 2 seconds of CPU time in the VM. With no per-IP, per-user, or per-endpoint throttling, this enables denial of service through sustained CPU consumption.

title: No security logging of code execution attempts or order creation on B2B endpoint
description: The b2bOrder handler performs security-relevant operations — executing user-supplied code in a VM sandbox and creating B2B orders — but logs nothing. There is no logging of successful order creation, no logging of VM execution failures, no logging of potentially malicious code evaluation attempts, and no logging of access to this unauthenticated endpoint. The only error handling passes errors to next(err) or returns a 503, with no security event recorded. This means an attacker exploiting the RCE or abusing the order creation endpoint would leave no auditable trail, making incident detection and investigation impossible.

A code execution attempt that fails (e.g., an attacker probing the RCE) produces no log entry, leaving no evidence of attack attempts.

title: Mass assignment of UserId in addMemory allows creating memories under another user's identity
description: The addMemory handler constructs the memory record using `UserId: req.body.UserId` (line 15), a field directly controlled by the caller. Although the route is guarded by `security.appendUserId()` middleware, the handler itself does not derive the UserId from the authenticated session (e.g., req.user.id) — it trusts the request body. If the middleware only appends UserId when absent, or if the caller can influence the body after middleware processing, an attacker can set UserId to another user's ID, creating memories attributed to a victim. This is both a mass assignment (API3 — caller controls a sensitive ownership field) and a broken object level authorization issue (the server does not independently verify ownership).

Whether this is exploitable depends on whether appendUserId() overwrites or only supplements req.body.UserId — but the handler's design of reading UserId from the body rather than the session is the defect.

title: getMemories endpoint has no authentication and returns all memories with associated user data
description: The getMemories handler (GET /rest/memories) has no authentication middleware applied to its route. It calls MemoryModel.findAll({ include: [UserModel] }), returning every memory record in the database joined with the associated user model. This exposes all users' memories and potentially sensitive user information (depending on UserModel's fields) to any unauthenticated caller. There is no per-user scoping, no authentication check, and no authorization filter.

title: getMemories returns unbounded result set with no pagination or limit
description: The getMemories handler calls MemoryModel.findAll() with no limit, offset, or pagination parameters. A single request retrieves every memory record in the database plus all associated user records (via the UserModel include). As the memories table grows, a single GET request can pull an arbitrarily large result set into memory, causing excessive memory consumption and degraded service. There is no rate limiting on the endpoint (auth: none) and no pagination control.

The entire result set is serialized to JSON and sent in the response. An attacker can repeatedly call this endpoint to consume server memory and database resources, or a single call on a large dataset can exhaust memory.

description: The addMemory handler stores req.body.caption directly into the MemoryModel record without any sanitization, encoding, or validation. If this caption is later rendered in an HTML context without proper output encoding (the render sink is outside this file), it becomes a stored XSS vulnerability. title: Private asset served without authentication via obfuscated URL (security through obscurity)
description: The handler servePrivacyPolicyProof() serves a file located in a directory named 'private' (frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/thank-you.jpg) without any authentication or authorization. The route is registered with auth: none, meaning anyone who discovers the URL can access the resource. The only protection is the obscurity of the long, obfuscated URL path (/we/may/also/instruct/you/to/refuse/all/reasonably/necessary/responsibility). This is a misconfiguration exposing an internal/restricted resource, a broken access control (no auth check on a resource that is clearly meant to be private), and an insecure design that relies solely on URL secrecy instead of enforced access controls.

The caller/router is outside this file.

Because the route has no authentication (auth: none) and the handler performs no authorization check, any user — authenticated or not — who discovers the obfuscated URL receives the file. The design relies entirely on URL obscurity as the sole access control, which is not a security control. An attacker can discover the URL through brute-forcing, directory enumeration, or information leakage and access the private asset.

title: UserId field exposed to caller control via auto-generated CRUD surface
description: The Feedback model declares UserId as a plain DataTypes.INTEGER field (lines 31-33) with no setter override, no exclude from mass assignment, and no ownership enforcement. Unlike the comment field (which has a custom setter at line 41) and the rating field (which has a custom setter at line 54), UserId has no setter at all, meaning Sequelize binds caller-supplied values directly. The auto-generated CRUD surface at /api/Feedbacks (POST, PUT) binds request body fields to model properties. An attacker can include a UserId field in the request body to create feedback attributed to another user or reassign existing feedback's ownership. This is both a mass assignment issue and a broken access control issue, because the server never verifies that the supplied UserId matches the authenticated user.

No authorization check ensures the supplied UserId matches the authenticated session user.

The UserId field is persisted as-is. An attacker sends {"UserId": 2, "comment": "...", "rating": 5} to POST /api/Feedbacks, creating feedback that appears to belong to user 2. No authorization check ensures the supplied UserId matches the authenticated session user.

title: Stored XSS via conditional sanitization of comment field
description: The comment field is declared as DataTypes.STRING (line 40), accepting free-form text. The setter (lines 41-49) applies different sanitization depending on whether the persistedXssFeedbackChallenge is enabled (line 43). When the challenge is enabled, security.sanitizeHtml is used (line 44). When it is NOT enabled, security.sanitizeSecure is used instead (line 46). The sanitized value is then persisted via setDataValue at line 48. This means the strength of XSS prevention on a persisted free-text field depends on a challenge configuration flag rather than always applying the strongest control. If sanitizeSecure is weaker than sanitizeHtml, then when the challenge is disabled, attacker-controlled HTML/script content in the comment field will be stored insufficiently sanitized. The stored comment will later be rendered in the application UI (render sink is outside this file), resulting in stored XSS.

The resulting value is persisted via this.setDataValue('comment', sanitizedComment) on line 48. If sanitizeSecure does not remove script payloads, stored XSS content is persisted. The render sink is outside this file.

title: Rating field accepts arbitrary integers without bounds validation
description: The rating setter (lines 54-56) accepts any integer value and stores it directly via setDataValue without validating that it falls within an expected range (e.g., 1-5). The model declares rating as INTEGER with allowNull: false but provides no min/max constraint or business-logic validation. An attacker can submit extremely large positive values, zero, or negative values. This is a design flaw because the server never establishes or enforces the invariant that a rating must be within the valid range — it trusts the client-supplied value entirely. The impact includes skewed aggregate ratings, corruption of rating averages, and potential downstream issues if rating values are used in calculations or display logic.

title: Account takeover via body-controlled UserId on deluxe upgrade endpoint
description: The upgradeToDeluxe handler determines which user to upgrade based on req.body.UserId (line 19) rather than deriving the identity exclusively from the authenticated session. The route's only middleware is security.appendUserId(), whose name indicates it appends the user ID to the body but does not enforce authentication — it does not reject requests lacking a valid session. Even if appendUserId sets req.body.UserId from a valid JWT, the handler never independently verifies that the body UserId matches the session user. If the middleware fails silently (no token, invalid token), req.body.UserId remains fully attacker-controlled. An attacker can POST with any victim's UserId, causing the handler to look up that user (line 19), upgrade their role to deluxe (line 43), generate a new authentication token for them (line 45), register it in the authenticated users store (line 46), and return it to the attacker (line 47). This grants the attacker a valid session token for the victim's account — full account takeover. Additionally, if paymentMode is 'wallet', the attacker can drain 49 from the victim's wallet (line 30).

title: Free deluxe membership by bypassing payment via unsupported paymentMode value
description: The upgradeToDeluxe handler checks for two specific payment modes: 'wallet' (line 24) and 'card' (line 34). If the caller supplies any other value for paymentMode (or omits it entirely), both conditional blocks are skipped and execution falls through to the user upgrade logic at line 42, which upgrades the user to deluxe and issues a new token without any payment being processed. The design validates only the two expected payment modes but never enforces that a valid payment mode is required before proceeding. An authenticated user can obtain deluxe membership for free by sending paymentMode set to any string other than 'wallet' or 'card'.

title: Privilege escalation (customer → deluxe) performed without any security logging
description: The upgradeToDeluxe handler performs a role change from customer to deluxe (line 43), which is a security-relevant privilege escalation event. The handler contains no logging statement before, during, or after the role change — no log entry records who was upgraded, who initiated the request, or when it occurred. In an incident investigation, there would be no application-level audit trail of this privilege change. This is especially critical given that the same handler is vulnerable to account takeover (Finding 1), meaning an attacker could escalate any user's privileges with no log evidence.

const user = await UserModel.findOne(...) — the target user is identified. No log records which user is being targeted for upgrade.
if (user == null) { — the null-check either returns an error (line 21) or falls through. Neither path logs the lookup result or the attempt.
const userWithStatus = utils.queryResultToJson(updatedUser) — the updated user object is prepared. No log records the successful role change or the new role.
const updatedToken = security.authorize(userWithStatus) — a new token is minted for the upgraded user. No log records token issuance for the privilege change.
security.authenticatedUsers.put(updatedToken, userWithStatus) — the token is registered as a live session. No audit entry records this session creation event.

res.status(200).json({ status: 'success', data: { confirmation: '...', token: updatedToken } }) — the success response is sent. At no point in the handler (lines 17-53) is any security log written for the privilege escalation, the token issuance, or the session creation. The response is sent with no audit trail of the role change.

user.update({ role: security.roles.deluxe }) — the user's role is changed from customer to deluxe. This privilege escalation event is not logged anywhere in the handler. The response is sent (line 47) with no audit trail of the role change.

title: Unauthenticated notification triggering for solved challenges
description: The GET /rest/repeat-notification route is registered with no authentication middleware (auth: none). The handler accepts a challenge name from the query string, looks up the challenge, and if it is solved, sends a notification via challengeUtils.sendNotification. There is no authentication or authorization check anywhere in the handler. Any anonymous client can supply an arbitrary challenge name and trigger a notification for that challenge if it has been solved. This is a broken function-level authorization defect: a privileged action (triggering notifications about challenge completion) is exposed to unauthenticated callers. It is also an insecure design defect because the notification side-effect is a server-decided action (whether to notify) that the design allows any caller to invoke repeatedly and for any challenge.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an HTTP request. The route is registered as GET /rest/repeat-notification with auth: none (confirmed by the architecture context). The handler destructures { query } from the request, accepting caller-controlled input with no authentication gate.
The caller-supplied query.challenge value is URL-decoded via decodeURIComponent and assigned to challengeName. No validation or authorization is performed on this value.
challengeUtils.findChallengeByName(challengeName) performs a lookup using the caller-supplied name. The caller controls which challenge record is retrieved.

The conditional if (challenge?.solved) is evaluated. If the looked-up challenge is solved, control passes to the notification sink. There is no authentication or authorization check between the entrypoint and this decision — the only gate is whether the challenge happens to be solved, not whether the caller is authorized to trigger a notification.

If the looked-up challenge is solved (challenge?.solved on line 14), challengeUtils.sendNotification(challenge, true) is called. This privileged action — sending a notification about a solved challenge — executes with no authentication or authorization check anywhere in the handler. An anonymous attacker can trigger notifications for any solved challenge by supplying its name.

title: No rate limiting on unauthenticated notification endpoint enables notification flooding
description: The GET /rest/repeat-notification endpoint has no authentication and no visible rate limiting. Each successful call triggers challengeUtils.sendNotification, which likely sends push notifications, WebSocket messages, or other network-delivered alerts. An attacker can repeatedly call this endpoint with the name of a solved challenge to flood the system with notifications. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated, the attack requires no credentials and can be parallelized across IPs. The handler performs a database lookup (findChallengeByName) and a notification dispatch on every request with no throttle, cooldown, or deduplication.

trace.description: The handler is reachable via GET /rest/repeat-notification with auth: none. No rate-limiting middleware is visible in this handler or in the route registration.
Every request performs a database lookup via challengeUtils.findChallengeByName(challengeName), consuming database resources on each call.
The solved check (challenge?.solved) is evaluated on every request with no caching or throttling.
decodeURIComponent(query.challenge as string) is executed on every incoming request, processing the caller-supplied value with no rate gate.

challengeUtils.sendNotification(challenge, true) is called on every request where the challenge is solved. No rate limit, cooldown, or deduplication mechanism is present. An attacker can issue unlimited requests to repeatedly trigger notifications, consuming notification infrastructure resources and potentially flooding notification recipients.

title: Prometheus metrics endpoint exposed without authentication
description: The serveMetrics() function serves the full Prometheus metrics registry without any authentication or authorization check. The route registration confirms auth: none for GET /metrics. The metrics exposed include sensitive operational data: total number of registered users by role, aggregate wallet balances, order counts, challenge solving status (which reveals which security challenges have been solved), cheat scores, coding challenge accuracy, and feedback/complaint counts. An unauthenticated attacker can access this endpoint to gain intelligence about the application's state, user base, and security posture — including which hacking challenges have been solved, which could aid in understanding what vulnerabilities exist and have been exploited.

trace.description: serveMetrics() is exported as a route handler. Per the route registration, GET /metrics has auth: none — no authentication or authorization middleware protects this endpoint. The caller (route registration) is outside this file.

The handler calls register.metrics() which returns the entire Prometheus registry contents. The registry (populated in observeMetrics()) contains gauges for user counts by role, total wallet balance, order counts, challenge solving status, cheat scores, and more — all set in the update loop at lines 183-213.

The register constant (Prometheus.register) is the default Prometheus registry. It holds all metrics auto-registered by the Gauges created in observeMetrics() (lines 96-156), which are populated in the update loop (lines 158-218) with sensitive data: user counts by role (lines 190-191), total wallet balance (line 193), order/review/feedback/complaint counts (lines 188-195), challenge solving status (lines 168-181), and cheat/accuracy scores (lines 202-204).

The function returns an async Express handler (req, res, next). This handler is what Express invokes on each request to GET /metrics. No authentication check, authorization check, or role verification is performed inside the handler body.

res.set('Content-Type', register.contentType) sets the response Content-Type to the Prometheus exposition format. Still no auth check has been performed — the handler proceeds directly to serving data.

The full metrics payload is written to the response with res.end(await register.metrics()). No access control check is performed anywhere in the handler. Any unauthenticated user can retrieve all operational metrics.

title: Unbounded Prometheus label cardinality via attacker-controlled file MIME type
description: The observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware() uses file.mimetype as a Prometheus label. The MIME type is derived from the uploaded file and is fully attacker-controlled. Prometheus creates a new time series for each unique combination of label values. An attacker can upload files with arbitrary or subtly different MIME type strings (e.g., 'application/octet-stream-1', 'application/octet-stream-2', ...) to create an unbounded number of time series. This leads to memory exhaustion and degraded Prometheus performance — a well-known cardinality explosion attack. There is no allow-list, sanitization, or cardinality cap on the label value. This middleware is applied to multiple file upload routes including POST /file-upload and POST /profile/image/file, both of which have auth: none.

trace.description: observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware() is exported as middleware. Per the route registration, it is applied to POST /file-upload and POST /profile/image/file, both with auth: none. The caller (route registration) is outside this file. The middleware destructures { file } from the request — file is the multer-parsed upload whose mimetype is set from the Content-Type header, fully attacker-controlled.

file.mimetype is passed directly to fileUploadsCountMetric.labels(file.mimetype) or fileUploadErrorsMetric.labels(file.mimetype) without any validation, allow-listing, or cardinality limiting. Each unique mimetype string creates a new Prometheus time series.

The returned handler destructures { file } from the Request object. The file object is populated by multer (uploadToMemory.single('file') middleware that runs before this middleware). The file.mimetype field is derived from the Content-Type header of the multipart upload, which is fully attacker-controlled. No validation or allow-listing is applied to the mimetype value at this point.

onFinished(res, () => { ... }) registers a callback that executes when the HTTP response finishes. This defers the metric recording until after the upload handler has run, but the file.mimetype value captured in the closure remains the attacker-controlled value from line 74.

if (file != null) checks only that a file was uploaded. If a file exists, execution proceeds to line 77. This conditional gates on file presence, not on the validity of the mimetype value — any non-null file with any mimetype string passes this check.

The .inc() call creates a new time series for each unique mimetype label value. An attacker can send thousands of requests with distinct MIME types, causing unbounded growth in the number of time series tracked by Prometheus, leading to memory exhaustion and potential denial of service.

title: Path traversal via insufficient slash-only filter in serveKeyFiles
description: The serveKeyFiles handler takes a user-controlled `file` path parameter and passes it directly into `res.sendFile(path.resolve('encryptionkeys/', file))`. The only protection is a check that the parameter does not contain a forward slash (`!file.includes('/')`). This blocklist approach is insufficient: (1) on Windows, backslash path separators are not blocked, allowing traversal like `..\..\config\secrets.yml`; (2) the code never verifies that the resolved absolute path remains inside the `encryptionkeys/` directory, so any future routing or encoding variant that bypasses the slash check immediately yields arbitrary file read. A robust control would resolve the path and compare it against the allowed directory's absolute path. Additionally, no authentication or authorization is performed before serving files from a directory named `encryptionkeys`, meaning any caller — authenticated or not — can retrieve cryptographic key material.

trace.description: The exported middleware handler receives `params.file` from the incoming request. The caller (route registration) is outside this file, but the handler accepts an arbitrary file name from the request path parameter.
`const file = params.file` — the user-controlled value is captured into a local variable with no sanitization or allow-listing.

The sole validation check is `!file.includes('/')`. This only blocks forward slashes. Backslashes (Windows path separators), the `..` component itself, and other traversal vectors are not blocked. There is no authentication check anywhere in the handler.
The exported function `serveKeyFiles` is defined. The caller (route registration) is outside this file, but this function constructs and returns the vulnerable request handler.

`res.sendFile(path.resolve('encryptionkeys/', file))` — the user-controlled `file` value is concatenated into a filesystem path and served. `path.resolve` will normalize `..` segments and backslashes on Windows, allowing the resolved path to escape the `encryptionkeys/` directory. The resolved path is never compared against the allowed directory boundary.

title: Encryption key files served without authentication or authorization
description: The serveKeyFiles handler serves files from the `encryptionkeys/` directory to any caller. There is no authentication check (no session/token verification), no authorization check (no role or ownership verification), and no access logging. The directory name `encryptionkeys` indicates these files are cryptographic key material — secrets that should never be publicly retrievable. Any unauthenticated user who can guess or enumerate filenames in this directory can download encryption keys, potentially decrypting protected data or forging tokens.

trace.description: The middleware handler begins. There is no authentication middleware referenced, no session check, no token verification, and no role check. The handler proceeds directly to serving the file.
The only check performed is a path-slash filter for traversal prevention. No access-control decision of any kind (authentication, authorization, role check) is made before the file is served.
`res.sendFile(path.resolve('encryptionkeys/', file))` — the file from the encryption keys directory is sent to the caller regardless of their identity or authentication status.

title: No security logging for access to encryption key files
description: The serveKeyFiles handler serves cryptographic key material but performs no logging of any kind — not of who accessed which key file, not of failed access attempts, and not of the source IP. Access to encryption keys is a security-relevant event that should be logged for audit and incident response. Without logging, an attacker who retrieves encryption keys leaves no trace, and the organization cannot detect or investigate the exfiltration of cryptographic secrets.

trace.description: The handler begins processing a request for a key file. No logging statement appears anywhere in the handler — neither before, during, nor after the file is served.
Even the error path (forward slash detected) does not log the rejected attempt — it only sends a 403 and passes an error to `next`.
On the success path, `res.sendFile` delivers the key file with no audit log entry recording the access. The complete absence of logging for retrieval of cryptographic material is the finding.

title: Lossy email masking in order lookup enables cross-user order history exposure
description: The orderHistory handler authenticates the user and then masks their email by replacing all vowel characters with '*'. This masked email is used as the sole query key to retrieve orders. Because the masking is a many-to-one (lossy) transformation, any two users whose emails differ only in vowels (e.g., 'alice@test.com' and 'elice@test.com') produce the identical masked string. When either user calls this endpoint, the query returns orders belonging to both users. The design uses a collision-prone derived identifier instead of the user's unique ID, breaking object-level authorization at the design level.

trace.description: orderHistory() handler for GET /rest/order-history receives the request. Auth middleware is 'none' at the route level; the handler performs its own authentication check on line 13.
The logged-in user is resolved from the Bearer token via security.authenticatedUsers.get(). The user's email and id are checked on line 14.

The user's email is transformed by replacing all vowel characters (a, e, i, o, u, case-insensitive) with '*'. This is a lossy, many-to-one transformation: 'alice@test.com' and 'elice@test.com' both become '*l*c*@t*st.c*m'.
The async route handler function is invoked with req, res, and next.
The code verifies that loggedInUser has both an email and an id, letting the request continue down the success path.
The user's actual email is extracted into the email variable.

ordersCollection.find({ email: updatedEmail }) retrieves all orders matching the masked email. Because the masked email is not unique per user, orders belonging to a different user (whose email differs only in vowels) are returned and sent to the caller on line 18. There is no secondary ownership check using the user's unique ID.

title: allOrders endpoint returns unbounded result set with no pagination
description: The allOrders handler calls ordersCollection.find() with no filter, no limit, and no pagination, then calls .reverse() on the result, which loads the entire orders collection into memory. An authenticated accounting user (or anyone who can bypass or satisfy the isAccounting check) can trigger a request that loads every order record into server memory. As the orders table grows, a single request can consume excessive memory and degrade or crash the service.

trace.description: allOrders() handler for GET /rest/order-history/orders. Protected by security.isAccounting() middleware.
The async route handler function is invoked with req, res, and next.

ordersCollection.find() is called with no query filter, no limit, no skip, and no pagination parameters. Line 28 calls .reverse() on the full result array, materializing the entire collection in memory before sending the response.

title: Successful order history access is not logged for audit
description: The orderHistory handler logs failed authentication attempts (line 20) by creating an error containing the client IP, but it does not log successful order history accesses. Order history contains financial and PII data (order details tied to a user). Without an audit log entry for successful access, the application cannot detect or investigate unauthorized data access, insider threats, or account compromise after the fact. The presence of logging on the failure path (line 20) demonstrates the code recognizes this as a security-relevant event, yet the success path has no equivalent.

trace.description: orderHistory() handler for GET /rest/order-history processes a request to view order history.
Authentication succeeds: loggedInUser.data.email and loggedInUser.data.id are both present. The code proceeds to retrieve and return order data.
The async route handler function is invoked.
The logged-in user is resolved from the Bearer token.
The user's email is extracted from the session data.
The email is transformed into updatedEmail by masking vowels.
The order history is retrieved from the database for the user.

The response with order data is sent with status 200. No logging or audit entry is created for this successful access. Contrast with line 20, where the failure path does create a log entry via next(new Error(...)), confirming the handler is aware this is a security-relevant event.

title: SQL injection in login query via interpolated email field enables authentication bypass
description: The login handler constructs a raw SQL query by directly interpolating req.body.email into the query string on line 33 using template literal interpolation. There is no parameterization, escaping, or allow-listing applied to the email value before it is embedded in the query. An attacker can supply a crafted email value such as `' OR 1=1--` to manipulate the query structure, causing it to return a user record regardless of the password provided. This bypasses the credential check entirely and grants the attacker an authenticated session for whatever user record the database returns first. Because the defect is in the credential-verification query and changes who the application believes the caller is, it establishes both the injection class and the authentication-bypass class on the same trace.

trace.description: The exported login() returns an Express route handler that receives req, res, next. The route POST /rest/user/login has no auth middleware (confirmed by the route registration context). req.body.email and req.body.password arrive from the caller.

req.body.email (defaulting to '') is taken directly from the request body with no sanitization, escaping, or parameterization. It is interpolated into a raw SQL query string via template literal: `SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '${req.body.email || ''}' AND password = '${security.hash(req.body.password || '')}' AND deletedAt IS NULL`.
Inside afterLogin, an authenticatedUser object is created: { data: user, bid: basket.id }, binding the attacker to the victim's basket.
security.authorize(authenticatedUser) issues a valid session token for the attacker-selected user identity.
security.authenticatedUsers.put(token, authenticatedUser) registers the forged session in the application's authenticated-users store.
The token is returned in the JSON response as { authentication: { token, bid, umail } }, completing the authentication bypass. The attacker now holds a valid session token for the victim's account.
verifyPreLoginChallenges(req) is called. Its body (lines 56-57) is an empty stub — no input validation, sanitization, or escaping is applied to req.body.email before it reaches the query.
The .then() callback receives the query result as authenticatedUser. Due to SQL injection, this is a real user record that the attacker did not authenticate as.
utils.queryResultToJson(authenticatedUser) converts the raw query result into a user object with a .data property containing the user fields.

The conditional checks user.data?.id and user.data.totpSecret. Because injection returned a real user record, user.data.id is truthy. If the returned user has no TOTP secret (totpSecret === ''), the else-if branch on line 46 is taken.
The else-if branch for a user with an id but empty totpSecret is entered, bypassing the MFA challenge path (lines 37-45).
afterLogin(user.data, res, next) is called with the attacker-selected user's data, treating the attacker as that authenticated user.
On a failed guess, only a 401 response is returned. No failed-attempt counter is incremented, no lockout is triggered, and no delay is introduced before the next attempt.

verifyPreLoginChallenges function body (line 56-57) is completely empty, confirming that no rate-limiting, throttling, or attempt-tracking logic exists anywhere in the login flow. The application has no defense against unlimited rapid credential submissions.
The security module is imported from '../lib/insecurity' as `import * as security from '../lib/insecurity'`. The module name itself signals deliberately insecure implementations.

The interpolated string is passed to models.sequelize.query() as a raw SQL query. An attacker supplying email=`' OR 1=1--` produces: SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = '' OR 1=1--' AND password='...' AND deletedAt IS NULL, which returns the first user record. On line 34-47, the returned user is used to issue a full authentication token via security.authorize() and security.authenticatedUsers.put(), completing the authentication bypass.

title: Login endpoint lacks rate limiting, enabling credential brute-force attacks
description: The login handler performs no rate limiting, throttling, or account lockout. An attacker can repeatedly submit password guesses against known email addresses without any server-side cap on attempt frequency. Per the crypto-auth playbook, a missing rate limit on a login endpoint permits credential brute force and establishes both the resource-consumption class and the authentication class, because the missing control directly enables defeating the authentication mechanism.

trace.description: The POST /rest/user/login route handler is registered with no authentication middleware and is publicly accessible. Every invocation performs a database query and password comparison.

The handler processes each login attempt by executing a full SQL query and hash comparison (lines 33-49) with no rate-limiting middleware, attempt counter, lockout mechanism, or delay between attempts visible anywhere in the handler. An attacker can issue unlimited rapid requests to brute-force user passwords. On success (line 46-47), a valid session token is issued, defeating the authentication control.

title: No security logging of login attempts (successful or failed)
description: The login handler does not log any security-relevant events. Neither successful authentications nor failed login attempts produce a log entry. The functions verifyPreLoginChallenges (line 56-57) and verifyPostLoginChallenges (line 59-60) are empty stubs, suggesting security checks and logging hooks were intended but never implemented. Without logging of authentication events, the application cannot detect, investigate, or respond to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, or account takeover attempts.

trace.description: The login route handler receives credential submissions from external callers via POST /rest/user/login with no auth middleware.
verifyPreLoginChallenges(req) is called — this is where pre-login security logging (e.g., logging the incoming attempt) should occur, but the function body is empty.
The credential-verification query is executed. No log statement records the attempt, the email used, or the source IP.
The query result is received. No logging occurs at this step.
utils.queryResultToJson converts the result to a user object. No logging of the resolved identity occurs.
The conditional branches based on authentication outcome (TOTP required, success, or failure). No branch logs the authentication decision.
The success path is entered when a valid user is found. No log statement records the successful authentication.
afterLogin is called, which issues a token (line 23) and registers a session (line 24). No logging of the session creation or token issuance occurs.
verifyPreLoginChallenges function body (lines 56-57) is an empty stub — no pre-login security event logging was implemented.

verifyPostLoginChallenges function body (lines 59-60) is an empty stub — no post-login security event logging (successful login, session creation) was implemented. The application has no logging coverage for any authentication event.

On failed authentication (line 49), the handler only sends a 401 response with no log statement. On successful authentication (lines 22-25), a token is issued and returned with no log statement. The empty stub functions verifyPreLoginChallenges (line 56-57) and verifyPostLoginChallenges (line 59-60) confirm no logging or security-event recording occurs at any point in the login flow.

title: Password hash function sourced from 'insecurity' library may use weak algorithm without salt
description: The login handler hashes the submitted password using security.hash() (line 33), where security is imported from '../lib/insecurity' (line 11). The library name 'insecurity' strongly suggests intentionally weak cryptographic implementations, consistent with Juice Shop's known use of unsalted MD5 for password hashing. If the hash function uses MD5 or SHA-256 without a salt or key-stretching function (bcrypt/Argon2/scrypt), an attacker who obtains the password column can recover plaintext passwords via precomputed rainbow tables or fast offline brute force. This cannot be fully confirmed from this file alone since the hash implementation is in a different file, but the import from a module named 'insecurity' is a strong indicator.

trace.description: The security module is imported from '../lib/insecurity'. The module name itself signals deliberately insecure implementations.

security.hash(req.body.password || '') is called to hash the password before comparison. The hash function's algorithm, salt usage, and work factor are defined in the external insecurity module and cannot be verified here. If it uses an unsalted fast hash (MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 without key stretching), password storage is vulnerable to precomputed lookup attacks.

title: CAPTCHA answer exposed in API response, making verification trivially bypassable
description: The imageCaptchas handler creates a CAPTCHA and stores it in the database, but it also returns the CAPTCHA answer (captcha.text) directly in the JSON response alongside the image. The response object at lines 24-28 includes both 'image' (the SVG challenge) and 'answer' (the solution text). Any client requesting a CAPTCHA receives the solution, so the CAPTCHA provides no protection. The downstream verifyImageCaptcha middleware (used to gate POST /rest/user/data-export) can be satisfied by simply echoing back the answer received from the creation endpoint. This completely defeats the purpose of the CAPTCHA as an anti-automation control on the sensitive data-export endpoint.

trace.description: GET /rest/image-captcha handler exported as imageCaptchas(). The caller (route registration) is outside this file; the route is registered with auth: none.
svgCaptcha.create() generates both captcha.data (the SVG image) and captcha.text (the answer).
The imageCaptcha object is constructed containing both 'image: captcha.data' and 'answer: captcha.text', plus 'UserId: user.data.id'.
Dynamically imports svg-captcha module, which will be used to generate the challenge and its solution.
const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) extracts the authenticated user from the request.
if (!user) checks whether a user was found; if not, returns 401 at line 20. If found, execution continues to construct the captcha object.
answer: captcha.text places the plaintext CAPTCHA solution directly into the imageCaptcha object alongside the image.
UserId: user.data.id associates the CAPTCHA with the requesting user.
ImageCaptchaModel.build(imageCaptcha) constructs a model instance from the object containing both image and answer.
await imageCaptchaInstance.save() persists the captcha record (including answer) to the database.
res.json(imageCaptcha) sends the full object — including the 'answer' field — back to the client. The client now possesses both the challenge and its solution.

title: CAPTCHA verification bypassed when no CAPTCHA record exists or has expired
description: In verifyImageCaptcha (line 52), the condition `!captchas[0] || req.body.answer === captchas[0].answer` calls next() (passes verification) when no CAPTCHA record is found. This means: (1) if a user never requests a CAPTCHA, verification passes automatically; (2) if a user waits 5 minutes (the Op.gt window at line 47) after requesting a CAPTCHA, all records expire and verification passes. The CAPTCHA gate on POST /rest/user/data-export can be bypassed simply by not requesting a CAPTCHA first, or by waiting for expiry. The logic should reject when no valid CAPTCHA exists, not pass. This is an insecure design flaw: the absence of a challenge is treated as a successful challenge response, allowing an attacker to trigger data exports without any CAPTCHA interaction.

trace.description: verifyImageCaptcha is exported as middleware for POST /rest/user/data-export, protected by security.appendUserId(). The caller is outside this file.
Query searches for CAPTCHA records for the user created within the last 5 minutes (line 47: Op.gt new Date(Date.now() - 300000)). If none exist, captchas array is empty.
Condition `!captchas[0] || req.body.answer === captchas[0].answer` — the first disjunct (!captchas[0]) is true when no CAPTCHA record is found.
const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) extracts the authenticated user from the request to scope the CAPTCHA lookup.
const UserId = user ? user.data ? user.data.id : undefined : undefined safely resolves the user's ID, or undefined if no user/session data is present.
limit: 1 restricts results to one record, but the query may still return zero rows if no CAPTCHA was ever created or all have expired.
where: { ... } begins the query conditions that determine which CAPTCHA records are eligible.
UserId scopes the query to the current user's CAPTCHAs — but if UserId is undefined (no user found), this will match records with null UserId.
createdAt: { ... } opens the time-window condition that filters CAPTCHA records by recency.
[Op.gt]: new Date(Date.now() - 300000) only matches CAPTCHAs created in the last 5 minutes. Records older than 5 minutes are excluded, so captchas array will be empty after expiry.
order: [['createdAt', 'DESC']] sorts results newest-first, but has no effect on whether any records exist.
Closing of the findAll call; the query executes and returns results (or an empty array).
next() is called when no CAPTCHA exists, bypassing verification entirely. An attacker can invoke the data-export endpoint without ever solving (or even requesting) a CAPTCHA.

title: No rate limiting on CAPTCHA generation endpoint enables database and CPU exhaustion
description: The GET /rest/image-captcha endpoint has no rate limiting or throttling. Each request invokes svgCaptcha.create() (CPU-intensive SVG generation) and persists a new row to the ImageCaptchaModel table (line 29-30). An authenticated attacker can flood this endpoint with rapid requests, consuming CPU for SVG generation and filling database storage with CAPTCHA records. There is no cap on how many CAPTCHAs a single user can generate. The CAPTCHA records are only cleaned up by the 5-minute expiry window in queries, but old records are not deleted from the database, so storage grows unboundedly.

trace.description: GET /rest/image-captcha handler. No rate-limiting middleware is applied to this route (auth: none in route registration; the handler does its own auth check at line 18).
svgCaptcha.create() is called on every request with no throttling — each call generates an SVG image with 5 characters and 2 noise lines, which is CPU-intensive.
return async (req: Request, res: Response) => { ... } defines the async handler that will run on every request with no throttling wrapper.
try block opens the request processing path; no rate-limit check or counter exists before the expensive operations begin.
await import('svg-captcha') dynamically loads the module on each request — this import and the subsequent generation are CPU-intensive and unthrottled.
const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) — the only check is authentication, not rate limiting. An authenticated user can make unlimited requests.
if (!user) gates only on authentication; once past this check, every subsequent operation runs without any usage cap.
const imageCaptcha = { ... } constructs a new object for every request, with no deduplication or caching to reduce per-request cost.
image: captcha.data stores the full SVG string, which can be large and is generated fresh each time.
ImageCaptchaModel.build(imageCaptcha) creates a new model instance for each request — no limit on how many records a single user can create.

imageCaptchaInstance.save() persists a new row to the database on every request with no limit on the number of CAPTCHAs per user. An attacker can flood this endpoint to exhaust CPU and database storage.

title: No security logging of CAPTCHA verification outcomes or bypass attempts
description: The verifyImageCaptcha middleware gates access to the sensitive data-export endpoint (POST /rest/user/data-export). Neither successful nor failed CAPTCHA verifications are logged. When the verification is bypassed via the no-record path (!captchas[0] on line 52), there is no audit trail. When a wrong answer is submitted (line 55), the failure is not logged. This means an attacker brute-forcing CAPTCHA answers or exploiting the bypass cannot be detected or investigated from logs. The absence of logging on a verification gate for a sensitive data-export operation is a security monitoring gap.

title: Unauthenticated challenge solving via forgeable continue codes with hardcoded Hashids salt
description: All three restoreProgress endpoints (PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:continueCode, PUT /rest/continue-code-findIt/apply/:continueCode, PUT /rest/continue-code-fixIt/apply/:continueCode) have no authentication middleware. The continue code that gates which challenges are marked as solved is encoded using the Hashids library — which is explicitly an obfuscation tool, not a cryptographic primitive — with a hardcoded salt that is plainly visible in the source code ('this is my salt', 'this is the salt for findIt challenges', 'yet another salt for the fixIt challenges'). Since Hashids is symmetric and deterministic, anyone who knows the salt can encode arbitrary challenge IDs into a valid continue code. An attacker can create their own Hashids instance with the same salt, encode any set of challenge IDs, and submit the resulting code to have all those challenges marked as solved without actually solving them. This entirely defeats the challenge-solving workflow of the application: the server trusts a client-supplied token whose integrity depends solely on a secret that is published in the source code, and it performs the solve operation without verifying the caller's identity or authorization.

title: Unauthenticated progress restoration endpoints with no rate limiting iterate over all challenges
description: All three restoreProgress endpoints have no authentication and no rate limiting. Each handler iterates over Object.values(challenges) — the entire challenge set — and for each challenge checks if the decoded ID array includes the challenge's ID. Because Hashids can encode arbitrarily large arrays of integers and the endpoints are unauthenticated, an attacker can repeatedly submit crafted continue codes containing large numbers of IDs. Each request triggers a full scan of the challenge set with an O(ids × challenges) inner loop. With no rate limiting, this can be abused to consume CPU and potentially degrade service. Additionally, the Hashids decode operation itself on a maximally-long input string (up to the regex-validated 60+ character alphanumeric input) can produce large decoded arrays, amplifying the per-request cost.

title: SQL Injection in product search via 'q' query parameter
description: The `searchProducts` handler accepts a search term from the `q` query parameter and interpolates it directly into a raw SQL query string without parameterization. Although the input is truncated to 200 characters, this length is sufficient to break out of the intended string context and inject arbitrary SQL. An attacker can exploit this to bypass the `deletedAt IS NULL` filter (gaining access to deleted products they should not see) or extract arbitrary data from the database via UNION-based or error-based injection.

title: Missing pagination on product search endpoint allows unbounded result sets
description: The `searchProducts` endpoint executes a `SELECT *` query against the Products table based on user input. There is no `LIMIT` clause in the query and no pagination logic applied to the result set before returning it via `res.json`. An attacker can supply a wildcard search term (e.g., `%`), which is accepted by the length check, to force the database to return the entire table. This can consume excessive memory and bandwidth, degrading application performance or causing a denial of service.

title: No rate limiting on unauthenticated password reset endpoint enables security answer brute-force
description: The password reset endpoint (POST /rest/user/reset-password) requires no authentication (auth: none) and has no rate limiting, throttling, or lockout mechanism. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for the security answer until they find the correct one. Security answers typically have very low entropy (e.g., a mother's maiden name, a favorite color), making brute-force feasible. Once the answer is guessed, the attacker can set a new password and take over the account. The absence of rate limiting also enables denial-of-service through repeated expensive database queries (Sequelize joins) and HMAC computations.

const answer = body.answer — the security answer guess is extracted from the request body.
Input validation only checks that email and answer are present (non-empty). No rate limit, no attempt counter, no lockout state is consulted or updated.

The comparison `security.hmac(answer) === data.answer` uses the standard `===` operator, which is not constant-time. The HMAC is computed on the attacker's input and immediately compared. This is the authentication decision point — the comparison result determines whether the password is reset. A timing side-channel here could leak information about the correct HMAC value, and by extension the correct security answer.

If the attacker guesses the correct security answer, line 44 directly updates the user's password (user.update({ password: newPassword })). There is no rate limiting, no account lockout, no CAPTCHA, and no email confirmation step anywhere in this flow. An attacker can brute-force the security answer with unlimited attempts, each costing one HTTP request.

title: Non-constant-time comparison of HMAC security answer permits timing side-channel

While timing attacks over networks are noisy, the comparison short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking timing information that could theoretically help an attacker discover the correct security answer byte-by-byte. A constant-time comparison function (e.g., crypto.timingSafeEqual) should be used for security-critical comparisons.

title: Password reset events are not logged — successful resets, failed attempts, and account takeovers are undetectable
description: The password reset handler performs no security logging at any point. Failed reset attempts (wrong security answer), successful password resets (account takeover), and error conditions are all silently processed without any log entry. Password resets are high-risk security events that must be logged for audit, alerting, and incident investigation. Without logging, an attacker brute-forcing security answers or performing an account takeover is invisible to defenders. The only logging-adjacent code is on line 23 which passes an error to next() when email/answer are missing — but this covers only the input validation case, not the security-relevant authentication outcome.

title: Password reset relies solely on a single security question with no compensating controls
description: The password reset flow grants full password-changing capability based solely on knowing the answer to a single security question. There is no email confirmation step, no secondary channel verification, no notification to the account owner, and no step-up authentication. Security questions are inherently low-entropy and often guessable or discoverable via social media. The design allows account takeover by anyone who can guess or learn one piece of information, with no additional verification or delay. This is a design-level defect — the code works exactly as written, but the design itself permits account takeover through a weak recovery factor.

title: Wallet NFT verification accepts client-supplied wallet address without cryptographic proof of ownership
description: The walletNFTVerify endpoint is designed to confirm that a user has minted an NFT, granting challenge-completion status upon success. However, it accepts the wallet address directly from the request body (req.body.walletAddress) and checks only whether that address appears in the addressesMinted set. There is no signature verification, nonce challenge, or any other cryptographic mechanism to prove that the caller actually controls the wallet they are claiming. Any user can submit any known minted wallet address and receive credit for solving the challenge. The server should require the caller to sign a challenge message with their wallet's private key and verify that signature server-side before granting credit. This is a trust assumption violation (the server accepts a client-reported identity it should independently verify), a missing cryptographic authentication control, and a broken access control issue (any user can claim any other user's mint achievement).

title: Unauthenticated security-question disclosure and user enumeration via GET /rest/user/security-question
description: The handler accepts an arbitrary email query parameter with no authentication or authorization (route declared with auth: none) and returns the security question associated with that user's account. The response differs between existing and non-existing accounts (a populated `question` object vs. an empty `{}`), which enables user enumeration. For existing accounts it also discloses which security question was chosen, giving an attacker a targeted starting point for guessing or social-engineering the answer as part of an account-recovery bypass. The endpoint is an account-recovery / security-question decision point but has no rate limiting, no throttling, and no authentication, allowing mass automated enumeration of every email address against the user base.

Its absence means an attacker can enumerate the entire user base and harvest security questions with no auditable trail, preventing incident detection and response.

title: Sequelize operator and array injection via JSON.parse on path parameter in getRecycleItem
description: The getRecycleItem handler calls JSON.parse(req.params.id) and passes the result directly as the 'where.id' clause to RecycleModel.findAll(). Because JSON.parse can produce arrays or objects (not just scalars), an attacker can supply a JSON array like [1,2,3,...] as the path parameter to match and return arbitrary numbers of records in a single request, or supply a JSON object with Sequelize operator keys (e.g., {"$like":"%"} in Sequelize versions using string operators) to manipulate the query predicate. This bypasses the blockRecycleItems gate (lines 23-26) that was intended to prevent bulk listing of recycle items through the GET /api/Recycles endpoint. The individual-item endpoint becomes a bulk-listing endpoint via array injection, and an unbounded array can return arbitrarily large result sets without pagination.

An attacker can send a URL-encoded JSON array (e.g., /api/Recycles/%5B1%2C2%2C3%5D) to retrieve multiple records in one call, bypassing the list-blocking design. With Sequelize string-operator versions, an object like {"$like":"%"} injected via the path parameter would match all records. There is no pagination, no size limit on the array, and no operator allow-list.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization on GET /api/Recycles/:id — no authentication or ownership check
description: The getRecycleItem handler is registered on GET /api/Recycles/:id with auth: none. The handler looks up a recycle item by its ID and returns it to the caller without verifying that the caller is authenticated, let alone authorized to view that specific record. Any anonymous user can retrieve any recycle item by supplying its identifier. There is no session check, no ownership verification, and no role-based access control anywhere in the handler. This is a textbook BOLA: authentication is absent (not just insufficient), and per-resource authorization is never performed.

title: No security logging for 2FA verification, setup, or disable operations

An attacker brute-forcing TOTP codes via the verify endpoint, or an attacker disabling a user's 2FA after session theft, would leave no trace in application logs.

title: TOTP brute force enabled by permissive rate limit and absence of per-account lockout
description: The POST /rest/2fa/verify endpoint is protected only by an IP-based rate limit of 100 requests per 5 minutes and has no authentication middleware (auth: none). The handler performs no per-account failed-attempt tracking or account lockout. A 6-digit TOTP code has 1,000,000 possible values; with epochTolerance of 30 (±1 time step), approximately 3 codes are valid at any moment. At 100 attempts per 5-minute window, an attacker has roughly an 8% chance of guessing a valid TOTP per day from a single IP, scaling linearly with additional IPs (proxy/botnet). The absence of per-account lockout means this brute force cannot be stopped at the account level — the rate limit is per-IP only. This enables authentication bypass via systematic TOTP enumeration.

title: 2FA disable requires only password, not TOTP token — undermines second-factor protection
description: The disable() function requires only the user's password to disable 2FA. The setup() function, by contrast, requires password + a signed setupToken + a valid TOTP code. This asymmetry means that disabling 2FA is weaker than enabling it. If an attacker obtains a valid session token (e.g., via XSS, token theft, or session fixation) and knows the user's password (e.g., from a separate breach), they can disable 2FA without possessing the TOTP device. Once 2FA is disabled, the attacker can maintain persistent access using only the password, even after the stolen session expires. Requiring the current TOTP code for disable would ensure the person removing 2FA actually possesses the second factor, preserving the protection 2FA is meant to provide.
