The attacker who had a session token and the password — but not the TOTP device — has now permanently removed the second factor. They can authenticate with just the password going forward, defeating the purpose of 2FA. The design should require the current TOTP code as an additional confirmation factor for disabling, mirroring the stronger requirements of the setup flow.

title: Stored XSS via unsanitized true-client-ip header in lastLoginIp
description: The handler records the user's last login IP for security/audit purposes. However, it preferentially uses the `true-client-ip` request header (line 18) — which is set by the client and trivially forgeable — rather than the actual socket remote address. The fallback to `req.socket.remoteAddress` on line 27 only fires when `lastLoginIp` is `undefined`, but after the sanitization on line 24 (in non-challenge mode) the value becomes an empty string, not undefined, so the real socket address is almost never used. This means an attacker can spoof their login IP in audit records, defeating the purpose of IP-based login monitoring and incident reconstruction. The server should derive the client IP from the socket or from headers only after verifying the request traversed a trusted reverse proxy.

title: Payment card queries scoped by client-controlled req.body.UserId enabling BOLA
description: All three handlers in this file filter payment card records by `req.body.UserId`. While the route is protected by `security.appendUserId()` middleware, `req.body` is fundamentally client-controlled. The middleware name 'appendUserId' suggests it adds the user ID to the body rather than enforcing a server-derived identity. If the middleware does not strictly override any client-supplied UserId value (e.g., it only sets the field when absent), an authenticated attacker can send a different UserId in the request body and retrieve or delete another user's payment cards. Even if the middleware currently overrides, using req.body for identity scoping is an insecure design — it conflates client-supplied data with trusted identity, creating a fragile authorization boundary. For GET requests, if body parsing is absent or the middleware fails to populate the field, Sequelize may treat `UserId: undefined` as no filter at all, returning all cards in the system.

title: Open redirect via unauthenticated endpoint with opaque URL validation from 'insecurity' module
description: The GET /redirect endpoint (auth: none) accepts a user-supplied URL in the `to` query parameter and redirects the browser to it via `res.redirect(toUrl)`. The sole validation is delegated to `security.isRedirectAllowed()` imported from the `../lib/insecurity` module — a module whose name signals intentionally weak security controls. Additionally, the local (dead) function `isUnintendedRedirect` reveals the codebase's URL-validation philosophy: it uses `utils.startsWith(toUrl, allowedUrl)`, which is trivially bypassable (e.g., `https://allowed-domain.evil.com`). An attacker can craft a URL like `/redirect?to=https://evil.com` (or a bypass of the allowlist) to redirect victims to attacker-controlled sites, enabling phishing, OAuth flow hijacking, and SSRF-adjacent attacks. The endpoint requires no authentication, so any anonymous user can invoke it.

title: Path traversal via malicious zip entry names in extractZipBuffer
description: The zip extraction function constructs a file path by concatenating the user-controlled zip entry name with the target directory. The validation check on line 32 only verifies that the resolved path contains the current working directory as a substring — it does NOT verify that the path stays within the intended 'uploads/complaints/' directory. An attacker can craft a zip file with entry names like '../../config/config.yml' or '../../app/data/datacache.js' that resolve to paths within the CWD but outside the complaints directory, allowing arbitrary file writes within the application directory. The write on line 33 uses the unsanitized 'uploads/complaints/' + fileName path directly.

trace.description: handleZipFileUpload receives a file from the POST /file-upload route (route registration is outside this file; auth is 'none'). For .zip files it calls extractZipBuffer with the uploaded file buffer.
In extractZipBuffer, each zip entry's path (entry.path) is taken directly from the uploaded zip archive without sanitization. This is attacker-controlled data.

The entry path is concatenated into a filesystem path: 'uploads/complaints/' + fileName. path.resolve is applied, but the result is not used for the actual write — it is only used for the check on line 32.
extractZipBuffer receives the buffer parameter from the caller.
unzipper.Open.buffer(buffer) parses the zip archive in memory, producing a directory object with file entries.
The code iterates over directory.files — every entry in the zip archive is processed.

The guard check: if (absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))) — this only verifies the resolved path CONTAINS the CWD as a substring. It does NOT verify the path is within uploads/complaints/. Paths like '../../app/evil.sh' that resolve within the CWD pass this check.
The function checks if file.originalname ends with '.zip' (case-insensitive). If it does, processing continues; otherwise next() is called and the handler returns.
Checks that file.buffer is not null AND that the fileWriteChallenge is enabled. Both conditions must be true to proceed to extraction.
extractZipBuffer is called with file.buffer — the raw uploaded zip data.

fs.createWriteStream is called with the unsanitized 'uploads/complaints/' + fileName path. The check on line 32 (absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))) only ensures the resolved path contains the CWD as a substring, which allows writes anywhere within the CWD, not just within uploads/complaints/. An attacker who includes '..' segments that resolve to a location still within the CWD (e.g., '../../app/uploads/evil.sh') bypasses the check and writes outside the intended directory.

title: XXE vulnerability in XML file upload processing
description: The handleXmlUpload function parses user-uploaded XML content using parseXmlString. The comment on line 67 explicitly acknowledges XXE attacks are possible. If external entity processing is enabled in the XML parser, an attacker can craft an XML file with external entity references that cause the server to make outbound HTTP requests (SSRF) to internal services or read local files. The parsed content and error messages are then reflected back to the client in error responses, potentially leaking internal file contents or service responses.

trace.description: handleXmlUpload is middleware on POST /file-upload (route registration outside this file; auth is 'none'). For .xml files it processes the uploaded file buffer.

parseXmlString(data) is called on the user-supplied XML content (file.buffer.toString()). The comment on line 67 explicitly references XXE attacks. If the parser resolves external entities, this enables file disclosure, SSRF to internal services, and denial of service via entity expansion.
Checks if file.originalname ends with '.xml' (case-insensitive). Only XML-named files proceed to parsing.
Checks that file.buffer is not null AND that the deprecatedInterfaceChallenge is enabled. The comment explicitly references XXE attacks. Both conditions must be true to proceed.
data is assigned from file.buffer.toString() — converting the uploaded XML file content to a string. This is fully attacker-controlled.
If parseXmlString throws, the catch block captures the error as err.
errorMessage is extracted from err — either err.message or String(err). This error message may contain data exfiltrated via XXE (e.g., file contents included in parser error output).
Checks if errorMessage contains 'Script execution timed out' — if so, a generic 503 error is returned. Otherwise the flow continues to line 79.

The errorMessage (which may contain exfiltrated data from XXE) and file.originalname are interpolated into an error message passed to next(new Error(...)), reflecting attacker-influenced content back to the client.

The parsed XML result (xmlString) and the original filename are interpolated into an error message passed to next(). This reflects server-side data (potentially including file contents read via XXE) back to the client, confirming data exfiltration. The SSRF vector is the external entity resolution itself in step 2 — the parser makes outbound requests to attacker-specified URLs, which can target internal services.

title: Unsafe YAML deserialization with code execution via yaml.load in VM sandbox
description: The handleYamlUpload function deserializes user-uploaded YAML using yaml.load() (the unsafe variant that allows arbitrary object construction) inside a Node.js VM context. The vm module is explicitly documented as not being a security boundary. yaml.load with the default schema can construct arbitrary JavaScript objects via YAML tags. When JSON.stringify is called on the result, custom toString/toJSON methods on constructed objects can execute arbitrary code. The VM sandbox provides only the illusion of isolation.

trace.description: handleYamlUpload is the handler for POST /file-upload (route registration outside this file; auth is 'none'). For .yml/.yaml files it processes the uploaded file buffer.
The uploaded file buffer is converted to a string (file.buffer.toString()) as 'data', which is user-controlled YAML content.
Checks if file.originalname ends with '.yml' or '.yaml' (case-insensitive). Only YAML-named files proceed to parsing.
Checks that file.buffer is not null AND that the deprecatedInterfaceChallenge is enabled. Both conditions must be true to proceed.

A sandbox object is created: { yaml, data }. The yaml module (js-yaml) and the user-controlled data string are both placed into the sandbox context. The yaml module's load function is the unsafe variant that allows arbitrary object construction.
vm.createContext(sandbox) initializes the VM context with the sandbox object. The yaml module and user data are now accessible inside the VM context.
The result (yamlString, truncated to 400 chars) and file.originalname are interpolated into an error message passed to next(new Error(...)).
If the VM execution throws, the catch block captures the error as err.
errorMessage is extracted from err — either err.message or String(err).
Checks if errorMessage contains 'Invalid string length' or 'Script execution timed out'. If so, a generic 503 error is returned. Otherwise the flow continues to line 107.
The errorMessage and file.originalname are interpolated into an error message passed to next(new Error(...)), reflecting attacker-influenced content back to the client.

vm.runInContext('JSON.stringify(yaml.load(data))', sandbox, { timeout: 2000 }) executes yaml.load on user-controlled data. yaml.load (without SAFE_SCHEMA) allows arbitrary object instantiation via YAML tags. The vm sandbox is not a security boundary per Node.js documentation. Constructed objects with custom toString/toJSON methods can execute code when JSON.stringify processes them. This is unsafe deserialization leading to potential code execution.

title: Empty checkUploadSize middleware provides no file size enforcement
description: The checkUploadSize middleware function is intended to validate upload file sizes but its body is completely empty — the if block on lines 55-56 contains no logic. This means there is no server-side enforcement of file size limits on the upload endpoint. An attacker can upload arbitrarily large files, consuming memory (files are stored in memory via uploadToMemory.single) and potentially causing denial of service. Combined with the zip extraction (decompression bombs), XML parsing (billion laughs), and YAML parsing, this creates multiple resource exhaustion vectors.

trace.description: checkUploadSize is middleware on POST /file-upload (registration outside this file). It receives the uploaded file object.
The closing brace of the empty if block. No logic was added inside the conditional.

The function unconditionally calls next(), passing through any file regardless of size. A security control that exists in name only (no-op middleware) is an insecure design flaw. The file is stored in memory (uploadToMemory), so arbitrarily large uploads consume server memory directly and flow into downstream processors.

The if block (if file != null) on lines 55-56 is entirely empty — no size check, no limit enforcement. The function unconditionally calls next() on line 57, passing through any file regardless of size. A security control that exists in name only (no-op middleware) is an insecure design flaw. The file is stored in memory (uploadToMemory), so arbitrarily large uploads consume server memory directly.

title: Empty checkFileType middleware provides no file type validation
description: The checkFileType middleware extracts the file extension but performs no validation whatsoever — it immediately calls next(). This means any file type can be uploaded regardless of the intended restrictions. The subsequent handlers (handleZipFileUpload, handleXmlUpload, handleYamlUpload) process files based on extension, but there is no blocklist or allowlist preventing dangerous file types from being uploaded and processed.

trace.description: checkFileType is middleware on POST /file-upload (registration outside this file). It receives the uploaded file object.

The function extracts the file extension via file.originalname.substr(file.originalname.lastIndexOf('.') + 1).toLowerCase(). The extension is computed but never compared against any allowlist or blocklist — the result is discarded.

The function extracts the file extension (line 61) but never uses it for any validation — it immediately calls next() on line 62. No allowlist or blocklist is applied. This is a no-op security control that provides false assurance of file type validation while allowing all file types through.

title: No security logging for file upload events and processing failures
description: None of the file upload handlers log security-relevant events. File uploads with dangerous content (zip files with path traversal entries, XML with XXE payloads, YAML with deserialization attacks) are processed without any logging. Error conditions are passed to next() as Error objects but there is no explicit security logging of upload attempts, processing failures, or blocked operations. This means an attacker probing the upload endpoint with malicious files cannot be detected or investigated from application logs.

trace.description: handleZipFileUpload, handleXmlUpload (line 65), and handleYamlUpload (line 91) all process potentially malicious file uploads (zip, XML, YAML) from unauthenticated users.
Checks if the file is a .zip file. If so, processing continues to extraction.
Checks file.buffer and challenge enabled status before proceeding.
A try block begins around the extractZipBuffer call — no logging occurs before attempting extraction.
extractZipBuffer(file.buffer) is called. No security event is logged for the upload or extraction attempt.

When zip extraction fails (line 47), XML parsing fails (line 73), or YAML processing fails (line 101), errors are passed to next(err) or next(new Error(...)) but no security logging is performed anywhere in the file. No log statement records the upload event, the file type, the processing result, or the nature of the attack payload. There is no audit trail for file upload attempts on an unauthenticated endpoint that performs dangerous file processing.

title: User-controlled data reflected in error messages (potential XSS)
description: Multiple error messages interpolate user-controlled data — file.originalname and parsed content (xmlString, yamlString, errorMessage) — into strings passed to next(new Error(...)). If the Express error handler renders these error messages in an HTTP response without HTML encoding, this constitutes reflected/stored XSS. The originalname field is fully attacker-controlled, and the parsed content (xmlString, yamlString) may contain attacker-crafted markup. The rendering sink is outside this file, but the injection point is here.

trace.description: handleXmlUpload and handleYamlUpload (line 91) receive uploaded files from unauthenticated users. file.originalname and file.buffer are fully attacker-controlled.

User-controlled values are interpolated into error message strings: utils.trunc(xmlString, 400) and file.originalname on line 72; errorMessage and file.originalname on line 80; file.originalname on line 85. The same pattern appears in handleYamlUpload at lines 100, 108, and 113.

The error messages are passed to next(new Error(...)) which delegates to Express's error handler. If the error handler renders the message in an HTML response without escaping (rendering sink is outside this file), the attacker-controlled file.originalname or parsed content executes as script in the victim's browser. This is a reflected XSS injection point — the taint originates here even though the browser rendering happens elsewhere.

title: Zip extraction vulnerable to decompression bombs without entry count or size limits
description: The extractZipBuffer function iterates over all entries in an uploaded zip file and writes each to disk without any limit on the number of entries or the total decompressed size. Combined with the empty checkUploadSize middleware (no upload size limit), an attacker can upload a zip bomb — a small compressed file that decompresses to an enormous size — causing disk exhaustion and denial of service.

trace.description: extractZipBuffer receives a Buffer from an uploaded zip file (called from handleZipFileUpload at line 45). The caller is handleZipFileUpload, which is middleware on the unauthenticated POST /file-upload route.
unzipper.Open.buffer(buffer) parses the entire zip archive into memory. There is no limit on the size of the buffer or the number of entries the archive may contain.
The for...of loop iterates over directory.files — every entry in the zip archive is processed sequentially with no limit on entry count.
fileName is assigned from entry.path. No size or count check is performed before or after this assignment.
absolutePath is computed from the fileName. This is a path operation, not a size or count limit.
The if check (absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.'))) only validates the path location — it does not check entry size, decompressed size, or total accumulated size.

The for loop on line 29 iterates over all directory.files entries without any limit on count. Each entry is written to disk via fs.createWriteStream on line 33 with no decompressed size check. A zip bomb with thousands of entries or entries that decompress to gigabytes will exhaust disk space and I/O. There is no maximum entry count, no maximum total decompressed size, and no per-entry size limit.

title: Unauthenticated review ownership + NoSQL injection via unsanitized body.id with multi:true allows mass review hijacking
description: The handler retrieves the authenticated user (line 15) but never uses it to scope the update query. The MongoDB update filter is built directly from `req.body.id` without any sanitization, type-checking, or ownership constraint. Because MongoDB treats embedded objects as query operators, an attacker can supply `{"id": {"$ne": null}}` in the request body to match every document in the reviews collection. The `multi: true` option (line 19) ensures ALL matching documents are updated in a single operation. This creates three compounding defects: (1) Broken Object Level Authorization — any authenticated user can overwrite any other user's review by supplying its `_id`, because the query never checks `author` against the authenticated `user`; (2) NoSQL injection — the raw `req.body.id` in the filter object allows operator injection; (3) Resource consumption / insecure design — `multi: true` combined with an operator-injected filter can update the entire collection in one request, consuming database resources and corrupting all review data.

trace.description: The exported handler `updateProductReviews()` receives `req` from the PATCH /rest/products/reviews route. The route is protected by `security.isAuthorized()` (authentication only), which confirms the caller is logged in but does not authorize per-resource access. The handler begins processing the request body.

`const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req)` retrieves the authenticated user's identity. This variable is never referenced again in the handler — it is fetched but never used to scope or authorize the database operation.

`{ _id: req.body.id }` — the query filter is constructed by directly embedding `req.body.id` from the request body. No type validation, sanitization, or ownership clause (e.g., `author: user.email`) is applied. Any authenticated user can supply any review `_id` to modify another user's review (BOLA). Additionally, because MongoDB interprets object values as operators, `req.body.id` being `{"$ne": null}` would match all documents.

`{ multi: true }` — the update is executed with the `multi` flag, causing ALL documents matching the filter to be updated. Combined with the NoSQL-injectable filter from line 17, a single request with `{"id": {"$ne": null}, "message": "hacked"}` overwrites the `message` field of every review in the collection in one database operation. Combined with the missing ownership check, any authenticated user can silently modify any or all reviews belonging to other users.

title: Unvalidated user-controlled message stored to reviews enables stored XSS
description: The `message` field from the request body is written directly to the reviews collection via `$set: { message: req.body.message }` without any sanitization, encoding, or content validation. Reviews are user-generated content that is conventionally rendered in product pages. If the front-end renders review messages without context-appropriate output encoding (the render sink is outside this file), this creates a stored XSS vector. An attacker can inject `<script>` tags or event-handler attributes into any review's message field. Even with the access-control and injection flaws above set aside, the absence of any sanitization on a free-form text field that is persisted and later rendered is a stored XSS defect at the persistence point.

trace.description: The handler receives `req.body.message` from the PATCH /rest/products/reviews request body. No validation, length cap, or sanitization is applied to this field before it reaches the database.

`{ $set: { message: req.body.message } }` — the raw, unsanitized user-supplied message is persisted directly to the reviews collection. There is no allow-list, no HTML encoding, no content-type restriction. The render sink where this message is later displayed to users is outside this file, but the persistence of unsanitized free-form text is where stored XSS is introduced.

title: No security logging on review modification operation
description: The handler performs a data mutation (overwriting review messages, potentially across multiple documents via `multi: true`) but logs nothing — no audit entry for who modified which review, no logging of the modified count, no error-level logging when the database operation fails. On the error path (line 24), the raw error object is returned directly to the client as JSON rather than being logged server-side. This means an attacker exploiting the BOLA or NoSQL injection to mass-modify reviews leaves no trace in application logs, making incident detection and investigation impossible.

trace.description: The handler begins processing a review update request. This is a security-relevant data mutation that should be auditable.

`const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req)` — the authenticated user's identity is retrieved. This is the actor who should be recorded in an audit log entry for the mutation, but the variable is never passed to any logging facility.
`db.reviewsCollection.update(` — the database mutation is initiated. No logging occurs before, during, or after this call to record which user triggered it or what filter/update was applied.
`).then(` — the promise chain begins. Neither the success nor the error callback contains any logging statement.

`(result: { modified: number, original: Array<{ author: any }> }) => {` — the success callback receives the `modified` count and `original` array (containing author data). This is the point where an audit log entry should be emitted recording the user (from line 15), the filter, and the number of modified documents — but no such log call exists.
`res.json(result)` — the success path returns the result to the caller with HTTP 200. No log entry is written at any point on this path. The modification is invisible to security monitoring.

On the error path, `res.status(500).json(err)` returns the raw error to the client without logging it. On the success path (line 22), `res.json(result)` returns the result without any audit log of which user modified which review(s). No `console.log`, logger call, or audit event exists anywhere in the handler. The `user` identity retrieved at line 15 is discarded without being recorded, so there is no way to correlate a review modification to the user who performed it.

title: File processing occurs before authentication check, enabling unauthenticated resource consumption
description: The handler reads the uploaded file buffer into memory (line 18) and runs file-type detection on it (line 24) before checking whether the user is authenticated (line 35). Because the route is registered with auth: none (no auth middleware), an unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly upload files that consume memory and CPU for buffer loading and magic-byte detection, only to be rejected at line 36. The authentication check should be the first operation in the handler or enforced via middleware, so that unauthenticated requests are rejected before any file processing begins.

trace.description: Exported handler profileImageFileUpload() is registered as POST /profile/image/file with auth: none — no authentication or authorization middleware is applied to this route (caller is outside this file).
req.file is read; the file buffer is loaded into memory on line 18 before any authentication check.
fileType.fromBuffer(buffer) performs magic-byte detection on the entire buffer — a CPU operation — still before any authentication check.
const buffer = file?.buffer — the entire file contents are loaded into a memory buffer, still before any authentication check.
if (buffer === undefined) — the only guard at this stage is a null-check on the buffer, not an authentication check; a non-empty buffer from any caller continues.
if (uploadedFileType === undefined) — a type-detection guard, not an auth guard; any file whose type is detectable continues.

if (uploadedFileType === null || !utils.startsWith(uploadedFileType.mime, 'image')) — a MIME-type guard rejects non-image files, but an attacker can supply a valid image to pass this check, still without authentication.
const filePath = ... — the destination path is constructed; no size or quota check intervenes before the write.
await fs.writeFile(filePath, buffer) writes the full buffer to disk with no size check anywhere in the handler. No per-user or per-IP rate limiting prevents repeated large uploads.

Authentication check (security.authenticatedUsers.get) finally occurs here, after memory and CPU have already been consumed. An unauthenticated attacker can trigger all prior processing by simply uploading a file, then receive the error on line 37. Repeating this exhausts server resources without valid credentials.

title: No file size limit or rate limiting on profile image upload
description: The handler reads the entire uploaded file into a memory buffer (line 18) and writes it to disk (line 43) without checking the file size anywhere in the handler. No rate limiting is visible in the middleware chain (only uploadToMemory.single, ensureFileIsPassed, and metrics middleware). An attacker can upload arbitrarily large files or flood the endpoint with many requests, consuming memory and disk without bound. While multer may have a configured limit elsewhere, the handler itself enforces no size constraint, and the absence of rate limiting allows repeated abuse.

trace.description: Exported handler profileImageFileUpload() is registered as POST /profile/image/file. The route's middleware (caller is outside this file) includes uploadToMemory.single('file') but no rate-limiting middleware is listed.
const buffer = file?.buffer — the entire file contents are held in memory with no size validation.
await fs.writeFile(filePath, buffer) writes the full buffer to disk with no size check anywhere in the handler. No per-user or per-IP rate limiting prevents repeated large uploads.

title: Successful profile image uploads are not logged
description: The handler logs blocked unauthenticated access attempts (line 37) and file write errors (line 45), but there is no logging when a profile image upload succeeds. A successful profile image upload is a security-relevant event — it modifies user profile data and writes a file to the server's static assets directory. Without logging successful uploads, an incident responder cannot reconstruct which user uploaded which file, when, or from where. This is an OWASP A09 logging and monitoring gap.

trace.description: Handler profileImageFileUpload() processes file uploads that modify user profile data.
The file write (line 43) and database update (line 51) succeed, but the only logging in this try block is the warn on line 45 which only fires on error.
await fs.writeFile(filePath, buffer) — the file is written to disk successfully; no success log is emitted.
catch (err) — this catch block only logs on error (line 45); the successful path falls through with no logging.
try block begins for the database update; the catch on line 53 only forwards errors, does not log success.
const user = await UserModel.findByPk(loggedInUser.data.id) — the user record is retrieved for update.
if (user != null) — the user record exists; no logging of the impending profile image update.
await user.update({ profileImage: ... }) — the user's profileImage field is updated in the database; no log entry records which user, which file, or when.
The handler completes successfully — file written, user record updated, redirect sent — with no log entry recording the successful upload, the user ID, the file type, or the source IP.

title: Verbose error responses leak framework and internal path details to clients
description: The test file documents and asserts that the application returns HTTP 500 error responses containing internal implementation details. Specifically, error responses include the application name and the Express framework identifier within an HTML <h1> tag, as well as the raw unrecognized path string ('Unexpected path: /rest/unrecognized'). This indicates the server is configured to expose verbose, debug-style error output to clients rather than generic error messages. An attacker can use this leaked information to fingerprint the framework, identify the application name, and understand internal routing logic, which aids in further exploitation. The test confirms this is the application's normal (non-debug) behavior since the test does not toggle any debug mode.

trace.description: The test sends a GET request to /rest/unrecognized, an unrecognized path. The caller (test framework) exercises the application's error handling path.
The test asserts the response status is 500, confirming the server returns a server-error for an unrecognized path rather than a 404.

The test asserts that the response body contains '<h1>' + the application name + ' (Express', confirming the error response leaks the application name and the underlying web framework (Express) to the client.
The test initializes a request to the application using the supertest client against the configured app.
The request targets the GET /rest/unrecognized path, which triggers the application's internal error handling for unrecognized routes.

The test asserts that the response body contains 'Unexpected path: /rest/unrecognized', confirming the error response echoes the raw internal path-handling detail back to the client, revealing internal routing logic.

title: Path traversal via insufficient path separator validation in quarantine file serving
description: The serveQuarantineFiles handler accepts a user-controlled `file` path parameter and passes it directly to `path.resolve` and `res.sendFile`. The only validation is a check that the filename does not contain a forward slash (`/`). This control is insufficient: on Windows, backslashes (`\`) are valid path separators and are not blocked, allowing traversal sequences like `..\\..\\..\\some\\file` or absolute paths like `C:\\Windows\\System32\\drivers\\etc\\hosts` to pass the check and escape the quarantine directory entirely. Even on Linux, the design of blocking only one path separator character is a fundamentally flawed security control — it attempts to enumerate dangerous characters rather than validating the resolved path stays within the intended directory. The correct approach is to resolve the path first and then verify the resolved path starts with the intended base directory.

trace.description: The exported function serveQuarantineFiles returns an Express handler. The caller (route registration) is outside this file. The handler receives params.file from the request path parameter — this is the entrypoint for user-controlled input.
const file = params.file — the user-controlled path parameter is assigned directly to a local variable with no normalization, allow-listing, or encoding applied.

The only security check is `!file.includes('/')`, which rejects filenames containing a forward slash. This does not block backslashes (path separators on Windows), does not block absolute Windows paths (e.g., C:\...), and does not verify that the final resolved path remains within the ftp/quarantine/ directory. The validation strategy of blocking a single character is an insecure design — it does not constrain the resolved path.

res.sendFile(path.resolve('ftp/quarantine/', file)) — the user-controlled, insufficiently validated filename is resolved and served. On Windows, an attacker can supply `..\\..\\..\\etc\\passwd` or an absolute path to read arbitrary files outside the quarantine directory. path.resolve will honor backslash separators and absolute paths on Windows, escaping the intended directory.

title: Missing authentication and authorization for quarantine file access
description: The serveQuarantineFiles handler serves files from an `ftp/quarantine/` directory without any authentication or authorization check within this handler. Quarantine directories typically contain files that were isolated for security reasons (e.g., malicious uploads, flagged content). Any caller who can reach this route can download any file from the quarantine directory by supplying its name. There is no per-user ownership check, no role check, and no authentication verification in this code. If the route is registered without upstream authentication middleware, this is a broken access control vulnerability allowing unauthenticated access to quarantined files. Even if authentication middleware exists upstream, there is no authorization check verifying that the requesting user should be allowed to access quarantine files.

trace.description: The handler factory serveQuarantineFiles returns a middleware function that receives (req, res, next). The route registration that mounts this handler is outside this file. There is no authentication check, no session verification, no role check, and no authorization decision anywhere in this handler before files are served.

The only check performed is a path separator validation — it determines whether to serve the file or return 403. There is no check of the caller's identity, session, role, or authorization to access quarantined files.
const file = params.file — the requested filename is extracted from the request parameters to be used for the file lookup, without any identity or authorization context being established or checked.

res.sendFile serves the file to the caller. Any user who can reach this endpoint — authenticated or not, authorized or not — receives the file contents. An attacker who knows or guesses a filename in the quarantine directory can download it.

title: No security logging for denied or served quarantine file access attempts
description: When a file access is denied because the filename contains a forward slash (line 16-17), the handler returns a 403 and passes an error to next(), but does not explicitly log the security-relevant event. There is also no logging of successful file accesses from the quarantine directory. Security-relevant events — access to quarantined (potentially malicious) files, and blocked path traversal attempts — should be logged with correlation context to enable incident investigation. The absence of explicit security logging in this handler means that repeated traversal attempts or unauthorized quarantine file access would go undetected unless upstream error-handling middleware happens to log the error.

trace.description: The handler receives requests for quarantine files. Both successful and denied accesses are security-relevant events — quarantine files are sensitive by nature, and path traversal attempts indicate potential attacks.
When the forward-slash check fails, the code enters the else branch. No logging statement records who attempted the access, what filename was requested, or that a path traversal attempt was blocked.
const file = params.file — the requested filename is extracted, but no logging occurs to record which file a user is attempting to access.
The else branch is entered, indicating a denied access attempt due to an invalid filename. Still, no logging is triggered.
res.status(403) is set to deny the request. The denial is enacted but not recorded in any application log.

next(new Error('File names cannot contain forward slashes!')) — the error is passed to the next middleware. There is no explicit security log entry written here. Successful file serves (line 14) are also not logged. An attacker probing the quarantine endpoint with path traversal attempts or downloading quarantined files would leave no application-level audit trail.

title: Unrestricted Server-Side Request Forgery via user-controlled imageUrl in profile image upload
description: The handler accepts a user-supplied `imageUrl` from the request body and passes it directly to `fetch()` with no validation whatsoever — no scheme allow-list, no hostname/IP filtering, no blocklist for internal addresses. An attacker can supply URLs targeting internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/), localhost services, or any host on the internal network. The response body is read and written to disk, so response data is exfiltrated to a file the attacker can later access (the profile image is served publicly). The only URL-related check on line 20 does not restrict the destination; it merely sets a challenge-completion flag when the URL matches a specific pattern. This is a textbook SSRF: the server makes an outbound request to an attacker-controlled destination. The route is registered with `auth: none` middleware, and while the handler performs its own token check, the SSRF sink is reachable by any authenticated user with no additional authorization.

trace.description: The handler receives `req.body.imageUrl` from the POST /profile/image/url route. The caller (route registration) is outside this file; the route is registered with `auth: none` middleware.
The user-supplied value is assigned to `const url = req.body.imageUrl` with no sanitization or validation.

title: Stored XSS via unvalidated imageUrl persisted as profileImage on error fallback path
description: When the `fetch(url)` call fails (non-OK status, network error, etc.), the handler falls into a catch block and stores the raw, unvalidated user-supplied URL directly as the user's `profileImage` field in the database (line 36). Because the URL is never validated for scheme, an attacker can supply a `javascript:` URL (e.g., `javascript:alert(document.cookie)`) or a `data:` URL. When this value is later rendered as an image source or href in the frontend (the render sink is outside this file), it executes attacker-controlled script in the victim's browser context. The field accepts arbitrary scheme strings with no encoding or allow-listing. This is a stored/persisted XSS: the persistence point is line 36, and the rendering sink is in a different file.

title: Unbounded fetch and file write with no size limit or timeout on user-supplied URL
description: The handler calls `fetch(url)` on a user-controlled URL and pipes the entire response body to a file on disk (line 30) with no maximum response size limit, no timeout, and no rate limiting on the endpoint. An attacker can supply a URL pointing to an infinitely streaming endpoint or an extremely large file, causing the server to consume unbounded memory and disk as it pipes the response into a write stream. The route has `auth: none` middleware, so any authenticated user can repeatedly trigger this. Combined with the lack of rate limiting, this enables denial-of-service through disk exhaustion or memory pressure.

title: Security-relevant SSRF fetch is not logged and route lacks auth middleware
description: The route POST /profile/image/url is registered with `auth: none` middleware, meaning no authentication or authorization middleware is applied at the routing layer. While the handler performs its own token check (line 21), the absence of auth middleware is a misconfiguration — the handler's inline check is weaker than a proper auth middleware chain (no token expiry validation, no session refresh, no standardized error handling). Additionally, the handler performs a server-side fetch to a user-controlled URL (a security-critical operation) but does not log the URL being fetched. The only logging occurs on the error path (line 37) and logs the error message, not the URL itself. Successful SSRF requests to internal services leave no trace in the logs, preventing incident detection and response.

`const url = req.body.imageUrl` — the URL is assigned. No log statement records this value.
The regex check sets a challenge flag but does not log the URL being checked.
`const loggedInUser = security.authenticatedUsers.get(req.cookies.token)` — the inline auth check. No log of successful or failed authentication is emitted.

It logs `utils.getErrorMessage(error)` — the error text — but does not log the URL that was fetched, the user who requested it, or the target host. Successful fetches (the SSRF success path) produce no log entry at all.

`await fetch(url)` performs a server-side request to a user-controlled URL. There is no log statement recording which URL was fetched, which user initiated it, or when. The only logging is on the error path (line 37) and logs the error message, not the requested URL. Successful SSRF to internal services is completely unlogged, preventing detection and investigation.

title: Open redirect endpoint confirmed via /redirect?to= with external URLs in client-side bundle
description: The test asserts that the publicly served /main.js file contains URLs of the form /redirect?to=https://blockchain.info/..., /redirect?to=https://explorer.dash.org/..., and /redirect?to=https://etherscan.io/.... This confirms the application implements a redirect endpoint that accepts a user-controlled 'to' parameter and redirects to external domains. Such an endpoint is an open redirect — an attacker can craft /redirect?to=https://evil.test to phish users via a trusted origin. The redirect destination is not restricted to internal or allow-listed origins. While the actual redirect handler is outside this file, the test verifies the pattern is embedded in the application's client-side code, confirming the design uses unvalidated redirect destinations.

These strings are embedded in the client-side bundle, confirming the application constructs redirect URLs using a user-controlled 'to' query parameter that points to external domains.

The application does not restrict the 'to' parameter to same-origin or allow-listed destinations — it redirects to blockchain.info, dash.org, and etherscan.io, establishing the pattern that any URL can be supplied. An attacker can substitute any destination. The actual redirect handler is outside this file, but the test confirms the application's design embeds and uses this open-redirect pattern.

title: Internal password policy warning for support team exposed in publicly served main.js
description: The test asserts that the publicly served /main.js file contains a Romanian-language internal security note: 'The support team's password does not comply with the corporate policy for privileged accounts! Please change the password accordingly!' This is an internal administrative/security warning that has been included in the client-side JavaScript bundle served to all users. Exposing internal security posture information — specifically that a privileged account's password is non-compliant — in a public asset is a security misconfiguration. It reveals to attackers that the support team's privileged credentials are weak or non-compliant, directly guiding them toward a target. The information should never have been included in a client-side bundle.

title: Unrestricted username change enables account impersonation and potential privilege escalation
description: The route POST /profile is registered with auth: none, meaning no authentication or authorization middleware is applied before the handler runs. The handler performs its own ad-hoc authentication check at line 17 by looking up the token in security.authenticatedUsers. This is a misconfiguration: the endpoint that mutates user identity (username) and issues new session tokens relies on an in-handler check rather than the application's standard auth middleware. If the in-handler check has a bug — for example, if security.authenticatedUsers.get returns a falsy-but-not-null value, or if the map is shared across requests in a way that causes a race — the endpoint would be reachable by unauthenticated users. Even when the check works, the inconsistency with the rest of the application's auth pattern means this endpoint is a likely point of future regression.

title: Stored XSS via unsanitized username field persisted to user record
description: The username field from the request body is persisted directly to the user model at line 32 without any HTML encoding, sanitization, or character allow-list. Usernames are display-name fields that are conventionally trusted downstream and rendered in numerous locations (profile pages, comments, leaderboards, admin panels). If any rendering context outputs the username without escaping — which is the default behavior in many template contexts — an attacker who sets their username to a payload like '' achieves stored XSS. The render sink is outside this file, but the persistence of unsanitized free-form text into a display-name field is where the stored XSS defect is introduced.

title: No security logging for successful username/profile changes
description: The handler logs only blocked unauthenticated access attempts (line 20, via error forwarding). Successful profile updates — which change the user's username and issue a new session token — are not logged at all. Username changes are security-relevant events because they can be used for impersonation, evasion of audit trails, or social engineering. Without a log entry recording who changed their username, from what value to what value, and when, security teams cannot detect or investigate username-based impersonation attacks or reconstruct an attack timeline. The new token issuance at line 34-36 is also unlogged.

title: Server-side code injection via eval() on user-controlled username
description: The getUserProfile handler reads the authenticated user's username from the database (line 52) and checks whether it matches the pattern `#{(.*)}` (line 54). If it matches and the challenge is enabled, the handler extracts the content between `#{` and `}` and passes it to `eval()` (line 61). Because the username is user-controlled — set by the user during registration or profile update (the persistence point is outside this file) — an attacker can set their username to e.g. `#{require('child_process').execSync('whoami').toString()}` and then visit GET /profile to trigger arbitrary server-side code execution. The result of eval is then inserted unescaped into a Pug template (line 73) and rendered to the response (line 95), compounding the issue with potential SSTI/XSS. This is a critical code injection: the dangerous sink (eval) is reached by stored user input with no sanitization, allow-listing, or parameterization.

The authenticated user's username is read from the database via UserModel.findByPk. This value is user-controlled — the user set it during registration or profile update (persistence point outside this file).
The username is tested against the regex /#{(.*)}/. If it matches and the usernameXssChallenge is enabled, the captured group (the content between #{ and }) is extracted on line 56 as `code`.
The returned async handler function receives req, res, next. The request carries the user's authentication token in req.cookies.token.
loggedInUser = security.authenticatedUsers.get(req.cookies.token) — resolves the token to a logged-in user object. The user's data.id will be used to look up the database record.
if (!loggedInUser) check — if no user is resolved, the request is rejected. If a user is found, execution continues to the database lookup.

user = await UserModel.findByPk(loggedInUser.data.id) — fetches the full user record from the database. The username field on this record is user-controlled, having been set during registration or profile update (persistence point outside this file).

const code = username?.substring(2, username.length - 1) — extracts the content between #{ and } from the username. This captured substring is the attacker's payload, now stored in the variable `code` with no sanitization or allow-listing applied.
if (!code) throw new Error('Username is null') — guards against an empty extraction but does not validate or restrict the content of `code`. Any non-empty string passes this check.

The extracted code is passed to eval(): `username = eval(code)`. There is no sanitization, allow-listing, or sandboxing between the stored user input and the eval sink. An attacker who sets their username to #{<arbitrary JS>} achieves arbitrary code execution on the server when they load /profile. The eval result is then inserted into the Pug template on line 73 and rendered on line 95.

title: CSP header injection via user-controlled profileImage
description: On line 88, the Content-Security-Policy header is assembled by interpolating `user?.profileImage` directly into the CSP string: `img-src 'self' ${user?.profileImage}; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'`. The profileImage value is user-controlled (set through profile image upload endpoints outside this file) and is not validated, encoded, or quoted before insertion into the CSP header. An attacker who sets their profileImage to a value containing semicolons and additional CSP directives (e.g. `x; script-src 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval';`) can inject arbitrary CSP directives. Because browsers honor the first occurrence of a directive, the injected `script-src` would override the intended one, enabling inline script execution. This is both a header injection (injection) and a security misconfiguration that weakens the CSP enforcement on the profile page.

The user record is fetched from the database via UserModel.findByPk. The profileImage field on this record is user-controlled (set via profile image upload endpoints outside this file).

The user's profileImage is interpolated directly into the CSP string: `img-src 'self' ${user?.profileImage}; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-eval'`. No validation, encoding, or quoting is applied to the profileImage value before it is placed in the header.

loggedInUser = security.authenticatedUsers.get(req.cookies.token) — resolves the token to a logged-in user object whose data.id is used for the database lookup.

The constructed CSP string (containing the unvalidated profileImage) is set as the Content-Security-Policy response header via res.set(). An attacker who controls profileImage can inject semicolons and additional CSP directives, overriding the intended policy.

title: Content-Security-Policy allows 'unsafe-eval' in script-src
description: The CSP header set on line 88 includes `'unsafe-eval'` in the script-src directive. The unsafe-eval directive permits the use of eval() and similar functions in the browser context. While this is likely set to support the profile page's client-side functionality, it weakens the browser's ability to prevent script injection attacks. Any XSS or script injection vulnerability on this page would be exploitable because unsafe-eval allows dynamic code execution. This is a security misconfiguration — the CSP is present but configured with a dangerous permission that should be avoided unless strictly necessary.

This CSP is set as the Content-Security-Policy response header. The unsafe-eval directive weakens XSS protections by allowing eval() in the browser, making any script injection on the profile page exploitable.

title: Race condition in product review like workflow allows multiple likes per user
description: The like endpoint uses a non-atomic check-then-act pattern: it checks whether the user has already liked the review (line 31), then increments the like count (lines 35-38), then after an artificial 150ms delay (line 41) re-fetches the review and appends the user's email to likedBy (lines 43-52). The check at line 31 and the write at lines 35-52 are not protected by any locking, transaction, or atomic conditional update. An attacker can send multiple concurrent POST requests to /rest/products/reviews; all requests pass the 'already liked' check before any of them write. The 150ms artificial sleep dramatically widens the race window, making exploitation trivial even without precise timing. The result is that a single user can inflate a review's like count arbitrarily and insert duplicate entries into the likedBy array. The 'count' variable computed at line 47 is never used to prevent the duplicate — it is calculated and discarded.

trace.description: The handler receives req.body.id (the review to like) and resolves the authenticated user from the request. The caller (route registration) is outside this file; this file's exported function is the entrypoint.
The code checks if the user already liked this review via likedBy.includes(user.data.email). This is the access gate that should prevent duplicate likes, but it is a read-only check with no lock.
An artificial sleep(150) is inserted between the check and the write, widening the race window from negligible to trivially exploitable.
const user = security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) — the authenticated user is resolved from the request, providing the email used for the duplicate-like check.
if (!user) return res.status(401).json(...) — authentication gate. If the user is not authenticated, the request is rejected. Authenticated requests continue.
const review = await db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — the review record is fetched. This is the first read in the check-then-act sequence; no lock is acquired on the document.
if (!review) return res.status(404).json(...) — existence gate. If the review is not found, the request is rejected. Existing reviews continue to the duplicate check.

const likedBy = review.likedBy — the likedBy array is extracted from the fetched review for the duplicate check. This is a snapshot taken at a single point in time with no guarantee it remains current.

await db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $inc: { likesCount: 1 } }) — likesCount is incremented. This write is not conditioned on the likedBy check at line 31; it executes unconditionally for any request that passed the check. Multiple concurrent requests will each increment, inflating the count.

const updatedReview = await db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — the review is re-fetched after the sleep. This is another non-atomic read; the document may have been modified by concurrent requests between the original check and this re-fetch.

const updatedLikedBy = updatedReview.likedBy — the likedBy array is extracted from the re-fetched review. If concurrent requests have already pushed their emails, this array may already contain duplicates.
updatedLikedBy.push(user.data.email) — the user's email is appended to the array without re-checking whether it is already present. No duplicate prevention is applied at this step.

const count = updatedLikedBy.filter(email => email === user.data.email).length — the number of times the user's email appears is computed. This count is never used to gate or abort the write; it is calculated and discarded, confirming the design never enforces uniqueness.

The likedBy array (with the user's email pushed at line 45) is written back via update({ _id: id }, { $set: { likedBy: updatedLikedBy } }). Because the check at line 31 and this write are non-atomic and separated by a 150ms delay, concurrent requests can all pass the check and all write, inflating likesCount (incremented at line 37) and duplicating entries in likedBy.

title: NoSQL injection via unvalidated req.body.id in MongoDB queries
description: The review ID is taken directly from req.body.id (line 18) with no type validation, sanitization, or coercion to a string/ObjectId. This value is then used in MongoDB query operations: findOne({ _id: id }) at line 25, update({ _id: id }, ...) at lines 35-36, findOne({ _id: id }) at line 43, and update({ _id: id }, ...) at lines 49-50. In Express with JSON body parsing, a client can send id as an object rather than a scalar string. For example, sending {"id": {"$ne": null}} or {"id": {"$gt": ""}} causes the query to match documents based on MongoDB query operators rather than a literal ID equality check. This enables an attacker to match and manipulate reviews without knowing their actual IDs, potentially affecting unintended records. The update operations use the same tainted id value in their query filter, so the injected operator affects which documents are modified.

db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — the unvalidated id is used directly as the MongoDB query filter. If id is an object (e.g., {"$ne": null}), the query becomes an operator-based match rather than an equality check.

db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $inc: { likesCount: 1 } }) — the same tainted id is used in the update query filter, so the injected operator determines which document(s) the increment applies to.

{ _id: id }, — the tainted id is placed directly into the update query filter object. If id is an operator object, the update will target documents matched by the operator rather than a specific document by ID.

const updatedReview = await db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — the tainted id is re-used in another findOne query. The same injection vector applies: an operator object will match unintended documents.

db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $set: { likedBy: updatedLikedBy } }) — the tainted id is used again in the final update. No parameterization, type validation, or allow-listing intervenes between the source (req.body.id) and any of these MongoDB query sinks.

title: Raw error object leaked to client in 500 response
description: When the inner database operation (the final update at lines 49-52) throws an error, the catch block at line 54 catches it and responds with res.status(500).json(err) at line 55. This sends the raw error object directly to the client without filtering or sanitization. Depending on the MongoDB driver and error type, this can expose internal details such as database connection strings, collection names, query structures, stack traces, and server paths. This is a security misconfiguration: error responses should return a generic message to the client while logging the full error server-side.

trace.description: The async handler for POST /rest/products/reviews is exported. The caller (route registration) is outside this file.
try { — an inner try block begins, wrapping the re-fetch and final update operations. Any error thrown by these database operations will be caught by the corresponding catch block.

const result = await db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $set: { likedBy: updatedLikedBy } }) — this database update operation may throw an error (e.g., connection failure, validation error, write conflict). The error propagates to the catch block.
} catch (err) { — the raw error object is caught. No filtering, sanitization, or logging is applied before it is sent to the client.

title: Artificial 150ms sleep with no rate limiting enables connection pool exhaustion
description: The like endpoint inserts an artificial await sleep(150) at line 41, holding each request open for at least 150 milliseconds. The endpoint also performs two findOne queries and two update operations per request (lines 25, 35, 43, 49), each consuming a database connection. No rate limiting is visible in the file — the route is protected only by security.isAuthorized() authentication middleware, which does not throttle request frequency. An authenticated attacker can send a large number of concurrent requests, each of which holds server resources (HTTP connection, memory, database connections) for 150ms or more. This enables denial-of-service through connection pool exhaustion and memory consumption without requiring a large botnet or sophisticated tooling.

trace.description: return async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => { — the async handler for POST /rest/products/reviews. No rate limiting middleware is visible in this file; the route declaration shows only security.isAuthorized() authentication middleware.
const review = await db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — the first database query consumes a database connection. The request is held open while awaiting the result.
await db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $inc: { likesCount: 1 } }) — the first database update consumes another database operation. The request continues to hold server resources.

await sleep(150) — an artificial 150ms delay holds the request open, keeping the HTTP connection, memory, and any database connections in use. This is the most significant resource consumer per request, as it holds resources idle for a fixed duration with no productive work.

const updatedReview = await db.reviewsCollection.findOne({ _id: id }) — a second database query is performed while the request is still held open from the sleep. Another database connection is consumed.
const result = await db.reviewsCollection.update({ _id: id }, { $set: { likedBy: updatedLikedBy } }) — a second database update is performed. The request continues to hold resources.

res.json(result) — the request finally completes and releases resources. Each request holds server resources for at least 150ms (plus database query time) with no rate limiting. An attacker sending concurrent requests can exhaust connection pools and memory, degrading or denying service to legitimate users.

title: NoSQL/JavaScript Injection via $where with string interpolation of user input
description: The `trackOrder` handler interpolates the user-supplied `id` path parameter directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression on line 17. The `$where` operator executes arbitrary JavaScript on the database server for every document in the collection. When the `reflectedXssChallenge` is enabled (line 15), the input is only truncated to 60 characters — no characters are stripped — so an attacker can inject JavaScript operators and quotes. For example, an `id` value like `1' || '1'==='1` would produce the `$where` expression `this.orderId === '1' || '1'==='1'`, matching all documents. More complex payloads can exfiltrate data or cause excessive CPU consumption on the database server since `$where` executes JavaScript for every document. Even on the sanitized path (when the challenge is disabled), the regex strip only removes non-word characters — the use of `$where` with string interpolation is a fundamentally unsafe pattern that should use parameterized query criteria instead.

trace.description: The handler receives user input from req.params.id (the :id path parameter). The route GET /rest/track-order/:id has no authentication middleware (auth: none). When reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, the input is only truncated to 60 characters via utils.trunc — no character sanitization is applied. When disabled, non-word characters are stripped via regex.

The (partially or minimally) processed id value is assigned to a local variable. On the challenge-enabled branch, it retains any characters including quotes, pipes, and comparison operators up to 60 characters in length.
The route handler function is defined and receives the `req` object, which contains user-controlled path parameters.

The id variable is interpolated directly into a MongoDB $where JavaScript string: `this.orderId === '${id}'`. The $where operator executes this JavaScript on the MongoDB server for every document in the orders collection. An attacker can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary JavaScript predicates, enabling data extraction (e.g., matching all documents, timing-based blind exfiltration) and denial-of-service through expensive per-document JavaScript evaluation across the entire collection.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization — order lookup by orderId without authentication or ownership check
description: The `GET /rest/track-order/:id` endpoint has no authentication middleware applied (auth: none). The handler on line 17 queries the orders collection solely by `orderId` — a value supplied by the caller — with no verification that the requester is authenticated, let alone that they own the order being retrieved. Any anonymous user can retrieve any order's details by supplying or guessing its orderId. Order IDs are often sequential or predictable (e.g., integer-based), making enumeration feasible. This is a classic BOLA: the resource is identified by a client-supplied parameter and no per-resource authorization is performed.

trace.description: The handler is registered as GET /rest/track-order/:id with auth: none — no authentication or authorization middleware is applied. The caller is outside this file (the route registration). Any anonymous user can reach this handler.

The handler performs db.ordersCollection.find() using only the orderId derived from the request path parameter. There is no user identity context, no session check, and no ownership filter (e.g., no WHERE user_id = current_user).
The `req.params.id` value is extracted from the request path and assigned to the local `id` variable.
The query result is processed by `utils.queryResultToJson(order)` and assigned to the `result` object, preparing the order data for the response.

The query result — including full order data — is returned to the caller via res.json(result). An anonymous attacker who supplies or guesses any orderId receives that order's complete details without any authorization check having occurred.

title: Reflected XSS — unsanitized user input echoed into JSON response when challenge is enabled
description: When the `reflectedXssChallenge` is enabled (line 15), the `id` path parameter is only truncated to 60 characters but not sanitized for HTML/script content. On line 20, when no matching order is found, the handler sets `result.data[0] = { orderId: id }`, reflecting the raw user input back into the response body. The response is sent as JSON (line 22). If any client-side code renders this `orderId` value in an HTML context without escaping (the render sink is outside this file), the reflected content executes as script in the victim's browser. The challenge name itself (`reflectedXssChallenge`) confirms this is the intended attack surface. The unsanitized value is stored into the response object at the persistence point (line 20); the rendering sink is in a different file.

trace.description: User input from req.params.id is received. When reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, the input is truncated to 60 characters but no HTML/script sanitization is applied — quotes, angle brackets, and script content pass through.
When no order matches the query (result.data[0] === undefined), the handler assigns result.data[0] = { orderId: id }, placing the unsanitized user input directly into the response payload object.
The handler receives `req` and `res` from the incoming HTTP request.
The unsanitized `id` is interpolated into the MongoDB `$where` query to lookup the order.
The result of the database query is passed to `utils.queryResultToJson(order)` and converted into the `result` object.
A conditional checks if `result.data[0] === undefined` (i.e., if no matching order was found for the given id).

The response object containing the unsanitized id is serialized and sent to the client via res.json(result). The render sink where this value may be inserted into HTML is outside this file, but the defect — accepting and echoing unsanitized free-form input — is introduced here at line 20.

title: Unauthenticated access to application configuration endpoint
description: The test at lines 31-40 issues a GET request to /rest/admin/application-configuration without setting any authentication headers or credentials. The test asserts a 200 response and that the response body contains a non-null configuration object. This demonstrates that the application-configuration endpoint—despite being under the /rest/admin/ path prefix—does not enforce authentication. Exposing the full application configuration to unauthenticated callers is a security misconfiguration: it can reveal internal settings, secrets, endpoints, and feature flags that an attacker can use to find further vulnerabilities. The insecure-design aspect is that an admin-prefixed endpoint serving sensitive configuration data has no access-control design enforced.

The .get('/rest/admin/application-configuration') call sends the unauthenticated request to the admin-prefixed endpoint. The request reaches the route handler (outside this file) which must decide whether to serve the configuration.

The test asserts that res.body.config is a non-null object, confirming that the full application configuration is returned to the unauthenticated caller. This is the exposure: internal application configuration is served without authentication.

title: Unauthenticated access to application version endpoint exposes software version
description: The test at lines 20-28 issues a GET request to /rest/admin/application-version without any authentication headers. The test expects a 200 response returning the application version from package.json. Exposing the exact software version to unauthenticated users under an /rest/admin/ path (which implies admin-only access) is a misconfiguration that aids attackers in identifying known vulnerabilities for that version.

description: The tests for both /rest/admin/application-version and /rest/admin/application-configuration issue unauthenticated requests to admin-prefixed endpoints that succeed with 200 responses. Access to admin endpoints by unauthenticated users is a security-relevant event that should be logged and alerted on. The tests verify the response status and body but make no assertions about any logging or alerting side effects, and the test setup (createTestApp) does not configure any security logging interceptor. While the actual logging behavior is in the route handlers outside this file, the tests demonstrate a code path where unauthenticated admin access occurs with no evidence of security logging in the test's observable behavior.

The test treats the unauthenticated admin access as normal expected behavior, indicating no security logging is expected for this event.

title: Stored XSS via unencoded subtitle content injected into HTML
description: In the promotionVideo handler, subtitle file content is read from disk and then concatenated directly into the compiled HTML template inside a <script> tag without any HTML encoding. The variable `subs` (line 70) is inserted raw: `'<script id="subtitle" ...>' + subs + '</script>'`. If the subtitle file's content is ever attacker-controlled — through a file upload vulnerability elsewhere, a config override, or modification of the .vtt file on disk — arbitrary script will be rendered in the browser of any user viewing the promotion page. The data is inserted into an HTML context with no escaping, no sanitization, and no allow-listing. The render sink (browser rendering of the response) is outside this file, but the defect — persisting and interpolating untrusted text without encoding — is introduced here.

getSubsFromFile() reads the subtitle file content from disk. The file path is constructed from config value 'application.promotion.subtitles' (line 80) concatenated directly into a filesystem path (line 81). The returned string is raw file content with no encoding or sanitization.

const fn = pug.compile(template) — the pug template is compiled. The subtitle content is not yet involved; this prepares the template into which subs will be injected.

The `subs` string is concatenated directly into the HTML response inside a <script> tag: `'<script id="subtitle" type="text/vtt" ...>' + subs + '</script>'`. No HTML encoding is applied. Any script or HTML in the subtitle content will be rendered by the browser. The render sink is in the browser (outside this file), but the unencoded interpolation is the injection point.

title: Path traversal in subtitle file path due to missing filename sanitization
description: In getSubsFromFile() (line 81), the config value 'application.promotion.subtitles' is concatenated directly into a filesystem path without any sanitization: `'frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/videos/' + subtitles`. This is inconsistent with the sibling function videoPath() (line 87) which correctly passes the config value through `utils.extractFilename()` to strip path traversal sequences. If the subtitles config value contains path traversal sequences (e.g., `../../../../etc/passwd`), the application will read and return the contents of an arbitrary file on disk. The file content is then served to the client in the promotion page response (line 70-71), causing arbitrary file disclosure.

The subtitles filename is read from config: `config.get<string>('application.promotion.subtitles') ?? 'owasp_promo.vtt'`. No validation is applied to this value.

The unsanitized config value is concatenated directly into a file path: `'frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/videos/' + subtitles`. Compare with videoPath() at line 87 which uses `utils.extractFilename()` to sanitize the analogous video config value — that control is absent here.
