fs.readFileSync() is called with the traversable path. If the config value contains `../` sequences, an arbitrary file on disk is read. The content is then sent to the client via the response on line 71, resulting in arbitrary file disclosure.

title: Unvalidated HTTP Range header values in video streaming endpoint
description: The getVideo() handler (GET /video, auth: none) parses the HTTP Range header from user input and passes the parsed integer values directly to fs.createReadStream() without validating that start >= 0, end < fileSize, or start <= end. A malicious client can send a Range header with extreme values (e.g., `bytes=0-999999999999`) or malformed values that produce NaN, potentially causing unexpected stream behavior, excessive memory allocation for the chunk size calculation, or errors that crash the request handler. There is no rate limiting on this endpoint, allowing repeated exploitation.

trace.description: getVideo() is an exported handler reachable via GET /video with auth: none. It processes the Range header from the request.

The user-controlled Range header (req.headers.range) is parsed: `range.replace(/bytes=/, '').split('-')`. The resulting parts are passed to parseInt() with no bounds checking — start and end can be negative, NaN, or exceed fileSize.
The handler function receives (req, res) from the Express framework. The request object carries the user-supplied Range header.
const path = videoPath() — the video file path is resolved (hardcoded/config-derived, not user-controlled).
const stat = fs.statSync(path) — file statistics are retrieved to determine fileSize.
const fileSize = stat.size — the legitimate file size is established. This value is used in the default end calculation but never used to validate the user-supplied range bounds.
const range = req.headers.range — the user-controlled Range header is captured from the request. This is the tainted input source.
if (range) { — a conditional that lets processing continue for any truthy Range header value, with no format validation before proceeding.
const start = parseInt(parts[0], 10) — the start value is parsed. parseInt can return NaN for non-numeric input or accept negative values. No bounds check ensures start >= 0.
const end = parts[1] ? parseInt(parts[1], 10) : fileSize - 1 — the end value is parsed or defaulted. No bounds check ensures end < fileSize or that end >= start.

const chunksize = (end - start) + 1 — the chunk size is computed from unvalidated values. Extreme or negative values can produce an enormous or nonsensical chunksize, which is later used in the Content-Length header.

The unvalidated start and end values are passed directly to fs.createReadStream(path, { start, end }). No validation ensures 0 <= start <= end < fileSize. A crafted Range header can cause unexpected file read behavior or resource exhaustion.

title: registerAdminChallenge middleware is a no-op, allowing unauthenticated admin account registration
description: The `registerAdminChallenge` middleware is registered on `POST /api/Users` (auth: none) but the function body (lines 26-28) only calls `next()` without performing any validation. The function name strongly implies it should prevent users from registering with an admin role, but it enforces nothing. Because the route has no authentication and this middleware is the only gate, any unauthenticated caller can submit a registration request with an admin-level role flag and the middleware will pass it through unchallenged. This is both a broken function-level authorization gap (no role check) and an authentication failure (the identity/role of a new account is caller-controlled rather than server-decided). Additionally, no security event is logged when a registration reaches this middleware, so admin-registration abuse would be invisible in logs.

trace.description: The exported function `registerAdminChallenge` receives a Request from an outside caller. Per the route registration, this middleware is attached to `POST /api/Users` with auth: none, meaning the request arrives unauthenticated. The caller is outside this file.

The function body immediately calls `next()`. There is no inspection of `req.body`, no check for an `isAdmin` / `role` field, no validation that the registration payload does not contain privilege-escalation fields.

`next()` passes control to the subsequent handler with zero authorization or validation performed. An attacker POSTs to `/api/Users` with a body containing `{"role":"admin", ...}` and the request proceeds unchallenged. No log entry is written for this security-relevant event.

title: captchaBypassChallenge records timing but never validates captcha, enabling unlimited unauthenticated feedback submission
description: The `captchaBypassChallenge` middleware is registered on `POST /api/Feedbacks` (auth: none). Instead of verifying that the caller has solved a captcha, the function (lines 20-24) merely records a timestamp into an array and increments a counter, then calls `next()`. No captcha token is extracted, no verification is performed, and no rate-limit threshold is enforced even though the timing data is collected. An attacker can submit unlimited feedback entries without solving any captcha, enabling spam flooding and resource consumption. The collected timing data is never checked against any threshold to block rapid repeated submissions. No security event is logged when a captcha bypass is attempted.

trace.description: The exported function `captchaBypassChallenge` receives a Request from an outside caller. Per the route registration, this middleware is attached to `POST /api/Feedbacks` with auth: none. The caller is outside this file.

The function writes the current timestamp into `req.app.locals.captchaBypassReqTimes` at the current captcha request ID index. This is telemetry collection, not captcha validation — no captcha response is extracted from the request, no verification service is called.

`req.app.locals.captchaReqId` is incremented. This counter is used solely to index the next timestamp slot — it grows without bound and is never checked against any limit or used to trigger a throttle. No threshold comparison occurs at any point.

`next()` is called on line 23 without any captcha verification or rate-limit check. The timing array grows unboundedly (one entry per request with no cap), and the request proceeds to create feedback. An attacker can flood `POST /api/Feedbacks` with unlimited requests — no captcha solved, no throttle applied, no log written. Line 24 closes the function.

`next()` is called without any captcha verification or rate-limit check. The timing array grows unboundedly (one entry per request with no cap), and the request proceeds to create feedback. An attacker can flood `POST /api/Feedbacks` with unlimited requests — no captcha solved, no throttle applied, no log written.

title: accessControlChallenges computes a UI-bypass check but discards the result, enforcing no access control
description: The `accessControlChallenges` middleware (lines 34-38) computes `uiBypassed` by inspecting the `sec-fetch-dest` header and the absence of a `referer` header. This value is intended to detect when a request bypasses the intended UI navigation (e.g., direct API access). However, the computed value is never used — it is not passed to the response, not stored on the request object, and not used to block the request. The function unconditionally calls `next()`. The access control check exists in computation but is never enforced, making any route using this middleware effectively unprotected against direct access by non-browser clients or attackers who manipulate headers.

The function computes `uiBypassed` from `req.header('sec-fetch-dest')` and `req.header('referer')`. The variable is local and is never read again.
The function destructures `url` from `req`. This value is captured but never used — it is dead code that suggests an intended URL-based access check that was never implemented.

`next()` is called unconditionally. The `uiBypassed` result is discarded — no branch denies the request, no flag is set on `req` for downstream handlers, no warning is logged. Any client can set `sec-fetch-dest: document` or omit `referer` to pass, and even clients that don't are not blocked. The access control gate is decorative.

title: passwordRepeatChallenge and emptyUserRegistration are no-op middleware on unauthenticated user registration
description: Both `emptyUserRegistration` (lines 12-14) and `passwordRepeatChallenge` (lines 30-32) are registered as middleware on `POST /api/Users` (auth: none). Despite their names implying they should validate that required fields are non-empty and that password and password-repeat match, both functions only call `next()` with no validation logic. This allows registration with empty fields, mismatched passwords, or missing required data — the server-side enforcement that should exist at the point of identity creation is absent. An attacker can create accounts with arbitrary or malformed credential data, bypassing intended registration integrity checks.

`passwordRepeatChallenge` also immediately calls `next()`. There is no comparison of `req.body.password` against `req.body.passwordRepeat`. Both identity-integrity checks are absent, allowing malformed or inconsistent credential submissions to proceed to account creation.

title: forgedFeedbackChallenge is a no-op allowing feedback to be submitted under another user's identity
description: The `forgedFeedbackChallenge` middleware (lines 16-18) is registered on `POST /api/Feedbacks` (auth: none). The function name implies it should detect or prevent feedback forgery — submitting feedback attributed to a different user. However, the function body only calls `next()` with no inspection of the request body, no user-identity verification, and no cross-referencing of the submitted `UserId` against the authenticated session (which does not exist, since auth is none). An attacker can submit feedback with any `UserId` value in the request body, impersonating other users, because no server-side identity check exists.

title: Hardcoded Ethereum private key in test source code
description: The test file contains a hardcoded Ethereum private key ('0x5bcc3e9d38baa06e7bfaab80ae5957bbe8ef059e640311d7d6d465e6bc948e3e') on line 68, sent as the request body to the /rest/web3/submitKey endpoint. Hardcoded secrets in source code are a security misconfiguration: the private key is committed to version control and is visible to anyone with repository access. If this key corresponds to a real wallet (even a challenge wallet), its exposure in source could allow an attacker to derive or reuse it. The playbook states that hardcoded secrets in source code are always findings regardless of production usage.

The request method and target path are set: `.post('/rest/web3/submitKey')`. The POST target is the endpoint that receives the private key.

The request body is sent with privateKey set to the hardcoded value '0x5bcc3e9d38baa06e7bfaab80ae5957bbe8ef059e640311d7d6d465e6bc948e3e'. The test asserts (line 72) that this key is accepted by the server, confirming it is a real, valid secret rather than a placeholder.

title: API endpoint accepts private key via unauthenticated POST request without compensating controls visible in test
description: The test file reveals the design of the /rest/web3/submitKey endpoint: it accepts a private key directly in the request body (line 68) and returns a success response (lines 72-73) without any visible authentication, session, or challenge-verification step in the test flow. The test sends the request with no authentication headers or cookies. While this is a CTF challenge application (OWASP Juice Shop), the design pattern — accepting cryptographic private keys via an unauthenticated API endpoint — is an insecure design where the server trusts the client to supply a secret credential without any compensating control such as requiring prior authentication, rate limiting, or multi-step verification. An attacker who obtains or guesses the private key can submit it directly to unlock the challenge with no intermediate steps.

trace.description: Test case begins for POST /rest/web3/submitKey with a private key. The test constructs the request using supertest against the app.
The POST request is made to /rest/web3/submitKey. No authentication headers, cookies, or session tokens are set on the request, indicating the endpoint is reachable without prior authentication.
The test initializes the supertest request: `const res = await request(app)`. No authentication headers, cookies, or session tokens are attached at this point.

The request body is sent containing the privateKey field with a valid Ethereum private key. The caller is outside this file (the route handler in the server), but the test demonstrates the endpoint's design: an unauthenticated POST with a private key is accepted.
The test asserts `res.status === 200`, confirming the server accepted the unauthenticated request carrying the private key and returned a success HTTP status.

The caller is outside this file (the route handler in the server), but the test demonstrates the endpoint's design: an unauthenticated POST with a private key unlocks a challenge with no compensating controls visible.

title: Authentication tokens forged without credential verification via security.authorize()
description: On line 16, `security.authorize({ data: { email: 'admin@juice-sh.op' } })` is called to produce a Bearer token for the admin user. No password or credential is passed — only an email address. The resulting token is then used as a valid Authorization header on lines 27 and 42 to access authenticated endpoints. This demonstrates that the token-signing function (`authorize` from the `insecurity` library) accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied identity claim and issues a valid session token without any credential verification. An attacker who can reach this function (or the endpoint that wraps it) can forge a token for any user, including administrators, by simply supplying the target email. This is a complete authentication bypass.

trace.description: The module-level constant `authHeader` is constructed by calling `security.authorize({ data: { email: 'admin@juice-sh.op' } })`. This call — originating from the imported `insecurity` library (line 10) — generates a Bearer token for the admin identity using only an email payload, with no password or credential check.

The forged admin token is attached as the Authorization header on a GET request to `/rest/user/authentication-details`, and the server accepts it as a valid authenticated session (line 29 asserts a 200 response).

The `insecurity` library is imported as `security`, bringing the `authorize` function into scope. This is the library that provides the token-signing and token-verification machinery used by the application.
A `request(app)` call begins constructing the first HTTP request that will carry the forged token. The `authHeader` constant has not been transformed or validated between line 16 and here.
The request target is set to `GET /rest/user/authentication-details` — an authenticated endpoint that will process the Authorization header.

`assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms the server accepted the forged token and treated the request as an authenticated admin session. The authentication decision was made on the server side using the unverified email claim embedded in the token.

The server returns data for all users (line 30 iterates `res.body.data` searching across the full user set), confirming the forged admin token grants privileged access. The authentication decision was made solely on the unverified email claim embedded in the token.

title: Authentication-details endpoint returns all users' data without per-user ownership scoping
description: The GET `/rest/user/authentication-details` endpoint returns a collection containing every user's authentication details (emails, password representations, lastLoginTime) rather than only the requesting user's own record. Lines 30-31 iterate over `res.body.data` expecting to find at least one user across the full dataset, and lines 46-48 search the same dataset for a specific user (jim). The endpoint is under `/rest/user/` (a user-scoped path), yet it returns the entire user table. If any authenticated user — not just the admin token used in these tests — can reach this endpoint and receive the full dataset, it constitutes a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) issue: User A can enumerate and read User B's email and login metadata.

trace.description: A GET request is made to `/rest/user/authentication-details`. The caller is outside this file (the route handler is in `target-apps/juice-shop-blind/server.ts`), but the test receives the response here and verifies its structure.

The response body contains `res.body.data` as an array of user objects. The test searches this array with `.find()` across all users for one whose password field is 32 asterisks, confirming the endpoint returns the full user collection, not a single record scoped to the authenticated user.

The request path is set to `/rest/user/authentication-details`. The path contains no user-specific identifier (no `:id`), yet the endpoint name suggests per-user authentication details. This is the first signal that the endpoint may return data beyond the requesting user's own record.
The admin `authHeader` (from line 16) is attached. The request is authenticated, but the path still carries no per-user scoping parameter.
`assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms the server processed the request successfully. The response is now in `res` awaiting inspection.

A second test confirms that a different user (jim, logged in on line 35) appears in the same collection response, with their email and lastLoginTime exposed. There is no evidence in the test that the endpoint filters by the requesting user's identity; the response is the full user set. Any authenticated user who reaches this endpoint receives every other user's authentication metadata.

title: Successful retrieval of all users' authentication details has no observable security logging
description: The tests on lines 24-32 and 34-49 exercise a sensitive endpoint that returns all users' authentication details (emails, password representations, login timestamps). Neither test asserts or references any audit log entry being created for this access. While this is a test file and cannot prove the absence of server-side logging with certainty, the complete absence of any logging interaction in tests covering a data-export-grade operation (mass user credential metadata retrieval) suggests no security event is emitted. Without logging on this endpoint, an attacker extracting the full user credential dataset cannot be detected or investigated.

trace.description: GET `/rest/user/authentication-details` is called, returning the authentication details of all users. The route handler is outside this file; the test observes the response.
The response is confirmed to contain all users' data (password fields, emails). This is a security-relevant event — mass exposure of credential metadata — that should generate an audit log entry.
The request target `/rest/user/authentication-details` is set. The path identifies a sensitive data-export endpoint returning credential metadata across all users.

`assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms the request succeeded. A successful mass retrieval of authentication details is the exact event that should be logged — at this point the data has been served.

The test completes its assertions on the response data without referencing, checking, or interacting with any logging or audit mechanism. No log assertion appears anywhere in this test file for either test case, indicating the endpoint's data export operation is not instrumented with security logging.

title: Unauthenticated endpoint accepts arbitrary wallet addresses into shared security state without ownership verification
description: The POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress endpoint (registered with auth: none) allows any caller to add any wallet address to the global `walletsConnected` Set. There is no authentication and no cryptographic proof (e.g., message signature) that the caller actually controls the wallet address they submit. The `walletsConnected` Set is subsequently used in a security-relevant decision: when a 'ContractExploited' blockchain event fires for an address in the Set, that address is removed (lines 27-29), which appears to track which connected wallets have successfully exploited the contract. An attacker can submit another user's wallet address, or any arbitrary address, to pollute this tracking state or claim credit for an exploit they did not perform. The design trusts the client to report its own wallet address without any server-side verification of ownership.

trace.description: contractExploitListener() is exported as the handler for POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress. Per the route registration, no authentication or authorization middleware is applied (auth: none). The caller is outside this file (the route registration in server.ts).

The handler reads `req.body.walletAddress` directly — an attacker-controlled string from the request body. No authentication context is checked, and no cryptographic proof of wallet ownership (e.g., a signed message) is required or verified.
The handler returns an async function receiving `req: Request` and `res: Response`. The request object carries the external input into the handler scope.

The attacker-supplied walletAddress is added to the global `walletsConnected` Set. This Set is later consulted in the ContractExploited event handler (line 27) to make a security-relevant decision (removing the address). Because no authentication gates the endpoint and no proof of wallet ownership is required, any user can inject any address into this shared state, subverting the tracking mechanism.

title: Unbounded growth of global walletsConnected Set with no rate limiting
description: The `walletsConnected` Set (line 10) is a module-level global that grows without any cap. The POST endpoint adds an entry on every request (line 16) with no rate limiting, no pagination, and no maximum size check. An attacker can send thousands of requests with unique wallet addresses to grow the Set indefinitely, consuming server memory. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated, this is trivially exploitable.

trace.description: contractExploitListener() handles POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress with no auth middleware and no rate limiting. The caller registration is outside this file.
`walletsConnected` is declared as a module-level `new Set()` with no maximum size constraint and no eviction mechanism.
The async route handler receives the incoming request.
The request body value `walletAddress` is assigned to `metamaskAddress`.

Every request adds `req.body.walletAddress` to the Set via `walletsConnected.add(metamaskAddress)` with no rate limiting and no size cap. An attacker can flood unique addresses to exhaust memory, as the Set is never pruned except when a ContractExploited event matches a specific address (line 28), which is attacker-uncontrolled and infrequent.

title: WebSocket provider falls back to empty API key when environment variable is unset
description: On line 20, the WebSocketProvider URL is constructed with `process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY ?? ''`. If the ALCHEMY_API_KEY environment variable is not set, the provider connects to Alchemy with an empty API key segment in the URL. This is a dangerous default — the connection will either fail silently or use an unauthenticated/default-tier connection, and the empty key in the URL could cause unexpected behavior. The fallback should fail loudly rather than silently proceeding with a malformed credential.

contractExploitListener() is exported as the route handler for POST /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress. The caller triggers this path from outside this file.
The async route handler receives the request, initiating execution of the listener setup logic.
The execution enters a try block, which protects the subsequent dynamic provider and contract initialization.
The `ethers` library is dynamically imported, yielding the `WebSocketProvider` and `Contract` classes required for the next step.

`new WebSocketProvider(`wss://eth-sepolia.g.alchemy.com/v2/${process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY ?? ''}`)` — the nullish coalescing operator defaults to an empty string when ALCHEMY_API_KEY is unset, producing a malformed WebSocket URL with an empty key segment. No validation or hard failure occurs when the key is missing; the code proceeds to create the provider and contract listener with a potentially invalid credential.

title: Path traversal via `key` parameter in checkCorrectFix allows arbitrary file read
description: The `checkCorrectFix` handler accepts a `key` value from the POST request body (line 71) with no validation or sanitization. This value is directly concatenated into a filesystem path at line 80 (`'./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml'`) and then read and parsed at line 81. An attacker can supply a `key` containing path traversal sequences (e.g., `../../`) to read and parse any `.info.yml` file on the filesystem. The `.info.yml` suffix limits the target to files ending in that string, but combined with any file-upload capability elsewhere in the application (the architecture summary shows file-upload routes exist), an attacker could plant a malicious `.info.yml` file and have it parsed, or read sensitive YAML configuration files that happen to end in that suffix. Even without the suffix constraint being bypassed, the ability to traverse the filesystem and read arbitrary `.info.yml` files is a file-handling integrity failure.

trace.description: The exported `checkCorrectFix` handler is registered as POST /snippets/fixes with no authentication middleware. It receives `key` from `req.body.key` at line 71.

The user-supplied `key` is extracted from the request body with no validation, sanitization, or allow-listing. It is then passed to `readFixes(key)` at line 73 and later used directly in filesystem path construction at line 80.

`if (fixData.fixes.length === 0)` — this conditional checks whether fixes were found for the key. If fixes exist (even one), execution continues to the `else` branch at line 78, which proceeds to use `key` in filesystem path construction. The key passes through this check unsanitized.

`fs.readFileSync('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml', 'utf8')` — the same attacker-influenced path is passed to `readFileSync`, actually reading the file content from the traversed path. The content is then passed to `yaml.load()` on the same line, completing the arbitrary file read.

At line 80, `key` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path: `fs.existsSync('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml')`. At line 81, the same path is passed to `fs.readFileSync()` and the result to `yaml.load()`. No path normalization, traversal filtering, or allow-listing is applied to `key`. An attacker submitting `key = '../../../../some/path'` causes the application to read files outside the intended directory.

title: Unsafe YAML deserialization via yaml.load() on user-influenced file path
description: At line 81, `yaml.load()` is used to parse YAML content from a file whose path is constructed from user-controlled input (the `key` parameter). In js-yaml versions prior to 4.0, `yaml.load()` uses the DEFAULT_FULL_SCHEMA which can instantiate arbitrary JavaScript objects during parsing, enabling remote code execution if an attacker can control the YAML content. Even if the application uses js-yaml >= 4.0 (where `yaml.load` is safe by default), the use of the historically-unsafe API without an explicit safe schema is a defect. If an attacker can traverse the filesystem (see path traversal finding) to a YAML file they control — for example, a file uploaded through the application's file-upload endpoints — they could achieve code execution through unsafe YAML deserialization.

trace.description: The `checkCorrectFix` handler receives `key` from `req.body` (line 71). The caller (route registration) is outside this file; this is where the file receives outside data.

`yaml.load(fs.readFileSync('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml', 'utf8'))` — YAML content from a user-influenced file path is deserialized using `yaml.load()` without an explicit safe schema. In js-yaml < 4.0, this API can instantiate arbitrary objects, leading to code execution if the attacker controls the YAML content. The path to the file is attacker-influenced via the `key` parameter, expanding the set of files that can be parsed.

title: Unbounded in-memory cache allows memory exhaustion via unique keys
description: The `readFixes` function (lines 20-45) caches every result in the module-level `CodeFixes` object (line 18), which is a plain `Record<string, codeFix>` with no eviction, no size limit, and no TTL. Every call with a unique `key` — including keys that match no files — creates a new entry (lines 40-43). Both `serveCodeFixes` (GET /snippets/fixes/:key, no auth) and `checkCorrectFix` (POST /snippets/fixes, no auth) call `readFixes` with attacker-controlled keys. An attacker can send a large number of requests with unique random keys to grow the cache unboundedly, exhausting server memory. Each unique key also triggers a `fs.readdirSync` (line 26) and potentially multiple `fs.readFileSync` calls (line 29) before caching, adding filesystem I/O cost.

trace.description: Both exported handlers — `serveCodeFixes` (line 56, GET /snippets/fixes/:key) and `checkCorrectFix` (line 70, POST /snippets/fixes) — are registered with no authentication middleware and accept attacker-controlled `key` values.

Both handlers call `readFixes(key)` (lines 58 and 73) with the attacker-controlled key. Inside `readFixes`, if the key is not already cached, the function performs directory reads and file reads (lines 26-38), then unconditionally stores the result in the module-level cache at lines 40-43.
`export const readFixes = (key: string) => {` — the function receives the attacker-controlled key as its parameter.
`if (CodeFixes[key])` — the cache is checked for an existing entry. On a cache miss (unique key), execution falls through to line 24 and beyond.
`const files = fs.existsSync(FixesDir) ? fs.readdirSync(FixesDir) : []` — on every cache miss, a synchronous directory read is performed, adding filesystem I/O cost per unique key.
`const fix = fs.readFileSync(`${FixesDir}/${file}`).toString()` — for each matching file, a synchronous file read is performed. Multiple unique keys that match files amplify the I/O cost.
`const key = req.params.key` — the attacker-controlled key is extracted from the path parameter. (In `checkCorrectFix`, the equivalent extraction is at line 71: `const key = req.body.key`.)

Line 40-43: `CodeFixes[key] = { fixes, correct }` — the cache object has no maximum size, no eviction policy, and no TTL. An attacker sending many requests with unique keys causes unbounded memory growth. Additionally, each cache miss triggers synchronous filesystem I/O (readdirSync at line 26, readFileSync at line 29), compounding the resource consumption impact.

title: Challenge-solving endpoint reachable without authentication
description: The `checkCorrectFix` handler (POST /snippets/fixes) is registered with no authentication middleware. When the correct fix is submitted (line 85), the handler calls `challengeUtils.solveFixIt(key)` (line 86), which presumably marks a challenge as solved for the current user. Without any authentication, any unauthenticated caller can submit correct fixes and trigger challenge-solving logic. The correct answer can be obtained by reading the fixes from the unauthenticated GET /snippets/fixes/:key endpoint and identifying which fix matches the `.info.yml` metadata. This means the challenge-solving workflow can be completed entirely without authentication.

trace.description: The `checkCorrectFix` handler is exported and registered as POST /snippets/fixes with `auth: none` per the route declaration. The handler receives no authenticated user identity.
`const key = req.body.key` — the challenge key is extracted from the request body with no user identity context.
`const selectedFix = req.body.selectedFix` — the attacker's selected fix index is extracted from the request body.

`const fixData = readFixes(key)` — the fix data (including the correct answer index) is loaded using the attacker-supplied key. The correct index is derived from the file naming convention inside `readFixes` (lines 30-35).
`if (fixData.fixes.length === 0)` — if fixes exist for the key, execution proceeds to the `else` branch at line 78, which contains the solve logic.

`if (selectedFix === fixData.correct)` — the attacker-supplied `selectedFix` is compared against the correct answer. Since an unauthenticated attacker can also call GET /snippets/fixes/:key (line 56, also `auth: none`) to read the fixes, they can determine or brute-force the correct index. When this condition is true, execution proceeds to line 86.

When `selectedFix === fixData.correct` (line 85), the handler calls `challengeUtils.solveFixIt(key)` (line 86) with no user identity context. An unauthenticated attacker can read the fixes via GET /snippets/fixes/:key (also unauthenticated), determine the correct one, and submit it to trigger the solve action. The correct answer index is derivable from the file naming convention (lines 30-35) and the `.info.yml` metadata (lines 80-83).

title: NoSQL injection via $where clause concatenation enables arbitrary JavaScript execution in MongoDB
description: The handler receives `req.params.id` from the route (caller is the Express framework, outside this file). When the `noSqlCommandChallenge` is enabled, the id is truncated to 40 characters via `utils.trunc()` but is NOT sanitized or parameterized. It is then concatenated directly into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression: `'this.product == ' + id`. The `$where` operator executes arbitrary JavaScript inside the MongoDB server. An attacker can craft an id such as `1;sleep(2000)` (the global `sleep` function is defined on lines 17-26 for this purpose) or `1;while(1){}` to cause denial of service, or `1;return true` to exfiltrate all reviews regardless of product. Even when the challenge is disabled and `Number(req.params.id)` is used, the code structure itself is insecure — the safe path is a conditional fallback, not the default. The 40-character truncation still permits payloads like `1;sleep(2000)` or `1;return true`.

trace.description: The exported handler `showProductReviews()` receives `req` from the Express router. The route GET /rest/products/:id/reviews has auth: none, so any caller can reach this handler.

`req.params.id` is either converted to a Number (when challenge disabled) or truncated to 40 chars via `utils.trunc()` (when challenge enabled). In the challenge-enabled branch, the value remains an unsanitized string.

The id is concatenated into a MongoDB `$where` JavaScript expression: `db.reviewsCollection.find({ $where: 'this.product == ' + id })`. The `$where` operator evaluates the string as JavaScript inside the MongoDB server. No parameterization, escaping, or allow-listing is applied. An attacker-controlled string becomes executable code. The globally defined `sleep()` function (lines 17-26) is a blocking busy-wait, enabling DoS via a payload like `1;sleep(2000)`. Data exfiltration is possible via `1;return true` or similar.

title: Unauthenticated route exposes user email addresses from review likedBy arrays
description: The route GET /rest/products/:id/reviews has no authentication middleware (auth: none). The handler queries all reviews for a product and returns them via `res.json(utils.queryResultToJson(reviews))`. Each review object contains a `likedBy` array (referenced on line 40: `reviews[i].likedBy.includes(user.data.email)`), which stores user email addresses. This array is never stripped from the response before serialization. Any unauthenticated caller can retrieve the email addresses of all users who liked any review on any product, simply by iterating over product IDs. This is a broken object property level authorization / data exposure issue.

trace.description: The handler is registered on GET /rest/products/:id/reviews with auth: none. No authentication or authorization is required to reach this code.
Reviews are fetched from the database. The review objects include a `likedBy` field (an array of email strings), as evidenced by its use on line 40.

The code accesses `reviews[i].likedBy.includes(user.data.email)`, confirming `likedBy` is an array of email addresses present on each review object. The handler only adds a `liked` boolean; it never removes `likedBy` from the objects.
The `id` is processed from `req.params.id` to be used in the database query.
The handler iterates over the fetched `reviews` array in a for loop, exposing each element to modification.

`res.json(utils.queryResultToJson(reviews))` serializes the full review objects, including the `likedBy` email arrays, to the response. No field filtering or redaction is applied. An unauthenticated caller receives PII (email addresses) for all users who liked reviews on the requested product.

title: NoSQL DoS detection timing measured but never used or logged
description: The handler records timestamps `t0` (before the query, line 34) and `t1` (after the query resolves, line 37) with the stated intent to 'check if there was a nosql dos attack.' However, the elapsed time `t1 - t0` is never compared against any threshold, never logged, and never triggers any alert. The detection mechanism is stubbed out but non-functional. If an attacker exploits the `$where` injection to execute `sleep()` or an infinite loop, the application has no monitoring in place to detect, log, or alert on the anomalous query duration. This means security-relevant events (DoS attacks via NoSQL injection) go completely unlogged.

trace.description: The handler is invoked on every GET /rest/products/:id/reviews request, with no authentication required.

`const t0 = new Date().getTime()` records the start time before the database query. The comment on line 33 states the intent: 'Measure how long the query takes, to check if there was a nosql dos attack.'
The `id` is extracted and processed for the database query.
The `db.reviewsCollection.find` query is executed, which is the operation whose duration is being measured and the potential target of a DoS attack.

`const t1 = new Date().getTime()` records the end time after the query resolves. The values t0 and t1 are computed but never compared, logged, or acted upon. There is no `if (t1 - t0 > threshold)` check, no `logger.warn()`, and no alerting. The security monitoring that the code explicitly intends to perform is absent. A NoSQL DoS attack via the $where injection would be completely invisible to operators.

title: Global blocking sleep function enables thread-blocking denial of service
description: A global `sleep` function is defined that performs a busy-wait blocking loop. It is attached to the global object, making it available in any execution context including MongoDB's `$where` JavaScript evaluation. While the function caps the sleep duration at 2000ms, a single request can still block a server thread for 2 seconds. Combined with the `$where` injection on line 36, an attacker can send many concurrent requests each triggering `sleep(2000)`, consuming all available event loop threads and causing denial of service. Even without the injection, defining a blocking busy-wait on the global object is an insecure design choice that makes DoS trivially achievable once any code path reaches it.

trace.description: `global.sleep` is defined as a function that performs a blocking busy-wait loop (lines 22-25: `while (new Date().getTime() < stop + time) { ; }`). This blocks the Node.js event loop for up to 2000ms per call.

The `$where` injection on line 36 allows an attacker to call `sleep()` from within the MongoDB query context. An attacker can send a request like GET /rest/products/1;sleep(2000)/reviews (URL-encoded) to trigger the blocking sleep. Repeated concurrent requests exhaust server resources.
Inside the `sleep` function, `const stop = new Date().getTime()` calculates the target time to block until, based on the attacker-supplied duration.

The busy-wait loop `while (new Date().getTime() < stop + time)` blocks the executing thread. Multiple concurrent invocations (enabled by the unauthenticated, rate-limit-free route) consume all available threads, degrading or denying service to legitimate users.

title: Hardcoded TOTP secrets and account passwords in source code
description: The test file hardcodes TOTP secrets and account passwords for what appear to be application-seeded accounts (wurstbrot, J12934) that may exist in production deployments. TOTP secrets like 'IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH' and passwords like 'EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!' are committed in source. If these seeded accounts exist in production with these same credentials, an attacker who reads the source repository gains direct access to pre-configured accounts, including accounts with 2FA enabled (since the TOTP secret is also exposed). Hardcoded secrets in source code are always a finding regardless of whether they are used in production.

Hardcoded password 'EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!' for the wurstbrot account, an email constructed from config domain rather than a test-specific domain, suggesting it is a seeded application account.
Hardcoded password '0Y8rMnww$*9VFYE§59-!Fg1L6t&6lB' for the J12934 account, also constructed from the config domain, suggesting another seeded application account.
tmpTokenWurstbrot (produced by security.authorize at line 37) is sent in the request body to POST /rest/2fa/verify.
The TOTP token generated from the hardcoded secret is sent in the same request body as totpToken.
Response status 200 confirms that the hardcoded secret produces a valid authentication token for the wurstbrot account.
Assertion confirms the authenticated account is wurstbrot@<domain>, proving the hardcoded secret and token are for a real application-seeded account.

The combination of hardcoded email, password, and TOTP secret for a seeded account means anyone with repository access has full credentials (including 2FA bypass) for accounts that may exist in production deployments.

title: Authentication token payload contains password hash and TOTP secret
description: The test at lines 319-326 constructs an authentication token via security.authorize() with a payload that includes the user's hashed password and TOTP secret directly in the token data. The same structure is used at lines 407-414. If the application sends these JWT tokens to clients (as is typical for Bearer token authentication), then the token payload — which contains security.hash(password) and totpSecret — is exposed to the client. While the password is hashed, the TOTP secret is in plaintext within the token, which would allow a token holder to generate valid TOTP codes and would undermine the second factor entirely. Even if the token is not sent to clients, storing the TOTP secret inside the JWT payload is a design that risks exposure through token logging, interception, or debug output.

trace.description: The test calls security.authorize() with a data object containing id, email, password (as security.hash(password)), and totpSecret. The caller (test setup) is outside the production code path, but this reveals the token payload structure used by the application's authentication library.

The totpSecret field is included in the token payload data. For the disable test (line 412), totpSecret 'KDR5FXSOLNV6A5UAQYCKROSJZF7SVML7' is placed directly in the token. This is the same secret used to generate valid TOTP tokens.
The password field is set to security.hash(password), embedding the password hash directly into the JWT payload.
The security.authorize() call completes, producing a JWT token whose payload contains the password hash and totpSecret.

In the disable test, the same pattern is used: the token containing totpSecret (line 412) is placed into security.authenticatedUsers, confirming this payload structure is not test-specific but reflects the real token format.

The token containing the TOTP secret and password hash is placed into security.authenticatedUsers and used as a Bearer token (line 332). If JWT tokens with this payload structure are issued to clients during normal authentication, the TOTP secret is exposed in the token, allowing an attacker who captures or reads the token to generate valid second-factor codes, effectively bypassing 2FA.

title: No rate limiting verification on 2FA TOTP verification endpoint
description: The tests for POST /rest/2fa/verify verify that valid tokens succeed and invalid tokens fail with 401, but there is no test asserting rate limiting or lockout after repeated failed attempts. TOTP codes are 6 digits (1 million possibilities), and without rate limiting an attacker with a valid tmpToken (obtained after password verification) can brute-force the TOTP code. The test file does not demonstrate any throttling control exists on this endpoint. While the absence of a test does not prove the absence of a control, the test suite's complete silence on rate limiting for an authentication-critical brute-force-susceptible endpoint is notable. This is both a resource-consumption concern (unbounded requests) and a crypto-auth concern (brute-force enables 2FA bypass).

trace.description: The describe block for /rest/2fa/verify defines tests for the TOTP verification endpoint. The entrypoint is POST /rest/2fa/verify which accepts tmpToken and totpToken.

A 6-digit TOTP has only 1,000,000 possibilities; without throttling, an attacker with a valid tmpToken (obtained after correct password entry) can brute-force the TOTP, bypassing the second factor. This also enables denial-of-service through repeated verification attempts.

title: Encryption keys directory publicly accessible with directory listing enabled
description: The application serves a directory listing at /encryptionkeys, exposing all encryption key files to any unauthenticated user. The test confirms that a directory listing is returned (line 134) and that the 'Premium Content AES key' file (premium.key) is publicly downloadable with a 200 response (lines 143-147). The directory listing further reveals all available key files, expanding the attack surface.

description: The application serves access log files at /support/logs/access.log.<date> to any unauthenticated user. The test on lines 198-203 confirms that these log files are publicly downloadable (200 response, application/octet-stream content type). Access logs typically contain sensitive information such as IP addresses, request paths, user agents, and potentially authentication tokens or session identifiers. Serving these publicly allows attackers to harvest reconnaissance data, identify other users' behavior patterns, and potentially extract credentials or session tokens that may have been logged.

title: Path traversal protection on file-serving endpoint relies on filename check rather than path normalization
description: The test on lines 149-154 confirms that the application blocks a path traversal attempt on /encryptionkeys/ where the attacker encodes forward slashes to escape the directory (%2fetc%2fos-release%2500.md). The server returns a 403 with 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!'. However, this defense is a blacklist-style check (rejecting forward slashes in filenames) rather than a robust path normalization and allow-listing approach. The fact that this specific attack vector is being tested suggests the endpoint is known to be susceptible to path traversal, and the current defense may be bypassable with alternative encoding techniques or null-byte truncation. The endpoint serves files from the filesystem based on user-supplied input, which is an access control concern — without proper per-resource authorization and path containment, users could access files outside the intended directory.

The server responds with 403 and 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!' — confirming the endpoint takes user-supplied filenames and maps them to filesystem paths, with the only protection being a check that rejects forward slashes. This is a weak access control on a file-serving endpoint; the defense is a string-level filter rather than robust path containment or authorization.

title: Client-controlled wallet balance increment allows free money creation
description: The addWalletBalance handler accepts the monetary amount to add to a wallet directly from req.body.balance. There is no server-side derivation of the amount, no payment processing confirmation, no validation that the amount is legitimate, and no check against an actual card balance or external payment gateway. An authenticated user can submit any positive number as 'balance' and the server will increment their wallet by that amount. The only gate is that a valid cardId is provided and belongs to the user (line 24), but once that check passes, the arbitrary client-supplied balance is applied unconditionally. This breaks the economic invariant that wallet balance should only increase by amounts actually paid.

req.body.paymentId is read to look up a card. The card ownership check at line 24 scopes by UserId, so a valid card belonging to the user must exist.

This is the only authorization gate: it verifies that a card with the given id exists and is associated with the supplied UserId. If cardId is falsy, card is set to null and the flow falls to the else branch at line 32.

WalletModel.increment({ balance: req.body.balance }, { where: { UserId: req.body.UserId } }) persists the client-supplied amount as a real balance increase. An attacker submits { "paymentId": <own card id>, "balance": 9999999 } and receives that amount in their wallet.

title: Wallet lookup and mutation use caller-controllable req.body.UserId for identity
description: Both getWalletBalance and addWalletBalance use req.body.UserId as the user identity for wallet lookups and mutations. The route is protected by security.appendUserId() middleware which is presumably intended to set this field from the session, but the handlers themselves read identity from the request body — a caller-controllable surface — rather than from a trusted server-side source such as req.user or a decoded session token. If the middleware fails to overwrite a pre-existing body value, or if any code path reaches these handlers without the middleware, User A can supply User B's UserId in the request body and read or modify User B's wallet balance. The handler performs no independent ownership verification.

description: Wallet balance changes are financial events that require audit logging: who changed the balance, by how much, and when. Neither getWalletBalance nor addWalletBalance emits any log entry on success or failure. An attacker who exploits the client-controlled balance increment (or any other wallet abuse) would leave no trace in application logs, making incident detection and forensic investigation impossible.

title: CAPTCHA verification is optional for user data export, defeating anti-automation control
description: The tests confirm that the data-export endpoint at POST /rest/user/data-export succeeds (HTTP 200) and returns the user's full PII (username, email, orders, reviews, memories) even when no CAPTCHA answer is provided. The test on line 52 explicitly states 'still succeeds without CAPTCHA' and asserts a 200 response with an empty body ({}). Further tests on lines 72-87, 133-159, and 161-186 all perform successful data exports by sending only { format: '1' } with no CAPTCHA answer. The CAPTCHA is only enforced when the client chooses to engage it (by first requesting /rest/image-captcha and then sending an answer). This means an attacker with a valid session token can automate bulk data exfiltration without solving any CAPTCHA — the control is opt-in rather than mandatory, which is an insecure design that defeats the purpose of the CAPTCHA as an anti-automation safeguard.

authHeader is constructed as { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token, 'content-type': 'application/json' } — only the bearer token is included, no CAPTCHA session identifier.
The request body is sent as {} — no 'answer' field, no CAPTCHA reference, no format field even. The application receives a valid auth token but zero CAPTCHA-related input.

The test asserts res.status === 200 and res.body.confirmation === 'Your data export will open in a new Browser window.' — confirming the application processed the data export and returned user data without requiring CAPTCHA verification. The same pattern is repeated on lines 72-87, 133-159, 161-186, and 188-213, all exporting user PII (orders, reviews, memories) without CAPTCHA.

title: Internal error details and stack traces exposed in HTTP error responses
description: The test file contains multiple hardcoded credentials used to authenticate against the application. Notably, line 321 uses 'admin123' as the admin password, line 134 uses 'K1f.....................' for user amy, and line 162 uses 'ncc-1701' for user jim. The admin password 'admin123' is an extremely weak default credential. If these credentials match the application's configured defaults (as is common in deliberately vulnerable applications like Juice Shop), they represent hardcoded weak credentials that would allow trivial authentication as privileged users. Even in a test context, embedding plaintext weak credentials in source code that is version-controlled is a misconfiguration that risks credential exposure if the test suite is accessible.

title: Authentication token generated without user identity binding via insecurity.authorize()
description: On line 16, the test file generates an authentication token by calling `security.authorize()` from the `insecurity` module (imported on line 12). The `authorize()` function is called with no arguments — no user ID, no credentials, no session context. This produces a valid Bearer token that is sufficient to access the protected B2B order endpoint (demonstrated by the test at lines 37-51 which receives a 200 response). This reveals that the application's authentication mechanism issues tokens that are not bound to a specific user identity. Any caller who can invoke `authorize()` — or who knows the signing secret, which the module name `insecurity` implies is weak or hardcoded — obtains a token accepted by the server. This is both a cryptographic/authentication failure (tokens are forgeable or identity-free) and an access-control failure (the endpoint authenticates possession of a token but never authorizes a specific user, enabling BOLA).

Line 16 calls `security.authorize()` with no arguments — no user identity, no credentials, no scope. The returned value is concatenated into a Bearer token: `'Bearer ' + security.authorize()`. This token is then used as the Authorization header for all subsequent authenticated requests.
The test initiates a request to the application: `const res = await request(app)`, beginning the process of sending the identity-free token to the server.
The request targets the protected B2B order endpoint: `.post('/b2b/v2/orders')`.
The `authHeader` containing the forgeable token is applied to the request via `.set(authHeader)`, transmitting the credential to the server.
The request body is initiated with `.send({`, preparing to send an arbitrary payload.
The request body is closed with `})`, finalizing the POST request that carries the unbound token.

The test at lines 37-51 sends an arbitrary JSON body to POST /b2b/v2/orders with only this identity-free Bearer token and receives a 200 response (line 46). The endpoint accepts the request based solely on token possession — there is no per-user authorization check, and the token itself carries no user identity. An attacker who can replicate the token generation (implied weak/hardcoded secret in the `insecurity` module) gains full access to the B2B order API as any user.

title: B2B order endpoint accepts arbitrary unvalidated JSON as a valid order
description: The test at lines 37-51 demonstrates that POST /b2b/v2/orders accepts any valid JSON payload — `{foo: 'bar', test: 42}` — and returns a 200 response with an `orderNo` and `paymentDue`. A B2B order endpoint should enforce a server-side schema: product IDs, quantities, customer identity, pricing. The fact that arbitrary key-value pairs are accepted indicates the server does not validate or re-derive order data from trusted sources. The test at lines 53-63 further shows that the `cid` (customer ID) field is accepted from the client request body and reflected directly in the response, meaning the client controls the customer identity associated with the order rather than the server deriving it from the authenticated session. This is a trust-boundary violation: the server trusts client-supplied order structure and customer identity.

Combined with the acceptance of arbitrary JSON (line 46), the order endpoint has no server-side enforcement of order structure, data integrity, or customer identity — a client can submit orders with arbitrary fields and a spoofed customer ID.

title: Hardcoded default credentials (password 'ncc-1701') embedded in source
description: The test file embeds the password 'ncc-1701' for the 'jim' account in plaintext across multiple test cases. In the OWASP Juice Shop application, 'ncc-1701' is the actual default password for the jim user account in the running application — these are not throwaway test-only credentials but real default credentials that the production system ships with. Hardcoded default credentials in source code are a misconfiguration finding (OWASP A05) because they allow anyone with access to the source or knowledge of the defaults to authenticate. They also constitute a crypto-auth finding (OWASP A07) because the authentication system accepts a known, predictable default credential, enabling authentication bypass by any attacker who knows the published defaults. The credentials are used in the login helper (line 13 import) which authenticates against the real application instance, confirming they are valid production credentials, not randomized test fixtures.

First occurrence: email 'jim@' + application.domain and password 'ncc-1701' are hardcoded and passed to login(). These same credentials are repeated at lines 53, 66, 77, and 93.

The email field is assembled by concatenating 'jim@' with the application domain from config: `email: 'jim@' + config.get<string>('application.domain')`. This constructs the full login email for the jim account.

The credentials object literal is closed with `})`, completing the argument passed to login(). The fully constructed {email, password} object — containing the hardcoded default credential — is now handed to the login helper.

The login() call sends the hardcoded default credentials to the application's authentication endpoint. Since these are the application's shipped default credentials (not randomized per-test secrets), any attacker who knows the published defaults can authenticate as jim. This is the authentication-bypass impact: a known default password is accepted by the production auth system.

title: Permissive CORS configuration allowing all origins
description: The test asserts that the application's HTTP responses include `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, confirming that the server is configured to allow cross-origin requests from any origin. This is a permissive cross-origin configuration. For an application like Juice Shop that serves authenticated API endpoints and user data, allowing all origins means any malicious website can make cross-origin requests to the API. While `*` cannot be combined with `credentials: true` in browser-based fetch, it still permits unauthenticated cross-origin reads of any non-credentialed API responses and can be combined with other attack vectors.

Exposing detailed error messages in production responses is a security misconfiguration — it leaks internal application structure, path routing logic, and potentially stack trace or implementation details that aid attackers in reconnaissance. Production applications should return generic error pages without internal details.

Hardcoded credentials in source code are a misconfiguration finding regardless of whether they are used in production. The admin password 'admin123' is an extremely weak default credential for an administrative interface. These credentials are committed in plaintext and could be used to authenticate to the application if the same credentials exist in any deployed environment. The presence of weak default admin credentials ('admin123') establishes both a misconfiguration (hardcoded weak default credential) and a crypto-auth concern (weak credential that enables authentication bypass through guessing or credential reuse).

title: BOLA: Any authenticated user can retrieve any other user's basket by ID
description: The test at lines 100-112 explicitly verifies that a user logged in as bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com can GET /rest/basket/2 and receive a 200 response with the basket data. The test is titled 'GET existing basket of another user' and expects success (status 200, basket data returned). This confirms that the /rest/basket/:id endpoint performs authentication but no per-resource ownership authorization — any authenticated user can substitute another user's basket ID and retrieve their data. This is a classic Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability.

title: BOLA: Any authenticated user can apply coupons to and checkout another user's basket
description: Lines 134-145 use the authHeader belonging to jim@juice-sh.op (created at lines 30-37) to apply a coupon to basket 2 (PUT /rest/basket/2/coupon/...) and then checkout basket 2 (POST /rest/basket/2/checkout). title: Forgeable coupon system: arbitrary discount coupons can be generated and accepted
description: Line 23 generates a 'forgedCoupon' with a 99% discount using security.generateCoupon(99). Lines 134-145 confirm that this coupon is accepted by PUT /rest/basket/2/coupon/:coupon (returns 200, discount=99) and the basket can then be checked out successfully. This is both an insecure design flaw (the server trusts a client-generatable token for a financial decision) and a cryptographic/auth failure (the coupon token lacks integrity protection, making it forgeable).

title: Feedback creation accepts arbitrary UserId from client — broken object-level authorization and client-controlled identity
description: The POST /api/Feedbacks endpoint accepts a UserId field directly from the request body and persists it without verifying that the authenticated (or anonymous) caller is authorized to post feedback on behalf of that user. The server trusts the client-supplied UserId rather than deriving it from the authenticated session, which is both a broken object-level authorization defect and an insecure design flaw where the client controls a value the server should decide.

title: Authorization token generated without authentication grants access to protected endpoints

title: Unauthenticated checkout of any basket — missing ownership verification on order placement
description: The POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout endpoint is registered with auth: none. The handler takes a basket ID from the URL path (line 34), looks up the basket by that ID (line 35), and proceeds to generate an order confirmation, decrement product quantities, and insert an order record — all without verifying that the requesting user owns or is authorized to access that basket. The authenticated user is extracted at line 38 only to derive an email for the order PDF and order ID; if no user is authenticated (which is possible since auth is 'none'), the email silently becomes an empty string and the order still processes. Any caller can supply any basket ID and force a checkout of another user's basket, causing inventory decrements, wallet modifications, and order records for baskets they do not own.

No ownership check was performed at any point. An attacker can checkout any basket by substituting its ID in the URL.

title: Caller-controlled UserId enables wallet manipulation for arbitrary accounts
description: The handler accepts a UserId field directly from the request body (line 144) and uses it to perform wallet lookups, balance decrements (line 148), and balance increments (line 155). The server never validates that req.body.UserId matches the authenticated user's identity. An attacker can supply any UserId to (a) add bonus points (totalPoints) to any user's wallet via WalletModel.increment, and (b) if paymentId is 'wallet', debit any user's wallet for the order total. Since the route has auth: none, even an unauthenticated caller can credit bonus points to a wallet of their choosing by including any UserId in the request body. This breaks object-level authorization on wallet resources and enables economic exploitation (free bonus points credited to attacker's wallet).

For any other paymentId value (or when orderDetails is absent), no payment is verified or processed — the order proceeds to completion: product quantities are decremented, bonus points are credited, and an order confirmation is returned. The server trusts the client to specify a payment method but never validates that payment was actually completed for non-wallet methods. This is a design-level flaw: the workflow allows an order to be finalized without the server confirming that payment occurred.

An attacker can submit paymentId: 'credit_card' (or any value other than 'wallet') and receive a completed order with no payment processed.

title: Unauthenticated PDF generation on checkout enables denial-of-service
description: The checkout endpoint dynamically imports and instantiates a PDF document generator (pdfkit) on every request (lines 42-43), writes a PDF file to disk (line 45), and performs multiple database queries and updates (lines 77-80, 124, 146-148, 155, 162). The endpoint has auth: none and no visible rate limiting. An attacker can send repeated checkout requests with arbitrary basket IDs, each triggering PDF generation, file I/O, and multiple database operations, to exhaust server resources (memory, disk, database connections).

With no authentication and no rate limiting, an attacker can flood this endpoint to exhaust memory, disk space, and database connections.

title: No security logging for order placement — a financial transaction event
description: The placeOrder handler processes an order including payment (wallet debit), inventory changes (quantity decrements), bonus point allocation, and order record creation. No security-relevant logging is performed at any point: no log of who placed the order, which basket was checked out, what payment method was used, or any audit trail for the financial transaction. Given that this endpoint is also reachable without authentication (auth: none) and accepts caller-controlled UserId for wallet operations, the absence of logging makes it impossible to detect or investigate fraudulent order placements or wallet manipulation.

title: Authentication token generated without user identity binding enables identity-agnostic access to complaints
description: On line 14, `security.authorize()` is called with no arguments — no user ID, no username, no role. This generates a valid bearer token that is then used to authenticate against every complaint endpoint in the test suite. If the production authorization mechanism works the same way (issuing tokens without binding them to a specific user identity), then any holder of any valid token can act as any user. The token does not encode who the caller is, so the server cannot perform per-user authorization. This means the authentication mechanism fails to establish identity, which is the foundational requirement for all subsequent access-control decisions. The test on lines 42–47 confirms that this identity-less token is sufficient to GET all complaints (200), and the test on lines 22–34 confirms it is sufficient to POST a new complaint (201). Since the token carries no user identity, the complaints system has no way to scope data to the requesting user — every authenticated caller can read every complaint and create complaints attributed to no specific user.

`security.authorize()` is called with zero arguments. No user identity, role, or session context is passed. The return value is used as a bearer token in the Authorization header for all subsequent requests. This means the token is generated without binding to any user identity — the authentication mechanism produces a credential that does not establish who the caller is.

GET /api/Complaints is called with this identity-less token and the test asserts a 200 response (line 46). This confirms that the server accepts the token and returns all complaints without any per-user scoping. Any authenticated caller receives the full complaint set.

`.get('/api/Complaints')` sets the request method and path. No pagination parameters, user-scoping query parameters, or ownership filters are included.

`.set(authHeader)` applies the identity-less bearer token to the request. The server receives a valid authentication credential that encodes no user identity, so it has no basis to scope the response to a specific user's complaints.

The test POSTs a new complaint to /api/Complaints. The request body (lines 26–28) contains only a `message` field. No user identifier, ownership token, or user-scoping is included. The caller is outside this file (the test drives the API).

`.set(authHeader)` applies the identity-less bearer token (from line 14). The server authenticates the request but has no user identity to associate with the complaint being created.

`.send({ message: '...' })` sends the request body. The body contains only a `message` field — no `userId`, no owner reference. The server accepts complaint creation without any user ownership binding in the payload.
`assert.equal(res.status, 201)` confirms the complaint was successfully created. The server accepted a complaint without associating it with any user identity.
`assert.ok(res.headers['content-type']?.includes('application/json'))` confirms the response is JSON, indicating a structured data response is returned.

`assert.equal(typeof res.body.data.id, 'number')` checks the `id` field. The response contains an `id` but the test does not check for a `userId` field — because none exists in the response. The complaint is created with a system-assigned ID but no owner reference.

`assert.equal(typeof res.body.data.updatedAt, 'string')` checks the `updatedAt` timestamp. The complete set of response fields asserted is `id`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` — none of which is a user ownership reference. This confirms the data model design lacks the ownership relationship needed to enforce per-user access control.

The assertion `assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms that the identity-less token grants full read access to all complaints. Because the token on line 14 encodes no user identity, there is no mechanism for the server to filter complaints by owner. This is both an authentication failure (identity is never established) and an access-control failure (no per-resource ownership check is possible without identity).

title: Complaints are created and listed without user ownership binding, enabling cross-user data exposure
description: The test suite demonstrates that the complaints system has no user ownership model. On lines 22–34, a complaint is POSTed with only a `message` field — no user ID is sent, and the response (201) returns an `id`, `createdAt`, and `updatedAt` but no `userId` or owner field. On lines 42–47, GET /api/Complaints returns all complaints to any authenticated caller. The design never associates a complaint with the user who submitted it, so there is no basis for per-user access control. Any authenticated user can read every complaint submitted by every other user. This is an insecure design flaw because the data model itself lacks the ownership relationship needed to enforce access control, and it manifests as a BOLA vulnerability at the API level.

The response is asserted to contain `data.id` (a number), `data.createdAt`, and `data.updatedAt` — but there is no `userId` or owner field in the response. The complaint is created without being associated with any user identity. This demonstrates that the data model does not bind complaints to users, which is a design-level defect: the server never establishes ownership of the resource at creation time.

GET /api/Complaints with the same generic auth token returns 200. Because complaints were never associated with a user (line 31), the server has no basis to filter the response by ownership. Any authenticated user receives all complaints. The design lacks the ownership relationship needed to enforce per-user access control, and the GET endpoint returns the full unscoped result set.

title: GET /api/Complaints endpoint returns all complaints without pagination or rate limiting
description: The test on lines 42–47 demonstrates that GET /api/Complaints returns the full set of complaints in a single response. The test asserts only the status code (200) and does not check for pagination headers, cursors, or page limits. There is no evidence of pagination, rate limiting, or result-set capping on this endpoint. An attacker can repeatedly call this endpoint to retrieve unbounded data, or flood it with requests to consume server memory and database resources. Since complaints can be created by any authenticated user (lines 22–34), an attacker can first populate the complaints table and then exhaust server memory by requesting the full unpaginated result set.

`.set(authHeader)` applies the authentication header. The request is authenticated but contains no constraints on the size of the response — no page size, no max results, no rate-limiting token.

The test asserts `res.status === 200` but does not check for any pagination metadata (total count, next page link, Link headers). The response is expected to contain all complaints. Combined with the unauthenticated POST endpoint that allows complaint creation (lines 22–34), an attacker can inflate the complaints table and then issue GET requests that force the server to serialize and return the entire dataset in a single response, consuming memory and CPU.

title: Log files served over HTTP without authentication
