The test asserts res.status === 200, confirming the endpoint returns the log file content to the unauthenticated caller.
createTestApp() builds the Express application instance whose routes include the /support/logs/:file endpoint. No authentication middleware is configured or asserted at this level.
The app instance is stored so that tests can issue requests against it. No credentials or auth tokens are provisioned alongside it.
The request URL is assembled from '/support/logs/access.log.' concatenated with the current date. The request is sent to the server with no authentication context.
The test asserts the content-type includes application/octet-stream, confirming the full log file body is served to the requester. Internal access logs are publicly exposed without authentication.

title: Path traversal protection limited to forward-slash check only
description: The test at lines 29-35 verifies that a file name containing URL-encoded forward slashes (%2f) is rejected with a 403 and the error message 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!'. This reveals that the endpoint's only path-traversal defense is a check for forward slashes in the file name. The design does not account for backslashes (relevant on Windows), double-encoding, null bytes, or other path traversal vectors. A control that blocks only one form of path separator while serving arbitrary files from the filesystem is a design flaw: an attacker could potentially use alternative encoding or platform-specific separators to traverse directories and read arbitrary files through the /support/logs/:file endpoint. The route handler is outside this file; the trace begins where the test exercises the endpoint.

trace.description: The test issues a GET request to /support/logs/%2fetc%2fpasswd — a path traversal attempt using URL-encoded forward slashes. The test does not test any other traversal vector (backslashes, double-encoding, null bytes, ../ without encoded slashes).

The test asserts a 403 response, confirming the endpoint does block this specific vector. The error message text asserted on line 34 ('File names cannot contain forward slashes!') indicates the check is specifically and only a forward-slash presence check.
The URL-encoded path /support/logs/%2fetc%2fpasswd is sent to the application. The server's route handler (outside this file) receives the :file parameter and applies its forward-slash check.

The asserted error message 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!' reveals the design of the path traversal control: it rejects only forward slashes. No canonicalization, no allow-list of filenames, no backslash check, no null-byte check. The endpoint serves files from the filesystem with a single-string-contains check as its only defense, which is bypassable by design on platforms or encodings that don't use forward slashes.

title: Log file endpoint serves entire files without size limits
description: The test at lines 21-27 retrieves an entire access log file via GET /support/logs/:file and receives it as application/octet-stream. There is no indication of pagination, byte-range limits, or maximum file size enforcement. Access log files can grow to hundreds of megabytes on a busy server. An unauthenticated attacker (per Finding 1) could repeatedly request large log files, consuming server memory and network bandwidth. The route handler is outside this file; the trace begins where the test exercises the endpoint.

trace.description: The test requests the full access log file for the current day. No pagination, offset, or limit parameter is passed, and the response is expected to contain the entire file body.
The request path is built as '/support/logs/access.log.' concatenated with the current date via utils.toISO8601(new Date()). The server is expected to locate and serve the entire file at this path.
The test asserts res.status === 200, confirming the server successfully reads and returns the complete file content in the response body.

The test asserts the response content-type is application/octet-stream and status 200, confirming the entire file is streamed back to the caller. No size cap or pagination is evident from the test's expectations.

title: Server accepts executable file uploads — file type validation is client-side only
description: The test at lines 39–45 explicitly proves that the /file-upload endpoint accepts an .exe file (a type classified as 'illegal for client validation') and returns HTTP 204 (success). This demonstrates that file type filtering is enforced only on the client and is absent on the server. An attacker can bypass client-side validation by crafting a direct API request, uploading executable or otherwise dangerous file types to the server. The test itself validates this bypass path as expected behavior.

trace.description: Test 'POST file with illegal type for client validation but valid for API' uploads an .exe file to the /file-upload endpoint. The test name itself states the file type is 'illegal for client validation' but 'valid for API', indicating that client-side validation is the only barrier.
The file uploaded is '../files/invalidTypeForClient.exe' — an executable binary file that client-side validation would reject.
The resolved file path is passed into request(app) to begin constructing the HTTP request to the /file-upload endpoint.
The request is directed to the POST /file-upload route — the attacker-facing endpoint that the server exposes for file ingestion.

The .attach('file', file) call attaches the .exe binary as a multipart file upload payload, simulating a direct API call that bypasses any client-side validation UI. No server-side type check intervenes before the file reaches the server handler.

The assertion assert.equal(res.status, 204) confirms the server accepts the .exe upload with a success response. The server performs no server-side file type validation, relying entirely on client-side checks that can be trivially bypassed with a direct API call.

title: Server accepts files exceeding client-side size limits — no server-side enforcement of client size thresholds
description: The test at lines 31–37 demonstrates that the /file-upload endpoint accepts a file described as 'too large for client validation' and returns HTTP 204. The server does not enforce the same size thresholds that the client uses. While a separate test (lines 73–79) shows a higher server-side limit exists, the gap between the client's threshold and the server's threshold means an attacker can upload files significantly larger than what the application's own client-side rules permit. Combined with the .exe acceptance, this shows the server treats client-side validation as the primary control rather than a defense-in-depth layer.

trace.description: Test 'POST file too large for client validation but valid for API' uploads a file that exceeds client-side size limits to the /file-upload endpoint.
The file is '../files/invalidSizeForClient.pdf' — sized to exceed client-side validation thresholds but within server limits.
The resolved file path is passed into request(app) to begin constructing the HTTP request against the test application instance.
The request is directed to POST /file-upload — the server-side endpoint that receives and processes the multipart upload.

The .attach('file', file) call attaches the oversized PDF as the upload payload. The file passes through to the server handler without any server-side enforcement of the client-side size threshold that the test name identifies.

The assertion assert.equal(res.status, 204) confirms the server accepts the oversized file. The server has no enforcement of the client-side size threshold, meaning the effective upload size limit is higher than what the application's own validation rules intend, increasing the attack surface for resource consumption via large uploads.

title: Oversized file upload returns HTTP 500 instead of 413 — internal error leakage on size limit violation
description: When a file exceeds the server's maximum upload size, the endpoint returns HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error) rather than the appropriate HTTP 413 (Payload Too Large). A 500 response typically indicates an unhandled exception, which may leak stack traces, internal paths, or framework-specific error messages. The test at line 97 also asserts that the response body contains 'Unexpected end of form' — a framework-level error message exposed to the client.

trace.description: Test 'POST file too large for API' uploads a file exceeding the server's own size limit to /file-upload.
The file path is resolved to '../files/invalidSizeForServer.pdf' — a file sized to exceed the server's own maximum upload limit.
The resolved file path is passed into request(app) to construct the HTTP request against the test application instance.
The request is directed to POST /file-upload — the server-side endpoint that will attempt to process the oversized payload.
The .attach('file', file) call attaches the oversized PDF. When the server's size limit is exceeded, the multipart parser throws an unhandled error rather than returning a controlled 413 response.

The assertion assert.equal(res.status, 500) confirms the server returns HTTP 500 for an oversized upload. Line 97 further shows res.text.includes('Unexpected end of form'), confirming internal framework error messages are exposed to the client. The correct response would be 413 with a generic error message.

title: Empty test blocks for XXE and YAML bomb challenges indicate untested dangerous upload processing paths
description: Lines 63–71 contain conditional blocks guarded by checks for xxeFileDisclosureChallenge, xxeDosChallenge, and yamlBombChallenge. These blocks are completely empty — no tests are implemented for XML External Entity (XXE) attacks or YAML bomb (billion laughs) attacks against the file upload endpoint. The presence of these challenge guards indicates the application is known to be vulnerable to these attack classes via file upload, yet the test suite provides no coverage. The earlier tests (lines 47–61) confirm XML files are processed by the endpoint (returning 410 for deprecated XML types, but the endpoint still receives and begins processing them). This is an insecure design issue: the upload endpoint processes potentially malicious XML/YAML content without demonstrated server-side protections, and the test suite explicitly leaves these attack vectors untested.

trace.description: Conditional block checks if xxeFileDisclosureChallenge or xxeDosChallenge are enabled. The block body (lines 64–68) is entirely empty — no test cases for XXE attacks are implemented despite the endpoint accepting XML uploads.

Test 'POST file type XML deprecated for API' uploads an XML file (../files/deprecatedTypeForServer.xml) to /file-upload. This establishes that the endpoint receives and processes XML file uploads — the server begins parsing the XML content before returning the 410 deprecated response at line 52. The endpoint's XML parsing path is the entrypoint for XXE attacks.

Test 'POST large XML file near upload size limit' uploads another XML file (../files/maxSizeForServer.xml) to /file-upload, further confirming the endpoint actively processes XML content up to the server's size limit. The endpoint does not reject XML at the boundary — it accepts and parses it.

The block body for the XXE challenge conditional (lines 64–68) is entirely empty — no test cases verify that the server rejects or safely processes malicious XML with external entity declarations. The endpoint parses XML (as proven by lines 47–61) but no test validates that XXE attacks are blocked, meaning the server's XML parser may resolve external entities without any demonstrated protection.

Conditional block checks if yamlBombChallenge is enabled. The block body (line 71) is entirely empty — no test cases for YAML bomb denial-of-service attacks are implemented. The existence of these challenge guards confirms the application's own design acknowledges these attack vectors exist via file upload, but no protective tests or validation checks are present.

title: Directory listing enabled on /ftp endpoint exposes internal file structure without authentication
description: The /ftp endpoint serves a full directory listing in HTML to any requester without authentication. The test confirms that a GET to /ftp returns a 200 with content-type text/html containing a '<title>listing directory /ftp</title>'. This exposes the names and structure of all files in the FTP directory, including backup files, configuration files, and sensitive documents, allowing an attacker to enumerate available files and then attempt to access them individually.

trace.description: Test issues an unauthenticated GET request to /ftp endpoint and asserts a 200 response with directory listing HTML content containing '<title>listing directory /ftp</title>'. This confirms the server exposes a directory listing of the /ftp folder without any authentication.

Assertion confirms the directory listing is returned (line 29 checks for the listing title), and the test expects status 200 (line 27), proving the listing is publicly accessible with no access control.

title: Null byte encoded bypass of file type restriction allows access to restricted .bak files
description: The /ftp endpoint enforces file type restrictions, returning 403 for disallowed extensions like .bak (confirmed by tests at lines 56-66 for coupons_2013.md.bak and package.json.bak). However, the design of the access control check can be bypassed by appending a URL-encoded null byte followed by an allowed extension (%2500.md). The test at lines 127-133 confirms that GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md returns 200 and discloses the contents of the restricted package.json.bak file, including dependency information. This is an insecure design flaw because the file type validation mechanism is fundamentally bypassable through encoding manipulation — the check operates on the URL string rather than the actual file being served.

trace.description: Test confirms that GET /ftp/package.json.bak returns 403, establishing that .bak files are restricted by the file type access control.

Test issues GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + .md appended), and asserts status 200 (line 131) with the response containing '"epilogue-js": "~0.7",' (line 132). This proves the access control on .bak files is bypassed via null byte encoding, allowing an attacker to read restricted configuration and backup files.

title: KeePass password database and confidential acquisition documents publicly accessible via /ftp without authentication
description: The /ftp endpoint serves sensitive files without authentication. The test at lines 74-79 confirms that GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returns 200 with confidential content about '# Planned Acquisitions'. The test at lines 81-85 confirms that GET /ftp/incident-support.kdbx returns 200, making a KeePass password database file publicly downloadable. Exposing a password database file and confidential business documents without any authentication is a critical misconfiguration.

trace.description: Test issues an unauthenticated GET request to /ftp/acquisitions.md and asserts 200 with confidential content '# Planned Acquisitions' (line 78). A separate test at line 81-85 issues an unauthenticated GET to /ftp/incident-support.kdbx (KeePass database) and asserts 200. Both confirm sensitive files are publicly served without authentication.

Assertion at line 84 confirms the KeePass database file is returned with status 200 to an unauthenticated requester, and line 77-78 confirms the confidential acquisitions document content is disclosed.

title: Malware payload .url files in quarantine directory publicly accessible without authentication
description: The /ftp/quarantine/ directory serves .url files (Windows URL shortcut files) for multiple platforms without authentication. Tests at lines 135-157 confirm that GET requests to /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_linux_amd_64.url, juicy_malware_linux_arm_64.url, juicy_malware_macos_64.url, and juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url all return 200. These files are described as malware and are in a 'quarantine' directory, yet they are publicly downloadable. Serving quarantined malware files to any requester is a misconfiguration that could facilitate malware distribution.

trace.description: Test issues unauthenticated GET requests to /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_linux_amd_64.url (line 137), /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_linux_arm_64.url (line 143), /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_macos_64.url (line 149), and /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url (line 155), all asserting 200 responses.
All four tests assert status 200, confirming that quarantined malware .url files are publicly accessible without authentication to any requester.

title: HTTP fetch calls to external resources have no timeout configuration
description: Every fetch() call in this test file (lines 12, 20, 29, 39, 51, 61, 69, 76) makes requests to external third-party services (pastebin.com, listverse.disqus.com, stackoverflow.com) without specifying any timeout. Node.js fetch() has no default timeout, meaning any slow or unresponsive external server will cause the test process to hang indefinitely. An attacker who compromises or is in a position to throttle one of these external endpoints (e.g., Pastebin rate-limiting or a network-level MITM introducing delay) can cause the entire CI/CD test suite to stall, creating a denial-of-service condition against the build pipeline. The fix is to wrap each fetch in an AbortController with a reasonable timeout or use a configured HTTP client with timeout defaults.

trace.description: First of eight bare fetch() calls to external URLs. Each call passes only a URL string with no options object, no AbortSignal, and no timeout. The same pattern repeats at lines 20, 29, 39, 51, 61, 69, and 76.

Last fetch() call in the file, same unconfigured pattern. All eight calls target third-party domains (pastebin.com, listverse.disqus.com, stackoverflow.com) over the public internet with no client-side timeout or connection limit.
const body = await res.text() — the response body is consumed. If the server accepted the TCP connection but sends the body very slowly, this await blocks indefinitely with no timeout.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) — test asserts on the response status, but this line is only reached after the fetch promise on line 12 resolves, which has no upper time bound.
assert.ok(body.includes('Hueteroneel')) — body content assertion. The entire test case blocks if either the fetch or the body read hangs.
assert.ok(body.includes('this coupled with Eurogium Edule...')) — second body assertion, same blocking behavior.
Second instance of the same unconfigured pattern: fetch('https://pastebin.com/8SMbWPxc') with no timeout option. The response is consumed identically on lines 21-25.
const body = await res.text() for the second fetch — same missing-timeout exposure on body read.
Third instance: fetch('https://pastebin.com/G47LrDr0') with no timeout. Response consumed on lines 30-35.
const body = await res.text() for the third fetch — same missing-timeout exposure.
Fourth instance: fetch('https://pastebin.com/t8jqE1y7') with no timeout. Response consumed on lines 40-47.
const body = await res.text() for the fourth fetch — same missing-timeout exposure.
Fifth instance: fetch('https://pastebin.com/RXrihEMS') with no timeout. Response consumed on lines 52-56.
const body = await res.text() for the fifth fetch — same missing-timeout exposure.
Sixth instance: fetch('https://listverse.disqus.com/.../latest.rss') with no timeout. Different external domain, same unconfigured pattern. Response consumed on lines 62-65.
const body = await res.text() for the sixth fetch — same missing-timeout exposure on body read.
Seventh instance: fetch('https://pastebin.com/4U1V1UjU') with no timeout. Response consumed on lines 70-72.
const body = await res.text() for the seventh fetch — same missing-timeout exposure.
const body = await res.text() for the eighth fetch — same missing-timeout exposure on body read. Any of these eight calls can hang indefinitely.

The unconfigured fetch() will hang indefinitely if the remote server accepts the TCP connection but never responds, or responds very slowly. Since Node's fetch has no built-in default timeout, there is no upper bound on how long any of these requests can block the test runner, enabling a denial-of-service against the test pipeline.

title: Password change succeeds via GET without verifying the current password
description: The test at lines 92–103 explicitly demonstrates that an authenticated user (Bender) can change their password through a GET request to /rest/user/change-password WITHOUT providing the 'current' password parameter. The test only sends 'new' and 'repeat' and expects HTTP 200 success. This means the current-password verification — which is present for the same endpoint when called with a wrong current password (lines 41–53, expecting 401) — is bypassed when the current parameter is omitted entirely on a GET request. An attacker who obtains a valid session token (via XSS, token theft, or any other means) can immediately change the victim's password without knowing it, achieving full account takeover. This is both an authentication failure (the credential check that guards password change is bypassable) and an access-control failure (the user's identity re-authentication for a sensitive mutation is skipped).

trace.description: Test 'GET password change for Bender without current password using GET request' — the entrypoint is the GET /rest/user/change-password endpoint being tested. The caller (route handler) is outside this file.
The request is sent to /rest/user/change-password?new=slurmCl4ssic&repeat=slurmCl4ssic with a valid Bearer token but NO 'current' password parameter.

Contrast: this test sends a wrong current password (line 48) and correctly receives 401 (line 51), proving the current-password check exists in the handler but is bypassed when the parameter is simply omitted on a GET request.
The test first logs in as Bender to obtain a valid session token, establishing that the user is authenticated but that no current-password re-verification will follow.

The test asserts res.status === 200, confirming the password change succeeds without current password verification. Compare with lines 41–53 where a wrong current password correctly yields 401 — the check exists but is bypassed when the parameter is absent on a GET request.

title: Passwords transmitted in GET query parameters exposing them in logs and browser history
description: The password change endpoint /rest/user/change-password accepts the current password, new password, and repeated password as URL query parameters on GET requests (lines 35, 48, 99). URLs with query strings are routinely recorded in web server access logs, proxy logs, browser history, and can leak via Referer headers to third-party resources. This means plaintext passwords — including the user's current password — are written to logs wherever the request passes through. This is an insecure design choice (GET should never be used for state-changing operations involving secrets) and a logging-monitoring failure (sensitive credential data ends up in log files in plaintext).

trace.description: Test sends a GET request with current=kunigunde&new=foo&repeat=foo as query parameters. The actual route handler is outside this file.
Additional confirmation: another test sends new=slurmCl4ssic&repeat=slurmCl4ssic in the GET query string. All password-change tests use GET with credentials in the URL.
Another test sends current=definetely_wrong&new=blubb&repeat=blubb in the GET query string, confirming the pattern is systemic to this endpoint, not a single test's choice.

The full URL /rest/user/change-password?current=kunigunde&new=foo&repeat=foo contains plaintext passwords in the query string, which will be logged by any HTTP server, reverse proxy, or intermediary that records request URLs.

title: Password reset via security questions with no evidence of rate limiting enables brute force
description: The password reset endpoint POST /rest/user/reset-password (lines 107–261) authenticates the reset request solely via a security question answer. The tests show that a correct answer (e.g., 'Samuel' for Jim, 'Stop\'n\'Drop' for Bender) immediately resets the password. There is no indication of any rate limiting, lockout, or throttling on this endpoint — the test at lines 177–190 sends a wrong answer and gets a clean 401 with no mention of remaining attempts or cooldown. An attacker can brute-force security question answers (which are typically low-entropy and guessable — 'Samuel' is a common name) without any lockout mechanism. This is both a resource-consumption issue (no rate limiting on an authentication-adjacent endpoint) and a crypto-auth issue (the security question answer acts as a credential and can be brute-forced).

trace.description: Test POSTs to /rest/user/reset-password with email, answer, new, and repeat in the JSON body. The route handler is outside this file.

Test 'POST password reset with wrong answer to security question' sends a wrong answer and expects a simple 401 with 'Wrong answer to security question.' — no rate-limit header, no lockout indicator, no 429 response.
The request body includes email, answer, new, and repeat — the security question answer is the sole credential gate for the password reset.
The answer 'Samuel' is a low-entropy, guessable value, illustrating that security question answers serve as weak credentials protecting account takeover.
The 401 response with a plain error message and no throttling confirms that repeated guesses are accepted, enabling brute-force attacks on security question answers to reset any user's password.

title: Unauthenticated coupon generation via AI chat tool call
description: The test at lines 356–383 demonstrates that the `/rest/chat` endpoint allows an unauthenticated user to trigger the `generateCoupon` tool through the LLM. The test sends no Authorization header, yet the tool successfully generates a coupon with a discount of 5. By contrast, the `getOrderById` tool (lines 303–327) does enforce authentication and returns 'Customer not authenticated' when no token is present. This inconsistency shows that the `generateCoupon` tool — a financially sensitive operation — has no authorization check, and the LLM is granted the agency to execute it based solely on the model's decision without verifying the user's permissions. An attacker can simply send a chat message like 'Give me a coupon' and receive a valid discount code without ever logging in.

trace.description: The test sends a POST to /rest/chat with content-type application/json and a user message 'Give me a coupon'. No Authorization header is set, meaning the request is unauthenticated.

The mock LLM responds with a tool_call for generateCoupon with arguments {"discount":5}. The application's chat handler receives this tool call and executes the generateCoupon tool server-side. The caller (route handler) is outside this file.
On the second LLM request, the tool result message is present in the request body, confirming the generateCoupon tool was executed and its result fed back into the conversation.
Test definition: 'POST handles generateCoupon tool call and includes coupon code in tool response'. The test will send an unauthenticated request expecting a coupon to be generated.
callCount variable initialized to 0. This counter will track the two LLM round-trips: the first returns a tool call, the second returns the final response after tool execution.
onLlmRequest callback is assigned. This mock stands in for the real LLM API; the application's chat handler (outside this file) will call it.

The toolCallChunk specifies id 'call_cpn', name 'generateCoupon', and args '{"discount":5}'. The application receives this tool call from the LLM and must decide whether to execute it — the agency boundary is crossed here.
The tool result is extracted from parsed.messages by finding the message with role 'tool'. This confirms the tool was executed and its output was captured.
.set({ 'content-type': 'application/json' }) — only content-type is set. No Authorization header, no token. The request is fully unauthenticated.
.send({ messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Give me a coupon' }] }) — the user message that triggers the coupon generation flow.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) — the unauthenticated request succeeded with HTTP 200, confirming the endpoint and tool execution were not blocked by authentication.
const parsed = JSON.parse(toolResult) — the tool result is valid JSON, meaning a structured coupon object was generated.
assert.equal(parsed.discount, 5) — the coupon has a discount of 5, confirming the tool accepted the LLM-supplied discount value without authorization.

assert.ok(parsed.couponCode !== undefined) — a coupon code was generated. An unauthenticated user has obtained a valid discount coupon through the LLM tool call, proving the access-control and agency boundary was crossed.

The test asserts toolResult is truthy, then parses it as JSON and asserts parsed.discount === 5 and parsed.couponCode !== undefined (lines 380-382). These assertions pass, proving a coupon was generated for an unauthenticated user. The generateCoupon tool executed a financial action without verifying the caller's identity or authorization — a Broken Function Level Authorization gap combined with excessive AI agency.

title: Chat endpoint accessible without authentication with privileged tool access
description: Multiple tests (lines 118–258, 356–383) send requests to `/rest/chat` without any Authorization header and receive 200 responses. The chat endpoint exposes four tools to the LLM (line 187–191): searchProducts, generateCoupon, getOrderById, and getProductReviews. While getOrderById individually checks authentication (lines 303–327), the endpoint itself does not require authentication, and tools like generateCoupon do not enforce their own authorization. This is an insecure design: the chat endpoint is a privileged interface that can trigger server-side actions (coupon generation, order lookup, product search) but is not gated behind authentication at the endpoint level.

trace.description: The first test (lines 118-137) sends a POST to /rest/chat with no Authorization header and receives a 200 response with streamed content. This establishes that the chat endpoint is accessible without authentication.

The test at lines 173-192 verifies that the LLM request includes 4 tool definitions: searchProducts, generateCoupon, getOrderById, and getProductReviews. These tools are exposed to the model even for unauthenticated users.

The test at lines 356-383 demonstrates that an unauthenticated request can trigger the generateCoupon tool, which produces a valid coupon. The endpoint-level lack of authentication, combined with tool-level inconsistency in authorization checks (getOrderById checks, generateCoupon does not), is a broken function-level authorization and insecure design defect.

title: Hardcoded credentials in test source
description: The test file contains hardcoded credentials at line 261 (email and base64-encoded password for an admin account) and line 330 (email and plaintext password for a regular user). While these are test credentials for the OWASP Juice Shop deliberately vulnerable application, hardcoded credentials in source code are always a security finding. The admin credential `bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=` (base64) and user password `ncc-1701` are committed in plaintext. If this test file is deployed or accessible, these credentials could be used to authenticate to a production instance.

trace.description: Hardcoded admin credentials are used directly in the login call: email 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' with password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI='. Line 330 contains another set: email 'jim@juice-sh.op' with password 'ncc-1701'.

let parsedBody: any — variable declared to capture the LLM request body. This is setup for the test, not directly part of the credential flow, but shows the test proceeds to use the authenticated session.
onLlmRequest = (_req, body, res) => { ... } — the mock LLM callback is assigned. The authenticated request will be sent next.
const res = await request(app).post('/rest/chat') — the authenticated chat request is constructed using the token obtained from the hardcoded credentials.
.set({ 'content-type': 'application/json', Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token }) — the token derived from hardcoded admin credentials is used in the Authorization header.
A second set of hardcoded credentials: email 'jim@juice-sh.op' with password 'ncc-1701'. These are used in another login() call for a different test.
const res = await request(app).post('/rest/chat') — another authenticated chat request using the second set of hardcoded credentials.
.set({ 'content-type': 'application/json', Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token }) — the token from the second hardcoded credential pair is used.
These credentials are passed to the login() helper and used to obtain authentication tokens (line 270: 'Bearer ' + token). The credentials are embedded in the source file permanently.

title: User-supplied chat messages flow into LLM context without prompt injection fencing visible in test
description: The tests send arbitrary user content (e.g., 'What is your name?', 'Do you have apple juice?', 'Give me a coupon') as message content to the `/rest/chat` endpoint. The test at lines 154-171 confirms that a system prompt is prepended and user messages are sent directly to the LLM. The test does not show any fencing, delimiter, or separation between user-controlled content and system instructions. While this test file cannot confirm the exact server-side implementation, the test structure shows raw user text reaching the LLM alongside a system prompt containing application context (including the user's name when authenticated, per line 274). An attacker could inject instructions in the user message to override the system prompt and manipulate tool calls — for example, tricking the LLM into calling generateCoupon with a higher discount value.

trace.description: User message content 'What is your name?' is sent in the request body as messages: [{role:'user', content:'...'}]. The test confirms this reaches the LLM as the second message (line 169-170).

The test confirms parsedBody.messages[0] is a system prompt and parsedBody.messages[1] is the user's message. The user content is sent directly alongside the system prompt with no visible fencing or delimiter in the test assertions.
Test definition: 'POST includes system prompt and user messages in LLM request'. This test verifies that the system prompt and user messages are forwarded to the LLM.
let parsedBody: any — variable declared to capture the LLM request body for inspection.

onLlmRequest = (_req, body, res) => { ... } — the mock LLM callback captures the request body. This is where the application forwards user content to the LLM (the caller that constructs this body is outside this file).
parsedBody = JSON.parse(body) — the LLM request body is parsed. This body contains both the system prompt and the user's message.

title: POST /api/PrivacyRequests accepts client-supplied UserId, enabling cross-user privacy request creation
description: The test at lines 22-35 sends a POST to /api/PrivacyRequests with a UserId field in the request body (UserId: 1) and expects a 201 response. This demonstrates that the API accepts a client-controlled user identifier rather than deriving the user from the authenticated session token. If the server trusts this client-supplied UserId, any authenticated user can create privacy (deletion) requests on behalf of other users by simply changing the UserId value. The server should derive the user identity from the session token, not from a body field the caller can set to any value. This is a Broken Object Level Authorization issue: the resource (privacy request) is created under a user ID supplied by the caller, with no verification that the caller owns that identity.

The authentication outcome (who the caller is) is not anchored to a trusted identity claim — it is left to the client to declare.

title: Data erasure endpoint does not actually delete user data
description: The POST /dataerasure/ endpoint is intended to handle GDPR-style data erasure requests, but the test explicitly demonstrates that after submitting an erasure request, the user can still successfully authenticate with the same credentials. This means the erasure workflow is a no-op — the design of the erasure process allows it to complete successfully (HTTP 200) without performing the deletion it claims to perform. A user who requests data erasure has no guarantee their data is removed, which is a fundamental design flaw in a privacy-critical workflow.

title: NoSQL injection in PATCH /rest/products/reviews enables mass modification of all reviews
description: The PATCH /rest/products/reviews endpoint accepts the `id` field as an arbitrary object and passes it directly to a MongoDB query without validating that it is a simple identifier. The test at lines 120-136 demonstrates this by sending `id: { $ne: -1 }`, which matches every review in the database, and asserts that `res.body.modified` equals `totalReviews` — the count of all reviews across all products. This means any authenticated user can overwrite the message of every review in the system in a single request. The design flaw is that the server never enforces that `id` must be a scalar string; it accepts a MongoDB query operator object and uses it as a filter. Beyond the design defect, this is also a broken access control: the endpoint modifies reviews belonging to other users/products without any per-resource ownership check — the only gate is authentication, not authorization.

The request includes an Authorization header from a generic token generated by security.authorize() with no user arguments (line 18), meaning the only access gate is authentication, not per-resource ownership.
The `id` field in the request body is set to { $ne: -1 }, a MongoDB 'not equal' operator object, rather than a scalar review identifier. The server accepts this without validation.
The server responds with status 200, confirming the bulk modification succeeded.
totalReviews is computed from config products by reducing over all reviews across all products. This value is used later to prove the modification affected every review.
