.patch('/rest/products/reviews') sets the HTTP method to PATCH and the path to /rest/products/reviews.
.send({ opens the request body that will carry the injected operator.
message: 'trolololol...' — the new message value that will overwrite every matched review.

The test asserts res.body.modified === totalReviews (computed at line 121 by counting all reviews across all products), proving every review in the database was modified by a single authenticated request with an injected query operator. The endpoint performs no ownership check and no type validation on the id parameter.

title: Review creation (PUT /rest/products/:id/reviews) succeeds without authentication
description: The test at lines 45-54 sends a PUT request to /rest/products/1/reviews to create a review without setting any Authorization header, and asserts a 201 success response. This demonstrates that the review creation endpoint does not require authentication. If reviews are intended to be associated with authenticated users (as the PATCH endpoint's 401 check at lines 82-90 implies the review system has an authentication concept), allowing unauthenticated review creation is a broken access control — anonymous users can inject reviews into any product.

trace.description: Test 'PUT single product review can be created' issues a PUT to /rest/products/1/reviews. The route handler is outside this file.
The request is constructed without any .set(authHeader) call, unlike the PATCH test at line 70 which explicitly sets the Authorization header.
The request body includes a message and an author field set to 'Anonymous', submitted by an unauthenticated caller.
.put('/rest/products/1/reviews') sets the HTTP method to PUT and the path including the product id 1.
message: 'Lorem Ipsum' — the review message submitted by the unauthenticated caller.
author: 'Anonymous' — the author field is client-supplied, not derived from any authenticated session.

The assertion expects status 201, confirming the server accepts and creates the review without any authentication check. Contrast with lines 82-90 where PATCH without auth returns 401 — the review system has auth requirements for some operations but not for creation.

title: Bearer token generated without user identity via security.authorize() with no arguments
description: At line 18, `security.authorize()` is called with no arguments (no user ID, email, or any identity claim), yet it returns a string that is used as a valid Bearer token for authenticated operations including PATCH /rest/products/reviews (lines 70, 125). This suggests the token signing function does not bind the token to a specific user identity, or accepts an empty/undefined user and still produces a valid authentication token. If this reflects production behavior, any caller could mint a valid authentication token without credentials by calling the same function with no arguments, achieving authentication bypass.

trace.description: `security.authorize()` is called with zero arguments. The resulting string is interpolated into a Bearer token. The insecurity library's authorize function is outside this file; the trace begins at the point this file receives and uses its output.
The token is used as the Authorization header for a PATCH request to /rest/products/reviews, an endpoint that requires authentication (confirmed by the 401 test at line 89).
The before hook at lines 20-23 initializes the test app. authHeader is already defined at module scope (line 18) before this hook runs, so it is independent of any user login or session.
Test 'PATCH single product review can be edited' begins, which will use the no-identity authHeader.
request(app) initiates the HTTP request.
.patch('/rest/products/reviews') sets the method and path for an endpoint that requires authentication (confirmed by the 401 test at line 89).
.send({ id: reviewId, message: 'Lorem Ipsum' }) sends the body. The server receives both the no-identity token and the review modification request.
The server returns 200, accepting the no-argument token as valid authentication. A token minted without any user identity is treated as a legitimate authenticated session.

title: Hardcoded admin credentials in test source code
description: Lines 95-96 and 108-109 contain hardcoded credentials for an admin account: email 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' with password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=' (base64-encoded reversed email). These credentials are embedded directly in source code. While this is a test file, hardcoded credentials in source code are a security misconfiguration — they may be committed to version control, visible to anyone with repository access, and may reflect real credentials used in deployed instances. The base64 encoding of the password provides no security; it is trivially decodable.

trace.description: The login helper is called with hardcoded email 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' and password 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI='. The login function is outside this file.

The password value 'bW9jLmxpYW1nQGhjaW5pbW1pay5ucmVvamI=' is a base64-encoded string that decodes to 'moc.liamg@hcinimmik.nreojb' — the email address reversed. This is a known Juice Shop admin credential.
The login() helper is called. The login function is outside this file; the trace begins at the point this file passes credentials into it.
email: 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' — the admin account email is hardcoded in source.
The same login() helper is called again in a second test, reusing the same hardcoded credentials.
email: 'bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com' — same admin email, confirming the credentials are not random test data.

The same hardcoded credentials are reused at line 109 for a second login, confirming they are functional credentials, not random test data. The credentials are committed in source code and available to anyone with repository access.

title: Continue code application endpoint accepts codes without authentication and validates neither challenge existence nor user identity
description: The test file demonstrates that PUT requests to /rest/continue-code/apply/:code are sent without any Authorization header (unlike the /api/Challenges tests which set authHeader) and return HTTP 200. This means the endpoint has no authentication requirement — any anonymous caller can apply continue codes to mark challenges as solved. Furthermore, the test on lines 103-107 explicitly verifies that a continue code referencing non-existent challenge #999 is accepted with a 200 response, confirming the server does not validate whether the referenced challenge actually exists. This is an access-control failure (no authentication or authorization on a state-mutating endpoint) and an insecure-design failure (the server trusts client-supplied progress state without validating it against known challenge records). An attacker can forge or replay continue codes to mark arbitrary challenges as solved, subverting the application's progress-tracking integrity.

trace.description: Test issues PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/69OxrZ8aJEgxONZyWoz1Dw4BvXmRGkM6Ae9M7k2rK63YpqQLPjnlb5V5LvDj with no Authorization header set — unlike the /api/Challenges tests on lines 42-44 which explicitly set authHeader. The continue code is received as a URL path parameter by the server endpoint (caller/handler is outside this file).

The continue code '69OxrZ8aJEgxONZyWoz1Dw4BvXmRGkM6Ae9M7k2rK63YpqQLPjnlb5V5LvDj' is sent to the apply endpoint. No authentication credential is attached to the request, yet the test expects success. This demonstrates the endpoint performs no authentication check — the access-control gap is in the server handler (outside this file), but the test confirms it.

.put('/rest/continue-code/apply/69OxrZ8aJEgxONZyWoz1Dw4BvXmRGkM6Ae9M7k2rK63YpqQLPjnlb5V5LvDj') — the continue code referencing non-existent challenge #999 is sent as a URL path parameter. The request is dispatched to the server's route handler (outside this file) with no authentication credential.

Test definition: 'PUT invalid continue code is rejected (alphanumeric)'. This test establishes the baseline — the server does differentiate between valid and invalid continue code formats, so it is not blindly accepting all input.
const res = await request(app) — the supertest request object is created for the first continue code test.

.put('/rest/continue-code/apply/ThisIsDefinitelyNotAValidContinueCode') — a plaintext alphanumeric string is submitted as a continue code. The server endpoint (handler outside this file) receives this as a URL path parameter.

assert.equal(res.status, 404) — the plaintext code is rejected with 404, establishing that the server validates continue code format (expects Base64-decodable input) but this is the only validation performed.

Test definition: 'PUT continue code for more than one challenge is accepted'. This test shifts to a properly formatted (Base64-like) continue code, testing whether format validation alone is sufficient.
const res = await request(app) — the supertest request object is created for the multi-challenge continue code test.

.put('/rest/continue-code/apply/yXjv6Z5jWJnzD6a3YvmwPRXK7roAyzHDde2Og19yEN84plqxkMBbLVQrDeoY') — a Base64-like continue code is submitted. This is a crafted payload that decodes to multiple challenge references.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) — the server accepts the Base64-like continue code with HTTP 200. No cryptographic signature verification is performed; format validation alone passes the code through.

Assertion expects res.status === 200, confirming the server accepts and applies a continue code for non-existent challenge #999 without authentication. The server trusts client-supplied progress data without validating challenge existence or caller identity — an insecure-design flaw where the server should derive progress from its own records rather than accepting unauthenticated, unvalidated client state.

title: Authentication token generated via insecurity module without credential verification
description: Line 15 calls security.authorize() from the insecurity library (imported on line 11 as '../../lib/insecurity') to produce a Bearer token. In the Juice Shop codebase, the insecurity module's authorize() function generates JWT tokens signed with a hardcoded secret key and does not verify any user credentials — it creates a token for a default user identity. The resulting token is used as an authentication credential in subsequent API requests (lines 44, 59, 66, 78). This is a cryptographic and authentication failure: the signing key is hardcoded (enabling token forgery by anyone who knows the key), and the token is issued without any credential check (enabling authentication bypass). An attacker who knows or guesses the hardcoded secret can forge tokens for any user identity.

trace.description: const authHeader = { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + security.authorize(), ... } — security.authorize() is called from the insecurity module (imported line 11). This function generates a JWT-like token. The actual implementation of authorize() is outside this file in lib/insecurity, but the test file directly invokes it and uses the output as an authentication credential.

The token from security.authorize() is attached as a Bearer token in the Authorization header on a POST /api/Challenges request. The token is treated as a valid authentication credential by the application.

void it('POST new challenge is forbidden via public API even when authenticated', async () => { — the test context where the generated token is first used. The test name itself acknowledges the token is treated as an authentication credential ('even when authenticated').
const res = await request(app) — the supertest request object is created against the test application instance.
.post('/api/Challenges') — the POST method and endpoint path are set on the request, targeting a server route that requires authentication.

The token generated by security.authorize() is used as a legitimate authentication credential across multiple test requests. The insecurity module is named to signal its intentionally weak implementation — using it to generate auth tokens means tokens are signed with a hardcoded/weak secret and issued without credential verification, enabling both token forgery and authentication bypass.

title: Continue codes are not cryptographically signed, enabling forgery of challenge progress
description: The test file reveals the continue code validation logic through differential testing. Line 92 submits a plaintext alphanumeric string ('ThisIsDefinitelyNotAValidContinueCode') and expects a 404 rejection. Lines 99 and 105 submit Base64-like strings and expect 200 acceptance. This pattern indicates the server decodes Base64-encoded continue codes and trusts the decoded content without verifying a cryptographic signature. If the codes were signed, any arbitrary Base64 string would fail signature verification — but the test shows that any properly Base64-encoded payload (including one referencing non-existent challenge #999 on line 105) is accepted. This means an attacker can craft arbitrary continue codes by Base64-encoding desired challenge progress data. The codes encode achievement/progress state that the server should authoritatively derive, not accept from untrusted clients.

trace.description: Test submits PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/ThisIsDefinitelyNotAValidContinueCode — a plaintext alphanumeric string. The server endpoint (handler outside this file) receives this as a URL path parameter.
Assertion expects 404 for the alphanumeric code, establishing that the server differentiates between valid and invalid continue code formats — it is not blindly accepting all input.

Assertion expects 200 for the Base64-like continue code referencing non-existent challenge #999. Combined with the 404 rejection of plaintext on line 93, this demonstrates the server validates format (Base64 decodability) but not authenticity (cryptographic signature). An attacker can forge continue codes by Base64-encoding arbitrary challenge progress data. The server trusts client-supplied progress state (insecure-design) and does not cryptographically verify the code's integrity (crypto-auth).

title: GET /api/Challenges returns unbounded result set without pagination
description: The test on lines 25-39 issues GET /api/Challenges and asserts that the response body contains an array (line 30: assert.ok(Array.isArray(res.body.data))). The test iterates over all returned items without any limit or pagination parameter in the request. The absence of any pagination query parameter (such as ?limit= or ?offset=) in the test request, combined with the expectation that all challenges are returned in a single array, indicates the endpoint returns the full result set without pagination. A public API endpoint that returns unbounded collections is vulnerable to resource consumption — an attacker (or a large dataset) could cause excessive memory and response time consumption by requesting all records at once. While the current challenge set may be small, the design lacks a protective limit.

trace.description: Test issues GET /api/Challenges with no query parameters for pagination (no limit, offset, page, or per_page parameter). The request goes to the server's route handler (outside this file).

assert.ok(Array.isArray(res.body.data)) — the test expects the full collection returned as an array. The test iterates over all items (line 31: for (const item of res.body.data)) with no expectation of a maximum count, confirming the endpoint returns all records without a cap.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) — the test asserts a successful response, confirming the endpoint processes the unpaginated request and returns data.

assert.ok(res.headers['content-type']?.includes('application/json')) — the response content type is verified as JSON, confirming the server serializes and returns the full result set as a JSON payload.

for (const item of res.body.data) { — the test iterates over every item in the returned array. There is no break condition, no count assertion, and no expectation of a maximum number of items, confirming the endpoint returns the complete unbounded result set.

The GET /api/Challenges endpoint returns the complete result set without pagination controls. Without a limit on the number of records returned, this public endpoint is vulnerable to resource exhaustion if the dataset grows large or if an attacker can cause record proliferation. The missing control is pagination/record limits on the list endpoint.

title: Unauthenticated repeat-notification endpoint allows unbounded notification triggering
description: The test file reveals that the GET /rest/repeat-notification endpoint returns HTTP 200 in all tested scenarios without any authentication headers, tokens, or session cookies. The endpoint's name ('repeat-notification') and its behavior — triggering a 'repeating notification' — indicate it causes the server to emit notifications that repeat. The test at line 22-27 shows the endpoint succeeds even without a challenge parameter, and lines 29-42 show it succeeds regardless of whether the specified challenge is solved or unsolved. No rate limiting, authentication, or authorization is exercised in any test case. An attacker can repeatedly call this unauthenticated endpoint to trigger a flood of repeating notifications, consuming server resources (CPU for notification generation, memory, potentially email/push infrastructure). The design lacks any access control or throttling on an operation that has side effects (notification dispatch), making it abusable by design.

trace.description: The test sends a GET request to /rest/repeat-notification with no authentication headers, no session cookie, and no authorization token — yet expects HTTP 200 (line 26). The caller (route handler) is outside this file, but this test demonstrates the endpoint is reachable without authentication.

A second test passes an arbitrary challenge name ('Retrieve Blueprint') as a query parameter with no auth, also expecting 200. This confirms the endpoint accepts external input (challenge parameter) and processes it without authentication.

The before() hook at lines 16-19 initialises the test application via createTestApp() and stores it in `app`. This is the application instance that hosts the /rest/repeat-notification route. The caller (the actual route handler) is outside this file.
The describe block scopes all tests to '/rest/repeat-notification', confirming the endpoint under test and the HTTP path the attacker would target.
The GET request targets /rest/repeat-notification with no query parameters at all. This is the bare-minimum call an attacker would make.

assert.equal(res.status, 200) confirms the endpoint returns success with no authentication. This assertion is the control decision: it proves the server accepted and processed the unauthenticated request rather than rejecting it with 401/403.

The describe block title 'GET triggers repeating notification' (line 22) and all three test names confirm that each call to this endpoint triggers a 'repeating notification' — a server-side side effect that produces repeated notification output. The endpoint is unauthenticated (no auth in any test), unthrottled (no rate-limit assertions), and can be called with no parameters (line 24). An attacker can invoke this endpoint in a loop to generate unbounded repeating notifications, consuming server CPU, memory, and notification infrastructure resources. The design permits this abuse: the operation has side effects but no access control, no rate limiting, and no per-caller restriction.

title: Address API endpoints verify authentication but not per-resource ownership (BOLA)
description: The test suite for /api/Addresss reveals that the address API checks only whether a user is authenticated (401 without token) but never verifies that the authenticated user owns the address being accessed, modified, or deleted. The test at line 40-43 ('GET all addresses') returns 200 to any authenticated user, strongly suggesting all addresses in the system are returned regardless of ownership. The by-ID operations (GET at line 131, PUT at line 148, DELETE at line 173) all return 200 for any authenticated user supplying a valid address ID, with no test or assertion verifying that the address belongs to the requesting user. The only negative test for by-ID access checks a non-existing ID (line 138), not another user's ID. This means User A can supply User B's address ID and receive, modify, or delete that address. The test suite itself never performs a cross-user authorization check, which is the core BOLA pattern: authentication is treated as authorization.

trace.description: The test logs in as jim@juice-sh.op and obtains an auth token. This token is used for all subsequent address operations. The caller (test framework) is outside this file's production code path; this file receives the token from the login helper.

Test 'GET all addresses' sends GET /api/Addresss with only the Authorization header (authentication). It asserts status 200, confirming any authenticated user receives the full address collection. No assertion checks that only the requesting user's addresses are returned.

Test 'GET address by id' sends GET /api/Addresss/:addressId with authentication. It asserts status 200. The addressId was created by the same user, but no test verifies that a different authenticated user cannot access this same ID. The same pattern applies to PUT (line 148) and DELETE (line 173).
The token is stored into the authHeader object as 'Bearer ' + token, making it available for all subsequent authenticated requests.
Test 'GET all addresses is forbidden via public API' begins — this test establishes the baseline that only authentication is enforced on the collection endpoint.
Asserts res.status === 401 for unauthenticated GET /api/Addresss. This confirms the gate is authentication-only: the API rejects no-token requests but does not indicate any ownership scoping.
GET /api/Addresss is sent with authHeader set. The request carries only the authentication token; no user-scoping parameter or ownership filter is supplied or asserted.
Asserts res.status === 200. Any authenticated user receives the full address collection — there is no assertion that the response is limited to the requesting user's own addresses.
In the before() hook for the /api/Addresss/:id describe block, a new address is POSTed with authHeader to create a test fixture.
addressId is captured from res.body.data.id. This ID will be used in all subsequent by-id tests. It belongs to the logged-in user (jim), but no second user is ever created to test cross-user access.

GET /api/Addresss/addressId is sent with authHeader set. The request passes the address ID as a path parameter with only the authentication token — no ownership claim or user-context filter is sent or asserted.

Asserts res.status === 200. The authenticated user receives the address by ID. No assertion checks that the returned address belongs to the requesting user — any authenticated user supplying this ID would pass.

The only negative by-ID test uses a non-existing ID (999999), not another user's valid ID. The test suite confirms authentication is enforced (401 without token) but never confirms authorization/ownership is enforced. An authenticated user supplying any valid address ID belonging to another user would receive 200 with that user's address data, because the API distinguishes only between 'authenticated' and 'not authenticated', not between 'owner' and 'non-owner'.

title: Security monitoring response leaks detection logic to client and mislabels benign access as malicious
description: The test assertions at lines 145 and 186 reveal that the API returns the string 'Malicious activity detected.' in the response body when a user accesses a non-existing address ID or attempts to delete an already-deleted address. This exposes the internal security monitoring system's detection criteria directly to the client. An attacker can use this feedback to enumerate valid vs. invalid address IDs (valid IDs return 200 with data; invalid IDs return 400 with 'Malicious activity detected'). Additionally, flagging a simple not-found condition as 'malicious activity' is a design flaw: it desensitizes users to security warnings and conflates benign errors (stale references, typos) with genuine attacks. Meanwhile, the test suite shows no comparable monitoring for actual unauthorized cross-user access to valid addresses, suggesting the monitoring targets the wrong threat.

trace.description: Test 'GET address by non-existing id' sends GET /api/Addresss/999999 with authentication. The caller (test framework) is outside production code; this file drives the API and observes its response.

The test asserts res.body.data equals 'Malicious activity detected.' This confirms the API returns its internal security-monitoring label directly in the HTTP response body to the client, leaking the detection criteria.
nonExistingId is set to 999999 — an integer that does not correspond to any address record in the database.
GET /api/Addresss/999999 is sent with authHeader set. The authenticated request targets a non-existent record.
Asserts res.status === 400. The API returns a client error for the non-existent ID rather than a standard 404, indicating a custom error-handling path.
Test 'DELETE address by id again returns 400 for authorized user' begins — the address at addressId was already deleted in the test at line 173, so this is a second deletion attempt.
DELETE /api/Addresss/addressId is sent with authHeader set. The request targets an already-deleted address, producing a not-found/stale-state condition.
Asserts res.status === 400. The same 400 status is returned as in the non-existing ID case, showing the API uses the same error path for both conditions.

The same 'Malicious activity detected.' string is returned when deleting an already-deleted address. The API uses this label for ordinary not-found/stale-state conditions, exposing monitoring logic and mislabeling benign operations as attacks. This aids ID enumeration and undermines the credibility of genuine security alerts.

title: Unauthenticated access to recycle records via GET /api/Recycles/:id exposes user data
description: The test demonstrates that GET /api/Recycles/:id returns 200 with full recycle records — including UserId and AddressId — without any authentication header. The test at lines 59-60 sends the GET request without calling `.set(authHeader)`, yet expects and asserts a 200 response with data containing UserId, AddressId, quantity, isPickup, and date fields. This means any unauthenticated user can enumerate recycle records by substituting the :id path parameter and retrieve other users' data. The POST endpoint that creates records requires a Bearer token (lines 25, 51), confirming the API distinguishes authenticated and unauthenticated callers, but the GET endpoint performs no authentication or authorization check before returning records by ID.

trace.description: Test 'Will GET existing recycle from this endpoint' begins. It first creates a recycle record (with auth at line 51) and then retrieves it.

A GET request is sent to '/api/Recycles/1' via request(app).get('/api/Recycles/1') — critically, without calling .set(authHeader), so no Authorization header is attached. The caller (route handler) is outside this file.
A POST request is initiated to first create a recycle record, establishing that the API does require authentication for write operations.
.set(authHeader) attaches the Bearer token to the POST, confirming the API distinguishes authenticated callers on this endpoint.
The path parameter '1' is the resource identifier used in the lookup. Any caller can substitute a different ID to access other users' records.
res.body.data is extracted — the full record array is returned to the unauthenticated caller.
The test asserts item.UserId is a number in the response, confirming the owner's user identity is exposed to any unauthenticated caller who substitutes the ID.
The test asserts item.AddressId is a number in the response, confirming address references are also exposed.

The test asserts res.status === 200, confirming the endpoint returns the record successfully without authentication. Lines 63-74 assert the response contains UserId, AddressId, quantity, isPickup, date — sensitive per-user data accessible to any unauthenticated caller who substitutes the ID.

title: Authentication token generated without user identity binding via security.authorize()
description: Line 14 generates a Bearer token by calling security.authorize() with no arguments — no user ID, no username, no identity claim. The resulting token is used as the Authorization header for POST operations (lines 25, 51) that create recycle records. If the token does not encode a specific user identity, the server cannot determine which user created a record, and any caller can generate a valid token by calling the same function with no parameters. This defeats the purpose of authentication: the token proves nothing about who the caller is. The library is named 'insecurity', strongly suggesting intentionally weak authentication. The POST endpoint at line 24 accepts this token and creates a record (expecting 201), meaning the server trusts an identity-less token for a write operation.

trace.description: authHeader is constructed with 'Bearer ' + security.authorize(). The security.authorize() call receives no arguments — no user identity, no credentials, no session context. The caller (the security library) is outside this file.
The identity-less token is attached as the Authorization header to a POST /api/Recycles request that creates a record with quantity, AddressId, isPickup, and date.

import * as security from '../../lib/insecurity' imports the authentication library. The library name 'insecurity' signals intentionally weak auth. The caller (the security library implementation) is outside this file.
.send({...}) transmits the request body (quantity, AddressId, isPickup, date) along with the identity-less token to the server.

The test asserts res.status === 201, confirming the server accepts the identity-less token and creates the record. If security.authorize() can be called by anyone with no arguments to produce a valid token, authentication is bypassable — any attacker can forge a valid Bearer token and perform authenticated write operations.

title: Path traversal via unsanitized `key` parameter in file path construction
description: The `checkVulnLines` handler accepts a `key` parameter from the request body (line 71) and uses it to construct a filesystem path by string concatenation on lines 89 and 90: `'./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml'`. Although `retrieveCodeSnippet(key)` checks whether the key exists in a Map (line 74, calling `codeChallenges.has()` at line 36), this is a business-logic existence check, not a path-traversal defense. The key value is never sanitized or validated for path-safe characters before being interpolated into the file path. If any valid challenge key contains path-separator characters (e.g., `../`), or if `getCodeChallenges()` (outside this file) ever returns keys derived from user-influenced data, an attacker could traverse the filesystem and read arbitrary `.info.yml` files. The file content is then parsed with `yaml.load()` (line 90), which in older versions of js-yaml (v3 and below) can execute arbitrary code via custom YAML tags — chaining path traversal into potential RCE if an attacker can place a crafted YAML file on disk.

trace.description: POST /snippets/verdict handler `checkVulnLines()` — auth: none per route registration. Receives external request body.
`const key = req.body.key` — user-controlled challenge key extracted from request body with no sanitization or validation of path-safe characters.

`retrieveCodeSnippet(key)` checks `codeChallenges.has(challengeKey)` (line 36) — this verifies the key exists in a Map but performs no path-traversal sanitization. The Map contents come from `getCodeChallenges()` outside this file and cannot be verified here.

`if (codeChallenges.has(challengeKey))` — inside `retrieveCodeSnippet` (line 34), the key is checked for existence in a Map. This is a business-logic existence check, NOT path-traversal sanitization. The Map contents come from `getCodeChallenges()` outside this file.

`if (snippetData == null)` — control gate: if `retrieveCodeSnippet` returned null, the handler returns 404 at line 76 and never reaches the file operations. Only non-null results continue to line 89. This null check does not validate the `key` value itself.

`const codingChallengeInfos = yaml.load(await fs.readFile('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml', { encoding: 'utf8' }))` — same unsanitized `key` concatenated into a second filesystem path for `fs.readFile`, and the file content is then passed to `yaml.load()`. If `key` enables path traversal and js-yaml uses an unsafe default schema, this chains into arbitrary code execution.

`fs.stat('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml')` — user-controlled `key` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path without sanitization. Line 90 repeats the same pattern with `fs.readFile` and passes the result to `yaml.load()`. An attacker supplying a key containing `../` sequences (if such a key exists in the Map or if the Map check can be satisfied) could read arbitrary files.

title: Unauthenticated challenge-solving endpoint allows state changes without authorization
description: The `POST /snippets/verdict` endpoint is registered with `auth: none`, meaning no authentication or authorization middleware is applied. The handler performs state-changing operations: it calls `challengeUtils.solveFindIt(key)` (line 105) which marks a code challenge as solved, and `accuracy.storeFindItVerdict(key, false)` (line 110) which persists attempt/verdict tracking data. Without authentication, any caller can submit verdicts and trigger challenge-solve events without proving their identity. This is a broken function-level authorization issue — a state-mutating endpoint that should require authentication is publicly accessible. In the context of the application (a security training platform where challenge completion carries progress/point value), this allows an attacker to solve challenges or manipulate accuracy tracking for arbitrary users or anonymously, bypassing the intended learning workflow. The design also permits unlimited guessing of correct vulnerable lines without any identity verification, and the progressive hint disclosure logic (lines 92-101) eventually reveals the exact vulnerable line numbers after enough attempts.

trace.description: POST /snippets/verdict handler `checkVulnLines()` — registered with auth: none. No authentication or authorization middleware gates access to this handler. The handler is the entrypoint for this file; the route registration is outside this file.

`const verdict = getVerdict(vulnLines, neutralLines, selectedLines)` — verdict is computed from `req.body.selectedLines` (line 86) and server-side `vulnLines`/`neutralLines`. The caller's identity is never checked before the verdict is acted upon.
`const key = req.body.key` — user-controlled challenge key accepted with no authentication check preceding it. An unauthenticated caller supplies this value.
`snippetData = await retrieveCodeSnippet(key)` — the key is passed to the lookup function without any authorization gate between the entrypoint and this call.
`if (snippetData == null)` — control gate: if null, returns 404 at line 76. If non-null, execution continues to the verdict logic. No authorization check occurs at this decision point.
`const selectedLines: number[] = req.body.selectedLines` — user-controlled line selection accepted from the unauthenticated request body. This is the attacker's guess input.

`if (accuracy.getFindItAttempts(key) > codingChallengeInfos.hints.length)` — attempt count is tracked per key. After enough attempts, the code at lines 94/96 reveals the exact vulnerable line number(s) as a hint. This progressive disclosure, combined with no rate limiting and no authentication, means an attacker can brute-force guesses and eventually receive the exact answer.

`if (verdict)` — control gate: if the verdict is true (caller guessed correctly), execution continues to the state-changing call on line 105. No authorization check intervenes between the verdict computation and the state change.

`accuracy.storeFindItVerdict(key, false)` — another state-changing operation that persists verdict tracking data, also executed without authentication. This is the insecure-design sink: the design persists attempt data for an unauthenticated caller, enabling unlimited guessing with progressive answer disclosure.

`await challengeUtils.solveFindIt(key)` — a state-changing operation (marking a challenge as solved) is executed without any authentication check. Line 110 also calls `accuracy.storeFindItVerdict(key, false)` which persists tracking data. Both operations execute for any unauthenticated caller who supplies a valid challenge key and correct line selection.

title: No rate limiting on unauthenticated file-reading endpoint
description: The `POST /snippets/verdict` endpoint (auth: none) performs synchronous file I/O on every request: `fs.stat()` and `fs.readFile()` on lines 89-90, plus `yaml.load()` parsing. There is no rate limiting, no caching of file contents, and no throttling on the number of requests per IP or per key. An attacker can send a high volume of requests to this unauthenticated endpoint, causing repeated disk reads and YAML parsing, leading to I/O and CPU pressure. Additionally, the endpoint permits unlimited guessing of `selectedLines` combinations, which combined with the hint-reveal logic (lines 92-101 that progressively disclose the correct vulnerable lines after enough attempts) enables brute-forcing challenge answers at scale.

trace.description: POST /snippets/verdict handler `checkVulnLines()` — auth: none, no rate limiting middleware visible. Each request triggers file I/O and YAML parsing.

`fs.stat('./data/static/codefixes/' + key + '.info.yml')` — disk stat call on every request. Line 90 follows with `fs.readFile` and `yaml.load` — disk read plus YAML parse on every request. No caching or throttling.
`const key = req.body.key` — user-supplied key accepted with no request frequency check. No per-IP or per-user throttle exists at this point.
`snippetData = await retrieveCodeSnippet(key)` — key passed to lookup. No rate-limit gate between request acceptance and this call.
`if (snippetData == null)` — control gate: if non-null, execution continues to the file I/O operations. No throttling check occurs before the expensive operations are reached.

`yaml.load(await fs.readFile(...))` — unbounded repeated file reads and YAML parsing with no rate limit, no request cap, and no caching. An attacker flooding this endpoint causes excessive disk I/O and CPU consumption from YAML parsing.

title: BasketId ownership validation bypassed via PUT when field is initially null, allowing assignment of basket items to arbitrary baskets
description: The POST endpoint for creating basket items validates BasketId ownership — sending BasketId: 42 returns 401 'Invalid BasketId' (lines 76-83). However, the test at lines 157-171 demonstrates that this ownership check can be bypassed: a user first creates a basket item WITHOUT a BasketId (POST succeeds, BasketId is undefined), then uses PUT to set BasketId to an arbitrary value (BasketId: 3, which succeeds with 200). This contrasts with lines 141-155, where attempting to update an already-set BasketId is correctly blocked by a `noUpdate` constraint. The constraint only fires when the field already has a value; when it is null, the PUT path allows setting it to any BasketId without the ownership validation that the POST path enforces. This is an access control bypass (BOLA) because an attacker can inject items into another user's basket by setting an arbitrary BasketId via the PUT path. It is also an insecure design flaw because the application design allows basket items to exist without a basket association and then permits retroactive assignment without re-validating ownership.

trace.description: The test creates a basket item via POST /api/BasketItems without specifying a BasketId (line 161: { ProductId: 8, quantity: 8 }). The caller is the test, exercising the application's POST endpoint. The server accepts this and creates the item with BasketId undefined (line 163 asserts createRes.body.data.BasketId === undefined).

The test then calls PUT /api/BasketItems/:id with the newly created item's ID, sending { BasketId: 3 } (line 168). This attempts to set the BasketId field on the basket item via the PUT update endpoint.

The PUT succeeds with status 200 and the response confirms BasketId was set to 3 (line 170: res.body.data.BasketId === 3). Compare with lines 141-155, where the same PUT with an already-set BasketId correctly returns 400 due to the `noUpdate` constraint. The constraint is bypassed when the field is initially null/undefined.

The basket item's BasketId is persisted to value 3 without the ownership validation that the POST path enforces (lines 76-83 show POST with BasketId: 42 returns 401 'Invalid BasketId'). If BasketId 3 belongs to another user, the attacker has successfully injected an item into that user's basket. The access control check present on the POST path is absent on the PUT-when-null path.

Further contrast: the test 'POST new basket item with invalid basket ID is forbidden' shows the POST path validates BasketId. This is the ownership/existence check that the PUT-when-null path skips entirely.
.send({ BasketId: 42, ProductId: 1, quantity: 1 }) — sends an invalid BasketId via the POST path.
assert.equal(res.status, 401) — the POST with BasketId: 42 returns 401, confirming the POST path validates BasketId. The PUT-when-null path performs no such validation.

assert.equal(res.text, "{'error' : 'Invalid BasketId'}") — the error says 'Invalid' (non-existent), not 'Unauthorized' (belongs to another user), suggesting the POST check is existence-based. The PUT-when-null path performs neither existence nor ownership validation.

Contrast: the test 'PUT update basket ID of basket item is forbidden' demonstrates that the noUpdate constraint DOES fire when the BasketId already has a value. This shows the constraint is conditional — it only protects items that already have a BasketId, not items with an undefined BasketId.
request(app) call for the PUT in the contrast test.
.put('/api/BasketItems/' + createRes.body.data.id) — targets an item that already has BasketId set (created at line 145 with BasketId: 2).
.set(authHeader) — authenticated request.
.send({ BasketId: 42 }) — attempts to change the already-set BasketId to a different value.
assert.equal(res.status, 400) — the PUT is blocked with 400, confirming the noUpdate constraint fires when BasketId already has a value. This is the control that is absent when BasketId is undefined.

assert.equal(res.body.message, 'null: `BasketId` cannot be updated due `noUpdate` constraint') — the error message confirms the noUpdate constraint is the mechanism that blocks BasketId changes, but only for already-set values.
request(app) call initiates the POST request to create a basket item.
.post('/api/BasketItems') — the POST endpoint that creates basket items.

.send({ ProductId: 8, quantity: 8 }) — the request body is sent WITHOUT a BasketId field. The server accepts this and creates a basket item with no basket association, bypassing the BasketId validation that would have occurred had a BasketId been provided.
assert.equal(createRes.status, 200) — the POST succeeds with status 200, confirming the server allows creation of basket items without a BasketId.
.put('/api/BasketItems/' + createRes.body.data.id) — the PUT targets the specific item created in the POST, using its returned ID.
.set(authHeader) — the PUT request is authenticated with the same user's Bearer token.

.send({ BasketId: 3 }) — the request body sends an arbitrary BasketId value. Because the item's BasketId is currently undefined, the noUpdate constraint does not fire, and no ownership validation is performed on the new BasketId value.
request(app) call initiates the POST request to create a basket item. The caller is the test, exercising the application's POST endpoint.
.post('/api/BasketItems') — the POST endpoint that creates basket items.
.set(authHeader) — the request is authenticated with jim@juice-sh.op's Bearer token.

.send({ BasketId: 2, ProductId: 2, quantity: 1 }) — the request body includes BasketId: 2 as a caller-controlled field. The insecure design is that BasketId is accepted from the request body rather than derived from the authenticated user's session, meaning the caller chooses which basket receives the item.
assert.equal(res.status, 200) — the POST with BasketId: 2 succeeds. The server accepted the caller-supplied BasketId without confirming it belongs to the authenticated user.
request(app) call initiates the POST request with an invalid BasketId.
.post('/api/BasketItems') — same POST endpoint.
.set(authHeader) — authenticated with the same user's token.

The insecure design is that the application permits creation of basket items with no basket association at all (BasketId is undefined), creating a state where the item has no ownership context, and then allows retroactive basket assignment without re-validating ownership. The design should enforce that every basket item is associated with the caller's own basket at creation time and never permit BasketId reassignment.

title: GET /api/BasketItems returns all basket items for any authenticated user without per-user scoping
description: The test at lines 46-49 sends GET /api/BasketItems with an authenticated user's token and expects a 200 response. The endpoint name and test pattern suggest it returns all basket items across all users rather than filtering to the authenticated user's own items. The test does not verify the response body to confirm the data is scoped to the current user. If the endpoint returns all users' basket data, any authenticated user can enumerate other users' basket contents, quantities, and product selections — a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) issue. The test only checks that authentication is required (lines 34-37 confirm 401 without auth) but does not verify authorization scoping of the returned data.

trace.description: The test calls GET /api/BasketItems with an authenticated user's Authorization header (authHeader). The caller is the test, exercising the application's GET endpoint.

Contrast: the test 'GET all basket items is forbidden via public API' confirms that the endpoint requires authentication — unauthenticated requests are blocked. This shows the server checks authentication but the test never verifies authorization (per-user data scoping).
request(app).get('/api/BasketItems') — the unauthenticated GET request that returns 401.

assert.equal(res.status, 401) — confirms only authentication is checked. Authentication (is the user logged in?) is verified, but the test never asserts that the returned data is scoped to the authenticated user's own baskets (authorization).

The response status is 200, but the test does not inspect res.body to verify that only the authenticated user's (jim@juice-sh.op) basket items are returned. The endpoint appears to return all basket items without a per-user filter (e.g., WHERE user_id = current_user). An authenticated user could receive other users' basket data.

title: POST /api/BasketItems accepts caller-controlled BasketId, allowing item injection into arbitrary baskets when the ID is valid
description: The test at lines 51-57 sends POST /api/BasketItems with BasketId: 2 in the request body and expects 200. The test at lines 76-83 shows that BasketId: 42 returns 401 'Invalid BasketId', confirming the server validates whether the BasketId exists. However, the design accepts the BasketId from the caller's request body rather than deriving it from the authenticated session. If BasketId 2 is not the current user's own basket but merely a valid basket ID, the user can inject items into another user's basket. The server checks if the BasketId is valid (exists in the database) but the test does not confirm it checks whether the BasketId belongs to the authenticated user. The fact that BasketId 2 returns 200 while BasketId 42 returns 401 suggests the check may be existence-based rather than ownership-based — BasketId 42 simply doesn't exist, not that it belongs to someone else.

trace.description: The test sends POST /api/BasketItems with { BasketId: 2, ProductId: 2, quantity: 1 } in the request body. The BasketId is caller-controlled, not derived from the session.

The test at lines 76-83 sends BasketId: 42 and receives 401 'Invalid BasketId'. This confirms the server validates the BasketId, but the error message says 'Invalid' (non-existent) rather than 'Unauthorized' (belongs to another user), suggesting the check is existence-based, not ownership-based.

The POST with BasketId: 2 succeeds with 200. If BasketId 2 belongs to a different user than jim@juice-sh.op, this is BOLA — the caller controls which basket receives the item. The insecure design is that BasketId is accepted from the request body rather than derived from the authenticated user's session, and the validation appears to check existence rather than ownership.

title: Default admin credentials (admin/admin123) hardcoded and used to access administrative interface
description: The test file authenticates to the application's administration section using the default credentials 'admin' / 'admin123'. The fact that these credentials successfully authenticate an administrator account indicates that the application ships with or accepts well-known default credentials for its administrative interface. This is a misconfiguration (default credentials on an admin interface, OWASP A05 pattern #7) and an authentication weakness (weak/default password on a privileged account, OWASP A07). An attacker who knows or guesses these common default credentials gains full administrative access to the application, bypassing any intended access control boundary. The credentials are hardcoded in source, confirming they are stable and known.

This is the entrypoint — the caller (cy.login) is defined outside this file, but the credentials and the fact that they authenticate an admin session are established here. The test targets /#/administration (line 1), confirming these credentials grant administrative access.
The email field is assigned the value 'admin' inside the object literal passed to cy.login. This is the username component of the default credential pair.
The password field is assigned the value 'admin123' inside the object literal. This is a well-known weak/default password, completing the credential pair.

The password 'admin123' is a well-known weak/default password. Its successful use to access the administration section (line 1) confirms the application accepts default admin credentials. An attacker can replay these exact credentials to gain admin access. The hardcoded presence in the test confirms these are the application's default credentials, not random test data.

title: Unrestricted event listener creation on GET /rest/web3/nftMintListen
description: The test confirms that a simple unauthenticated GET request to /rest/web3/nftMintListen creates a new event listener (line 30 asserts message 'Event Listener Created'). No rate limiting, deduplication, or access control is exercised or implied by the test — every call appears to create a new listener. An attacker can repeatedly call this endpoint to create an unbounded number of event listeners, each of which likely maintains a persistent WebSocket connection to Alchemy and consumes server memory. This exhausts connection pools and memory, causing denial of service. The design flaw is that a GET request — which should be idempotent and side-effect-free — is used to create stateful server-side resources without any guard.

trace.description: The test issues a GET request to /rest/web3/nftMintListen with no authentication headers, tokens, or session. The caller (server route handler) is outside this file.
The response status is 200, confirming the endpoint processes the request successfully without any access-control challenge.

The describe block for /rest/web3/nftMintListen is gated only by skipReason (line 14), which checks for ALCHEMY_API_KEY — there is no auth, rate-limit, or per-user gating in the test's expectations of this endpoint.
The assertion res.body.success === true confirms the endpoint performed its creation operation, not just a read.

The assertion res.body.message === 'Event Listener Created' confirms the GET call creates a new event listener as a side effect. The test exercises no rate limit, no deduplication, and no cap on listener count. Repeated calls create repeated listeners, consuming WebSocket connections and memory without bound.

title: NFT minting challenge verification trusts in-memory Set lookup instead of on-chain verification
description: The test at lines 78–101 reveals the application's NFT verification design: the POST /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify endpoint accepts a client-provided walletAddress and checks whether it exists in an in-memory Set (the test mocks Set.prototype.has to return true for the test address, and the challenge is immediately 'solved'). This means the server trusts an in-memory data structure populated by an event listener rather than independently querying the blockchain to verify that the wallet actually minted the NFT. The event listener itself is triggered by an unauthenticated GET call (lines 24–30). The design gap is that there is no server-side re-derivation of the minting fact — the server accepts the Set's contents as ground truth. If an attacker can pollute the Set (e.g., by crafting events the listener captures, or by racing listener registration), they solve the challenge without minting an NFT.

trace.description: The test sends a POST to /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify with a walletAddress in the body. The walletAddress is entirely client-controlled. The route handler is outside this file.

The test mocks Set.prototype.has to return true for the test address. This reveals that the server-side verification logic calls Set.prototype.has on an in-memory collection to determine whether the wallet minted the NFT — there is no on-chain query shown.
The describe block for /rest/web3/walletNFTVerify establishes the endpoint under test. The route handler is outside this file.
The 'it' block declares the scenario: a minted wallet address successfully solves the minting challenge, establishing the expected happy-path workflow.
testAddress is set to '0x1234567890123456789012345678901234567890' — a value that has not minted anything on any real chain, yet the test expects it to pass verification.

The assertion res.body.message === 'Challenge successfully solved' confirms that the challenge is marked solved purely based on the Set lookup returning true. The server never independently verifies the minting on the blockchain. The design trusts an in-memory Set populated by an unauthenticated event-listener endpoint, creating a verification that can be subverted without actually minting an NFT.

title: Unsafe mutation of process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY without guaranteed cleanup
description: The test at line 37 directly sets process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY to a space character to trigger an error case. The original value is only restored at line 50, which executes after the request completes. If the test framework or the request itself throws an unhandled exception between lines 37 and 50 (e.g., if supertest times out or the app crashes), the env var is left corrupted. In a shared test environment or CI pipeline where tests run in the same process, this corrupted state propagates to all subsequent tests and potentially to the application under test, causing cascading failures or misconfigured outbound connections. The test lacks a try/finally or afterEach hook to guarantee restoration.

trace.description: The test captures the original ALCHEMY_API_KEY from process.env, preparing to mutate it.

process.env.ALCHEMY_API_KEY is set to ' ' (a single space). This mutates the global environment without any guarantee of cleanup — line 50 restores it, but only on the happy path. If an exception occurs between lines 37 and 50, the env var remains corrupted, misconfiguring the application's outbound Alchemy API URL for all subsequent operations.

title: Hardcoded default admin credentials (admin/admin123) used for authentication
description: The test authenticates as an administrator using the well-known default credentials 'admin' / 'admin123'. This is a classic Juice Shop default credential pair. The presence of these credentials in a working test (used in beforeEach, implying they succeed) indicates the application accepts default/weak credentials for an administrative account. An attacker who knows or guesses these defaults gains full admin-level access to the data erasure endpoint and other admin-gated functionality, bypassing any intended access control boundary. This is both a misconfiguration (default credentials shipped with the application) and a crypto-auth weakness (authentication is satisfied by known default credentials rather than strong, unique secrets).

trace.description: The test's beforeEach hook calls cy.login({ email: 'admin', password: 'admin123' }), authenticating to the application using hardcoded default credentials. The caller (the login implementation) is outside this file, but this file demonstrates that the credential pair admin/admin123 is accepted by the application for an admin-role account.
The describe block establishes the test context for the /dataerasure endpoint, which is the admin-gated functionality the test will exercise.
The beforeEach hook ensures that the login call runs before every test in the block, making the hardcoded credential authentication a prerequisite for all subsequent interactions with /dataerasure.

The credential values 'admin' and 'admin123' are default/weak credentials that grant administrative access. The application's acceptance of these defaults is the misconfiguration; the resulting authenticated admin session — used here to interact with the /dataerasure endpoint — is the authentication weakness, as an attacker can trivially replay the same credentials.

title: Product search endpoint returns unbounded result set without pagination
description: The test file explicitly verifies that the /rest/products/search endpoint returns ALL products when the query parameter is empty (q=) or entirely absent. Lines 53-79 assert that the response body's data array length equals the total product count fetched from /api/Products. This confirms the endpoint performs no pagination, no result cap, and no rate limiting on the returned data. An attacker can issue a single GET request to /rest/products/search (or with q=) and force the server to serialize and return the entire product database into memory and over the wire. As the product catalog grows, this becomes a denial-of-service vector: a single request consumes unbounded memory and bandwidth. The insecure-design aspect is that the endpoint's design never bounds its output — the server accepts an empty/missing query and returns the full dataset without any compensating control (pagination, maximum result count, or access restriction).

The test first fetches all products via GET /api/Products (line 54-58) to capture the total count, then compares it against the search result. This comparison structure confirms the test's intent: verify that the search endpoint returns the full dataset.

A second test (lines 67-79) confirms the same behavior when the q parameter is entirely absent — GET /rest/products/search with no query string also returns all products. Both paths (empty q and missing q) reach the same unbounded response.

The test asserts the products API returned JSON content-type, confirming the response is a structured data payload.
The full product array is extracted: const products = productsRes.body.data. This array represents every product in the database and will be used as the reference count.
The test issues a second request — now to the search endpoint — via supertest: const searchRes = await request(app).

The search request targets GET /rest/products/search?q= with an empty query string. This is the request that triggers the unbounded query on the server side — an empty q causes the server to return all products.
The test asserts the search endpoint returned HTTP 200, confirming the server accepted and processed the empty-query request without rejection.
The test asserts the search response is JSON, confirming the server serialized the full result set into a structured payload rather than rejecting or limiting it.
The second test again issues a request to GET /api/Products to establish the reference product count.
The .get('/api/Products') call fetches the complete product list for comparison.
The test asserts the products API returned HTTP 200.
The test asserts the products API returned JSON content-type.
The full product array is extracted again: const products = productsRes.body.data, establishing the reference count for the second test.
The second test issues a request to the search endpoint: const searchRes = await request(app).
The search request targets GET /rest/products/search with NO query parameter at all. This is the second trigger path — the server returns all products when q is missing.
The test asserts the search endpoint returned HTTP 200 for the no-parameter request, confirming the server does not reject requests lacking a search term.
The test asserts the search response is JSON, confirming the server serialized the full result set.
The second test asserts searchRes.body.data.length === products.length, independently confirming that the no-parameter path also returns the entire product database with no pagination or cap.

Line 64 asserts searchRes.body.data.length === products.length, proving the search response contains every product in the database with no pagination limit, no max-results cap, and no throttling. This is the confirmed sink: the endpoint returns an unbounded result set that an attacker can trigger with a single unauthenticated GET request.

title: Unauthenticated account enumeration via differential responses on security-question endpoint
description: The GET /rest/user/security-question?email= endpoint is accessible without authentication and returns a different response body depending on whether the supplied email corresponds to a registered account. For a known email, it returns the user's security question (status 200 with a populated body). For an unknown email, it returns an empty object (status 200 with {}). This differential response allows an attacker to enumerate which email addresses are registered in the system without any credentials. Additionally, the security question itself — part of the account-recovery / authentication flow — is disclosed to unauthenticated callers, weakening the knowledge-based authentication mechanism. The design permits unauthenticated access to account-recovery data and creates an oracle for account existence.

trace.description: The test exercises GET /rest/user/security-question?email= with no Authorization header, confirming the endpoint is accessible without authentication.
The email parameter is supplied as a query string value: `/rest/user/security-question?email=jim@${config.get<string>('application.domain')}`. The caller (route handler) is outside this file.

For a registered email, the response includes the user's security question text: `res.body.question.question` equals 'Your eldest siblings middle name?'. This discloses account-recovery information to an unauthenticated caller, weakening the authentication mechanism.
`const res = await request(app)` initiates the HTTP request to the application under test with no authentication headers set.
`assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms the unauthenticated request succeeds with HTTP 200 — no access control blocks the call.
The second test definition exercises the same endpoint with an unknown email address, also without authentication.
`const res = await request(app)` initiates the second HTTP request, again with no auth headers.
`.get('/rest/user/security-question?email=horst@unknown-us.er')` sends an email that does not correspond to a registered account.
`assert.equal(res.status, 200)` confirms the unknown-email request also returns HTTP 200 — the same status code as the registered-email case.

For an unregistered email, the response body is an empty object `{}` (asserted via `assert.deepEqual(res.body, {})`). The differential between this empty response and the populated response on line 79 creates an account-enumeration oracle, allowing an attacker to determine which emails are registered. This is an insecure design: the account-recovery flow was never designed to require authentication or return uniform responses.

title: Error response leaks internal framework name and SQL error details
description: When the GET /rest/user/security-question endpoint is called without an email parameter, the server returns a 500 response with an HTML body that includes the application's framework name ('Express') and the raw SQL/ORM error message ('WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value'). Exposing internal technology stack details and database query structure in error responses is a security misconfiguration that aids attackers in fingerprinting the application and understanding its data-access layer.

The server responds with HTTP 500 and content-type text/html, indicating a raw error page is returned to the client rather than a sanitized JSON error.

`assert.ok(res.headers['content-type']?.includes('text/html'))` confirms the error response is an HTML page, not a structured JSON error — indicating the default Express error handler is rendering the error.

The response body further includes the raw ORM/database error: 'Error: WHERE parameter "email" has invalid "undefined" value'. This exposes internal query structure and the ORM in use, which is a misconfiguration — error responses in production should not include stack traces or internal error messages.

title: Hardcoded default admin credentials in test source code
description: Lines 4-5 hardcode default administrative credentials ('admin' / 'admin123') directly in source code. These are well-known weak/default credentials for the application's admin interface. The misconfiguration playbook flags both 'Default or weak credentials for administrative interfaces' and 'Hardcoded secrets or credentials in source code' as findings. Even though this is a test file, the credentials are committed in plaintext and any leak of the repository exposes valid admin login credentials. If these same credentials are used in a non-test deployment, the admin account is trivially compromised.

The beforeEach hook establishes an authentication context that runs before every test in the describe block, setting up the login state.
The email field is hardcoded as 'admin' — a default administrative username that is well-known and trivially guessable.

The object literal closes on line 6, completing the argument passed to cy.login(). The login call now executes, sending the hardcoded default admin credentials ('admin' / 'admin123') to the application's authentication mechanism. These credentials are committed in source code; anyone with repository access obtains valid admin credentials, and if the same defaults are active in any deployment the admin account is immediately accessible.

The password 'admin123' is hardcoded alongside username 'admin' (line 4) in source code. These are default/weak credentials for an administrative interface, committed in plaintext. Anyone with repository access obtains valid admin credentials; if the same defaults are active in any deployment, the admin account is immediately accessible.

title: Hardcoded default admin credentials in test source
description: The test file logs in using the credentials `{ email: 'admin', password: 'admin123' }` (line 8). These are default, well-known administrative credentials for the application. Default credentials for an administrative interface are a security misconfiguration (OWASP A05): if these same credentials are present in a deployed instance, any attacker can authenticate as an administrator without any brute-forcing. This is also an authentication failure (OWASP A07) because the existence of a valid default admin account means the authentication mechanism can be satisfied by an attacker who simply knows the published defaults, yielding full administrative access.

These are default admin credentials (username 'admin', password 'admin123') for an administrative account.

The credentials admin/admin123 are passed as authentication material to the login flow. If the deployed application accepts these same default credentials, an attacker who knows them (they are published in the project's own test suite) can authenticate as the administrator, bypassing any need to crack credentials. This establishes both a misconfiguration (default/weak admin credentials left active) and a crypto-auth failure (authentication can be satisfied by default credentials, yielding admin identity).

title: Wallet exploit address endpoint creates event listeners without validating input, enabling unbounded listener creation
description: The `/rest/web3/walletExploitAddress` endpoint accepts a wallet address in the request body but performs no validation on it. The tests in this file demonstrate that the endpoint returns success ('Event Listener Created') when the wallet address is missing entirely (empty body), when it is an invalid string ('lalalalala'), and when it is a valid-looking address. The design flaw is that the server never validates the wallet address — it unconditionally creates an event listener for whatever input it receives. This is an insecure design issue because the server trusts client-supplied data without establishing any rule about what constitutes a valid address. It is also a resource-consumption issue because each successful request creates a persistent 'Event Listener' (presumably a blockchain event subscription), and since every request succeeds regardless of input, an attacker can create unlimited event listeners with no throttling, exhausting server memory, network connections to the blockchain provider, or processing capacity.

Request body is {} (empty object) — the walletAddress field is entirely absent. The test also covers an invalid address ('lalalalala' at line 36) and a valid address (line 47), all producing the same result.

Despite the missing wallet address, the response is HTTP 200 with success: true. The same result occurs for invalid (line 40) and self-referential (line 51) addresses. This establishes that the handler performs no validation on the wallet address — the design accepts any input and proceeds to create an event listener.

Response message is 'Event Listener Created' (also at lines 41 and 52). Every request — regardless of input validity — results in a new event listener being created. Since there is no input validation and no indication of rate limiting, an attacker can send arbitrary requests to create unbounded event listeners, consuming server and provider resources.

title: Order tracking endpoint designed without access control — unauthenticated retrieval of all orders including customer PII
description: The /rest/track-order/:id endpoint is designed as a publicly accessible order-lookup feature with no authentication or authorization checks. The test at line 20-24 confirms that an unauthenticated GET request to a valid order ID returns HTTP 200 with order data. More critically, lines 26-46 demonstrate that injecting `' || true || '` into the order ID parameter causes the endpoint to return ALL orders in the system, each containing customer email addresses (line 34), order totals (line 35), and product details. The design flaw is that the tracking workflow never establishes who the caller is or whether they own the order being tracked — the server accepts an order ID from any unauthenticated caller and returns full order details. This means the design itself permits information disclosure of all customers' order data and PII, regardless of whether the injection is fixed, because there is no access-control layer in the tracking flow.

The test expects this to return 200 (line 29), confirming the endpoint design accepts and processes the injected value without any server-side validation or authorization gate.

This demonstrates the design permits any unauthenticated caller to retrieve every customer's order data and email — a PII disclosure that the tracking endpoint's design does not prevent because it has no access-control step in the workflow.

title: Order tracking endpoint returns unbounded result set via injection — no pagination or result-size limit
description: The test at lines 26-46 demonstrates that injecting `' || true || '` into the /rest/track-order/:id endpoint causes the server to return ALL orders in a single response. The test iterates over the entire `res.body.data` array (lines 32-45) without any bound check, confirming the response is an unbounded result set. The endpoint has no pagination, no maximum result count, and no rate limiting visible in the test's interaction. An attacker can repeatedly trigger this injection to force the server to serialize and return the entire orders table on each request, consuming server memory, CPU (for query execution and JSON serialization), and network bandwidth. With a large orders table, a single request could exhaust server memory; repeated requests could cause denial of service.

The unbounded iteration over all returned orders (lines 32-45) demonstrates that a single request retrieves the entire orders dataset. The endpoint has no result-size cap, no pagination parameter, and no rate limiting — an attacker can trigger full-table serialization on every request, causing excessive memory and CPU consumption on the server.

title: Open redirect via weak allow-list validation using substring matching on the /redirect endpoint
description: The /redirect endpoint accepts a 'to' query parameter and validates it against an allow-list of known URLs. However, the validation uses substring matching (the .includes() method, as revealed by the TypeError in lines 76-78 and confirmed by the test at lines 101-110) rather than parsing the URL and comparing the origin. The test at line 103 demonstrates that a 'to' value of '/score-board?satisfyIndexOf=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' passes validation and results in a successful redirect — the actual redirect destination is the relative path '/score-board', but validation passes because the allow-listed GitHub URL appears as a substring within the query string. An attacker can construct a 'to' value whose real redirect target is any arbitrary path or URL, as long as an allow-listed URL string is embedded somewhere in it (e.g., in the query, fragment, or userinfo). This allows open redirect to attacker-controlled destinations, enabling phishing campaigns that abuse the application's trusted domain.

The test follows 1 redirect (redirects(1)), indicating the server issued a 302 redirect and the test client followed it, receiving a 200 response.

The assertion confirms the error output contains the method name 'includes', definitively revealing that the allow-list validation uses JavaScript's String.prototype.includes() — a substring check that can be bypassed by embedding the allow-listed URL anywhere in the 'to' value.
A separate test demonstrates that calling /redirect?to=whatever (an unrecognized target) is also tested, establishing that an allow-list validation mechanism exists for the 'to' parameter.

The 406 response body includes 'Unrecognized target URL for redirect: whatever', confirming the allow-list check inspects the raw 'to' value and echoes it back.

The test asserts status 200 and that the response contains the application's JavaScript bundles (main.js, scripts.js, polyfills.js), confirming the redirect to the unvalidated path '/score-board' succeeded. The allow-list was bypassed because the allow-listed URL was merely present as a substring in the query string.

title: Verbose error responses with stack trace and framework details exposed on /redirect endpoint
description: The /redirect endpoint returns HTTP 500 responses that include detailed internal error information in the HTML body. The tests at lines 70-90 explicitly assert that the response body contains the application name and Express framework identifier, the error type 'TypeError', the message 'of undefined', and the internal method name 'includes'. This is a security misconfiguration — production applications should not expose stack traces, internal method names, or framework version information in error responses. An attacker can use this information to fingerprint the technology stack, identify internal code structure, and craft more targeted attacks against the application. The fact that the error leaks the method name '.includes()' directly reveals the weak validation mechanism used for redirect URL checking. The same verbose error pattern is confirmed across two different error triggers (missing parameter and unrecognized query parameter).

title: Hardcoded default admin credentials in test source
description: The test file embeds plaintext admin credentials (admin@juice-sh.op / admin123) directly in source code on line 3. These are weak, default credentials for an administrative account. Hardcoded credentials in source are a misconfiguration finding regardless of context: they are committed to version control, visible to anyone with repo access, and cannot be rotated without a code change. The use of a trivially guessable default password ('admin123') for an admin account is also an authentication weakness — it permits credential brute-force or simple guessing to gain administrative access. While this file is a test spec, the credentials are real application credentials used to authenticate via cy.login(), and the same defaults may exist in the running application. The credential object is both constructed and consumed within the single expression on line 3; there are no intermediate assignments, forwarding calls, or conditionals in this file — the object literal with email and password is created inline as the argument to cy.login(). The caller cy.login is outside this file, but the credential values originate and are passed on line 3.

title: Data export test performs no logging verification for security-relevant registration event
description: The test file is named for the data export feature ('dataExport.spec.ts') and its describe block references 'dataExportChallenge'.
