The test performs a user registration (lines 3-20) — itself a security-relevant event (account creation) — but includes no assertion that the registration or any subsequent data export action produces a log entry. While the absence of a test assertion does not prove the application lacks logging, it indicates that logging of account creation and data export is not verified or enforced through testing, leaving a gap in detectability if logging is removed or broken in the application code.

title: Security answer creation accepts arbitrary UserId with a non-user-bound token, enabling account takeover
description: The test file demonstrates that POST /api/SecurityAnswers creates a security answer for any UserId supplied in the request body using a generic authentication token that is not bound to that user. At line 14, `security.authorize()` is called with no arguments, producing a Bearer token that carries no specific user identity. A new user is registered at lines 56–62, and the 201 assertion at line 64 confirms the user was created so `userRes.body.id` is populated. At lines 66–73, the generic token from line 14 is sent in the Authorization header (line 68) while the request body specifies `UserId: userRes.body.id` (line 70) for that newly registered user. The 201 response at line 75 confirms the security answer was created. This means any authenticated caller can set or replace the security answer for any user account. Since security answers are used in password reset / account recovery flows, an attacker who sets a known security answer on a victim's account can subsequently use it to reset the victim's password and take over the account. The GET, PUT, and DELETE operations on /api/SecurityAnswers are correctly blocked (401 at lines 27, 52, 90, 98), but the POST operation — the most dangerous one for account takeover — is left open. The token generation at line 14 is a crypto-auth weakness because `security.authorize()` produces a valid authentication token without binding it to a user identity, and the application accepts this token for user-scoped operations. The insecure-design weakness is that the security answer creation workflow never re-derives or validates ownership of the UserId from the authenticated session — the server trusts the client-supplied UserId for a security-critical recovery credential.

trace.description: A generic Bearer token is generated via `security.authorize()` with no user identity argument. This token is stored in `authHeader` and reused across all test requests. The token is not bound to any specific user, yet it is accepted as valid authentication by the application.

A new user is registered via POST /api/Users (lines 56–62), and the response body's `id` field is captured at line 64 (`userRes.body.id`). This ID belongs to the newly created user, not to the identity (or lack thereof) represented by the generic authHeader token.

The POST /api/SecurityAnswers request body includes `UserId: userRes.body.id` (line 70), passing an arbitrary user ID that is not derived from the authenticated session. The request is sent with the generic authHeader (line 68). The endpoint does not verify that the token's user identity matches the UserId in the body.
A new user registration request is initiated. `const userRes` captures the response from POST /api/Users. The request is built over the next several lines.
The request targets POST /api/Users — the user creation endpoint. The response will contain the new user's `id` in its body.
The email field `new.user@te.st` is set in the registration request body.
The password field `12345` is set in the registration request body.
A second request is initiated: `const res` captures the response from POST /api/SecurityAnswers. This is the request that will create a security answer.
The request targets POST /api/SecurityAnswers — the security answer creation endpoint.

`.set(authHeader)` attaches the generic Authorization header from line 14 to the SecurityAnswers request. The token carries no user identity, so the server cannot determine which user is making this request — yet it accepts it as authenticated.

The response returns 201 (line 75), confirming the security answer was created successfully for the specified UserId without any ownership or authorization check. An attacker can repeat this with any UserId to set a known security answer on a victim's account, then use the password reset flow to take over the account.

title: Client-controlled wallet charge amount enables arbitrary balance inflation
description: The PUT /rest/wallet/balance endpoint accepts a `balance` field directly from the client request body and adds it to the user's wallet. The test at line 51 sends `balance: 10` alongside a `paymentId`, and the follow-up GET at line 59 confirms the wallet went from 200 to 210 — proving the server trusts the client-supplied amount rather than deriving the charge amount from the payment instrument or a server-side price lookup. An attacker can send `balance: 99999999` with their own valid paymentId and inflate their wallet balance to any amount. This is a trust assumption violation: the server must decide how much credit to add, not accept it from the caller. The paymentId authorization check (tested at lines 62-68, which correctly returns 402 for a foreign card) only validates *which* card is used, not *how much* is charged.

title: Wallet charge endpoint lacks rate limiting enabling wallet inflation via repeated small charges
description: The PUT /rest/wallet/balance endpoint is tested without any evidence of rate limiting or throttling. The tests show no mention of rate limits, and the endpoint performs a financial mutation (adding credit to a wallet) which is an expensive write operation that should be throttled. The test at lines 47-60 makes a single charge request that succeeds, and nothing in the test suite or endpoint behavior indicates per-user or per-IP throttling on this financial write endpoint.

title: Hardcoded weak default admin credentials in source code

If these credentials mirror or are reused in any non-test environment, an attacker who reads the source repository obtains direct administrative access. Even in a test-only context, committing credentials to version control risks leakage and establishes a pattern of embedding secrets in code.

Email 'admin' is passed as a hardcoded string literal in the login call.

title: eval() on DOM-sourced captcha text enables code injection
description: The solveNextCaptcha function reads text content from the #captcha DOM element and passes it directly to eval() without any validation or sanitization. eval() interprets its argument as executable JavaScript code. If the application under test is compromised or returns attacker-controlled captcha text (e.g., through stored XSS or server-side manipulation), the eval call will execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Cypress test runner's browser context. The eslint-disable comment on line 85 acknowledges the intentional use of eval, but no safer alternative (e.g., parsing the arithmetic expression) is used. The input is external data from the DOM of the application under test, and it reaches a code-execution sink with no intervening control.

The eslint-disable-next-line no-eval comment suppresses the linter warning, acknowledging eval is being used deliberately.

const answer = eval(val).toString() — the DOM-sourced captcha text (val) is passed directly to eval(), which interprets it as executable JavaScript. No validation, allow-listing, or safe arithmetic parsing intervenes between the DOM read and the eval call.

title: Hardcoded administrative credentials in test source
description: The test file hardcodes administrative credentials (email: 'admin', password: 'admin123') directly in source code at two locations. While this is a test file for an intentionally vulnerable application (OWASP Juice Shop), hardcoded credentials in source code are a security concern: they may be reused in non-test environments, leaked via version control, or inadvertently copied into production code. These credentials authenticate as an admin-level user, making them particularly sensitive.

trace.description: cy.login({ email: 'admin', password: 'admin123' }) hardcodes admin credentials in the beforeEach block of the 'forgedFeedback' challenge test suite.
The same hardcoded credentials are repeated in a second beforeEach block for the 'persistedXssFeedback' challenge test suite, confirming this is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The hardcoded credentials are passed to cy.login(), authenticating as an admin user. The credentials are embedded in source code committed to version control with no indirection through environment variables or secrets management.

title: Hardcoded plaintext credentials in test source code
description: The test file embeds plaintext passwords directly in source code: 'focusOnScienceMorty!focusOnScience' (the login and current password for the 'morty' account) and 'GonorrheaCantSeeUs!' (the new password). Hardcoded secrets in source code are a misconfiguration finding regardless of whether they are used in production. If these credentials are shared with any non-test environment, they provide direct authentication bypass. Even in a test-only context, committing real passwords to version control means anyone with repository access gains valid credentials, and the passwords may be reused across environments.

The #changeButton is clicked, submitting the password change with the hardcoded old and new passwords. The entire credential lifecycle — old and new — is now in version control.

The hardcoded plaintext password is the credential used for authentication (line 6) and the password-change flow (lines 12-14). Any party with access to this source file obtains working credentials for the 'morty' account, and the new password value is also disclosed.

title: Test reveals valid credentials enabling authentication bypass
description: The test file contains a complete, valid credential pair for the 'morty' account (email and password on lines 5-6) and performs a password change to another known value (lines 13-14). By exposing working credentials in source code, this file enables any reader to authenticate as 'morty' and potentially as any account that shares the same password. This is an authentication failure because the secret used to verify identity is disclosed, removing the barrier that the authentication mechanism is supposed to provide. The password change operation (lines 13-14) also sets the account password to a value known to anyone reading the repository, so the post-test state of the account is predictable and accessible.

title: Quarantined files served without authentication
description: The test at line 21-24 issues a GET request to /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url with no authentication headers, cookies, or tokens, and asserts a 200 response. This establishes that the quarantine endpoint—the server's own test expects—serves quarantined files (including a file whose name suggests it is quarantined malware) to any unauthenticated caller. A quarantine directory exists specifically to isolate dangerous or suspicious files; serving them without access controls is both a misconfiguration (exposed internal/dangerous resources) and an insecure design (no compensating control for an inherently risky operation). An attacker can retrieve any quarantined file by guessing or enumerating filenames.

trace.description: The test constructs a GET request to /ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url using supertest. No Authorization header, cookie, or API token is set on the request, meaning the test expects the endpoint to serve the file without authentication.
The request targets a quarantined file (juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url). The caller is the test; the actual route handler is outside this file in the server implementation.

The assertion assert.equal(res.status, 200) confirms the server's expected behavior: it returns the quarantined file content to the unauthenticated caller. The quarantine endpoint has no access control, exposing quarantined (potentially malicious) files to any requester.

title: Path traversal protection only checks for forward slashes, leaving backslash and encoding bypasses untested
description: The test at lines 27-34 verifies that a filename containing an encoded forward slash (../package.json → ..%2Fpackage.json) is rejected with 403 and the message 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!'. This is the only path-traversal test. On Windows (and in many Node.js path resolution contexts), backslashes (..\) are also valid path separators. The check described by the error message is specific to forward slashes only, meaning backslash-based traversal, double-encoding (%252F), or null-byte injection may bypass the filter and allow reading arbitrary files from the server filesystem. The design chose a narrow denylist (forward slashes) rather than validating that the resolved path stays within the quarantine directory.

trace.description: The test constructs a GET request to /ftp/quarantine/ + encodeURIComponent('../package.json'), which produces /ftp/quarantine/..%2Fpackage.json. The caller is the test; the route handler is outside this file.

The assertion verifies the error message 'File names cannot contain forward slashes!' — this message reveals the server's validation logic: it specifically and only checks for forward slashes in the filename, not for backslashes, double-encoding, null bytes, or resolved-path containment.

The .get() call sets the path to '/ftp/quarantine/' + encodeURIComponent('../package.json'), which produces /ftp/quarantine/..%2Fpackage.json. This is the path-traversal payload that reaches the server's filename validation logic.
assert.equal(res.status, 403) confirms the server rejected the request. The rejection confirms a validation check exists, but does not reveal its full scope.
assert.ok(res.headers['content-type']?.includes('text/html')) confirms the server responded with an HTML error page, not a file download — the traversal was blocked for this specific payload.

The narrow check ('cannot contain forward slashes') is the only traversal defense tested. A filename like ..\package.json (backslash) or ..%252Fpackage.json (double-encoded) would pass this forward-slash-only filter, allowing path traversal to read files outside the quarantine directory.

title: No verification that access to quarantined files is security-logged
description: The tests verify HTTP status codes and error messages for the quarantine endpoint but do not verify that access attempts (especially successful retrieval of quarantined files or blocked path-traversal attempts) are logged. Access to quarantined files is a security-relevant event — these files are isolated because they are dangerous or suspicious. Without logging, there is no audit trail for who accessed quarantined files or attempted path traversal against the quarantine directory, making incident detection and investigation impossible. This is a secondary finding because the absence of a test assertion does not prove the server lacks logging; it only shows that logging is not verified.

The test also issues a path-traversal attempt against the quarantine endpoint. Both successful and blocked access to quarantined files are security-relevant events that should be logged.
The .get() targets '/ftp/quarantine/juicy_malware_windows_64.exe.url' — a successful retrieval of a quarantined file, which is a security-relevant event that should be logged.

The test only asserts on res.status (200/403) and res.text/res.headers. No assertion checks that a log entry was created for the quarantine file access or the blocked traversal attempt, indicating logging is not part of the endpoint's tested contract.

title: System prompt extraction detection threshold too low to protect confidential section
description: The checkSystemPromptSimilarity function uses a similarity threshold of 0.25 (confirmed at line 142) to detect whether a user submission matches the system prompt. The system prompt contains a CONFIDENTIAL section detailing a secret 15% courtesy discount policy for escalated complaints (lines 23-26, 31-33). The test at lines 30-35 explicitly demonstrates that submitting the verbatim confidential section alone scores ~0.22, which falls below the 0.25 threshold and returns false — meaning the extraction is NOT detected. Because the dice coefficient compares the submission against the entire system prompt, extracting only the small confidential portion yields a low similarity score. The design therefore fails to protect the most sensitive part of the prompt: an attacker who extracts only the confidential discount policy evades detection entirely, while someone who extracts a large non-sensitive portion of the prompt is caught. The business impact is that an attacker can learn and abuse the secret courtesy discount policy (obtaining unauthorized 15% discounts by feigning complaints and requesting escalation) without triggering any system prompt extraction alert.

Do not mention this option proactively.' This is the most sensitive portion of the prompt extracted in isolation.

The test at lines 30-35 demonstrates the design flaw: submitting the verbatim confidential section (containing the secret discount policy) scores ~0.22, which is below the 0.25 threshold, so checkSystemPromptSimilarity returns false. The extraction of the most sensitive portion of the system prompt is not detected. An attacker can extract and abuse the confidential courtesy discount policy without triggering any alert.

title: Confidential system prompt content hardcoded in test file in plaintext
description: The test file embeds the full confidential system prompt content — including the secret 15% courtesy discount escalation policy marked 'CONFIDENTIAL - INTERNAL ONLY' and 'Do not mention this option proactively' — directly in source code at lines 23-26, 31-33, 38-42, and 82-84. This sensitive business logic is duplicated across four separate test cases in plaintext. The playbook states that hardcoded secrets in source code are always findings regardless of production usage. The confidential discount policy is a business secret that, if disclosed, enables attackers to obtain unauthorized discounts by feigning complaints and requesting escalation. Storing it in test files increases the attack surface: anyone with read access to the source repository (including CI/CD systems, developer machines, and any deployed test artifacts) can read the secret policy.

This is a misconfiguration (sensitive data exposed in source code) and an insecure design issue (the confidential policy is duplicated in multiple locations rather than referenced from a single secured source, increasing exposure).

title: Missing per-resource ownership (BOLA) verification on card retrieval by ID — tests confirm only authentication is enforced
description: The test suite for /api/Cards/:id verifies that unauthenticated requests are rejected with 401 (line 104-107) and that an authenticated user can retrieve a card by ID with 200 (line 119-122). However, the entire test flow uses a single user ('jim') who both creates and retrieves the card. There is no test asserting that a different authenticated user cannot retrieve another user's card by substituting the card ID. The test at line 130-136 shows that a non-existing ID returns 400 'Malicious activity detected,' confirming the server does perform some validation on the ID — but this check is about existence/anomaly detection, not ownership. If the server's GET /api/Cards/:id handler performs a lookup by primary key without filtering on the authenticated user's identity, any logged-in user can enumerate and read other users' payment card records (masked number, full name, expiry). This is the classic BOLA pattern: authentication is enforced, per-resource authorization is not.

The endpoint returns 200 for any authenticated user supplying a valid card ID. The absence of any ownership-scoping assertion — combined with the fact that the 'Malicious activity detected' response at line 135 only triggers for non-existing IDs, not for IDs owned by other users — indicates the server looks up the card by ID without filtering on the authenticated user's identity. User A can supply User B's cardId to retrieve User B's payment card details (masked number, name, expiry).

title: Mass assignment of role field on user registration enables privilege escalation without authentication
description: The POST /api/Users endpoint accepts a `role` field in the request body and persists it directly. The test at lines 62-78 demonstrates that sending `role: 'admin'` during registration creates a user with admin privileges (response 201, role confirmed as 'admin'). The same pattern is shown for 'deluxe' (lines 130-146) and 'accounting' (lines 148-164). Crucially, these requests use only `jsonHeader` (content-type) with no authentication header, meaning an unauthenticated attacker can self-register as admin. The server does not apply an explicit allow-list for writable fields; it accepts caller-supplied role values and persists them. This is a classic mass assignment / broken object property level authorization flaw that enables broken function level authorization (anyone can become admin) and reflects an insecure design (role assignment is client-controlled rather than server-derived).

title: Password hash exposed via fields query parameter on /rest/user/whoami
description: The /rest/user/whoami endpoint accepts a `fields` query parameter that controls which user properties are returned. The test at lines 303-316 demonstrates that requesting `fields=id,email,password` causes the endpoint to return the user's password hash as a string. There is no server-side filtering of sensitive fields — the caller controls which properties are serialized. This is a broken object property level authorization issue (the caller selects which properties to read, including sensitive ones) and a cryptographic/authentication failure (password hashes are exposed to the client, enabling offline cracking).

title: Any authenticated user can retrieve any other user's data by ID via GET /api/Users/:id
description: The test at lines 205-208 demonstrates that GET /api/Users/1 with a generic Bearer token returns HTTP 200. title: JWT token payload contains user password hash, exposing sensitive credential data

title: Authentication token stored in localStorage and replayable across origins (CSRF vector)

title: Track-order feature reflects unsanitized user input in order ID parameter (Reflected XSS)
description: The track-order result page accepts an `id` query parameter and reflects it directly into the DOM without sanitization or validation. The test at line 12 demonstrates that injecting an `<iframe src="javascript:alert(`xss`)">` payload through the `id` parameter causes arbitrary JavaScript execution when the page renders. This is an insecure design flaw: the application trusts client-supplied input (the order ID) and renders it without encoding or validation. The order ID should be validated against an expected format (e.g., alphanumeric order reference) before being reflected or used in a lookup. The design never establishes what a valid order ID is, so arbitrary content is accepted and rendered, enabling reflected XSS attacks that could steal session tokens, perform actions on behalf of the user, or redirect users to phishing pages.

title: Tests validate that access control failures return HTTP 500 with error detail exposure instead of 401/403

The test validates and enforces this insecure behavior, meaning any future fix to return proper 401/403 responses would cause these tests to fail. The design treats unauthenticated access as an exceptional error ('illegal activity') rather than a normal access-control decision, which is an insecure design choice in how authentication enforcement is structured.

title: Unsafe js-yaml load() on data file used in test
description: The file uses the unsafe `load` function from the `js-yaml` library (line 12) to parse `data/static/challenges.yml`. In js-yaml versions prior to v4, `load` (as opposed to `safeLoad`) can instantiate arbitrary JavaScript objects via custom YAML tags, which can lead to code execution during parsing. While the parsed file is a static repository asset rather than direct user input, the use of the unsafe parser variant means that a supply-chain compromise or malicious modification of the YAML file would achieve arbitrary code execution during the test run. The safe alternative (`safeLoad`, or `load` with `schema: DEFAULT_SAFE_SCHEMA`) would prevent object instantiation from untrusted YAML.

The import statement `import { load } from 'js-yaml'` imports the unsafe load function rather than the safe variant. In js-yaml v3 and earlier, load() uses the DEFAULT_FULL_SCHEMA which allows construction of arbitrary JS objects via custom tags (e.g., !!js/function).

import path from 'path' — the path module is imported, providing path.resolve() which constructs the filesystem path to challenges.yml on line 12. This determines which file's contents flow into the deserializer.

import fs from 'fs' — the filesystem module is imported, providing the readFileSync function that reads the untrusted YAML file content from disk on line 12. Without this import the file content could not be loaded.

load() is called on the file contents without specifying a safe schema option. If the YAML content contains malicious custom-type tags (possible via supply-chain tampering of the static data file), the parser will instantiate arbitrary objects or execute embedded code during deserialization. No checksum, signature, or safe-schema option is applied.

title: Server accepts forged coupon with arbitrary discount percentage
description: The test demonstrates that a coupon granting a 90% discount can be generated client-side (via the GenerateCoupon task, which simulates what an attacker computes) and then submitted to the server, which accepts it. The challenge name 'forgedCoupon' confirms the coupon system is designed such that coupon validity can be computed or forged by the client rather than being issued and verified server-side. The server trusts a client-produced coupon string without independently validating it against a server-side record of issued coupons. This is an insecure design flaw: the application's own logic permits an attacker to create arbitrary discounts by forging coupons.

trace.description: The test calls cy.task<string>('GenerateCoupon', 90), which generates a coupon string with a 90-percent discount. This simulates an attacker forging a coupon client-side — the discount amount is a parameter controlled by the caller, not decided by the server.
The forged coupon string is typed into the coupon input field (#coupon).
The test visits /#/payment/shop, navigating to the payment page where the coupon attack is executed. This is the start of the attack flow.
The test clicks #collapseCouponElement to expand the coupon input panel, exposing the UI element through which the forged coupon will be submitted.

The applyCouponButton is clicked, submitting the forged coupon to the server. The server accepts it and applies the 90% discount. The design never requires the coupon to be server-issued; the client can produce a valid coupon.

title: BasketId is client-controlled and sent to API without per-resource ownership verification
description: The test sends a POST to /api/BasketItems/ with a BasketId read from sessionStorage. The BasketId is a client-supplied value in the request body — the server endpoint accepts it as a parameter. If the server does not verify that the supplied BasketId belongs to the currently authenticated user (Bearer token), any logged-in user could substitute another user's BasketId and add items to or manipulate their basket. The empty test blocks for 'basketAccessChallenge' and 'basketManipulateChallenge' (lines 11-15) reinforce that basket-level access control is a known weak point in this application. The actual entrypoint (the route handler for POST /api/BasketItems/) is outside this file, but the test code shows the client controls the BasketId parameter that reaches the API.

trace.description: The BasketId is read from sessionStorage.getItem('bid') — a client-side storage value that the user can read and modify. This value is placed into the request body as BasketId. The caller (the route handler for POST /api/BasketItems/) is outside this file.
The fetch call sends the request body containing the client-controlled BasketId to /api/BasketItems/ with the user's Bearer token for authentication.

The Authorization header is set to `Bearer ${localStorage.getItem('token')}`, providing authentication. This is the only identity proof sent — there is no per-resource authorization check on the BasketId. Authentication is present; authorization is absent.
The BasketId value is passed into JSON.stringify({ ... }) as a property of the request body object. The body is being constructed to be sent as JSON.

The POST to /api/BasketItems/ accepts the BasketId from the request body. The test provides only authentication (Bearer token) but the BasketId itself is whatever the client supplies. A user could substitute another user's BasketId (e.g., by guessing or extracting it) to add items to another user's basket, which is a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) issue.

title: Hardcoded authentication credentials and TOTP secret in source code
description: The test file contains plaintext passwords and a TOTP shared secret directly in source code. The password for 'wurstbrot' ('EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!') and its TOTP secret ('IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH') are on lines 6-7. The password for 'amy' ('K1f.....................') appears on lines 20, 31, and 37. Per the misconfiguration playbook, hardcoded secrets in source code are always findings regardless of whether they are used in production. The TOTP secret is a cryptographic authentication secret whose hardcoding establishes a crypto-auth failure as well: if this secret is a real shared secret used for 2FA, anyone with source access can generate valid TOTP codes and bypass the second authentication factor.

trace.description: Test setup calls cy.login() with credentials passed as a literal object. The caller is outside this file (Cypress test framework), but the secret values originate here in source.
Email field 'wurstbrot' set in the credential object literal passed to cy.login().
Password 'EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!' hardcoded as a plaintext string in the credential object.
Second cy.login() call for user 'amy', constructing another credential object literal with hardcoded values.
Email field 'amy' set in the credential object literal.
Password 'K1f.....................' hardcoded as a plaintext string in amy's credential object.
The same hardcoded password 'K1f.....................' is typed into the #currentPasswordSetup field, reusing the committed secret.
The same hardcoded password 'K1f.....................' is typed into the #currentPasswordDisable field, a third use of the committed plaintext credential.

TOTP secret 'IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH' is hardcoded on line 7. Passwords are hardcoded on lines 6 ('EinBelegtesBrotMitSchinkenSCHINKEN!'), 20 ('K1f.....................'), and reused on lines 31 and 37. These secrets are committed in source code.

title: Commented-out logging of TOTP secret value
description: Line 30 contains a commented-out console.log statement that would print the TOTP secret ($val) retrieved from the DOM attribute 'data-test-totp-secret'. While currently commented out, this line demonstrates intent to log a sensitive cryptographic secret (the TOTP shared secret) to the console during test execution. If uncommented, or if similar logging exists in other test or production code, the TOTP secret would be exposed in console output, undermining the 2FA mechanism. The value being logged is the TOTP secret obtained from the DOM attribute.

cy.get('#initialToken') selects the DOM element that contains the TOTP secret in its data attributes.

A commented-out console.log($val) would log the TOTP secret to the console. The variable $val is the TOTP secret obtained from the DOM attribute in the previous step.

title: TOTP secret exposed in DOM data attribute accessible to any client-side script
description: The test on line 28 reads the TOTP shared secret from a 'data-test-totp-secret' attribute on the #initialToken DOM element. This reveals that the application exposes the TOTP secret in a DOM attribute that is accessible to any JavaScript running in the page context, including third-party scripts, browser extensions, or XSS payloads. While the TOTP secret must be displayed to the user during setup, placing it in a machine-readable data attribute (as opposed to displaying it in a controlled manner such as a QR code) is an insecure design choice that makes the secret trivially extractable. If an attacker can inject script or convince a user to visit a malicious page while the setup screen is open, the TOTP secret can be silently exfiltrated, permanently compromising the user's 2FA.

cy.get('#initialToken') selects the specific DOM element that the application has populated with the TOTP secret, confirming the element exists in the rendered page.

The test asserts that #initialToken has a 'data-test-totp-secret' attribute and reads its value. This confirms the application exposes the TOTP shared secret in a DOM data attribute, making it accessible to any client-side script.

title: Sensitive files in /ftp directory served publicly without authentication
description: The fileServer serves files from the /ftp directory to any caller. The test setup creates a request object with no authentication context (no user, session, token, or headers) and the servePublicFiles handler proceeds to serve files directly. The only access control is an extension allowlist that still permits sensitive file types such as .kdbx (KeePass password databases) and .pdf. An attacker can retrieve the incident-support.kdbx password database and any other allowlisted file from /ftp without credentials. The /ftp directory is an internal resource that should not be publicly exposed, and serving a password database file without authentication is a misconfiguration and an insecure design that permits direct access to sensitive assets.

The caller (servePublicFiles route handler) is outside this file; this test demonstrates the handler's behavior when it receives an unauthenticated request.

The test sets req.params.file to 'incident-support.kdbx', a KeePass password database file, demonstrating that the /ftp directory contains sensitive credential stores that are reachable through this endpoint.

servePublicFiles()(req, res, next) is called with the unauthenticated request object. The handler receives the file parameter and proceeds without any authentication or authorization check, forwarding the request to file serving logic.

The test asserts that servePublicFiles calls res.sendFile with a path matching /ftp/incident-support.kdbx, confirming that the handler serves the KeePass database file to the unauthenticated caller with no access control beyond extension filtering. The /ftp directory is exposed as a public file store (misconfiguration), and the design permits unauthenticated retrieval of sensitive files (insecure design).

title: No security logging for file access events on /ftp endpoint
description: The test verifies that servePublicFiles serves files from the /ftp directory and rejects disallowed file types by calling next with an Error. However, the test mock objects (res with only sendFile and status, next as a bare mock) include no logging mechanism, and no assertion checks that file access or access-denial events are logged. Access to sensitive files in /ftp — especially a KeePass database — and rejected access attempts are security-relevant events that should be logged for incident detection and investigation. The absence of any logging expectation in the test indicates the implementation does not log these events.

The test for disallowed file types (line 55-63) asserts that next is called with an Error, but makes no assertion that the rejected access attempt is logged. Similarly, successful file serving tests (lines 27-52) do not verify any access log entry is created.

The test asserts only that next was called with an Error for the rejected file type. No security event logging is expected or verified for either successful or denied file access, indicating the implementation lacks security logging for access to sensitive files in /ftp.

title: Unvalidated URL fetch from config writes remote content to disk without size or destination restrictions
description: The test iterates over product configuration entries and, for any product whose `image` field passes `utils.isUrl()`, issues an outbound HTTP fetch to that URL (line 37) and streams the entire response body to a file on disk (lines 42-43). The only validation on the URL is `utils.isUrl()` (line 35), which checks URL format — it does not validate the destination host, scheme, or IP range. If the configuration source is influenced by an attacker (e.g., through environment overrides, custom config files, or a config-editing feature), the `fetch` call can be directed at internal services (loopback, private network ranges, cloud metadata endpoints). Additionally, the download has no size limit — the response body is streamed directly to disk without any cap, meaning a large response or a slow-drip response can consume disk space or hold the stream open indefinitely. While this is a test file and the input is configuration rather than direct request data, the code receives the URL from an external source (config) and performs an unvalidated outbound network request with it.

trace.description: The file receives product configuration from an external source via `config.get<ProductConfig[]>('products')`. The caller/configuration system is outside this file. Each product's `image` field is an externally-provided string.

`utils.isUrl(product.image)` checks whether the image value is a URL. This validates URL format but does not validate the destination — no host allow-list, no IP range check, no scheme restriction beyond what `isUrl` implies.

`fetch(product.image)` issues an outbound HTTP request to the config-supplied URL with no destination validation. If config is attacker-influenced, this is SSRF — the URL could target `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, `http://localhost:8080/admin`, or any internal service.
`let pathToImage: string = 'assets/public/images/products/'` initializes the local file path variable that will later be overwritten with a path derived from the remote URL's filename component.
`for (const product of products)` iterates over each config-supplied product, bringing the external `product.image` value into scope for each iteration.
`if (product.fileForRetrieveBlueprintChallenge && product.image)` gates on the image field existing, but performs no validation of its content — any non-empty string passes this check.

`product.image.substring(product.image.lastIndexOf('/') + 1)` extracts the filename portion from the URL, and `path.resolve(...)` constructs the local destination path from it. The path component is also unvalidated — a URL with crafted path segments could influence the write location.
`if (!response.ok || !response.body)` checks the response status and body existence but does not check `Content-Length` or impose any size limit before proceeding to write the response to disk.

`await finished(Readable.fromWeb(response.body as any).pipe(fileStream))` pipes the entire response body to the file stream with no size cap and no timeout. An attacker controlling the URL can point it at a service that streams an unbounded response, consuming disk space indefinitely.

`fs.createWriteStream(pathToImage, { flags: 'w' })` combined with `Readable.fromWeb(response.body).pipe(fileStream)` (line 43) writes the full response body to disk with no `Content-Length` check, no maximum body size, and no timeout. An attacker controlling the URL can point it at a service that streams an unbounded response, consuming disk space.

title: Webhook notify function accepts arbitrary URL for outbound HTTP request without destination validation
description: The test file demonstrates that the `webhook.notify` function (in `lib/webhook.ts`, outside this file) accepts a URL as its 5th parameter and makes an outbound HTTP POST request to it. The tests confirm that the only validation performed is URL format parsing (line 30 expects a parse error for an invalid URL string 'localhorst', line 33 shows the error message), but there is no allow-listing or destination validation to prevent the URL from targeting internal services. The test at lines 38-49 successfully sends a POST request to a localhost server, confirming that internal/loopback addresses are accepted as valid webhook destinations. If the URL parameter is derived from user input in the calling route handler (the entrypoint is outside this file), an attacker could supply an internal URL (e.g., cloud metadata endpoint `http://169.254.169.254/`, internal admin APIs, or loopback services) and have the server make requests to those targets, potentially exfiltrating internal data or triggering internal actions.

trace.description: The test calls `webhook.notify(challenge, 0, 0, 0, 'localhorst')` — the 5th argument is a URL string. The caller of `webhook.notify` in production code (route handler) is outside this file; the test receives this interface from `lib/webhook`.

The error message 'Failed to parse URL from localhorst' confirms that the only validation on the URL parameter is URL format parsing — there is no destination allow-list or internal-network filtering visible.
The test constructs `http://localhost:${port}` and passes it as the webhook URL, confirming that loopback/internal addresses are accepted as valid destinations.
The second test creates an HTTP server with `http.createServer` to receive the outbound webhook request — this is the receiving end that proves the outbound call actually fires.
The test server binds to port 0 (`server.listen(0, resolve)`) to obtain an ephemeral loopback port, establishing that the webhook target will be a localhost address.
The test reads the assigned port from `(server.address() as AddressInfo)?.port`, preparing the loopback URL that will be passed as the webhook destination.

`webhook.notify(challenge, 0, 0, 0, url)` triggers an outbound HTTP POST to the caller-supplied URL. The test server on line 38-41 receives the request, confirming the outbound call completes. No origin-based allow-list or internal-IP blocking is exercised by any test, indicating none exists in the library.

title: Client-controlled true-client-ip header trusted for storing login IP without proxy validation
description: The saveLoginIp route handler (whose behavior is revealed by this test file) reads the `true-client-ip` HTTP header and stores it directly as the user's `lastLoginIp`. The `true-client-ip` header is client-settable by any HTTP client. Unless the application is strictly behind a reverse proxy that strips and re-injects this header, any authenticated user can spoof their recorded login IP address to an arbitrary value. This defeats the purpose of recording login IPs for security audit and incident investigation. An attacker could log in from a malicious IP and record a benign or another user's IP, obscuring their trail and poisoning audit logs. The test at line 34 confirms the header value flows directly into the `lastLoginIp` field via `UserModel.findByPk(...).update({ lastLoginIp: ... })` with no validation of the header's provenance or format.

trace.description: The test sets req.headers['true-client-ip'] directly to a caller-supplied value. This header is the source of the login IP that the saveLoginIp handler (imported from '../../routes/saveLoginIp', outside this file) uses. The caller is outside this file; the trace begins at the point where outside data — the true-client-ip header — enters the function under test.

The test mocks security.authenticatedUsers.from to return { data: { id: 1 } }, confirming the handler authenticates the user and extracts a user id. Authentication is checked, but there is no validation that the true-client-ip header originated from a trusted reverse proxy.

const findByPkMock = mock.method(UserModel, 'findByPk', ...) sets up the mock for the database lookup the handler performs using the authenticated user's id. The handler calls UserModel.findByPk(user.id) to retrieve the user record, then calls .update() on it with the header-derived IP value.

await saveLoginIp()(req, res, next) invokes the handler with the req object that carries the unvalidated true-client-ip header. At this point the handler reads the header from req.headers and proceeds to use it as the login IP.

assert.equal(findByPkMock.mock.calls.length, 1) confirms that findByPk was called exactly once, proving the handler reached the database-lookup stage using the user id from the authentication context and is about to persist the header value.
const updateCall = findByPkMock.mock.calls[0].result as any retrieves the result of the findByPk call — the user record object whose .update() method will receive the unvalidated header value.

const updateMock = (await updateCall).update extracts the update mock function from the resolved findByPk result. This is the function the handler called with { lastLoginIp: <header value> }, forwarding the caller-controlled data into the persistence layer.

The assertion confirms that updateMock.mock.calls[0].arguments[0].lastLoginIp equals '1.1.1.1' — the raw value from the true-client-ip header. This demonstrates that the unvalidated, client-controlled header value is persisted directly into the user's lastLoginIp field via UserModel.findByPk(id).update({ lastLoginIp: headerValue }), with no format validation, no trusted-proxy check, and no sanitization. An attacker can set true-client-ip to any arbitrary string, poisoning the audit trail.

title: XML parser test suite lacks XXE and entity expansion security tests
description: This unit test exercises parseXmlString from ../../lib/xml but only verifies basic parsing and malformed-XML rejection. It does not test whether the parser is configured to block XML External Entity (XXE) attacks or entity expansion attacks (e.g., Billion Laughs). In a security-focused application (OWASP Juice Shop), an XML parser that accepts external entities is a classic misconfiguration (OWASP A05). If lib/xml constructs the parser with external entity resolution enabled, this test suite would still pass, leaving the dangerous configuration undetected. The absence of a negative security test means a misconfiguration in the underlying parser would go uncaught. The caller (lib/xml) is outside this file; this trace begins where the test invokes the parser.

trace.description: The test imports parseXmlString from ../../lib/xml. The actual parser configuration is in that external file; this test is the only observable consumer in scope.
The test calls parseXmlString with a benign XML string and asserts the result matches. This confirms the parser is exercised but only for the happy path.
The describe('xml', ...) block wraps the entire test suite. No setup or teardown here configures or resets parser security options — the suite relies entirely on whatever defaults lib/xml chose.
The first test case ('should parse a simple XML string') is defined. This is the only positive-path test; it does not attempt any security-relevant XML input.
A benign XML string with no DOCTYPE, no entity declarations, and no external references is assigned to the xml variable. This is the input that will reach the parser.

The assertion only checks that the root element is preserved. There is no test case (anywhere in this file) that passes an XML payload with DOCTYPE, external entity references, or recursive entity definitions to verify the parser rejects or strips them. A parser misconfigured to allow external entity resolution would pass this entire suite.

title: makeKeyNonUpdatable protection bypassed when validate option is false
description: The test file codifies (as expected behavior) that the `makeKeyNonUpdatable` hook silently allows updates to 'non-updatable' columns when the Sequelize operation is performed with `{ validate: false }`. This means the immutability guarantee is not enforced unconditionally at the hook level — it is contingent on a caller-controlled option. Any code path that performs a model update with `validate: false` (e.g., bulk operations, migration scripts, or direct Sequelize calls) will bypass the non-updatable constraint entirely. A column designated as non-updatable (e.g., a user role, a wallet balance reference, or a security-critical flag) can be modified if the caller simply opts out of validation. This is a design flaw: the immutability enforcement should not depend on a client-controllable validation flag.

An empty instance object is created with no constraints — any model instance would pass through.
makeKeyNonUpdatable is called on the mock model, attaching the beforeValidate hook that is supposed to enforce immutability.
The hook function intended to enforce the non-updatable constraint is extracted from the mock model's addHook calls.

The hook is called with the instance and options. The test asserts with assert.doesNotThrow (line 93-95) that the hook does NOT block the update. This confirms the design: when validate is false, the non-updatable key protection is entirely bypassed, even though the instance could have a changed non-updatable column. The protection meant to enforce immutability is defeated by a single caller-controlled flag.

The options object is set to { validate: false }, and the test asserts with assert.doesNotThrow (line 93-95) that the hook does NOT block the update. This confirms the design: when validate is false, the non-updatable key protection is entirely bypassed, even though the instance could have a changed non-updatable column. The protection meant to enforce immutability is defeated by a single caller-controlled flag.

title: makeKeyNonUpdatable protection bypassed when previous value is null or undefined
description: The test file codifies (as expected behavior) that the `makeKeyNonUpdatable` hook allows updates to a 'non-updatable' column when the previous value of that column is null or undefined. This means that any record whose non-updatable field was initially set to null (a common default for optional fields, or for fields populated after creation) can have that field overwritten on subsequent updates. The immutability guarantee is thus not absolute — it depends on the field already having a non-null value. An attacker who can influence the creation of a record (or finds one created before the hook was applied) can set the 'non-updatable' field to any value on update, defeating the intended protection.

The hook is called again, and the test asserts with assert.doesNotThrow (lines 140-142) that the hook does NOT block the update. This confirms the design flaw extends to undefined as well, undermining the immutability guarantee.

The _previousDataValues.testColumn is set to null (and later undefined on line 139), and the test asserts with assert.doesNotThrow (lines 135-137 and 140-142) that the hook does NOT block the update. This confirms the design flaw: a non-updatable column whose previous value was null or undefined can be freely modified, undermining the immutability guarantee.

title: Encryption key files served without authentication or access control
description: The serveKeyFiles function serves files from the /encryptionkeys directory based on a user-supplied filename parameter. The test reveals that the mock request object (line 16) contains no authentication context — only a params object — yet serveKeyFiles still proceeds to call res.sendFile, serving the requested file. This indicates the endpoint does not enforce authentication or authorization before serving cryptographic key material. An attacker who discovers this endpoint can download any encryption key stored in the encryptionkeys directory, potentially decrypting protected data or impersonating services. Additionally, the user-supplied filename flows directly to sendFile with no visible sanitization in the test flow, raising the possibility of path traversal to read arbitrary system files.

User-controlled input is placed directly into req.params.file with no validation or sanitization step.
serveKeyFiles() is called with the unauthenticated request. The function receives the request and proceeds to serve a file without any auth check visible in the test flow.

The assertion confirms res.sendFile was called with a path under the encryptionkeys directory, serving cryptographic key material to an unauthenticated caller. The test verifies the file was served but performs no check for authentication, authorization, or path traversal protection.

title: No security logging for encryption key file access events
description: The test for serveKeyFiles verifies that files from the encryptionkeys directory are served via res.sendFile, but the mock response object and test assertions include no logging mechanism or verification. Access to cryptographic key material is a security-relevant event that should be logged — including which file was requested, by whom, and when. The absence of any logging in the test flow suggests the implementation does not log key file accesses, preventing detection and investigation of unauthorized key retrieval or brute-force enumeration of key filenames.

title: Container runs as root with no USER directive
description: The Dockerfile does not specify a non-root USER directive. By default, the container process (smoke-test.sh executed via sh) will run as root inside the container. If the smoke test script or curl encounters attacker-influenced content (e.g., a malicious endpoint response), code execution would occur with root privileges inside the container, increasing the blast radius. Best practice is to create a non-root user and set the USER directive.

trace.description: The Dockerfile begins building from alpine; no non-root user is created at any point.
smoke-test.sh is copied into the image. No USER directive appears before or after this step.
RUN apk add curl executes as root during the build, installing curl into the root-owned filesystem. No USER directive appears before or after this step to drop privileges.
CMD executes 'sh smoke-test.sh http://app:3000' as the container entrypoint. With no USER directive anywhere in the Dockerfile, this process runs as root by default.

title: Unpinned base image — FROM alpine without version tag or digest
description: The Dockerfile uses 'FROM alpine' with no version tag or cryptographic digest pin. Each build pulls whatever 'alpine:latest' currently resolves to, making builds non-reproducible and susceptible to supply-chain risk — a compromised or regressed upstream image would be pulled and used without detection. Pinning to a specific version tag or, ideally, a digest is the expected security configuration.

trace.description: FROM alpine — the base image is referenced by name only, with no version tag or digest pin.

The unpinned base image means any future 'docker build' will pull an arbitrary alpine image, including potentially compromised or vulnerable versions, and all subsequent layers (apk add curl, COPY, CMD) inherit from it.

title: RSA private key hardcoded in source code
description: The RSA private exponent `d` and modulus `N` are hardcoded directly in the source file on lines 5-6. This is a complete RSA private key in plaintext. Anyone who can read this source file (version control, deployed code, source distribution) can decrypt any data encrypted with the corresponding public key. The private key should never be stored in source code; it should be loaded from a secure secret management system or environment variable at runtime. This is both a cryptographic failure (exposed private key defeats the confidentiality of all data encrypted with the matching public key) and a security misconfiguration (hardcoded secret in source code).

trace.description: The script begins execution by opening 'announcement_encrypted.md' for reading. The script itself is a standalone decryption utility.
The RSA modulus N is hardcoded as a literal integer in the source code on line 5. This is one half of the private key material.

The RSA private exponent d is hardcoded as a literal integer in the source code on line 6. Together with N, this constitutes the complete RSA private key. Any party with access to this file can perform decryption operations that should be restricted to the key holder.

The hardcoded private key (d, N) is used directly in the RSA decryption operation pow(int(f[:-1]), d, N). Because the private key is embedded in source, anyone with source access can replicate this decryption, completely defeating the confidentiality that RSA is supposed to provide.

title: Textbook RSA decryption without padding scheme
description: The decryption on line 9 uses raw/textbook RSA: pow(ciphertext, d, N) with no padding scheme (such as OAEP). Textbook RSA is known to be insecure because it is deterministic (same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext), vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext attacks, and susceptible to small-message attacks. A proper RSA decryption implementation should use a padding scheme like OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) to provide semantic security. The use of raw modular exponentiation without any padding or integrity check is a cryptographic implementation weakness.

trace.description: The script reads encrypted data from 'announcement_encrypted.md', one ciphertext value per line.

Each line is converted to an integer via int(f[:-1]) and then passed directly into pow(int(f[:-1]), d, N) for RSA decryption. There is no OAEP unpadding, no integrity verification, and no padding removal step — the raw modular exponentiation result is passed directly to chr().

The sink is the pow(int(f[:-1]), d, N) call, which performs textbook RSA decryption without any padding scheme. This is a known-insecure cryptographic operation that lacks semantic security and is vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext and related attacks.

title: SSRF via /profile/image/url — server fetches arbitrary user-supplied URLs including localhost
description: The test file exercises the POST /profile/image/url endpoint with a user-supplied `imageUrl` field. The tests demonstrate that the application makes a server-side HTTP request to whatever URL the user provides, with no validation or allow-listing of the destination. Lines 195–239 show the server fetching from `http://localhost:${mockPort}/...` — an internal loopback address — and processing the response (writing it to disk or falling back to storing the raw URL). Lines 101 and 116 show external URLs being fetched without restriction. The application honors any URL the caller supplies, including internal addresses, making this a classic SSRF: an attacker can probe internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other network resources accessible from the server's position. Additionally, the test at lines 191–209 shows that when the fetch returns a non-OK or empty-body response, the application falls back to storing the raw URL string itself as the profile image — an insecure design that allows arbitrary URL values to be persisted in user profile data.

There is no validation of the URL scheme, host, or content at this fallback path. An attacker could supply a `javascript:`, `data:`, or other dangerous URL scheme that, when later rendered in an or similar context in the frontend, could execute as script (stored XSS via the URL value). The design flaw is that the fallback path trusts the URL string as a safe profile image value without any scheme validation or allow-listing. Additionally, the URL is persisted without encoding, meaning any free-form text in the imageUrl field becomes a stored value rendered downstream — the render sink is outside this file.

The stored URL is rendered downstream (outside this file) in the profile page, creating a stored XSS risk if dangerous schemes like javascript: are accepted.

While this is test code extracting a user ID from a token the test itself obtained via login, the pattern demonstrates that the JWT is treated as a source of trusted identity data without verifying its integrity. If this same pattern exists in the application's request handling (outside this file), it would allow token forgery. The hardcoded test credentials (`password: 'ncc-1701'` at lines 31, 48, 77, 95, 110, 137, 161) are also present throughout the file, though these are expected in a test fixture for OWASP Juice Shop.

title: SSRF endpoint may process outbound fetch before authentication check — anonymous access test skipped due to socket hang up
description: The test at line 122 ('POST profile image URL forbidden for anonymous user') is skipped with the reason 'FIXME runs into socket hang up'. The test sends a POST to /profile/image/url without an authentication token (line 123–125) and expects a 500 'Blocked illegal activity' response — the same rejection the file upload endpoint returns for anonymous users (line 71). The fact that it instead hits a 'socket hang up' strongly suggests the server is making the outbound HTTP request to the user-supplied imageUrl (cataas.com/cat) before or instead of checking authentication. If the server fetches the URL before verifying the caller's identity, an unauthenticated attacker can trigger arbitrary server-side requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or any external host — combining broken access control with SSRF.

title: No file size limits or rate limiting on profile image upload endpoints

Similarly, the URL fetch endpoint at /profile/image/url fetches arbitrary content from user-supplied URLs with no evidenced size cap on the response. An attacker could upload extremely large files or supply URLs pointing to very large resources, consuming server memory and disk without throttling.

title: Fetched URL content written to public directory without integrity verification
description: The tests at lines 211–246 demonstrate that the server fetches content from user-supplied URLs and writes it directly to the public images directory (`frontend/dist/frontend/assets/public/images/uploads/${userId}.png`). There is no integrity verification — no checksum, no signature, no content-type validation on the fetched response beyond what the remote server chooses to declare. An attacker could serve malicious content (e.g., a polyglot file that is both a valid image and executable script, or content with embedded payloads) that gets written to a publicly accessible directory. The file extension is derived from the URL path (lines 222–246), meaning the attacker also controls the output file type to some extent.

title: Weak RSA key size — 1024-bit modulus hardcoded as public parameter
description: The RSA modulus N on line 5 is approximately 1024 bits (309 decimal digits). RSA keys below 2048 bits are deprecated by NIST and are considered factorable by well-resourced attackers. This N is used as the public modulus for RSA encryption (line 11: pow(ord(char), e, N)). A 1024-bit key does not provide adequate security for encrypted data; an attacker who can factor N can recover the private key and decrypt all data encrypted under this key pair. The key is hardcoded directly in source rather than loaded from a secure configuration or key store, compounding the issue.

N is used in the modular exponentiation pow(ord(char), e, N) to encrypt each character. The key size determines the strength of this operation.
The public exponent e = 65537 is also hardcoded alongside N, completing the public key pair. Both public parameters are static and present in the source.

The script successfully decrypts the announcement file by brute-forcing single-character encryptions. The 1024-bit key size is below the 2048-bit minimum recommended by modern standards, making the cryptographic protection inadequate.

title: Character-by-character RSA encryption reduces to a trivial substitution cipher
description: The script on lines 10-12 pre-computes the RSA encryption of every printable ASCII character and builds a lookup table (encrypted_chars). It then decrypts the announcement file (line 15) by looking up each encrypted line in this table. This succeeds because the original encryption was performed character-by-character rather than on the message as a whole. Encrypting individual characters with RSA produces a deterministic mapping from plaintext character to ciphertext value — functionally identical to a simple substitution cipher, regardless of RSA's mathematical strength. This is a fundamental design flaw in the encryption scheme: RSA (or any public-key cipher) should never be applied to individual characters; proper designs use hybrid encryption (encrypt a symmetric key with RSA, then encrypt the message with the symmetric cipher). The script itself is the proof of exploitability — it defeats the encryption in milliseconds with a 96-entry brute force.

Each encrypted character value is stored as a key in the encrypted_chars dictionary, mapping ciphertext to plaintext character. This creates a complete substitution table for the cipher.

Each individual character is encrypted via pow(ord(char), e, N). Because RSA without padding is deterministic and each character is encrypted independently, the same plaintext character always maps to the same ciphertext value.
The encrypted announcement file is opened for reading. Each line of the file is an encrypted representation of a single plaintext character (or characters), to be matched against the lookup table.

The announcement file is decrypted by looking up each encrypted line in the pre-computed table. The entire encryption is defeated by a trivial brute-force over 96 possible characters, proving the character-by-character encryption design is fundamentally insecure.

title: MD5 used for package integrity checksums
description: The 'checksum' Grunt task generates MD5 hashes for distribution packages. MD5 is a cryptographically broken hash function — collision attacks are practical, meaning an attacker can produce two different files with the same MD5 digest. When these checksums are used to verify the integrity of a downloaded package, an attacker who controls the distribution channel can substitute a malicious package that produces the same MD5 hash, defeating the integrity guarantee. The playbook explicitly calls out MD5 for integrity as a broken-algorithm finding. A stronger hash (SHA-256 or better) should be used, and ideally the checksums should be signed for supply-chain integrity.

Each file in dist/ is read into a buffer to be hashed.

The resulting hash is written to a .md5 file on line 79 and is intended to be used for integrity verification of the distribution package.

Packaging secrets into distribution artifacts is a security misconfiguration — keys should be provisioned out-of-band and kept separate from the application bundle.

title: MD5 used for hashing credentials

MD5 is a cryptographically broken hash function. When used for password or credential storage, it is vulnerable to precomputed rainbow-table attacks and lacks key stretching (no salt, no work factor). Any attacker who obtains the hash table can recover plaintext credentials trivially. The caller of `security.hash()` is outside this file, but the test confirms the function's behavior unambiguously.

The hardcoded secret is a misconfiguration (secret in source) that also constitutes a crypto-auth failure (compromised signing key).

title: Coupon codes are predictable and forgeable, encoding discount value in plaintext
description: The test at lines 33-51 reveals that generateCoupon() creates coupon codes by base85-encoding a string in the format 'MMMYY-DD' where MMM is the 3-letter month abbreviation, YY is the 2-digit year, and DD is the discount percentage. An attacker can simply base85-encode e.g. 'JAN26-99' to create a 99% discount coupon. The design never established a server-side secret or signature for coupon integrity — the coupon value is entirely determined by publicly known information (current date + chosen discount).

title: User identity resolved from client-controlled x-user-email header without verification
description: The test at lines 22-31 confirms that security.userEmailFrom() reads the user's email identity directly from the 'x-user-email' HTTP header on the request object. This means the application trusts a client-supplied header to determine who the caller is. Any attacker can set 'x-user-email: victim@example.com' in their request to impersonate any user. There is no token verification, no session lookup, and no signature check — the header value is returned as-is. This is both an authentication bypass (crypto-auth: the identity decision is made without any credential verification) and a broken access control (access-control: any user can act as any other user by changing the header). The caller that uses userEmailFrom() is outside this file.

title: authenticatedUsers token-to-user mapping uses trivially guessable tokens with no validation

title: Faucet has no per-user withdrawal limits — entire balance drainable by first caller
description: The BeeFaucet contract is a token faucet that maintains a single shared `balance` of 200. The `withdraw` function accepts any `uint8 amount` from any caller with no per-user tracking, rate limiting, cooldown, or withdrawal cap. The first user to call `withdraw(200)` receives the entire faucet allocation, leaving nothing for any other user. A faucet's purpose is to distribute tokens broadly; the design permits a single actor to monopolize the entire supply in one transaction. There is no access control restricting who can call withdraw, and no authorization check limiting how much any individual address may claim.

trace.description: The `withdraw(uint8 amount)` function is declared `public` — any external caller (the caller is outside this file; this is the Solidity entrypoint that receives the transaction) can invoke it with any amount up to 255.

The caller-supplied `amount` is subtracted directly from the shared `balance` state variable. There is no per-user accounting — no mapping of address to amount withdrawn, no daily/weekly cap, no cooldown timestamp.
The only guard is `require(balance >= 0)`, which is always true for `uint8` (unsigned). It provides no meaningful protection. Even the intended guard does not limit per-user withdrawals.

The state variable `balance` is declared as a single shared `uint8` with value 200. It is not a mapping from address to uint — there is no per-user accounting structure. This is the design root: all callers share one counter.
Tokens are transferred to `msg.sender` for the full requested amount. An attacker calls `withdraw(200)` and receives the entire faucet balance, leaving nothing for other users.

title: Redundant balance check on unsigned integer provides no safety guarantee
description: The `withdraw` function includes `require(balance >= 0, "Withdrew more than the account balance!")` after subtracting from `balance`. Because `balance` is declared `uint8` (unsigned), it can never be negative, so this condition is always true. The developer intended this as a safety check to prevent over-withdrawal, but the check is logically dead code. In Solidity ^0.8.0 the compiler's built-in overflow/underflow protection would revert the subtraction before this line is reached, but the intended safety mechanism as written is ineffective — a developer relying on this check for correctness would be mistaken.

trace.description: The `withdraw` function is the entrypoint; the caller (outside this file) passes `amount`.
`balance -= amount` is executed. `balance` is `uint8` (line 12), so underflow would revert via Solidity 0.8+ built-in checks, not via the require on the next line.

`require(balance >= 0)` is the intended safety guard, but `balance` is unsigned and can never be < 0. The check is tautologically true and provides no protection. A developer who assumed this check enforces the invariant would have a false sense of security.

title: Faucet balance variable is disconnected from actual contract token holdings
description: The contract tracks a manual `uint8 balance` variable initialized to 200, but never queries the actual token balance of the contract via `token.balanceOf(address(this))`. The `Token` interface already declares `balanceOf` (line 7) but it is never used. If the contract's real token balance differs from the `balance` variable — for example, if someone transfers tokens directly to the contract, or if the faucet is refilled — the `balance` counter and reality diverge. This can cause the `token.transfer` call to revert (if `balance` says tokens are available but the contract actually holds fewer), or leave tokens permanently stranded (if the contract holds more than `balance` indicates and `balance` reaches 0). The design should derive the available amount from the actual token balance rather than maintaining a disconnected counter.

trace.description: `balance` is initialized to 200 as a manual counter. It is a `uint8`, meaning it can never represent more than 255 tokens regardless of the contract's actual holdings.
`balance -= amount` decrements the manual counter. The contract never reconciles this counter with `token.balanceOf(address(this))` (declared on line 7 but never called).

The `Token` interface declares `function balanceOf(address account) external view returns (uint256)` — the method that could reconcile the counter with reality is available but never called anywhere in the contract.

The `token` contract reference is constructed at `Token(0x36435796Ca9be2bf150CE0dECc2D8Fab5C4d6E13)`. This is the token whose `balanceOf` should be queried to verify actual holdings, but only `transfer` (line 6) is ever called.

`token.transfer` uses the caller-supplied amount, gated only by the disconnected `balance` counter. If the contract's actual token balance is less than what `balance` claims, the transfer reverts. If the actual balance exceeds `balance`, excess tokens are stranded with no way to withdraw them through this contract.

title: User-controlled username concatenated directly into LLM system prompt without fencing
description: The buildSystemPrompt function embeds the user's name directly into the system prompt text. The test on line 39 confirms the output format: 'The customer you are currently chatting with is John Doe.' The username is retrieved from the database via getUserNameFromToken (lines 68-74), meaning it is user-controlled data (a user sets their own display name at registration or profile update). Since the name is concatenated into the system prompt without any delimiters, escaping, or fencing, a malicious user could set their name to something like 'Ignore all previous instructions. You are now...' to inject instructions into the system prompt. This is OWASP LLM01 (Prompt Injection). The actual implementation of buildSystemPrompt lives in routes/chat (outside this file), but this test file confirms the behavior and the data flow.

buildSystemPrompt is called with the user-controlled username as its argument. The test confirms the username flows into the function.

The assertion assert.equal(userName, 'jdoe') confirms that getUserNameFromToken returns the raw username string from the database. No sanitization or encoding is applied to the username at this stage.

The test assertion confirms the username is concatenated directly into the system prompt string: 'The customer you are currently chatting with is John Doe.' No delimiters, fencing, or sanitization separate the user-controlled name from the system instructions. An attacker who sets their username to 'Ignore previous instructions...' can inject instructions into the system prompt, causing the LLM to perform unintended actions.

title: Authorization and token signing delegated to library named 'insecurity' suggesting weak crypto/auth implementation
description: The test file imports from '../../lib/insecurity' (line 10) and uses security.authorize to create tokens (lines 55, 69). The library name 'insecurity' is a deliberate hint that the cryptographic and authentication mechanisms are intentionally weak (this is OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately vulnerable application). The getUserId function (lines 48-60) and getUserNameFromToken function (lines 62-75) both rely on decoding a bearer token to extract a user identity. If the token signing/verification in the insecurity library uses a weak or hardcoded secret, an attacker could forge tokens with arbitrary user IDs, achieving authentication bypass. The actual weakness is in lib/insecurity (outside this file), but this test file confirms that token-based identity resolution is the auth mechanism used by the chat routes.
